title: Introduction to physical geology
summary: A first-year survey of how Earth works, from its internal layers and plate tectonics through minerals, rocks, geologic time, earthquakes, mountain building, water and ice. Students learn to identify minerals and rocks from hand samples and to read maps and cross sections. Lectures follow Earle's Physical Geology, and weekly labs apply each topic.
brief: Introduction to physical geology for first-year undergraduates: a 12-week term, each week two 50-minute lectures and a two-hour lab. Textbook: Steven Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition (BCcampus open textbook). Week by week: 1, Earth's layers and plate tectonics; 2, minerals; 3, igneous rocks and volcanoes; 4, weathering, erosion and soils; 5, sedimentary rocks; 6, metamorphic rocks and the rock cycle; 7, geologic time and how rocks are dated; 8, earthquakes; 9, folds, faults and mountain building; 10, streams and floods; 11, groundwater; 12, glaciers and climate. Labs, done in pairs with the department's hand samples: mineral identification, igneous and sedimentary rock identification, metamorphic rocks, topographic maps, geologic maps and cross sections, and a stream table. Grading: lab reports 30% (each due at the start of the next lab), two midterm exams in weeks 5 and 9 (15% each), weekly online quizzes 10%, and a final exam after week 12 (30%).
policies:
Lab safety: closed-toe shoes in the lab, and the acid bottle (dilute HCl, for the fizz test) is used only with goggles on. Hand samples stay in their trays and go back where they came from.

Lab reports are due at the start of the next lab; a missed lab can be made up in the same week’s open lab hour.

Pairs write the one question they most want answered about the course, and the instructor answers two or three.

segments.title: How do we know what is inside Earth?
segments.description:
The instructor shows the depth of the deepest borehole beside Earth’s radius.
Each student writes one kind of evidence geologists could use to learn about the interior without drilling to it.
Pairs compare for two minutes, then two pairs report.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: earthquake waves, meteorites, Earth’s density, the magnetic field, rocks brought up from depth by volcanoes. The Kola borehole (12.262 km) reached about 0.19% of the way to the center (12.262 ÷ 6,371). Collect ideas on the board and return to them.
shown: The Kola Superdeep Borehole in Russia reached 12,262 m, the deepest hole ever drilled. Earth’s radius is 6,371 km.
Prompt: Name one kind of evidence that tells us what Earth’s interior is made of, without drilling to it.

segments.title: Compositional layers and the seismic evidence
segments.description:
The instructor presents the crust, mantle and core with thickness, material and density, using the table.
Evidence follows: Earth’s mean density of 5.51 g/cm³ is far above surface rocks, and seismic waves change speed and direction at boundaries such as the Moho (identified in 1909).
Before the shadow zone is shown, every student writes what stations on the far side of Earth would record from an earthquake’s S waves if the whole interior were solid. Pairs compare, then the instructor shows that S waves stop at the core, so the outer core is liquid, and that Lehmann (1936) found the inner core, later shown to be solid.
segments.teacherNotes: Common error: the mantle is liquid. It is solid rock that flows very slowly; only the outer core is liquid. Expected prediction: S waves could travel through a wholly solid interior to the opposite side; a liquid outer core blocks their direct passage. Keep P (compressional, through solids and liquids) and S (shear, solids only) distinct.
shown: Table: Layer | Thickness or depth | Main material | Approximate density (g/cm³) / Continental crust | about 35 km | granitic rock | 2.7 / Oceanic crust | about 7 km | basalt | 3.0 / Mantle | to 2,890 km depth | peridotite | 3.3 at the top / Outer core | 2,890 to 5,150 km depth | liquid iron-nickel alloy | 10 to 12 / Inner core | 5,150 to 6,371 km depth | solid iron-nickel alloy | about 13
Prompt: If Earth’s whole interior were solid, what would a seismic station on the opposite side of Earth record from the S waves of a large earthquake? Explain in one or two sentences.

segments.title: Drawing Earth to scale
segments.description:
Pairs draw a quarter-section of Earth on plain paper at 1 cm for every 1,000 km.
They mark the inner core (radius 1.2 cm), the core-mantle boundary (radius 3.5 cm) and the surface (radius 6.4 cm).
Each student then works out how thick the continental crust would be on the drawing and compares it with a pencil line.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: 35 km is 0.035 cm, or 0.35 mm, comparable to a fine pencil line, so the crust is a skin like an apple’s. Core-mantle boundary radius: 6,371 − 2,890 = 3,481 km. Freehand arcs through ruler ticks are fine without a compass.
shown: Scale: 1 cm on paper = 1,000 km. Earth’s radius 6,371 km; core radius 3,481 km; inner core radius 1,220 km; continental crust about 35 km thick.

segments.title: Written check on layers and evidence
segments.description:
Each student answers three short prompts in writing, alone, for four minutes.
Pairs then compare answers for two minutes and settle any difference.
The instructor goes over the answers with the class.
segments.teacherNotes:
Answers.
1. Outer core; S waves do not pass through it.
2. The interior must hold far denser material than surface rock, which fits an iron-nickel core.
3. Continental crust is thicker (about 35 km against 7), granitic and less dense (2.7 against 3.0 g/cm³); oceanic is basaltic.

segments.title: Summary and what comes next time
segments.description:
The instructor sums up: three compositional layers, known from seismic waves, density, meteorites and the magnetic field.
Next time covers the lithosphere and asthenosphere, the evidence that plates move, and the three kinds of plate boundary.
Students are told to read Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, ch. 10 (Plate Tectonics) before then, and that the reading note starts at the next meeting.
segments.teacherNotes: Write the chapter on the board. The reading note is ungraded and short; remind students to bring one clear point and one question.

segments.title: Reading note
segments.description:
Each student writes one point from Earle ch. 10 that was clear and one question it raised, for two minutes.
Pairs swap notes and try to answer each other’s question for two minutes.
The instructor collects two or three unanswered questions on the board to return to later.
segments.teacherNotes: Students who did not manage the reading can write a question from last time’s lecture instead. Keep this brisk. Likely questions: why plates move, whether continents were once joined. Park them for the discussion segment.
shown: Prompt: Write one point from Earle ch. 10 (Plate Tectonics) that was clear and one question it raised.

segments.title: From drifting continents to moving plates
segments.description:
The instructor contrasts compositional and mechanical layers: the lithosphere (crust plus rigid uppermost mantle, about 100 km thick) rides on the weak asthenosphere, which flows very slowly, and the lithosphere is broken into plates.
Evidence is presented: Wegener’s 1912 fit of the continents and matching Glossopteris fossils across the southern continents, Hess’s seafloor spreading, and symmetrical magnetic stripes on either side of ridges (Vine and Matthews, 1963).
Before the seafloor ages are shown, every student writes whether seafloor gets older or younger away from a mid-ocean ridge, and why. Pairs compare, then the instructor shows that it gets older, with most younger than 200 million years, while continents hold rocks about 4 billion years old.
segments.teacherNotes: Common error: plates are the same as continents, or the lithosphere is the crust. A plate includes oceanic or continental crust plus uppermost mantle. The asthenosphere is solid but weak, not a liquid layer.
shown: Layers: Lithosphere (rigid, about 100 km) → Asthenosphere (weak, flows slowly) → Lower mantle (stronger) → Outer core (liquid) → Inner core (solid)
Prompt: Moving away from a mid-ocean ridge, does the seafloor get older or younger? Give a reason.

segments.title: How old is the seafloor?
segments.description:
The instructor works one example at the board: seafloor 1,000 km from a ridge, moving away at 2.5 cm per year, using the shortcut that 1 cm per year equals 10 km per million years.
Each student then finds the age at 1,500 km, and the distance of seafloor 100 million years old. Pairs check each other.
segments.teacherNotes: Worked: 2.5 cm/yr = 25 km per million years; 1,000 ÷ 25 = 40 million years. Students: 1,500 ÷ 25 = 60 million years; 100 × 25 = 2,500 km. Common error: mixing cm and km; convert first.

segments.title: Three kinds of plate boundary
segments.description:
The instructor presents divergent, convergent and transform boundaries using the table, with a named example and landforms for each.
Before the transform row is shown, pairs predict which landforms and hazards to expect where plates slide past without making or destroying lithosphere.
The instructor adds that not every volcano is at a boundary: Hawaii lies over a hot spot, a plume of hot mantle beneath the interior of the Pacific plate, and its island chain records plate motion.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected prediction: faults and earthquakes, no volcanoes. Oceanic-oceanic convergence builds island arcs; Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench is nearly 11 km deep. Subduction earthquakes occur down to about 700 km.
shown: Table: Boundary | Plate motion | Landforms | Volcanoes and earthquakes | Example / Divergent | plates move apart | mid-ocean ridge, rift valley | basaltic volcanoes, shallow earthquakes | Mid-Atlantic Ridge, East African Rift / Convergent, oceanic-continental | oceanic plate subducts | trench, volcanic arc on the continent | explosive volcanoes, earthquakes to about 700 km | Andes, Cascades / Convergent, oceanic-oceanic | one oceanic plate subducts | trench, island arc | volcanoes, deep earthquakes | Mariana Islands / Convergent, continental-continental | collision | mountain belt, thick crust | earthquakes, few volcanoes | Himalaya / Transform | plates slide past | strike-slip fault, offset ridges | shallow earthquakes, no volcanoes | San Andreas Fault

segments.title: Find and fix the mistakes in a boundary table
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Find and fix the mistakes in a boundary table”.
Each student gets the instructor’s hypothetical completed boundary table shown on the sheet; some rows contain a mistake about what happens at the boundary.
Students work alone for four minutes to find each mistake and write a one-sentence correction.
Pairs compare for two minutes, then the instructor takes the corrections from two pairs.
segments.teacherNotes: Rows 1, 2 and 5 are correct. Row 3 is wrong: Himalaya is a collision; buoyant continental lithosphere resists continued subduction, so collision thickens the crust rather than sustaining a typical subduction volcanic arc. Row 4 is wrong: transform boundaries neither create nor destroy lithosphere, and have earthquakes but no volcanoes.

segments.title: Why does oceanic lithosphere sink?
segments.description:
Each student writes a two-sentence answer using densities from last meeting’s table, then pairs compare for three minutes.
The class discusses, with students answering each other, and the instructor returns to one parked question from the reading notes.
segments.teacherNotes: Key points: oceanic crust (3.0 g/cm³) over mantle (3.3) is denser than continental crust (2.7). Explain that cooling causes thermal contraction and increases mantle-rock density. Old oceanic lithosphere can therefore become denser overall than the warmer asthenosphere beneath it and sink. Continental lithosphere resists subduction and crumples into mountains.
shown: Prompt: Why does oceanic lithosphere subduct at a trench while continental lithosphere resists? Use densities and age in your answer.

segments.title: Summary and the lab ahead
segments.description:
The instructor sums up the three boundary types and the landforms, volcanoes and earthquakes at each.
Next time is the lab: pairs will measure the density of hand samples that stand for the crust and mantle, and classify plate boundaries on a world map.
Students are reminded that closed-toe shoes are required in the lab.
segments.teacherNotes: Nothing needs preparing for the lab beyond shoes.

segments.title: Lab rules and density method
segments.description:
The instructor states the rules: closed-toe shoes, hand samples stay in their trays and go back where they came from, and work is done in pairs with the department’s hand samples. The dilute HCl bottle, used in later labs, is used only with goggles on.
Using a spare sample, the instructor demonstrates weighing in a tared sample tray and finding volume by water displacement in a graduated cylinder set inside the tray. Samples remain within their trays throughout the procedure.
Pairs decide who lowers the sample and who records. Use a cylinder large enough for full immersion without overflow. Demonstrate reading the bottom of the meniscus at eye level, removing trapped bubbles, and using 1 mL = 1 cm³.
segments.teacherNotes: Safety: lower samples on a thread, never drop them, since glass cylinders crack. Carry trays with both hands and keep samples away from table edges. Wipe spills at once so floors are not slippery. Samples are not to be taken from the room.
shown: Steps: Weigh the sample on the balance → Fill the cylinder deep enough to cover the sample and read the water level → Lower the sample on a thread and read the new level → Subtract to get the volume → Divide mass by volume

segments.title: Predict the densities
segments.description:
Each student writes a ranking of granite, basalt and peridotite from least to most dense, and which Earth layer each best represents.
Pairs compare for two minutes, then two or three pairs report and give reasons.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: granite < basalt < peridotite; granite stands for continental crust, basalt for oceanic crust, peridotite for the upper mantle. Do not confirm yet; the measurements do.
shown: Prompt: Rank granite, basalt and peridotite from least to most dense. Which Earth layer does each best represent? Give a reason.

segments.title: Measuring density of crust and mantle samples
segments.description:
Pairs weigh the granite, basalt and peridotite hand samples to 0.1 g and find each volume by water displacement.
They record mass, volume and density (mass divided by volume) in the table and compare the rank order with their prediction.
All samples go back to their trays, and the benches are wiped dry.
segments.teacherNotes: Typical results: granite 2.6 to 2.7, basalt 2.8 to 3.0, peridotite 3.2 to 3.4 g/cm³. Measurement errors can reverse the expected rank order. If the ranking differs from the prediction, repeat the measurements and assess volume-reading uncertainty before interpreting the result. Use pieces that fit the cylinder; if the tray has no peridotite, use dunite.

segments.title: Break
segments.description: Students take a break while the instructor checks that samples are back in their trays and the benches are dry.

segments.title: What the densities say about Earth’s interior
segments.description:
Using their own results, pairs write what Earth’s mean density of 5.51 g/cm³ implies about the interior.
Pairs then join another pair to answer why oceanic lithosphere sinks at trenches while continental lithosphere does not, and each group explains its answer to the class.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: Earth’s mean density exceeds the measured sample densities, so substantial regions of its interior must be denser. Pressure increases rock density at depth; seismic and meteorite evidence additionally support a dense iron-rich core. Subduction follows from density and cooling with age.
shown: Earth’s mean density: 5.51 g/cm³
Prompt 1: What must be true of Earth’s interior, given your measured densities and a mean density of 5.51 g/cm³?
Prompt 2: Why does oceanic lithosphere sink at trenches while continental lithosphere does not?

segments.title: Classifying plate boundaries on a world map
segments.description:
Pairs receive the Plate boundaries world map sheet, which the instructor prepares in advance from a printed plate-boundary world map (no map is included in these materials): a world map showing plate outlines, relative-motion arrows, earthquake depths, and volcano locations, with the Nubian, Somali, Arabian, Pacific, Tonga, Anatolian, Eurasian, Juan de Fuca, North American and Adriatic plates labeled (the Nubian plate is the African plate), plus a recording table for the six named locations.
For each location they mark it on the map, decide the boundary type or none, name the plates, and record the landforms and hazards expected.
Pairs then state one pattern in where earthquakes and volcanoes occur, and two pairs share.
segments.teacherNotes:
Answers.
1. Afar Triangle, Ethiopia: divergent, continental rift; Nubian, Somali and Arabian plates; rift valley, basaltic volcanoes.
2. Tonga Trench: convergent, oceanic-oceanic; Pacific plate sinks beneath Tonga; trench, island arc.
3. North Anatolian Fault near Istanbul: transform; Anatolian and Eurasian plates; strike-slip earthquakes, no volcanoes.
4. Mount Rainier: convergent, oceanic-continental; Juan de Fuca beneath North America; volcanic arc.
5. The Alps: convergent, continental collision of Africa and Eurasia; folded mountain belt.
6. Yellowstone: no boundary; hot spot beneath the North American plate.
Pattern: most earthquakes and volcanoes follow boundaries; hot spots are exceptions.

segments.title: Plate speed from the Hawaiian hot spot
segments.description:
Pairs use rounded values to find how fast the Pacific plate moved while Kauai drifted away from the hot spot.
They give the speed in km per million years and in cm per year, and say which direction the plate moves, using the fact that the chain gets older toward Kauai.
Two pairs report their answers.
segments.teacherNotes: Worked: 500 km ÷ 5 million years = 100 km per million years = 10 cm per year, near the upper range of Pacific plate speeds (about 7 to 10 cm/yr). The chain is older to the northwest, so the plate moves northwest. Values are rounded.

segments.title: Assignments and what comes next
segments.description:
The instructor sets the Lab reports assignment (30% of the course grade), due at the start of the lab of Minerals. Each student writes their own.
The instructor separately sets the Weekly online quizzes assignment (10% of the course grade), due at the first meeting of Minerals. Each student completes their own work and submits it online before that meeting.
A short practice quiz on this lesson is available to take after class; it counts toward no grade.
Later in the course, students will study atomic structure, the definition of a mineral, the silicate tetrahedron and the physical properties used to identify common rock-forming minerals. Students read Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, ch. 2 (Minerals) first.
segments.teacherNotes: Say the due times in these words. Check that every tray is complete and every sample is back where it came from before students leave.

keyIdeas: Earth has three compositional layers: a thin crust (about 7 km of basalt under oceans, about 35 km of granitic rock under continents), a thick peridotite mantle to 2,890 km depth, and an iron-nickel core with a liquid outer part and a solid inner part.

Nobody has drilled past about 12 km, so the layers are known from indirect evidence: seismic waves (P waves pass through solids and liquids, S waves only through solids), Earth’s mean density of 5.51 g/cm³, meteorites and Earth’s magnetic field.

The lithosphere (crust plus rigid uppermost mantle, about 100 km thick) is broken into plates that move over the weak asthenosphere. Evidence includes matching continental margins and fossils, magnetic stripes on the seafloor, and the generally young ocean floor, mostly younger than 200 million years.

Plates meet at three kinds of boundary. Divergent boundaries make ridges and rifts, convergent boundaries make trenches, volcanic arcs and collision mountains, and transform boundaries make strike-slip faults and earthquakes without volcanoes.

Plate motion is slow but measurable: a few centimeters a year, which is 10 km per million years for each 1 cm per year. Hot spots such as Hawaii and Yellowstone lie away from boundaries, and their volcano chains record plate motion.

vocabulary.definition: Earth’s thin, outermost compositional layer: about 7 km of basalt under oceans and about 35 km of granitic rock under continents.
The rigid outer shell of Earth, about 100 km thick, made of the crust and uppermost mantle, broken into plates.
The weak part of the upper mantle beneath the lithosphere, which flows very slowly and lets plates move.
A wave of energy from an earthquake. P waves pass through solids and liquids; S waves pass only through solids.
A plate boundary where plates move apart and new lithosphere forms, as at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
A plate boundary where plates move together, by subduction or by collision, as in the Andes and the Himalaya.
A plate boundary where plates slide past each other, as along the San Andreas Fault.
The sinking of one lithospheric plate beneath another into the mantle, forming a trench and, often, a volcanic arc.

slides.title: Earth’s compositional layers
bullets: Mean density of Earth: 5.51 g/cm³, far above surface rocks
Seismic waves change speed and direction at boundaries such as the Moho (1909)
slides.notes:
Present the crust, mantle and core with thickness, material and density. Point out that the crust is very thin compared with the whole planet.

Then the evidence. Earth’s mean density of 5.51 g/cm³ is far above the density of surface rocks (2.7 to 3.0), so the interior must hold much denser material. Seismic waves change speed and direction where the material changes; the Moho, the base of the crust, was identified in 1909.

Clarify early: the mantle is solid rock that flows very slowly. Only the outer core is liquid.

slides.title: Predict the S waves
bullets: Prompt: If Earth’s whole interior were solid, what would a seismic station on the opposite side of Earth record from the S waves of a large earthquake? Explain in one or two sentences.
slides.notes:
Keep the answer off the screen. Each student writes a prediction alone, then pairs compare.

Expected prediction: S waves could travel through a wholly solid interior to the opposite side. Take a couple of predictions aloud, then move to the next slide.

Keep P and S waves distinct: P waves are compressional, S waves are shear.

slides.title: What the seismic waves show
bullets: Lehmann (1936) found the inner core, later shown to be solid
slides.notes:
Now reveal the result. Stations on the far side of Earth record no direct S waves from a large earthquake. S waves stop at the core, so the outer core must be liquid. P waves still arrive, bent at the boundaries.

Compare with the predictions students wrote. Those who predicted that S waves arrive were reasoning correctly from a solid interior; the missing waves are the evidence that the interior is not all solid.

In 1936 Inge Lehmann showed that faint P waves reaching the shadow zone require a distinct inner core inside the liquid outer core; later evidence showed that the inner core is solid.

sides.title: P waves
points: Cross the core, bent at its boundaries

sides.title: S waves

Write the chapter on the board: Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, ch. 10 (Plate Tectonics). Tell students the reading note starts at the next meeting and is short and ungraded: bring one clear point and one question.

slides.title: Earth’s layers and plate tectonics
bullets: Plates, boundaries and landforms
slides.notes: This meeting moves from Earth’s layers to the plates that ride on them, the three kinds of plate boundary, and why oceanic lithosphere sinks.

slides.title: Reading note
bullets: Prompt: Write one point from Earle ch. 10 (to confirm) (Plate Tectonics) that was clear and one question it raised.
Write alone for two minutes
Swap notes with your partner and try to answer each other’s question
slides.notes:
This is the reading note explained at the earlier meeting. Students write for two minutes, then pairs swap notes and try to answer each other’s question for two minutes.

Collect two or three unanswered questions on the board to return to later. Students who did not manage the reading can write a question from the earlier lecture instead. Keep this brisk.

Likely questions: why plates move, whether continents were once joined. Park them for the discussion later in the lecture.

slides.title: Mechanical layers: lithosphere and asthenosphere
bullets: Layers: Lithosphere (rigid, about 100 km) → Asthenosphere (weak, flows slowly) → Lower mantle (stronger) → Outer core (liquid) → Inner core (solid)
A plate is crust plus rigid uppermost mantle
slides.notes:
Contrast the two ways of dividing Earth. Compositional layers (crust, mantle, core) are defined by what they are made of. Mechanical layers are defined by how they behave.

The lithosphere is the crust plus the rigid uppermost mantle, about 100 km thick. It is broken into plates and rides on the asthenosphere, which is solid but weak and flows very slowly. Make clear that a plate is not the same as a continent, and the lithosphere is more than the crust: each plate carries oceanic or continental crust plus uppermost mantle. The asthenosphere is not a liquid layer.

slides.title: Evidence that plates move
bullets: Wegener, 1912: the continents fit together
Glossopteris fossils match across the southern continents
Hess: seafloor spreading
Symmetrical magnetic stripes either side of ridges (Vine and Matthews, 1963)
Prompt: Moving away from a mid-ocean ridge, does the seafloor get older or younger? Give a reason.
slides.notes:
Present the evidence first, line by line: Wegener’s 1912 fit of the continents and the matching Glossopteris fossils across the southern continents, Hess’s seafloor spreading, and the symmetrical magnetic stripes on either side of ridges (Vine and Matthews, 1963).

Then ask the question. Each student writes whether seafloor gets older or younger away from a ridge, and why. Pairs compare. Do not give the answer while the slide is up.

After the pairs have compared, say that the seafloor gets older away from the ridge. Most of it is younger than 200 million years, while continents hold rocks about 4 billion years old. Ocean floor is made at ridges and recycled at trenches, so it stays young.

slides.title: How old is the seafloor?
bullets: Work from the sheet “How old is the seafloor?”.
slides.notes:
The instructor works one example at the board: seafloor 1,000 km from a ridge, moving away at 2.5 cm per year, using the shortcut that 1 cm per year equals 10 km per million years.
Each student then finds the age at 1,500 km, and the distance of seafloor 100 million years old. Pairs check each other.

slides.title: Three kinds of plate boundary
bullets: Where plates slide past without making or destroying lithosphere, which landforms and hazards do you expect?
slides.notes:
Present divergent and convergent boundaries from the table, with a named example and landforms for each.

Before showing the transform row, pairs predict which landforms and hazards to expect where plates slide past each other. Expected prediction: faults and earthquakes, no volcanoes. Take two or three predictions, then move to the next slide.

rows: trench, volcanic arc on the continent
explosive volcanoes, earthquakes to about 700 km

slides.title: Three kinds of plate boundary
bullets: Not every volcano is at a boundary: Hawaii lies over a hot spot
A plume of hot mantle beneath the interior of the Pacific plate; its island chain records plate motion
slides.notes:
Add the transform row and compare it with the predictions: strike-slip faults and shallow earthquakes, no volcanoes, because lithosphere is neither made nor destroyed.

Oceanic-oceanic convergence builds island arcs; Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench is nearly 11 km deep. Subduction earthquakes occur down to about 700 km.

Then add that not every volcano is at a boundary. Hawaii lies over a hot spot, a plume of hot mantle beneath the interior of the Pacific plate, and its island chain records plate motion. Yellowstone is another hot spot.

rows: trench, volcanic arc on the continent
explosive volcanoes, earthquakes to about 700 km

slides.title: Find and fix the mistakes in a boundary table

slides.notes:

Each student gets the instructor’s hypothetical completed boundary table shown on the sheet; some rows contain a mistake about what happens at the boundary.
Students work alone for four minutes to find each mistake and write a one-sentence correction.
Pairs compare for two minutes, then the instructor takes the corrections from two pairs.

slides.title: Why does oceanic lithosphere sink?
bullets: Prompt: Why does oceanic lithosphere subduct at a trench while continental lithosphere resists? Use densities and age in your answer.
Write two sentences alone
Compare with your partner, then discuss as a class
slides.notes:
Each student writes a two-sentence answer using the densities from the layers table shown at the earlier meeting, then pairs compare for three minutes. Then open the discussion so students answer each other, and return to one parked question from the reading notes.

Key points for the teacher: oceanic crust (3.0 g/cm³) over mantle (3.3) is denser than continental crust (2.7). Cooling causes thermal contraction and raises the density of mantle rock. Old oceanic lithosphere can therefore become denser overall than the warmer asthenosphere beneath it, and sink. Continental lithosphere resists subduction and crumples into mountains.

Convergent: trenches, volcanic arcs, collision mountains

slides.notes:

Next time is the lab. Pairs will measure the density of hand samples that stand for the crust and mantle, and classify plate boundaries on a world map. Remind students that closed-toe shoes are required in the lab. Nothing needs preparing for the lab beyond shoes.

slides.title: What the densities say about Earth’s interior

Prompt 2: Why does oceanic lithosphere sink at trenches while continental lithosphere does not?

study.overview: Earth is layered in two ways. By composition it has crust, mantle and core. By mechanical strength it has a rigid lithosphere riding on a weak asthenosphere. Nobody has drilled deeper than about 12 km, so the layers are known from indirect evidence, mainly seismic waves. The lithosphere is broken into plates that move a few centimeters a year. Where plates meet, three kinds of boundary shape volcanoes, earthquakes and ocean basins. This guide gives the layers and the evidence behind them, the lithosphere and the proof that plates move, the three boundary types, and the arithmetic of plate speed.

points.heading: Compositional layers and how we know them
points.explanation:
By composition Earth has three layers. The crust is thin: about 7 km of basalt under the oceans and about 35 km of granitic rock under the continents. The mantle is peridotite and extends to 2,890 km depth. The core is an iron-nickel alloy with a liquid outer part and a solid inner part. The mantle is solid rock that flows very slowly. It is not a liquid.

The layers are known from indirect evidence because the deepest hole ever drilled, the Kola Superdeep Borehole in Russia, reached only 12,262 m. Earth’s radius is 6,371 km, so Kola went about 0.19% of the way to the center (12.262 ÷ 6,371). The main tool is seismic waves. P waves are compressional and travel through solids and liquids. S waves are shear waves and travel only through solids. Waves also change speed and direction where the material changes. In 1909 this revealed the Moho, the boundary between crust and mantle. In 1936 Inge Lehmann used faint P waves that arrived where the liquid outer core should have kept them out to show that Earth has a distinct inner core; later seismic work showed that the inner core is solid.

To use this evidence, ask which wave types a station on the far side of Earth records after a large earthquake. Then ask what the rules above imply about the material the waves crossed. Meteorites and Earth’s magnetic field are further lines of evidence. They agree with an iron-rich core.

points.heading: Lithosphere, asthenosphere and the evidence that plates move
points.explanation:
The mechanical layers divide Earth by strength, not by composition. The lithosphere is rigid. It is the crust plus the uppermost mantle and is about 100 km thick. Beneath it the asthenosphere is solid but weak, so it flows very slowly. Plates are pieces of lithosphere, so a plate is not the same thing as a continent. One plate can carry both continental and oceanic crust, with uppermost mantle under both.

Four lines of evidence support moving plates. (1) Continental margins fit together, as Wegener showed in 1912. (2) Fossils such as the plant Glossopteris occur on the matching southern continents. (3) Magnetic stripes on the seafloor are symmetrical on either side of a mid-ocean ridge, as Vine and Matthews pointed out in 1963. This fits Hess’s idea of seafloor spreading. (4) The ocean floor is young, mostly under 200 million years old, while continents hold rocks about 4 billion years old.

Example: suppose a rock sample dredged from the floor of the Atlantic is dated and found to be 3 billion years old. That result would contradict the pattern above, because rock that old is found on continents, not on the ocean floor.

points.heading: Three kinds of plate boundary and their landforms
points.explanation:
Plates meet in three ways.

At a divergent boundary the plates move apart. This makes mid-ocean ridges and rift valleys, with basaltic volcanoes and shallow earthquakes. Examples are the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and the East African Rift.

At a convergent boundary the plates move together, and the result depends on the plate types. With an oceanic plate and a continental plate, the oceanic plate subducts. This makes a trench and a volcanic arc on the continent, with explosive volcanoes and earthquakes down to about 700 km. The Andes and the Cascades are examples. With two oceanic plates, one subducts. This makes a trench and an island arc, as in the Mariana Islands, where Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench is nearly 11 km deep. When two continents collide, neither subducts easily, because continental lithosphere resists sinking. The crust thickens into a mountain belt with earthquakes and few volcanoes. The Himalaya are an example.

At a transform boundary the plates slide past each other. Lithosphere is neither made nor destroyed. The landforms are strike-slip faults and offset ridges, with shallow earthquakes and no volcanoes. The San Andreas Fault is an example.

For each boundary, ask what happens to lithosphere there. Whether it is created, destroyed or neither tells you which landforms and hazards to expect. Not every volcano lies on a boundary. Yellowstone sits over a hot spot, a plume of hot mantle beneath the interior of a plate.

points.heading: Plate speed: converting centimeters per year to kilometers per million years
points.explanation:
Plates move a few centimeters a year, about as fast as fingernails grow. Over geologic time that adds up. The shortcut is that 1 cm per year equals 10 km per million years. To check it, convert units. 1 cm per year is 1,000,000 cm per million years, and 1,000,000 cm is 10 km.

Worked example: seafloor lies 1,000 km from a ridge and moves away from it at 2.5 cm per year. First convert the speed to km per million years, so 2.5 cm per year becomes 25 km per million years. Then divide distance by speed: 1,000 km ÷ 25 km per million years = 40 million years. The seafloor there is about 40 million years old.

The same shortcut works in reverse. Distance = speed × age. Always convert the speed first, because mixing cm and km is the most common error. For hot-spot volcano chains the same idea applies: the distance between two volcanoes divided by the difference in their ages gives the plate speed.

handouts.title: Written check on layers and evidence
handouts.usedIn: Written check on layers and evidence

blocks.text: Answer each prompt alone and in writing. Then compare answers with your partner and settle any difference.
Which layer of Earth's interior is liquid, and how do S waves show it?

blocks.hint: Write your answer here.

blocks.text: Earth's mean density is 5.51 g/cm³. What does this tell you about the interior compared with surface rocks?

blocks.hint: Write your answer here.

blocks.text: Give two differences between continental crust and oceanic crust.

blocks.hint: Write your answer here.

handouts.key:
1. The outer core is liquid. S waves cannot travel through liquids, so direct S waves do not pass through the outer core. Look for the outer core specifically. Common slip: describing the mantle or the whole core as liquid.

2. Earth's mean density exceeds the density of typical surface rocks, so substantial regions of the interior must be denser than surface rocks. An iron-rich core contributes to this difference; pressure also increases density at depth. Common slip: treating 5.51 g/cm³ as the density of every layer.

3. Accept any two accurate contrasts: continental crust averages about 35 km thick, compared with about 7 km for oceanic crust; continental crust has an average density near 2.7 g/cm³, compared with about 3.0 g/cm³ for oceanic crust; continental crust is broadly granitic in composition, whereas oceanic crust is broadly basaltic. Common slip: confusing crust with the lithosphere.

handouts.title: How old is the seafloor?

blocks.text: Shortcut: a speed of 1 cm per year is the same as 10 km per million years. Convert the speed to km per million years before you divide. Show your working. Then check your answers with your partner.
Seafloor moves away from a mid-ocean ridge at 2.5 cm per year. How old is the seafloor 1,500 km from the ridge?

blocks.hint: Working and answer, in millions of years.

blocks.text: At the same speed, how far from the ridge is seafloor that is 100 million years old?

blocks.hint: Working and answer, in km.

handouts.key:
1. Convert the speed: 2.5 cm/year × 10 = 25 km per million years. Age = distance ÷ speed = 1,500 km ÷ 25 km per million years = 60 million years. Look for consistent units and the age of crust on one side of the ridge. Common slip: halving the speed as though the given value were the total separation rate across both sides.

2. Distance = speed × age = 25 km per million years × 100 million years = 2,500 km. This is the distance from the ridge. Common slip: dividing by age instead of multiplying.

blocks.text: This table was written for this exercise. Some rows contain a mistake about what happens at the boundary. Work alone. For each row, write "correct" or write a one-sentence correction. Then compare with your partner.

rows: Plates move apart and new oceanic lithosphere forms
Mid-ocean ridge, basaltic volcanoes, shallow earthquakes
Dense oceanic lithosphere sinks beneath continental lithosphere
Trench, volcanic arc on the continent, earthquakes at many depths
Oceanic lithosphere subducts and feeds a chain of volcanoes
San Andreas Fault (Pacific and North American plates)
Plates pull apart and new lithosphere forms along the fault
Mariana Trench (Pacific plate beneath the Mariana plate)
One oceanic plate sinks beneath another
Trench nearly 11 km deep at Challenger Deep, island arc, earthquakes down to about 700 km
blocks.caption: Hypothetical boundary table

handouts.key:
Row 1: Correct. Plates diverge, new oceanic lithosphere forms, and the ridge has basaltic volcanism and shallow earthquakes.

Row 2: Correct. The Nazca plate subducts beneath the South American plate, producing a trench, a continental volcanic arc and earthquakes at a range of depths.

Row 3: Correction: The Himalaya forms where continental lithosphere of India collides with Eurasia, shortening and thickening the crust to build mountains and generate earthquakes, rather than sustaining a typical oceanic-subduction trench and volcanic arc. Look for continental collision and crustal thickening. Common slip: assuming every convergent boundary produces a volcanic arc.

Row 4: Correction: The Pacific and North American plates slide past each other along the San Andreas Fault, neither creating nor destroying lithosphere, and produce shallow earthquakes without characteristic boundary-related volcanism. Look for lateral motion and earthquakes. Common slip: describing transform motion as pulling apart.

Row 5: Correct. The Pacific plate subducts beneath the Mariana plate, producing a deep trench, an island arc and earthquakes extending to about 700 km depth.

handouts.title: Measuring density of crust and mantle samples
handouts.usedIn: Measuring density of crust and mantle samples

blocks.text: Work in your pair with the department's hand samples. One partner lowers the sample and the other records.
Safety and handling

items: Wear closed-toe shoes.
Carry trays with both hands and keep samples away from table edges.
Lower samples on a thread. Never drop them: glass cylinders crack.
Wipe spills at once so the floor is not slippery.
Samples stay in their trays, go back where they came from, and do not leave the room.

blocks.text: Procedure

items: Put the sample tray on the balance and tare it so it reads 0.0 g.
Put the first sample in the tray. Record its mass to 0.1 g.
Fill a graduated cylinder with enough water to cover the sample completely without overflowing when it is lowered. Stand the cylinder inside the tray.
Read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level. Record this as the water level before.
Tie the sample to a thread and lower it slowly until it is fully under water. Tap the cylinder gently to remove trapped bubbles.
Read the bottom of the meniscus again. Record this as the water level after.
Volume (cm³) = water level after − water level before. 1 mL = 1 cm³.
Density (g/cm³) = mass ÷ volume.
Repeat for the other two samples. Use pieces that fit the cylinder. If your tray has no peridotite, measure the dunite.
Rank the three samples from least dense (1) to most dense (3).
If your rank order differs from your prediction, repeat the measurements and check how well you could read the volume before you interpret the result.
Put all samples back in their trays and wipe the bench dry.

blocks.hint: Your predicted ranking from earlier in this session, from least to most dense.
Does your measured rank order match your prediction? If not, say what you repeated and how well you could read the volume.

handouts.key:
Recording table, in row order:

Granite: Mass is the pair's measured sample mass in grams, recorded to 0.1 g after taring the tray. Water level before and water level after are the measured meniscus readings in milliliters. Volume = water level after − water level before, expressed in cm³. Density = measured mass ÷ calculated volume, expressed in g/cm³. Typical density is about 2.6–2.7 g/cm³. Expected rank: 1.

Basalt: Mass is the pair's measured sample mass in grams, recorded to 0.1 g. Water level before and water level after are the measured meniscus readings in milliliters. Volume = water level after − water level before, expressed in cm³. Density = measured mass ÷ calculated volume, expressed in g/cm³. Typical density is about 2.8–3.0 g/cm³. Expected rank: 2.

Peridotite or dunite: Mass is the pair's measured sample mass in grams, recorded to 0.1 g. Water level before and water level after are the measured meniscus readings in milliliters. Volume = water level after − water level before, expressed in cm³. Density = measured mass ÷ calculated volume, expressed in g/cm³. Typical density is about 3.2–3.4 g/cm³. Expected rank: 3.

For every row, look for calculations consistent with the recorded measurements. The rank must follow the calculated densities, even if it differs from the expected order. Common slips: including tray mass, using the final water level as sample volume, subtracting in the wrong order, inverting mass and volume, or reporting more precision than the volume readings support. Trapped bubbles increase apparent volume and lower calculated density.

Predicted ranking blank: Expected prediction is granite < basalt < peridotite or dunite. Accept a clearly stated original prediction even if it differs; this blank records the student's prediction before measurement.

Comparison blank: The answer must compare the measured order with the recorded prediction. If they match, a direct statement identifying that agreement is sufficient. If they differ, look for the measurements repeated, the resulting values, and an estimate of volume-reading uncertainty based on the cylinder graduations. The explanation should consider meniscus readings, trapped bubbles and complete immersion. Common slip: changing measured results merely to reproduce the expected ranking.

handouts.title: Classifying plate boundaries on a world map
handouts.usedIn: Classifying plate boundaries on a world map

blocks.text: Use the Plate boundaries world map your instructor gives each pair. It shows plate outlines, relative-motion arrows, earthquake depths and volcano locations. These plates are labeled: Nubian (African), Somali, Arabian, Pacific, Tonga, Anatolian, Eurasian, Juan de Fuca, North American and Adriatic.

For each location, mark it on the map using the approximate position given. Decide the boundary type (divergent, convergent, transform, or none), name the plates, and record the landforms and hazards you expect.

blocks.hint: State one pattern in where earthquakes and volcanoes occur.

handouts.key:
1. Afar Triangle, Ethiopia: Mark near 11° N, 41° E. Boundary type: divergent; a continental rift and triple-junction region. Plates: Nubian, Somali and Arabian. Landforms and hazards: rift valleys, normal faults, basaltic volcanoes, fissure eruptions and shallow earthquakes.

2. Tonga Trench: Mark near 22° S, 175° W. Boundary type: convergent, oceanic–oceanic subduction. Plates: Pacific and Tonga; the Pacific plate subducts beneath Tonga. Landforms and hazards: deep ocean trench, volcanic island arc, shallow through deep earthquakes, explosive eruptions and possible tsunamis. Common slip: reversing the subduction direction.

3. North Anatolian Fault near Istanbul: Mark near 41° N, 29° E. Boundary type: transform. Plates: Anatolian and Eurasian. Landforms and hazards: strike-slip faults, offset landforms, shallow earthquakes, strong shaking and surface rupture; no characteristic boundary-related volcanic arc. Common slip: predicting new oceanic lithosphere.

4. Mount Rainier, Washington: Mark near 47° N, 122° W. Boundary type: convergent, oceanic–continental subduction. Plates: Juan de Fuca and North American; Juan de Fuca subducts beneath North America. Landforms and hazards: Cascade volcanic arc, an offshore subduction zone, earthquakes, explosive eruptions and lahars. Rainier lies inland above the subduction system rather than directly on the plate boundary.

5. The Alps: Mark near 46° N, 8° E. Boundary type: convergent, continental collision. Plates: Adriatic and Eurasian; accept African and Eurasian as the broader regional description. Landforms and hazards: folded and faulted mountain belt, thickened crust, earthquakes and landslides. Common slip: expecting a typical active subduction volcanic arc.

6. Yellowstone: Mark near 44.5° N, 110.5° W. Boundary type: none; an intraplate hot spot. Plate: North American. Landforms and hazards: volcanic caldera, rhyolitic volcanic terrain, geysers and hot springs; earthquakes, volcanic hazards and hydrothermal explosions. Common slip: assigning Yellowstone to a plate boundary because it is volcanic.

Pattern blank: Most earthquakes and volcanoes cluster along plate boundaries. Earthquakes occur at all three boundary types; volcanoes are especially associated with divergent boundaries and subduction zones. Hot spots such as Yellowstone are exceptions to the boundary pattern. Accept a specific pattern supported by the map, such as increasing earthquake depths beneath the overriding plate at a subduction zone. Common slip: claiming all earthquakes and volcanoes occur at boundaries.

handouts.title: Plate speed from the Hawaiian hot spot
handouts.usedIn: Plate speed from the Hawaiian hot spot

blocks.text: Use these rounded values. The hot spot lies beneath the island of Hawaii and stays in place. Kauai lies northwest of it, about 500 km away. Kauai is about 5 million years old. Volcanoes in the chain get older toward Kauai.
Find how fast the Pacific plate moved while Kauai drifted away from the hot spot. Give the speed in km per million years.

blocks.hint: Working and answer.

blocks.text: Give the same speed in cm per year. (1 cm per year is 10 km per million years.)

blocks.hint: Working and answer.

blocks.text: In which direction does the Pacific plate move? Explain using the ages in the chain.

blocks.hint: Direction and reason.

handouts.key:
1. Speed = distance ÷ age = 500 km ÷ 5 million years = 100 km per million years. Look for distance divided by elapsed time and units of speed.

2. Since 1 cm per year = 10 km per million years, 100 ÷ 10 = 10 cm per year. Common slip: multiplying by 10 instead of dividing.

3. The Pacific plate moves northwest relative to the hot spot. Kauai lies northwest of the currently active hot spot beneath Hawaii and is older, so its volcanoes were carried northwest after forming above the hot spot. Common slip: reversing plate motion or describing the hot spot as moving northwest in this model.

segments.title: What counts as a mineral?
segments.description:
Weekly online quizzes: Earth’s layers and plate tectonics is due now, submitted online before this meeting.
Students write “mineral” or “not a mineral” for each of the three items on the screen, with no reasons yet, for 1 minute alone.
Pairs compare verdicts and give a reason for one item they differ on, for 1 minute.
The class shows hands for each item, then hears one reason for the item with the most split vote, for 2 minutes in all.
Leave the verdicts unsettled; the next segments return to them.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: glacier ice is a mineral (natural, solid, crystalline H₂O); window glass is not (made by people, no crystal structure); quartz is. Common error: ice is “not a mineral because it melts”. Do not correct yet. Ask for a reason on the item the class is most divided on, usually the ice.
shown: Glacier ice
Window glass
A crystal of quartz from a granite
Write “mineral” or “not a mineral” for each item. With your partner, give a reason for one item you differ on.

segments.title: Atoms, ions and bonds
segments.description:
Review protons, neutrons, electrons and atomic number. Show Na (11 protons) giving one electron to Cl (17 protons) to form Na⁺ and Cl⁻, held together in halite by an ionic bond.
Contrast covalent bonds, where atoms share electrons, as between silicon and oxygen.
Show that oxygen and silicon make up about three quarters of the crust by mass.
Everyone works out the ion that magnesium forms, then checks with a neighbor.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: Mg²⁺ has 12 protons, 10 electrons, charge +2. Common mistake: changing the number of protons when an ion forms. Allow about 6 minutes of explanation and 3 for the problem.
shown: Table: Element | Percent of crust by mass / Oxygen | 46.6 / Silicon | 27.7 / Aluminum | 8.1 / Iron | 5.0 / Calcium | 3.6
A magnesium atom has 12 protons and 12 electrons. It loses two electrons. How many protons and electrons does it now have, and what is its charge?

segments.title: The five criteria
segments.description:
Set out the five criteria: naturally occurring, inorganic, solid, crystalline, and a definite chemical composition.
Explain crystal structure as a repeating, ordered arrangement of atoms. Explain that composition may vary within limits, as Mg and Fe swap places in olivine.
Return to the opening items and ask which criterion each passes or fails.
Then switch the table off and pairs state the five criteria to each other.
segments.teacherNotes: Window glass fails “naturally occurring” and “crystalline”. Stress that “inorganic” means the substance is not an organic compound (the carbon-based material of coal), not “not a chemical” and not “no organism was involved”: calcite built by shell-forming organisms is still a mineral. “Solid” is judged under the conditions where the material occurs, which is why glacier ice counts. Remove the table before the pair statement so recall is real.
shown: Table: Criterion | Meaning / Naturally occurring | formed by geological processes, not made by people / Inorganic | not an organic compound; calcite in shells still counts / Solid | solid under the conditions where it occurs, as ice is in a glacier / Crystalline | atoms in a repeating, ordered pattern / Definite composition | a chemical formula, varying only within limits

segments.title: Apply the criteria
segments.description:
Students take the three cases on the screen one at a time. For each they write a verdict and the criterion that decides it, about 1 minute per case, 3 minutes in all.
Pairs compare for 2 minutes and prepare to defend one decision.
The class hears two pairs for 2 minutes in all, and the instructor confirms the verdicts.
segments.teacherNotes: Halite: mineral. Coal: not a mineral (organic origin, no crystal structure, no definite formula). Lab-grown ruby: not a mineral (not naturally occurring), though identical in structure and formula to corundum, Al₂O₃. Common mistake: calling the ruby a mineral because of its structure.
shown: Halite crystals left behind by a dried salt lake
Coal from a seam
A ruby grown in a laboratory (Al₂O₃)

segments.title: Find and fix: is obsidian a mineral?
segments.description:
Students read the claim on the screen and each finds the flaw, then rewrites it as a correct statement, for 3 minutes alone.
Pairs compare corrected versions for 2 minutes.
The class hears two versions for 3 minutes, and the instructor names the criteria that fail.
segments.teacherNotes: Obsidian meets the naturally occurring, inorganic and solid criteria, but lacks a definite mineral composition and fails “crystalline”: obsidian is volcanic glass from lava that cooled too fast for atoms to order. Its composition also varies without a fixed formula. Some students object that it is mostly SiO₂ like quartz; the arrangement of atoms differs. Correct: obsidian is not a mineral.
shown: Claim: Obsidian is a mineral. It forms naturally from lava, it is solid, it is inorganic, and it is mostly SiO₂, so it has a definite composition.

segments.title: The silicate tetrahedron
segments.description:
Draw one silicon ion inside a tetrahedron of four oxygen ions on the board. Show that the charges give (SiO₄)⁴⁻.
Explain that tetrahedra join by sharing corner oxygens or by bonding through cations such as Fe²⁺ and Mg²⁺.
Students work out the Si to O ratio when every oxygen is shared, for 2 minutes alone, then compare with a partner.
The instructor takes one answer and links it to the formula of quartz.
segments.teacherNotes: Net charge: 4+ and 4 × 2− gives 4−. In a framework each tetrahedron owns 4 × ½ = 2 oxygens, so the ratio is 1:2 and the formula SiO₂, quartz. Common error: counting all four oxygens for each silicon.
shown: In a framework, every oxygen is shared between two tetrahedra, and each silicon is bonded to four oxygens. What is the ratio of silicon to oxygen, and what is the formula?

segments.title: One-sentence definition
segments.description:
Each student writes a one-sentence definition of a mineral that names all five criteria, for 2 minutes.
Two students read theirs aloud and the class checks them against the criteria.
The instructor says that the next meeting covers how tetrahedra link into chains, sheets and frameworks, and the four properties used to identify minerals.
segments.teacherNotes: Listen for “definite chemical composition” and “crystal structure” as separate criteria; students often merge them or drop “inorganic”.

segments.title: Recall the five criteria
segments.description:
Students write the five criteria for a mineral from memory, with no notes, for 3 minutes.
Partners swap papers and check each other for 2 minutes.
segments.teacherNotes: Circulate and note which criterion is missed most often, usually “definite chemical composition”. Revisit it with the olivine example in the next segment.
shown: Write the five criteria for a mineral from memory.

segments.title: How tetrahedra link
segments.description:
Draw each arrangement on the board in turn: isolated tetrahedra in olivine, single chains in pyroxene, double chains in amphibole, sheets in mica and a framework in quartz and feldspar.
Show that chains give two cleavages, at about 90° in pyroxene and about 56° and 124° in amphibole.
Show that more shared oxygens means more silica, from olivine to quartz at 100% SiO₂.
Pairs predict for 2 minutes in which direction mica splits easily, then two pairs answer.
segments.teacherNotes: Mica: strong Si–O bonds within sheets, weak K⁺ bonds between them, so it splits parallel to the sheets in one direction. Common mistake: calling tetrahedra “molecules”. Quartz has no cleavage because bonds are strong in all directions.
shown: Table: Arrangement | Example mineral | Oxygens shared per tetrahedron / Isolated | olivine | 0 / Single chain | pyroxene (augite) | 2 / Double chain | amphibole (hornblende) | 2 and 3 / Sheet | mica, clay | 3 / Framework | quartz, feldspar | 4

segments.title: From break to structure
segments.description:
Students take the four descriptions of how a mineral breaks. For each they name the silicate structure and an example mineral, working alone for 4 minutes.
Pairs compare for 2 minutes.
The class hears answers for 2 minutes in all.
segments.teacherNotes: 1: sheet, muscovite or biotite. 2: single chain, pyroxene (augite). 3: double chain, amphibole (hornblende). 4: framework, quartz. Common mistake: swapping 2 and 3; pyroxene cleavages meet near 90°, amphibole near 56° and 124°.
shown: Splits into thin, flexible flakes in one direction
Two cleavages meeting at about 90°, in a dark green to black mineral
Two cleavages meeting at about 56° and 124°, in a dark mineral
Glassy, no cleavage, breaks along curved surfaces

segments.title: Hardness, cleavage, luster and streak
segments.description:
Introduce Mohs hardness, 1 (talc) to 10 (diamond), and the tools that bracket it: fingernail, copper coin, steel nail and glass plate.
Contrast cleavage, where a mineral breaks along flat planes, with fracture. Define luster as metallic or nonmetallic, and streak as the color of the powder on a porcelain plate.
Explain why color misleads, using hematite, which looks gray, black or red but always streaks red-brown.
Students work out the hardness range of a mineral that scratches calcite but is scratched by fluorite, alone for 1 minute, then in pairs.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: between 3 and 4. Common error: assuming a mineral that scratches glass must be quartz. Streak does not work for minerals harder than the plate (about 6.5), and quartz leaves none. Allow 8 minutes of exposition and 3 for the problem.
shown: Table: Hardness | Reference mineral / 1 | talc / 2 | gypsum / 3 | calcite / 4 | fluorite / 5 | apatite / 6 | orthoclase / 7 | quartz / 8 | topaz / 9 | corundum / 10 | diamond
Table: Common tool | Hardness / Fingernail | about 2.5 / Copper coin | about 3.5 / Steel nail | about 5.5 / Glass plate | about 5.5
A mineral scratches calcite, but fluorite scratches it. Between which two hardness values does it lie?

segments.title: Identify from descriptions
segments.description:
Students match each of the four descriptions to a mineral using the property table, alone for 4 minutes.
Pairs compare and settle any disagreement in 2 minutes.
The class hears the answers and the deciding property for each, for 2 minutes.
segments.teacherNotes: A: pyrite (hardness and black streak; gold is soft with a yellow streak). B: halite (three cleavages at 90°). C: calcite (rhombs plus fizz). D: quartz (no cleavage, scratches glass). Common mistake: using color alone for A. Quartz is harder than the streak plate, so it leaves no streak; scratching it only leaves white porcelain powder.
shown: Table: Mineral | Hardness | Cleavage | Streak / Calcite | 3 | three, not at 90° | white / Halite | 2.5 | three, at 90° | white / Pyrite | 6 to 6.5 | none | greenish black / Quartz | 7 | none | none (harder than the plate)
A: Brassy yellow, metallic luster, scratches glass, black streak
B: Colorless cubes, glassy, three cleavages at right angles, scratched by a copper coin
C: Colorless rhombs, three cleavages not at right angles, scratched by a copper coin, fizzes in dilute HCl
D: Glassy, gray and translucent, no cleavage, scratches glass, breaks along curved surfaces

segments.title: Summary and the quiz
segments.description:
Students list on paper the four identification properties and one mineral that each separates from a look-alike, for 2 minutes.
Preview the lab at the next meeting: pairs use the department’s hand samples, with closed-toe shoes required.
Set Weekly online quizzes (10%) for this lesson and say it is due at the first meeting of Igneous rocks and volcanoes. Each student completes their own work, done and scored alone, and submits it online before that meeting.
segments.teacherNotes: Example answers: streak separates hematite from magnetite; hardness separates pyrite from gold; cleavage angle separates calcite from halite. Remind students to bring closed-toe shoes.

segments.title: Lab start, safety and method
segments.description:
Lab reports: Earth’s layers and plate tectonics is due now, at the start of this lab.
State the rules: closed-toe shoes, goggles on whenever the dilute HCl bottle is open, and hand samples stay in their trays and go back where they came from.
Demonstrate observations and suitable tests on a calcite sample not in the unknown set: luster, color, cleavage, then hardness and streak on designated test spots. Explain that destructive tests are used only when they resolve an identification. Demonstrate one drop of dilute HCl to confirm suspected carbonate, with goggles on.
Pairs read the Mineral identification data sheet and the Mineral properties reference table, and each pair takes a hand lens.
segments.teacherNotes: The Mineral identification data sheet has one row per sample, with columns for sample number, luster, streak, hardness, cleavage and name; prepare copies. Record fracture in the Cleavage column and any acid reaction beside the mineral name. The Mineral properties reference table lists luster, streak, hardness, cleavage and acid reaction for every mineral in the unknown set and the specimen sets; prepare copies. Put out one hand lens per pair for judging luster and counting cleavage directions. Demonstrate on a sample not among the unknowns, so no reported sample is modelled. Each student writes their own report; the pair shares data. Safety: goggles for HCl, dropper only; rinse spills with water; no tasting any sample.

segments.title: Calibrating hardness and streak
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Hardness and streak record”.
Pairs scratch the reference minerals with a fingernail, copper coin, steel nail and glass plate. For each tool they record the hardest reference mineral it scratches and the softest it fails to scratch, giving a hardness bracket, for 14 minutes.
They streak hematite, pyrite and calcite on the plate and record the colors, for 4 minutes.
Pairs compare their tool brackets with the Mohs scale on the Mineral properties reference table, for 4 minutes.
segments.teacherNotes: Reference set: talc, gypsum, calcite, fluorite, apatite, orthoclase, quartz. Tool hardness varies with the individual coin, nail and plate, so students record their own brackets, e.g. “nail scratches fluorite, not orthoclase”, and use those brackets later rather than nominal values. Typical results: the fingernail scratches talc and gypsum; the coin adds calcite; the nail and glass add fluorite and apatite; none of these tools should scratch quartz; quartz should scratch the glass plate. Streaks: hematite red-brown, pyrite greenish black, calcite white. Wipe off powder to tell a true scratch. Use a copper coin or a pre-1982 U.S. penny. Newer U.S. pennies have a zinc core with copper plating; calibrate the actual coin against the reference minerals. Safety: tape the glass plate edges; scratch away from the body; do not blow dust.

segments.title: Cleavage and luster
segments.description:
Pairs examine six labeled specimens under the light, and for each count the cleavage directions, estimate the angles and name the luster, about 2.5 minutes each, 15 minutes in all.
They sketch the cleavage faces of two specimens on the data sheet.
Pairs compare results with the class for 5 minutes.
segments.teacherNotes: Set: halite, 3 cleavages at 90°, vitreous. Calcite, 3 not at 90°, vitreous. Muscovite, 1 perfect, pearly to vitreous. K-feldspar, 2 near 90°. Hornblende, 2 at 56° and 124°. Quartz, none, conchoidal. Common error: counting each flat face as a separate direction; parallel faces count once. Cleavage fragments are sharp; handle gently.

segments.title: Break
segments.description: Students leave the samples in their trays and step away from the lab benches.
segments.teacherNotes: Check that goggles, the HCl bottle and trays are tidy before restarting.

segments.title: Identify the unknown samples
segments.description:
Each pair receives a tray of eight numbered unknowns and identifies each, at about 4 minutes a sample. Partners share what they observe, and each fills in their own Mineral identification data sheet with luster, streak, hardness, cleavage and name.
Observe luster and existing cleavage or fracture first. Use hardness or streak only when it resolves an identification, on a designated test spot; write not tested for any property not tested. In the Cleavage column write the number of directions and their angles, or the type of fracture. Do not streak quartz or mica. Test mica hardness only with a fingernail on an edge. Use acid only to confirm a suspected carbonate, with goggles on.
When they finish, pairs compare names with the key and re-test any sample they got wrong, for the last 4 minutes. Students do not change their original entries and record each correction in the corrections table on the sheet: the sample, the corrected name and the evidence.
segments.teacherNotes: Suggested unknowns (adapt to the department’s trays): 1 muscovite: 1 perfect cleavage, hardness 2 to 2.5. 2 pyrite: brassy, hardness 6, greenish-black streak. 3 galena: metallic gray, 3 cleavages at 90°, gray streak. 4 quartz: no cleavage, conchoidal fracture, hardness 7. 5 calcite: fizzes in HCl. 6 halite: 3 cleavages at 90°, hardness 2.5. 7 K-feldspar: 2 cleavages near 90°, hardness 6. 8 fluorite: 4 cleavage directions, hardness 4. The sheet has no acid column; a student who confirms calcite with acid can note the fizz in the Name column or as evidence in the corrections table. The corrections table has three rows. Do not acid-test halite or galena, and test mica only with a fingernail on an edge, never the steel nail. Safety: dilute HCl from a dropper bottle, goggles on; wash hands after handling galena (lead sulfide); no tasting. Allow about 4 minutes a sample.

segments.title: Choose the test
segments.description:
Students read the prompt and write their choice and reason alone for 3 minutes.
Pairs then test two paired samples from the tray for 5 minutes and record the result.
The class hears two pairs for 4 minutes and the instructor confirms the decision.
segments.teacherNotes: Streak is better: hematite red-brown, magnetite black. Hardness overlaps (hematite 5 to 6.5, magnetite 5.5 to 6.5), and both can look metallic gray. A magnet would also work for magnetite. Common mistake: trusting color. Use a labeled hematite and magnetite pair that is not in the unknown set.

segments.title: Clean-up, assignments and what comes next
segments.description:
Pairs wipe the streak plates, return every sample to its tray and wash their hands, for 3 minutes.
Set Lab reports (30%) for this lab, with each student’s own work done and scored alone, and say it is due at the start of the lab of Igneous rocks and volcanoes.
Tell students to read Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, chapters 3, Intrusive Igneous Rocks, and 4, Volcanism, before the first meeting of Igneous rocks and volcanoes. It covers how magma forms and crystallizes, how felsic and mafic rocks and textures are classified, and how volcano types and eruption styles create hazards.
The practice quiz on this lesson is open after class and counts toward no grade.
segments.teacherNotes: Count trays and samples before students leave. Confirm the chapter numbers against the edition students own.

keyIdeas: A mineral is a naturally occurring, inorganic, solid with a crystal structure and a definite chemical composition. A material that fails any one of the five criteria, such as obsidian (no crystal structure) or coal (organic), is not a mineral.

Atoms become ions by gaining or losing electrons, and ionic and covalent bonds hold minerals together. Oxygen (about 47% of the crust by mass) and silicon (about 28%) dominate, so silicate minerals dominate the crust.

The silicate tetrahedron, one Si⁴⁺ surrounded by four O²⁻, links by sharing oxygens into isolated units, chains, sheets and frameworks. Each structure helps predict cleavage: mica splits in one direction, quartz in none.
Hardness (Mohs scale 1 to 10), cleavage, luster and streak identify common minerals in hand samples. Color alone misleads, because one mineral can show many colors.

vocabulary.definition: A naturally occurring, inorganic solid with a crystal structure and a definite chemical composition.
An atom that has gained or lost electrons and so carries an electric charge, such as Na⁺ or Cl⁻.
The repeating, ordered three-dimensional arrangement of atoms in a mineral.
The building block of silicate minerals: one silicon ion bonded to four oxygen ions, (SiO₄)⁴⁻.
A mineral’s resistance to scratching, ranked on the Mohs scale from 1 (talc) to 10 (diamond).
The tendency of a mineral to break along flat planes where bonds are weakest.
The way a mineral’s surface reflects light, such as metallic or vitreous (glassy).
The color of a mineral’s powder when rubbed on an unglazed porcelain plate.

Then everyone works out the ion magnesium forms, alone, and checks with a neighbor.
