Preview the lab at the next meeting: pairs use the department’s hand samples, and closed-toe shoes are required. Remind students to bring closed-toe shoes.

study.overview: A mineral is a specific kind of natural solid, and the minerals that make up most of the crust are silicates built from one repeating unit, the silicon-oxygen tetrahedron. This guide covers what qualifies a material as a mineral, how atoms bond, how tetrahedra link, and how to identify common minerals by hardness, cleavage, luster and streak. Read it alongside Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, the chapter on minerals.

points.heading: A mineral must pass all five criteria
points.explanation:
A mineral is naturally occurring, inorganic, solid, crystalline and of definite chemical composition. Failing any one criterion rules a material out.

Naturally occurring: formed by geological processes, not made by people. Inorganic: not an organic compound. Calcite built by shell-forming organisms still counts, because calcite is not a carbon-based organic compound. Solid: judged under the conditions where the material occurs, which is why glacier ice is a mineral (crystalline H₂O). Crystalline: atoms sit in a repeating, ordered pattern. Definite composition: a chemical formula, varying only within limits, as Mg and Fe swap places in olivine.

Example: coal from a seam is organic, has no crystal structure and has no definite formula, so it is not a mineral. A ruby grown in a laboratory has the same structure and formula (Al₂O₃) as natural corundum, but people made it, so it is not a mineral. Obsidian is natural, solid and inorganic, and it is mostly SiO₂, but it is volcanic glass. The lava cooled too fast for atoms to order, so it is not crystalline and has no fixed mineral formula. Mostly SiO₂ is not enough: quartz has the same chemistry with the atoms arranged in order. Halite crystals left by a dried salt lake pass all five.

points.heading: Ions and bonds explain why silicates dominate
points.explanation:
An atom becomes an ion by gaining or losing electrons. The number of protons never changes. A magnesium atom has 12 protons and 12 electrons. If it loses two electrons it becomes Mg²⁺ with 12 protons, 10 electrons and a charge of +2.

In an ionic bond, one atom gives electrons to another and the opposite charges attract. In halite, sodium (11 protons) gives one electron to chlorine (17 protons), forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻. In a covalent bond, atoms share electrons, as silicon and oxygen do.

Oxygen is about 46.6% of the crust by mass and silicon about 27.7%, followed by aluminum (8.1%), iron (5.0%) and calcium (3.6%). Together, oxygen and silicon make up about three quarters of the crust, so minerals built from silicon and oxygen, the silicates, dominate it.

points.heading: Silicate tetrahedra link in different ways, and structure predicts cleavage
points.explanation:
The building block is one Si⁴⁺ surrounded by four O²⁻ at the corners of a tetrahedron. The charges give 4+ and 4 × 2−, a net charge of (SiO₄)⁴⁻. This unit is an ion group, not a molecule. It is neutralized by sharing corner oxygens with other tetrahedra or by bonding to cations such as Fe²⁺ and Mg²⁺.

The pattern of sharing gives the main structures: isolated tetrahedra (olivine), chains (pyroxene, amphibole), sheets (mica, clay) and frameworks (quartz, feldspar). The more oxygens are shared, the higher the proportion of silica, up to quartz at 100% SiO₂.

Worked example: in a framework every oxygen is shared by two tetrahedra, so each tetrahedron owns 4 × ½ = 2 oxygens. The ratio of silicon to oxygen is 1:2, and the formula is SiO₂, which is quartz. A common error is counting all four oxygens for every silicon.

A mineral breaks most easily where its bonds are weakest. Quartz has strong bonds in every direction, so it has no cleavage and breaks along curved surfaces.

points.heading: Identify minerals by hardness, cleavage, luster and streak, not by color
points.explanation:
Color alone misleads, because one mineral can show many colors. Use these four properties instead.

Hardness is resistance to scratching, on the Mohs scale from 1 (talc) to 10 (diamond). Reference minerals are talc, gypsum, calcite, fluorite, apatite, orthoclase, quartz, topaz, corundum and diamond, numbered 1 to 10 in that order, with topaz at 8 and corundum at 9. Nominal tool values are a fingernail at about 2.5, a copper coin at about 3.5, and a steel nail or glass plate at about 5.5. Real tools vary, so use brackets you measured yourself. Example: a mineral that scratches calcite but is scratched by fluorite lies between 3 and 4. Do not assume that a mineral that scratches glass is quartz.

Cleavage is breaking along flat planes. Count directions, not faces, because parallel faces count once. Estimate the angles between directions. Fracture is any other break, such as curved (conchoidal) surfaces.

Luster is metallic or nonmetallic. Streak is the color of the powder on a porcelain plate. Hematite looks gray, black or red, but always streaks red-brown. The plate has a hardness of about 6.5, so a harder mineral such as quartz leaves only white porcelain powder, not a true streak.

Always combine properties. Halite (hardness 2.5, three cleavages at 90°) and calcite (hardness 3, three cleavages not at 90°) are told apart by the cleavage angles, and calcite also fizzes in dilute HCl.

handouts.title: Mineral identification data sheet
handouts.copies: One per student; the pair shares its data, and each student keeps their own sheet

blocks.text: Work with your partner on the tray of eight numbered unknowns. Share what you observe, and fill in your own sheet. Observe luster and any existing cleavage or fracture first. Use a hardness or streak test only when it helps settle an identification, on a designated test spot. Write not tested for any property you did not test. In the Cleavage column, write the number of directions and their angles, or write the type of fracture if the sample has no cleavage.
Safety

items: Closed-toe shoes at all times.
Goggles on whenever the dilute HCl bottle is open. Use one drop from the dropper, and only to confirm a suspected carbonate.
Do not streak quartz or mica. Test the hardness of mica only with a fingernail on an edge.
Samples stay in the tray and go back where they came from.
No tasting any sample. Wash your hands after handling the samples.

blocks.text: Corrections after comparing with the key
Do not change your entries above. For any sample you re-test, record the correction here.

handouts.key:
Expected entries for the suggested numbered tray follow. Accept not tested for tests that were unnecessary. Hardness entries should report the observed bracket from the calibrated tools; the values below are reference values.

Sample | Luster | Streak | Hardness | Cleavage | Name
1 | Pearly to vitreous | Not tested | 2–2.5, or not tested | 1 perfect direction; parallel sheets | Muscovite
2 | Metallic | Greenish black, or not tested | 6–6.5, or not tested | No cleavage; uneven fracture | Pyrite
3 | Metallic | Gray, or not tested | About 2.5, or not tested | 3 directions at 90° | Galena
4 | Vitreous | Not tested | 7, or an observed bracket consistent with 7 | No cleavage; conchoidal fracture | Quartz
5 | Vitreous | White, or not tested | 3, or not tested | 3 directions, not at 90° | Calcite; fizzing in dilute HCl supports identification if tested
6 | Vitreous | White, or not tested | About 2.5, or not tested | 3 directions at 90° | Halite
7 | Vitreous to pearly | White, or not tested | About 6, or not tested | 2 directions near 90° | K-feldspar
8 | Vitreous | White, or not tested | About 4, or not tested | 4 directions; octahedral cleavage | Fluorite

Look for names supported by several properties. Parallel faces count as one cleavage direction. Quartz has conchoidal fracture, not cleavage. White porcelain powder from scratching the plate is not a mineral streak. Muscovite hardness testing uses only a fingernail on an edge.

Corrections after comparing with the key: Each used row gives the sample number, the corrected mineral name and the observation that supports the correction. For example: 5 | Calcite | Three cleavage directions not at 90°; fizzed with dilute HCl. Accept other corrections supported by the student's observations. Original entries remain unchanged. Unused correction rows may remain blank.

blocks.text: Typical properties of the minerals in the unknown set and the specimen sets. Real samples vary, so treat hardness as a range and compare several properties before you decide.
The porcelain streak plate has a hardness of about 6.5. A mineral harder than the plate scratches it and leaves only white porcelain powder, not a true streak.

handouts.title: Hardness and streak record

blocks.text: Tools vary from one coin, nail or glass plate to the next, so record your own results. Try each tool on each reference mineral: talc, gypsum, calcite, fluorite, apatite, orthoclase and quartz. Wipe off the powder to tell a true scratch from a mark. Tape covers the glass plate edges; scratch away from your body and do not blow dust.

columns: Softest mineral it does not scratch
blocks.caption: Hardness bracket for each tool

blocks.hint: Compare your tool brackets with the Mohs scale on the Mineral properties reference table. Write down any tool whose bracket differs from the table.

handouts.key:
Hardness bracket for each tool: Entries depend on the actual tools. Each row names the hardest reference mineral genuinely scratched and the softest reference mineral not scratched. A rubbed-off mark is not a scratch. A consistent bracket requires the tool to scratch softer reference minerals and fail on harder ones.

Tool | Typical hardest mineral scratched | Typical softest mineral not scratched
Fingernail | Gypsum, 2 | Calcite, 3
Copper coin | Calcite, 3 | Fluorite, 4
Steel nail | Apatite, 5, for a nail between 5 and 6 | Orthoclase, 6, for that nail
Glass plate | Apatite, 5, for glass between 5 and 6 | Orthoclase, 6, for that plate

Accept different consistent brackets for the actual nail, coin or glass. If a tool scratches fluorite but fails on apatite, record fluorite and apatite, giving a bracket between 4 and 5. If it scratches apatite but fails on orthoclase, record apatite and orthoclase, giving a bracket between 5 and 6. Do not substitute nominal tool hardness for observations.

Streak on the porcelain plate:
Hematite: Red-brown.
Pyrite: Greenish black.
Calcite: White.

Comparison response: Name any tool whose observed bracket differs from the displayed expectation and give its observed bounding minerals. Accept a statement that all observed brackets agree if supported by the recorded results. The Mohs table ranks reference minerals; it does not assign a fixed hardness to every coin, nail or glass plate. Common slips are reversing the two bracket columns and recording a powder mark as a scratch.

handouts.title: Cleavage and luster record

blocks.text: Examine the six labeled specimens under the light. For each, count the cleavage directions, estimate the angles between them and name the luster. A set of parallel flat faces counts as one direction. If a specimen has no cleavage, write none and name its fracture. Cleavage fragments are sharp, so handle them gently.

blocks.hint: Sketch the cleavage faces of the first specimen you chose. Label the specimen letter and mark the angles.
Sketch the cleavage faces of the second specimen you chose. Label the specimen letter and mark the angles.

handouts.key:
For specimens labeled in the sequence specified in the plan:

Specimen | Directions | Angles | Luster
A, halite | 3 | 90° | Vitreous
B, calcite | 3 | Approximately 75° and 105° | Vitreous
C, muscovite | 1 perfect direction | Not applicable between cleavage directions | Pearly to vitreous
D, K-feldspar | 2 | Near 90° | Vitreous to pearly
E, hornblende | 2 | Approximately 56° and 124° | Vitreous
F, quartz | None; conchoidal fracture | Not applicable | Vitreous

Accept reasonable angle estimates from irregular hand samples. Count orientations, not individual faces. Opposite parallel faces belong to the same direction. Quartz crystal faces are not cleavage planes.

First chosen specimen sketch: The specimen letter matches the drawing. Look for the appropriate cleavage geometry and labeled angles: cubic faces for halite; an oblique rhomb for calcite; parallel sheets for muscovite; nearly perpendicular cleavage planes for K-feldspar; or oblique planes at about 56° and 124° for hornblende. For quartz, accept curved, shell-like fracture surfaces labeled no cleavage, with angles marked not applicable.

Second chosen specimen sketch: Apply the same criteria to the other selected specimen. For muscovite, the angle between separate cleavage directions is not applicable because there is only one direction. Common slips are drawing mica with several cleavage directions and drawing quartz as a cube.

handouts.title: Choose the test

blocks.text: Two minerals, hematite and magnetite, can both look metallic gray in a hand sample. You may use color, hardness or streak to tell them apart.

blocks.hint: Alone: choose the one test you would trust most and give your reason. Use the Mineral properties reference table.

blocks.text: With your partner, test the two labeled samples from your tray, P and Q, and record the result.

blocks.hint: After the class discussion, write whether your choice of test held up and why.

handouts.key:
Alone: Choose streak. Hematite produces a red-brown streak; magnetite produces a black streak. Their metallic gray appearance can overlap. Their hardness ranges also overlap: hematite 5–6.5 and magnetite 5.5–6.5. Look for a reason based on the contrasting powder colors.

Sample | Test | Result | Mineral
P | Streak | Red-brown if hematite; black if magnetite | Hematite if red-brown; magnetite if black
Q | Streak | The contrasting streak of the other specimen | Magnetite if black; hematite if red-brown

The labels P and Q do not establish which mineral occupies each position. Accept either arrangement when names match the observed streaks.

After discussion: A supported response states that streak distinguished the samples because their powder colors differed despite similar surface colors. If the original choice was color or hardness, look for a revision explaining why overlapping appearance or hardness made that choice less decisive. Common slips are recording the sample's surface color as its streak and treating black and red-brown as interchangeable.

ready: Teacher: a tray of eight numbered unknown samples for each pair, and the answer key for comparing names
Teacher: a reference set for each pair (talc, gypsum, calcite, fluorite, apatite, orthoclase, quartz)
Teacher: for each pair, a copper coin or pre-1982 penny, a steel nail and a glass plate with taped edges
Teacher: porcelain streak plates, and hematite, pyrite and calcite for the streak test
Teacher: six specimens labeled A to F, set out under a light
Teacher: a dropper bottle of dilute HCl and goggles for every student
Teacher: one hand lens per pair
Teacher: a calcite sample for the demonstration, and a labeled hematite and magnetite pair P and Q, none from the unknown set

l_52f93cce8e6d.title: Igneous rocks and volcanoes
l_52f93cce8e6d.summary: How magma forms and crystallizes, how felsic and mafic rocks and textures are classified, and how volcano types and eruption styles create hazards.
readings: Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, ch. 4 (to confirm) (Igneous Processes and Volcanoes)

segments.title: Due now, and how solid mantle melts
segments.description:
Weekly online quizzes: Minerals is due now, submitted online before this meeting. Repeat the reading assigned last time: Earle’s Physical Geology, 2nd edition, covers magma formation, crystallization and classification in sections 3.2–3.4 of chapter 3, Intrusive Igneous Rocks, and volcanoes in chapter 4, Volcanism.
The prompt on the screen says mantle peridotite at 100 km depth is solid. Each student writes one way it could become magma, for 2 minutes.
Pairs compare for 2 minutes, and the instructor hears one pair for 1 minute.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: lower pressure as mantle rises, added water, contact with hotter magma. Common error: it must simply get hotter. Do not confirm yet; the next segment names the three mechanisms.
shown: Mantle peridotite at about 100 km depth is about 1,300°C, yet it is solid. Write one way it could become magma.

segments.title: Three ways rock melts, and what magma is made of
segments.description:
Present decompression melting under ridges and hot spots, flux melting above a subducting plate, and heat transfer from basaltic magma into continental crust.
Explain partial melting: the lowest-melting minerals melt first, so the magma is richer in silica than its source. Peridotite at about 45% SiO₂ yields basalt at about 50%.
Introduce the four classes by silica content. Each student then writes the class of a magma with 55% SiO₂ and checks it with a neighbor, for 1 minute.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: intermediate. Common error: thinking magma forms only by heating. Adding water can melt sufficiently hot rock by lowering its melting temperature, and pressure release can melt hot, rising mantle. Link hot spots to the Hawaiian chain met earlier in the course.
shown: Table: Magma class | Silica (SiO₂) / Ultramafic | less than 45% / Mafic | 45–52% / Intermediate | 52–63% / Felsic | more than 63%
Write the class of a magma with 55% SiO₂.

segments.title: Match the setting to the melting mechanism
segments.description:
Students choose a melting mechanism for each of the four settings on the screen, alone for 3 minutes.
Pairs compare for 1 minute.
The instructor hears answers for 1 minute and names the deciding clue in each.
segments.teacherNotes: 1: decompression melting (mantle rises as plates part). 2: flux melting (water released from the slab). 3: decompression melting (rising plume). 4: heat transfer (stalled basalt melts crust, giving felsic magma). Common mistake: using flux melting for the hot spot.
shown: Choices: decompression melting, flux melting, heat transfer
1. A mid-ocean ridge where two plates pull apart
2. A volcanic arc above a subducting oceanic plate
3. The Hawaiian hot spot, where a hot mantle plume rises
4. Continental crust above a basaltic magma body that has stalled at the base of the crust

segments.title: Bowen’s reaction series
segments.description:
Students first predict to a partner, for 1 minute, which of olivine and quartz sits higher in Bowen’s reaction series, crystallizing at the higher temperature.
Show the series. The discontinuous branch runs olivine, pyroxene, amphibole, biotite. The continuous branch runs calcium-rich to sodium-rich plagioclase. K-feldspar, muscovite and quartz come last.
Link to the silicate structures from last time: isolated tetrahedra in olivine, a framework in quartz. Early crystals react with the melt or settle out, so mafic rocks hold early minerals and felsic rocks hold late ones.
segments.teacherNotes: Stress that it is a sequence of crystallization, not a list of rock types. A magma only reaches the minerals its composition allows, so many basaltic magmas never crystallize quartz. Common error: thinking each mineral fully replaces the last. Reaction is often partial, so several minerals coexist. In granite, quartz commonly crystallizes late and fills spaces between earlier crystals.
shown: Which sits higher in Bowen’s reaction series, olivine or quartz? Say why.
Side by side: Discontinuous branch: olivine; pyroxene; amphibole; biotite | Continuous branch: calcium-rich plagioclase; intermediate plagioclase; sodium-rich plagioclase
Steps: olivine and calcium-rich plagioclase, hottest → pyroxene → amphibole → biotite and sodium-rich plagioclase → K-feldspar and muscovite → quartz, coolest and last

segments.title: Can these minerals share a rock?
segments.description:
Students judge each of the four mineral groups on the screen as likely or unlikely in one rock, with a reason from the series, alone for 4 minutes.
Pairs compare for 2 minutes.
The instructor hears answers for 1 minute.
segments.teacherNotes: a: unlikely. Olivine reacts away before quartz forms. b: likely, as in basalt or gabbro. c: likely, as in granite. d: unlikely, since the minerals crystallize at opposite ends of the series. Common mistake: judging by color instead of position on the series.
shown: a. Olivine and quartz
b. Calcium-rich plagioclase and pyroxene
c. Quartz, K-feldspar and biotite
d. Olivine and K-feldspar

segments.title: Texture records cooling
segments.description:
Students first predict to a partner, for 1 minute, which cools faster, a magma body 5 km underground or a 3 m lava flow, and how crystal size differs.
Show phaneritic, aphanitic, porphyritic, glassy and vesicular textures with their cooling histories.
Return to obsidian from last time and explain why glass is not a mineral.
segments.teacherNotes: Crystals need time and atom mobility to grow. Common error: reading texture as composition. Granite and rhyolite share composition but differ in texture. Porphyritic means larger crystals set in a finer groundmass. In these volcanic examples, it commonly records crystal growth at depth followed by faster cooling.
shown: Table: Texture | Cooling history | Example / phaneritic | slow, deep, intrusive | granite, gabbro / aphanitic | fast, at the surface, extrusive | rhyolite, basalt / porphyritic | slow, then fast | porphyritic andesite / glassy | very fast | obsidian / vesicular | gas bubbles trapped in lava | pumice, scoria

segments.title: From cooling history to rock
segments.description:
The last segment read a history from a rock. Here students work it the other way, from the history on the screen to the texture and rock name, using the naming chart on the screen, alone for 5 minutes.
Pairs compare for 3 minutes.
Two pairs explain one case for 2 minutes.
segments.teacherNotes: A: porphyritic andesite, large plagioclase phenocrysts in an aphanitic groundmass. B: vesicular glassy rhyolite, pumice. Common mistake: calling A phaneritic because some crystals are large. Both cases are hypothetical, made up for practice. The full chart is taught at the next meeting; here only these entries are shown.
shown: Table: Magma class | Phaneritic, slow cooling at depth | Aphanitic, fast cooling at the surface / Felsic, more than 63% SiO₂ | granite | rhyolite / Intermediate, 52–63% SiO₂ | diorite | andesite
Suppose a magma with 55% SiO₂ sits for thousands of years in a chamber 8 km deep and grows 4 mm plagioclase crystals. Then it erupts and chills at the surface. Give the texture and the rock name.
Suppose a gas-rich magma with 72% SiO₂ erupts, froths as its gas escapes, and chills within minutes. Give the texture and the rock name.

segments.title: Which magma flows farther?
segments.description:
Students read the two magmas on the screen. Each writes which flows farther and which is more likely to erupt explosively, with a reason, for 2 minutes.
Pairs compare for 1 minute.
The instructor hears one pair for 1 minute and introduces the word viscosity.
segments.teacherNotes: With equal volume, discharge and slope, A flows farther. With equal gas content and ascent, B is more likely to erupt explosively. High silica means more linked tetrahedra, and low temperature adds to stickiness, so gas cannot escape. Common error: saying hotter magma is always more explosive.
shown: Two magmas erupt in equal volumes, at the same rate, onto the same slope. Each holds the same amount of dissolved gas and rises at the same speed.
Side by side: Magma A: 50% SiO₂, about 1,200°C | Magma B: 70% SiO₂, about 800°C

segments.title: Classifying igneous rocks
segments.description:
Show the chart that crosses silica content with texture. Composition fixes the row and cooling fixes the column.
Show how to read composition from hand samples: light rock with quartz is felsic, dark rock with pyroxene and olivine is mafic.
Pairs tell each other the intrusive and extrusive rocks of intermediate magma, for 1 minute.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: diorite and andesite. Gabbro and basalt are the same magma with different cooling. Common error: treating them as different compositions. Peridotite is mantle rock, rare at the surface. Rhyolite and andesite are often hard to tell apart by eye.
shown: Table: Magma class | Intrusive, phaneritic | Extrusive, aphanitic / Felsic, more than 63% SiO₂ | granite | rhyolite / Intermediate, 52–63% | diorite | andesite / Mafic, 45–52% | gabbro | basalt / Ultramafic, less than 45% | peridotite | rare komatiite

segments.title: Name these rocks
segments.description:
Students name each of the four rocks described on the screen and give its silica class, alone for 3 minutes.
Pairs compare for 2 minutes.
The instructor hears answers for 1 minute.
segments.teacherNotes: 1: granite, felsic. 2: basalt, mafic. 3: diorite, intermediate. 4: porphyritic rhyolite, felsic. Common mistake: naming 4 granite because quartz is visible; the matrix is too fine, so it is extrusive.
shown: 1. Light pink, crystals 3–5 mm, quartz and K-feldspar visible, about 72% SiO₂
2. Dark gray-black, no crystals visible, small gas holes, about 49% SiO₂
3. Coarse, salt-and-pepper, plagioclase and hornblende, no quartz, about 58% SiO₂
4. Pale gray, fine matrix with a few 2 mm quartz crystals, about 70% SiO₂

segments.title: Shield volcanoes and stratovolcanoes
segments.description:
Compare Mauna Loa, a shield volcano of runny basaltic lava above a hot spot, with Mount St. Helens, a stratovolcano of stickier magma above a subduction zone.
Link eruption style to silica, viscosity and gas: gas escapes from runny magma, but sticky magma holds it until it fragments.
Each student sketches the two profiles and labels the magma type on each, for 2 minutes.
segments.teacherNotes: Check that sketches show a broad, gentle shield and a steeper cone. Common error: calling shields harmless. Lava flows are slow but destroy property. Explosive Hawaiian eruptions are rare but possible.
shown: Side by side: Shield volcano: mafic magma; low viscosity; broad, gentle slopes; mostly lava flows; Mauna Loa | Stratovolcano: intermediate to felsic magma; high viscosity; steeper cone; layers of lava, ash and pyroclastic deposits; Mount St. Helens

segments.title: Which hazards can people escape?
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Which hazards can people escape?”.
The instructor introduces the three records shown on the screen, and reminds students that these deaths are real, so the talk is about decisions and evidence, for 1 minute.
For each case, each student writes one response the record supports and one question it leaves open, alone for 4 minutes.
Pairs compare for 3 minutes and agree on what these records can and cannot settle.
The instructor hears one pair per case for 4 minutes and lists the supported responses on the board.
segments.teacherNotes:
Ruiz: prompt evacuation to higher ground after a clear warning. Open: how much time each resident had, which routes were safe.
St. Helens: closed zones reduced exposure, but the blast passed their edge, so zones need a margin. Open: how far a blast can reach.
Pinatubo: evacuate threatened slopes beforehand and check roofs before ash fall. Open: ash thickness per village.
Discuss decisions and evidence; never have students play victims or officials.

segments.title: Invent a volcano that fits
segments.description:
Each student makes up a hypothetical volcano and writes its tectonic setting, magma silica percentage, volcano type, eruption style and most dangerous hazard, so that the parts fit, for 5 minutes.
Partners swap papers and identify any part that does not fit, or explain why the parts fit, for 3 minutes.
Two students read theirs aloud and the class tests the fit for 2 minutes.
segments.teacherNotes: A fitting example: arc volcano above a subducting plate, 60% SiO₂, stratovolcano, explosive, pyroclastic flows. A typical misfit is a shield built mainly from lava with 70% SiO₂. Mafic magma can erupt explosively, so assess the student’s explanation of gas behavior or interaction with water. Papers stay with students.

segments.title: Summary and the quiz
segments.description:
Summarize: silica content sets viscosity, minerals and eruption style, and texture records cooling.
Set Weekly online quizzes, which count for 10% of the course grade, and say it is due at the first meeting of Weathering, erosion and soils. Students submit it online.
Preview the lab at the next meeting: pairs use the department’s hand samples to identify igneous rocks, with closed-toe shoes required.
segments.teacherNotes: Remind students to bring closed-toe shoes. Confirm the chapter numbers against the edition students own.

segments.title: Lab start, safety and method
segments.description:
Lab reports: Minerals is due now, at the start of this lab.
State the rules: closed-toe shoes, goggles on whenever the dilute HCl bottle is open, and hand samples stay in their trays and go back where they came from.
Demonstrate the method on one sample not in the unknown set: texture first with a hand lens and ruler, then color and minerals, then the name from the naming chart. Each student calls the texture before it is named.
Pairs read the Igneous rock lab: rules and method sheet.
segments.teacherNotes: The Igneous rock lab: rules and method sheet holds the safety and handling rules, the three-step method, a table of texture terms, the naming chart, Bowen's reaction series and the pumice water test; prepare copies. Demonstrate on a labeled scoria, not among the unknowns. Each student writes their own report; the pair shares data. Safety: obsidian and broken basalt have sharp edges, so handle gently, never strike samples, and report cuts. Prepare hand lenses and millimeter rulers.

segments.title: Predict before handling
segments.description:
Students write answers to the three predictions on the screen, alone for 3 minutes.
Pairs compare for 2 minutes and agree on a prediction for each.
The instructor hears two pairs for 2 minutes. Pairs return to their predictions after the next two segments.
segments.teacherNotes: 1: granite, with crystals visible. 2: gabbro, same reason. 3: float, since gas bubbles trap air and make the density below water’s. Common mistake: expecting the dark rock to have larger crystals.
shown: 1. Granite and rhyolite have the same composition. Which has the larger crystals, and why?
2. Gabbro and basalt have the same composition. Which has the larger crystals, and why?
3. Will pumice float or sink in water? Say why.

segments.title: Texture station
segments.description:
Pairs examine six labeled reference samples under the hand lens. For each they record texture, grain size in millimeters, and vesicles or glass, about 3.5 minutes each.
Pairs then test pumice in a beaker of water for 2 minutes.
Pairs check their earlier predictions for 2 minutes.
segments.teacherNotes: Suggested set (adapt to the department’s trays): granite, phaneritic, crystals several mm. Rhyolite, aphanitic, pale. Obsidian, glassy, conchoidal fracture. Pumice, vesicular; select and pretest a dry specimen that floats for this demonstration. Basalt, aphanitic, dark. Gabbro, phaneritic, dark. Safety: set the beaker on a tray; dry spills at once; obsidian edges are sharp; samples stay in trays.

segments.title: Composition and the reaction series
segments.description:
Pairs examine granite, diorite and gabbro. For each they name the minerals seen, estimate the percent of dark minerals, and place the minerals on Bowen’s reaction series, about 5 minutes each.
Pairs write one sentence linking their minerals to the series, for 3 minutes.
The class hears two sentences for 2 minutes.
segments.teacherNotes: Granite: roughly 10–15% dark (biotite), with quartz and K-feldspar. Diorite: roughly 30–40% dark (hornblende), with plagioclase, no quartz. Gabbro: roughly 50% or more dark (pyroxene), with calcium-rich plagioclase. Common error: judging composition by overall brightness of a weathered face. Use fresh surfaces.

keyIdeas: Mantle rock melts partly, not wholly, by decompression, by added water (flux melting) or by heat from rising magma. Magmas are classed by silica: ultramafic below 45% SiO₂, mafic 45–52%, intermediate 52–63%, felsic above 63%.

Bowen’s reaction series gives the order in which minerals crystallize as magma cools: olivine and calcium-rich plagioclase first, quartz last. Mafic rocks therefore hold early, high-temperature minerals, and felsic rocks hold late ones. Olivine and quartz rarely share a rock.

Texture records cooling history. Slow cooling at depth gives phaneritic rock, fast cooling at the surface gives aphanitic rock, two stages give porphyritic rock, and gas gives vesicles. A rock’s name needs both silica content and texture, as in granite and rhyolite or gabbro and basalt.

Silica and dissolved gas control viscosity and eruption style. Runny mafic magma builds shield volcanoes such as Mauna Loa. Sticky intermediate to felsic magma builds explosive stratovolcanoes such as Mount St. Helens.

The hazards differ in reach and speed: lava flows, ash fall, pyroclastic flows, lahars and gas. Which response a case supports depends on that case’s evidence, such as travel time, warning, rain and wind.

vocabulary.definition: Igneous rock or magma rich in silica (more than 63% SiO₂), made mostly of quartz and feldspar, and light in color, such as granite and rhyolite.
Igneous rock or magma with 45–52% SiO₂, rich in magnesium and iron, made of pyroxene and calcium-rich plagioclase, and dark in color, such as basalt and gabbro.
The order in which minerals crystallize from cooling magma, from olivine and calcium-rich plagioclase at the hot end to quartz at the cool end.
An igneous texture with crystals large enough to see without a lens, formed by slow cooling at depth, as in granite.
An igneous texture with crystals too small to see without a lens, formed by fast cooling at or near the surface, as in basalt.
A fluid’s resistance to flow. Magma with more silica and a lower temperature is more viscous.
A broad volcano with gentle slopes built by many runny mafic lava flows, such as Mauna Loa.
A steep cone built from alternating layers of lava, ash and pyroclastic deposits, formed from stickier magma and often explosive, such as Mount St. Helens.

slides.title: Igneous rocks and volcanoes
bullets: How magma forms, crystallizes and takes its texture
slides.notes: Opening for this meeting. Today covers how solid mantle melts, how magmas are classed by silica, Bowen’s reaction series, and how texture records cooling. This builds toward classifying igneous rocks by texture and silica content, and explaining how Bowen’s reaction series relates to rock composition. Volcano types and hazards come next time.

slides.title: How can solid mantle become magma?
bullets: Mantle peridotite at about 100 km depth is about 1,300°C, yet it is solid. Write one way it could become magma.
slides.notes:
Weekly online quizzes: Minerals is due now. Students submitted it online before this meeting, so nothing is collected in class.

Reading reminder: Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, covers magma formation, crystallization and classification in sections 3.2–3.4 of chapter 3, Intrusive Igneous Rocks, and volcanoes in chapter 4, Volcanism. Say this aloud and ask students to note it.

Activity: each student writes one way the rock could become magma, 2 minutes. Pairs compare, 2 minutes. Hear one pair, 1 minute.

Expected answers: lower pressure as the mantle rises, added water, contact with hotter magma. Common error: it must simply get hotter. Do not confirm or correct yet. The next slide names the three mechanisms.

slides.title: Four classes of magma by silica content
bullets: Write the class of a magma with 55% SiO₂.
slides.notes:
Before showing the table, present the three ways rock melts. Decompression melting: hot mantle rises and pressure falls, as under ridges and hot spots. Flux melting: water released from a subducting plate lowers the melting temperature of hot mantle above it. Heat transfer: basaltic magma stalled at the base of continental crust melts the crust. Link hot spots to the Hawaiian chain met earlier in the course. Stress that heating alone is not the only route: adding water can melt sufficiently hot rock, and pressure release can melt hot, rising mantle.

Explain partial melting: the lowest-melting minerals melt first, so the magma is richer in silica than its source. Peridotite at about 45% SiO₂ yields basalt at about 50%.

Then show the table. Each student writes the class of a magma with 55% SiO₂ and checks with a neighbor, 1 minute. Answer: intermediate.

slides.title: Match the setting to the melting mechanism
bullets: Choices: decompression melting, flux melting, heat transfer
1. A mid-ocean ridge where two plates pull apart
2. A volcanic arc above a subducting oceanic plate
3. The Hawaiian hot spot, where a hot mantle plume rises
4. Continental crust above a basaltic magma body that has stalled at the base of the crust
slides.notes:
Students choose a mechanism for each setting, alone, 3 minutes. Pairs compare, 1 minute. Hear answers for 1 minute and name the deciding clue in each.

Answers: 1 decompression melting (mantle rises as plates part). 2 flux melting (water released from the slab). 3 decompression melting (rising plume). 4 heat transfer (stalled basalt melts the crust, giving felsic magma).

Common mistake: using flux melting for the hot spot. There is no subducting slab there, so the clue is the rising plume.

slides.title: Bowen’s reaction series
bullets: Which sits higher in Bowen’s reaction series, olivine or quartz? Say why.
slides.notes:
Ask the question aloud before advancing to this slide, so students predict without the series in view. Partners predict which of olivine and quartz crystallizes at the higher temperature, 1 minute. Then show the slide and take answers.

Walk through the series. The discontinuous branch runs olivine, pyroxene, amphibole, biotite. The continuous branch runs calcium-rich to sodium-rich plagioclase. K-feldspar, muscovite and quartz come last.

Link to the silicate structures from last time: isolated tetrahedra in olivine, a framework in quartz. Early crystals react with the melt or settle out, so mafic rocks hold early minerals and felsic rocks hold late ones.

Stress that this is a sequence of crystallization, not a list of rock types. A magma only reaches the minerals its composition allows, so many basaltic magmas never crystallize quartz. Reaction is often partial, so several minerals coexist. In granite, quartz commonly crystallizes late and fills spaces between earlier crystals.

slides.title: Bowen’s reaction series (continued)
slides.notes:
The prediction was taken on the previous slide; use this one to set the two branches side by side.
Show the series. The discontinuous branch runs olivine, pyroxene, amphibole, biotite. The continuous branch runs calcium-rich to sodium-rich plagioclase. K-feldspar, muscovite and quartz come last.
Link to the silicate structures from last time: isolated tetrahedra in olivine, a framework in quartz. Early crystals react with the melt or settle out, so mafic rocks hold early minerals and felsic rocks hold late ones.

slides.title: Likely or unlikely in one rock? Give a reason from the series
bullets: a. Olivine and quartz
b. Calcium-rich plagioclase and pyroxene
c. Quartz, K-feldspar and biotite
d. Olivine and K-feldspar
slides.notes:
Students judge each group as likely or unlikely in one rock, with a reason from the series, alone, 4 minutes. Pairs compare, 2 minutes. Hear answers for 1 minute.

Answers: a unlikely, because olivine reacts away before quartz forms. b likely, as in basalt or gabbro. c likely, as in granite. d unlikely, because the minerals crystallize at opposite ends of the series.

Common mistake: judging by color instead of position on the series.

slides.title: Texture records cooling history
slides.notes:
Before this slide, partners predict which cools faster, a magma body 5 km underground or a 3 m lava flow, and how crystal size differs, 1 minute. Take a few answers, then show the table.

Crystals need time and atom mobility to grow. Common error: reading texture as composition. Granite and rhyolite share composition but differ in texture. Porphyritic means larger crystals set in a finer groundmass. In these volcanic examples it commonly records crystal growth at depth followed by faster cooling.

Return to obsidian from last time. Glass is not a mineral because it has no ordered crystal structure: the atoms were frozen in place before they could organize.

slides.title: From cooling history to texture and rock name
bullets: Suppose a magma with 55% SiO₂ sits for thousands of years in a chamber 8 km deep and grows 4 mm plagioclase crystals. Then it erupts and chills at the surface. Give the texture and the rock name.
Suppose a gas-rich magma with 72% SiO₂ erupts, froths as its gas escapes, and chills within minutes. Give the texture and the rock name.
slides.notes:
The last slide read a history from a rock. Here students work the other way, from the history to the texture and rock name, using the naming chart. Alone, 5 minutes. Pairs compare, 3 minutes. Two pairs explain one case, 2 minutes.

Answers: A is porphyritic andesite, with large plagioclase phenocrysts in an aphanitic groundmass. B is vesicular glassy rhyolite, which is pumice.

Common mistake: calling A phaneritic because some crystals are large. Both cases are hypothetical, made up for practice. The full chart comes at the next meeting; only these entries are shown here.

columns: Aphanitic, fast cooling at the surface

slides.title: Igneous rocks and volcanoes
bullets: Classification, eruption styles and hazards
slides.notes: Opening for this meeting. At the earlier lecture we covered how mantle melts, the silica classes, Bowen’s reaction series and texture. Today those ideas become a full classification chart, and then we apply them to volcano types and to the hazards people have faced. This works toward classifying igneous rocks by texture and silica content, and comparing shield volcanoes, stratovolcanoes and their hazards.

slides.title: Which magma flows farther?
bullets: Two magmas erupt in equal volumes, at the same rate, onto the same slope. Each holds the same amount of dissolved gas and rises at the same speed.
slides.notes:
Students read the two magmas and each writes which flows farther and which is more likely to erupt explosively, with a reason, 2 minutes. Pairs compare, 1 minute. Hear one pair for 1 minute, then introduce the word viscosity.

With equal volume, discharge and slope, A flows farther. With equal gas content and ascent, B is more likely to erupt explosively. High silica means more linked tetrahedra, and low temperature adds to stickiness, so gas cannot escape. Common error: saying hotter magma is always more explosive.

visual.ask: Which flows farther, and which is more likely to erupt explosively? Give a reason.

slides.title: Classifying igneous rocks
bullets: Composition sets the row. Cooling sets the column.
Light rock with quartz is felsic. Dark rock with pyroxene and olivine is mafic.
slides.notes:
Show the chart that crosses silica content with texture. Composition fixes the row and cooling fixes the column. Then show how to read composition from hand samples: light rock with quartz is felsic, dark rock with pyroxene and olivine is mafic.

Activity: pairs tell each other the intrusive and extrusive rocks of intermediate magma, 1 minute. Answer: diorite and andesite.

Gabbro and basalt are the same magma with different cooling. Common error: treating them as different compositions. Peridotite is mantle rock, rare at the surface. Rhyolite and andesite are often hard to tell apart by eye.

slides.title: Name each rock and give its silica class
bullets: 1. Light pink, crystals 3–5 mm, quartz and K-feldspar visible, about 72% SiO₂
2. Dark gray-black, no crystals visible, small gas holes, about 49% SiO₂
3. Coarse, salt-and-pepper, plagioclase and hornblende, no quartz, about 58% SiO₂
4. Pale gray, fine matrix with a few 2 mm quartz crystals, about 70% SiO₂
slides.notes:
Students name each rock and give its silica class, alone, 3 minutes. Pairs compare, 2 minutes. Hear answers for 1 minute.

Answers: 1 granite, felsic. 2 basalt, mafic. 3 diorite, intermediate. 4 porphyritic rhyolite, felsic.

Common mistake: naming 4 granite because quartz is visible. The matrix is too fine, so it is extrusive.

slides.title: Shield volcanoes and stratovolcanoes
bullets: Sketch the two profiles. Label the magma type on each.
slides.notes:
Compare Mauna Loa, a shield volcano of runny basaltic lava above a hot spot, with Mount St. Helens, a stratovolcano of stickier magma above a subduction zone.

Link eruption style to silica, viscosity and gas: gas escapes from runny magma, but sticky magma holds it until it fragments.

Each student sketches the two profiles and labels the magma type on each, 2 minutes. Check that sketches show a broad, gentle shield and a steeper cone.

Shield volcanoes are not harmless. Lava flows are slow but destroy property, and explosive Hawaiian eruptions are rare but possible.

sides.title: Stratovolcano
points: intermediate to felsic magma; high viscosity
layers of lava, ash and pyroclastic deposits

slides.title: Which hazards can people escape?
bullets: Nevado del Ruiz, Colombia, 1985: lahars from melted summit ice
Mount St. Helens, Washington, 1980: a sideways blast after a landslide
Mount Pinatubo, Philippines, 1991: ash fall during a typhoon
For each case, write one response the record supports and one question it leaves open.
slides.notes:
Give out the sheet “Which hazards can people escape?”. Introduce the three records in about a minute. Remind students that these deaths are real, so the talk is about decisions and evidence. Never have students play victims or officials.

Background for the introductions, in outline: at Ruiz an eruption melted summit ice and lahars buried the town of Armero, with more than 20,000 deaths; a hazard map had shown Armero at risk, but no clear evacuation order reached the town in time. At St. Helens a landslide on the north flank released a sideways blast, and 57 people died, most of them outside the restricted zones. At Pinatubo, the main eruption coincided with a typhoon, and rain-soaked ash collapsed roofs. Keep to what each record shows.

Activity: each student writes one supported response and one open question per case, alone, 4 minutes. Pairs compare, 3 minutes, and agree on what these records can and cannot settle. Hear one pair per case, 4 minutes, and list the supported responses on the board.

Likely points. Ruiz: prompt evacuation to higher ground after a clear warning; open: how much time each resident had, which routes were safe. St. Helens: closed zones reduced exposure, but the blast passed their edge, so zones need a margin; open: how far a blast can reach. Pinatubo: evacuate threatened slopes beforehand and check roofs before ash fall; open: ash thickness per village.

slides.title: Invent a hypothetical volcano so that the parts fit
bullets: Tectonic setting
Magma silica (% SiO₂)
Volcano type
Eruption style
Most dangerous hazard
slides.notes:
Each student invents a volcano for practice. It is not a real one. Fill in the five parts so they fit together, 5 minutes. Partners swap papers and name any part that does not fit, or explain why the parts fit, 3 minutes. Two students read theirs aloud and the class tests the fit, 2 minutes.

A fitting example: arc volcano above a subducting plate, 60% SiO₂, stratovolcano, explosive, pyroclastic flows. A typical misfit is a shield built mainly from lava with 70% SiO₂. Mafic magma can erupt explosively, so assess the student’s explanation of gas behavior or interaction with water. Papers stay with students.

study.overview: Igneous rocks record two things: what the magma was made of and how it cooled. This guide follows that sequence from melting to classification to eruption. Silica content and cooling history together explain a rock’s name, its minerals, and how its volcano behaves. For further reading, Earle’s Physical Geology, 2nd edition, treats magma formation, crystallization and classification in sections 3.2–3.4 (to confirm) of chapter 3 (to confirm), Intrusive Igneous Rocks. It treats volcanoes in chapter 4 (to confirm), Volcanism.

points.heading: Mantle melts partly, and silica sorts the magmas
points.explanation: Solid mantle rock becomes magma in three ways. Decompression melting happens when hot rock rises and pressure drops. Flux melting happens when water released from a subducting plate lowers the melting temperature of the rock above it. Heat transfer happens when hot basaltic magma stalls and melts the crust around it. Heating alone is not required. Melting is partial: the lowest-melting minerals melt first, so the magma holds more silica than its source. Peridotite at about 45% SiO₂ yields basalt at about 50%. Magmas are classed by silica: ultramafic below 45%, mafic 45–52%, intermediate 52–63%, felsic above 63%. Example: a volcanic arc sits above a subducting oceanic plate. Water from the slab rises into hot mantle and triggers flux melting. The resulting magma is typically intermediate, for instance 55% SiO₂. Magma from crust melted by stalled basalt tends to be felsic.

points.heading: Bowen’s reaction series links minerals to composition
points.explanation: Bowen’s reaction series gives the order in which minerals crystallize as magma cools. Olivine sits at the hot end of the discontinuous branch, followed by pyroxene, amphibole and biotite. Plagioclase runs from calcium-rich to sodium-rich on the continuous branch. K-feldspar, muscovite and quartz come last. It is a sequence of crystallization, not a list of rock types. Early crystals react with the melt or settle out, but the reaction is often partial, so several minerals coexist. A magma only reaches the minerals its composition allows. Mafic rocks therefore hold early, high-temperature minerals, and felsic rocks hold late ones. Example: diorite, from a magma of about 58% SiO₂, contains plagioclase and hornblende and no quartz. It sits in the middle of the series. Olivine and quartz sit at opposite ends, so they rarely share a rock. Judge a mineral by its position in the series, not by color.

points.heading: Texture gives cooling history, and a name needs both texture and silica
points.explanation: Crystals need time and mobile atoms to grow, so texture records cooling. Slow cooling at depth gives phaneritic rock, with crystals visible to the eye. Fast cooling at the surface gives aphanitic rock, with crystals too small to see without a lens. Very rapid cooling gives glass, such as obsidian. Glass has no ordered atomic structure, so it is not a mineral. Gas bubbles trapped in lava leave vesicles, as in pumice and scoria. Texture is not composition. Silica content sets the row of the naming chart and cooling sets the column. Felsic gives granite (phaneritic) or rhyolite (aphanitic). Intermediate gives diorite or andesite. Mafic gives gabbro or basalt. Example: a magma of about 58% SiO₂ that cools slowly in a chamber becomes diorite. The same magma erupting as a 3 m lava flow chills quickly and becomes andesite. The composition is the same and the texture differs. Be careful with rhyolite and andesite, which are often hard to tell apart by eye.

points.heading: Viscosity controls eruption style, and hazard response depends on evidence
points.explanation: Viscosity is a magma’s resistance to flow. High silica means more linked silicate tetrahedra, and low temperature adds to stickiness. Gas escapes easily from runny mafic magma, which tends to flow, as at Mauna Loa above a hot spot. Sticky intermediate to felsic magma holds its gas until it fragments, giving explosive eruptions, as at Mount St. Helens above a subduction zone. Hotter magma is not always more explosive: a hot, runny magma loses gas easily, while a cooler, silica-rich one traps it. Hazards differ in reach and speed: lava flows, ash fall, pyroclastic flows, lahars and gas. Which response a case supports depends on that case’s evidence, such as travel time, warning, rain and wind. Example: before the 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens, closed zones were set around the volcano. The blast reached beyond the edge of the zone. The record supports closing areas, but it also shows that a zone needs a margin, and it leaves open how far a blast can reach.

blocks.text: Safety and handling

items: Closed-toe shoes in the lab.
Goggles on whenever the dilute HCl bottle is open.
Hand samples stay in their trays and go back where they came from.

blocks.text: Method for each sample

items: Texture first. Look at a fresh surface with the hand lens. Measure the typical crystal size in millimeters with the ruler. Look for vesicles (gas holes) or glass.
Then color and minerals. Light rock with quartz points to felsic. Dark rock with pyroxene and olivine points to mafic. Use a fresh surface, not a weathered face.
Then the name. Combine texture and composition using the chart below.

items: Set the beaker on a tray and fill it about two-thirds with water.
