Watch for about a minute and record what it does.
Dry the sample surface and the tray, and return the sample to its tray.

handouts.title: Igneous rock identification data sheet

blocks.text: Your pair examines the tray of numbered unknown samples and shares the data. For each sample, call the texture first, then name the rock by color and minerals. Record only the texture and the name today, and leave the other columns blank. Each student writes their own lab report from the shared data.

handouts.key:
Expected answers for the suggested unknown tray:
1. Texture: phaneritic. Name: granite.
2. Texture: phaneritic. Name: diorite.
3. Texture: phaneritic. Name: gabbro.
4. Texture: aphanitic. Name: rhyolite.
5. Texture: aphanitic. Name: andesite.
6. Texture: aphanitic. Name: basalt.
7. Texture: glassy. Name: obsidian.
8. Texture: vesicular; also glassy where visible. Name: pumice.
Leave grain size, vesicles or glass, minerals seen, color and silica class blank, as the sheet directs. Match names to the actual numbered department samples if the tray differs from the suggested set. Accept a justified provisional identification among rhyolite, andesite and basalt when fine grain size prevents mineral identification. Look for texture identified before composition. Common slips: calling any dark rock basalt, calling any light rock granite, and treating vesicles as mineral grains.

handouts.title: Texture station record

blocks.text: Examine each labeled reference sample under the hand lens. Record its label, its texture, its grain size in millimeters, and whether you see vesicles or glass.
Pumice in water

blocks.hint: What did the pumice do in the water?

blocks.text: Back to your predictions

blocks.hint: Which of your pair's three predictions did the samples support, and which did they not? Say what you saw.

handouts.key:
Expected entries for the suggested reference set, in the order listed in the plan. Follow the actual sample labels if the station order differs.
1. Label: granite. Texture: phaneritic. Grain size: measured value, typically several millimeters. Vesicles or glass: neither expected.
2. Label: rhyolite. Texture: aphanitic, unless the specimen also contains phenocrysts. Grain size: groundmass crystals unresolved with the available equipment; do not invent a measurement. Vesicles or glass: neither expected in the suggested specimen.
3. Label: obsidian. Texture: glassy. Grain size: not applicable to glass. Vesicles or glass: glass present; vesicles depend on the specimen.
4. Label: pumice. Texture: vesicular and commonly glassy. Grain size: not applicable to the glass; record a crystal size only if crystals are visible. Vesicles or glass: abundant vesicles; glass commonly present.
5. Label: basalt. Texture: aphanitic, unless phenocrysts are present. Grain size: groundmass crystals unresolved with the available equipment. Vesicles or glass: record the specimen's actual features; neither is required for basalt.
6. Label: gabbro. Texture: phaneritic. Grain size: measured value, commonly millimeter scale. Vesicles or glass: neither expected.
Accept measurements that represent typical crystals rather than the largest crystal. Common slips: recording vesicle diameter as grain size and assigning a crystal size of zero to glass.
Pumice in water: The selected dry specimen floats, at least initially. Its gas-filled pores lower its bulk density below that of water. Some specimens take up water and eventually sink.
Back to your predictions: Granite and gabbro both support the prediction of visible crystals produced by slow cooling. Their colors do not establish which has larger crystals. The selected pumice supports the prediction of floating. Students should name their original predictions and cite observations, including any result that differed.

handouts.title: Composition and the reaction series

blocks.text: Examine granite, diorite and gabbro on fresh surfaces. For each rock, name the minerals you see, estimate the percent of dark minerals, and place those minerals on Bowen's reaction series (early, middle or late in the sequence).

blocks.hint: Write one sentence with your partner that links the minerals you saw to Bowen's reaction series.

handouts.key:
Granite: Minerals seen—typically quartz, K-feldspar and plagioclase, with biotite and sometimes amphibole. Dark minerals (%)—the observed area estimate; about 10–15% is plausible for the suggested specimen. Place on Bowen's series—quartz and K-feldspar are late; biotite is toward the low-temperature end of the discontinuous branch; sodium-rich plagioclase is toward the low-temperature end of the continuous branch. Place any observed amphibole between pyroxene and biotite.
Diorite: Minerals seen—typically plagioclase and amphibole, with possible biotite or pyroxene. Dark minerals (%)—the observed area estimate; about 30–40% is plausible for the suggested specimen. Place on Bowen's series—amphibole is in the middle-to-later discontinuous sequence; intermediate plagioclase occupies the middle of the continuous sequence. Place additional identified minerals individually.
Gabbro: Minerals seen—typically calcium-rich plagioclase and pyroxene; olivine may occur. Dark minerals (%)—the observed area estimate; about 50% is plausible for the suggested specimen. Place on Bowen's series—calcium-rich plagioclase, pyroxene and any olivine belong toward the high-temperature end.
Partner sentence: Accept a statement such as: Gabbro contains minerals associated with higher crystallization temperatures, while granite contains late-crystallizing quartz and K-feldspar; diorite commonly contains amphibole and intermediate plagioclase between these ends of the series.
Look for mineral identifications supported by visible properties and percentages estimated from fresh surfaces. Percentages vary among samples. Common slips: counting dark shadows as dark minerals, identifying every dark mineral as biotite, and assigning the whole rock one crystallization temperature.

handouts.title: Which hazards can people escape?

blocks.text: The three records are on the screen. These deaths are real, so discuss decisions and evidence. For each case, write one response the record supports and one question it leaves open.
Nevado del Ruiz, 1985

blocks.hint: One response the record supports
One question the record leaves open

blocks.text: Mount St. Helens, 1980

blocks.hint: One response the record supports
One question the record leaves open

blocks.text: Mount Pinatubo, 1991

blocks.hint: One response the record supports
One question the record leaves open

blocks.text: With your partner

blocks.hint: Agree on what these records can and cannot settle.

handouts.key:
Nevado del Ruiz, 1985
Supported response: Evacuate threatened valleys to designated higher ground when a clear lahar warning is issued. Lahars can travel far downstream from a volcano.
Question left open: How much warning time did residents in a particular location have, and which routes remained safe?
Mount St. Helens, 1980
Supported response: Restrict access before an eruption and allow for uncertainty in hazard boundaries. The lateral blast extended beyond the restricted area.
Question left open: How far could a future lateral blast reach, and what evidence would justify changing the restricted area?
Mount Pinatubo, 1991
Supported response: Evacuate threatened areas before dangerous eruptive activity and assess roof vulnerability before ashfall. Wet ash can impose heavy roof loads.
Question left open: How much ash accumulated at each settlement, and which buildings were vulnerable to collapse?
With your partner: These cases support early action, clear warnings, evacuation routes suited to the hazard, and planning for uncertainty. They do not establish a universal safe distance, the warning time available to every person, or the effectiveness of every possible response. Look for each claim to be tied to a specific feature of its case. Common slips: treating lava, lahars, ashfall and pyroclastic density currents as equally escapable, or assuming residents all received the same warning and had the same means to leave.

handouts.title: Invent a volcano that fits

blocks.text: Make up a hypothetical volcano. This volcano is invented for practice and is not a real one. Fill in each part so that the parts fit together.
Partner's check

blocks.hint: Your partner swaps papers with you. Name any part that does not fit, or explain why the parts fit.

handouts.key:
One coherent hypothetical answer:
Tectonic setting: Continental volcanic arc above a subducting oceanic plate.
Magma silica (% SiO₂): 60%.
Volcano type: Stratovolcano.
Eruption style: Explosive eruption of gas-rich intermediate magma, with possible lava flows between explosive episodes.
Most dangerous hazard: Pyroclastic density currents threatening nearby valleys and slopes.
Partner's check: The setting supports flux melting and the production and evolution of arc magma. The silica content is intermediate. A stratovolcano and explosive activity fit this composition when gas is retained during ascent. Pyroclastic density currents are a consistent principal hazard.
Accept other internally consistent invented examples, including a basaltic shield volcano above a hot spot with approximately 50% SiO₂, mainly effusive activity and lava-flow hazards. A mafic explosive eruption can fit if the explanation includes gas behavior or interaction with water. Look for a specific setting, a numerical silica content and a defensible connection among composition, volcano shape, eruption style and hazard. Common slips: giving a mainly rhyolitic volcano a broad basaltic shield profile without explanation, or claiming that shield volcanoes cannot erupt explosively.

ready: Teacher: hand lenses and millimeter rulers for every pair
Teacher: a labeled scoria for the method demonstration, kept out of the unknown set
Teacher: six labeled reference samples for the texture station, and a tray of granite, diorite and gabbro with fresh surfaces
Teacher: a tray of eight numbered unknown samples for each pair, and the answer key for pairs to check against
Teacher: a beaker of water on a tray and a pretested dry pumice that floats, with paper towels for spills
Teacher: goggles and the dilute HCl bottle kept tidy and closed
Students wear closed-toe shoes

l_a931a830a08b.title: Weathering, erosion and soils
l_a931a830a08b.summary: Physical and chemical weathering, the movement of sediment by water, wind and gravity, and the horizons and controls of soil formation.
readings: Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, ch. 5 (to confirm) (Weathering and Soil)

segments.title: Quiz due now and a granite puzzle
segments.description:
Weekly online quizzes: Igneous rocks and volcanoes is due now.
The instructor puts two granite descriptions on the screen. Each student writes what has changed in the second sample and what might have caused it, then compares with a partner for one minute.
Two pairs report, and the instructor says that today is about how rock at Earth’s surface breaks down.
segments.teacherNotes: The quiz was submitted online before this meeting and is not collected in class. Expected: brown staining, loose grains, white patches and a crack. Feldspar alteration to clay is a hypothesis to test. Granite formed at depth, so it is out of equilibrium at the surface. Do not name the processes yet.
shown: Sample 1: fresh granite. Pink and white crystals interlocked, hard, a ringing sound when struck.
Sample 2: granite from a hillside outcrop. A rusty-brown surface, crumbling loose grains, white powdery patches, a crack along one side.

segments.title: Physical weathering and surface area
segments.description:
The instructor presents frost wedging, unloading (exfoliation, as in Half Dome in Yosemite), root wedging, salt wedging and abrasion. For each, the instructor says what force breaks the rock and notes that no new mineral forms.
Before the cube example, students predict by how much cutting a 1 cm cube into 1 mm cubes raises its total surface, and write a number.
The instructor then works it on the board: one cube has 6 cm². There are 1,000 small cubes of 6 mm² each, so 6,000 mm², which is 60 cm².
segments.teacherNotes: Water expands about 9% when it freezes; frost wedging needs repeated freeze-thaw cycles around 0 °C. Common error: predicting ‘about double’. Stress that more surface lets water and acid attack faster, so physical weathering feeds chemical weathering.
shown: Steps: Water enters a crack → freezes and expands → crack widens → block pries loose
A 1 cm cube cut into 1 mm cubes: what happens to the total surface area?

segments.title: Surface area in a second case
segments.description:
Pairs use the starting surface area of 24 cm² to calculate the total surface after a 2 cm cube is cut into eight 1 cm cubes.
They state the area ratio and indicate whether this proportional increase is bigger or smaller than the earlier tenfold increase. The screen supplies the starting area and asks for these same responses.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: before 6 × 4 = 24 cm²; eight cubes of 6 cm² give 48 cm², so surface doubles. The gain is smaller than the 10 times for 1 mm cubes: the smaller the final pieces, the greater the gain.
shown: A 2 cm cube is cut into eight 1 cm cubes. Find the total surface area before and after, and the ratio.

segments.title: Chemical weathering
segments.description:
The instructor shows that rainwater is weakly acidic: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid). Dissolution takes limestone (calcite) into solution, hydrolysis turns feldspar into clay, and oxidation turns iron in olivine and pyrite into rusty iron oxides.
Students then predict which of olivine and quartz, both in Bowen’s reaction series from last time, would survive longer at the surface, and why. They write it, then the instructor builds the answer.
The instructor links the order to silicate structure and to the conditions where each mineral formed.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: olivine weathers fastest, quartz survives longest; minerals that crystallize at the highest temperatures are furthest from surface conditions. Quartz persists as sand and clay forms from feldspar. Warm, wet climates weather faster than cold, dry ones.
shown: Table: Process | What happens | Example / Dissolution | CaCO₃ dissolves in carbonic acid | Limestone surface pitted / Hydrolysis | Feldspar changes to clay mineral | Granite crumbles to grus and clay / Oxidation | Iron in minerals reacts with oxygen | Rusty-brown crust on basalt

segments.title: Physical or chemical?
segments.description:
Pairs classify each case on the screen as physical or chemical.
Pairs check with the pair beside them, and the class hears the case where pairs disagreed and names its process.
segments.teacherNotes: Answers: 1 physical, frost wedging. 2 chemical, dissolution. 3 chemical, oxidation. 4 physical, root wedging. 5 chemical, hydrolysis. 6 physical, unloading. Case 3 draws ‘rust looks like a color change only’: new iron oxide minerals form. Name the process only for the disputed case.
shown: 1. Water in a crack in a granite cliff freezes and widens the crack.
2. Rainwater slowly dissolves a limestone surface, leaving it pitted.
3. A basalt surface turns rusty brown.
4. Tree roots grow into a joint in sandstone and pry blocks apart.
5. Feldspar grains in granite turn to soft white clay.
6. Granite exposed after the rock above is removed splits into curved sheets.

segments.title: Find and fix the mistake
segments.description:
Each student underlines what is wrong in the statement on the screen and rewrites it correctly in two or three sentences.
Pairs compare rewrites and agree on one version.
Two pairs read theirs, and the class settles what the statement confuses.
segments.teacherNotes: Errors: frost wedging is physical, so no new minerals form and the composition is unchanged. Clay comes from hydrolysis, not frost. Carrying pieces downslope is erosion, not weathering. Watch for ‘weathering means the rock moved’.
shown: Frost wedging is chemical weathering. The water changes granite into new minerals such as clay. When the broken pieces are carried down the slope, that movement is also weathering.

segments.title: Summary and what comes next time
segments.description:
Each student states in one sentence how physical and chemical weathering differ, using one example.
The instructor says that next time the class follows weathered material as it is moved by water, wind and gravity, then turns to soil.
Students who have not read Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, ch. 5 (Weathering and Soil), are told to do so before then.

segments.title: Where does weathered rock go?
segments.description:
Students write two ways that loose grains from a weathered hillside could end up in a river.
They compare with a partner, and two pairs report.
The instructor separates weathering, which breaks rock, from erosion, which moves it.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: rain wash, wind, landslide, slow creep downslope. Return to the corrected statement from the previous lecture if pairs blur the two words.
shown: Name two ways loose grains from a weathered hillside could reach a river.

segments.title: Erosion, transport and mass wasting
segments.description:
The instructor presents transport by water, wind and gravity, and the grain sizes each can carry: clay under 0.004 mm, silt to 0.0625 mm, sand to 2 mm, gravel above. Wind lifts sand by saltation and carries silt as dust, as in the 1930s Dust Bowl.
Students predict whether initially similar gravel of the same rock type would generally be more rounded after traveling 5 km or 100 km under comparable river conditions, and explain why. The instructor then shows how rounding and sorting give clues to distance and agent.
Mass wasting follows: rockfall, slump, debris flow and creep, with the 1903 Frank Slide at Turtle Mountain, Alberta, as a case.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: 100 km is more rounded, since collisions wear corners and soft grains break. Keep the Frank Slide factual, as many people died. The table gives common tendencies only: floods can deposit poorly sorted water-laid sediment, and gravity deposits are not always angular.
shown: Table: Agent | Typical grains moved | Often seen in the deposit / Water | Clay to boulders | Often rounded and sorted by size, but flood deposits can be poorly sorted / Wind | Sand and silt | Often well sorted, with frosted grains / Gravity | All sizes together | Often poorly sorted, and frequently angular

segments.title: Soil horizons and the factors that form soil
segments.description:
The instructor draws a soil profile on the board, layer by layer: O, A, E, B, C and bedrock. Water carries clay, iron and aluminum down from E to B. Before the B horizon is explained, students predict where clay and iron oxides will pile up, and write it.
The instructor then gives the five controls: parent material, climate, organisms, topography and time.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: lower, in the B horizon. O is organic, A is dark with humus, E is pale and leached, C is partly weathered parent material. Not every soil has an E. Soil takes centuries to thousands of years to form, so erosion loss is hard to replace.
shown: Layers: O organic litter → A dark topsoil with humus → E pale leached layer → B clay and iron oxides accumulate → C partly weathered parent material → Bedrock

segments.title: Read a profile
segments.description:
Pairs get a described profile on the screen and label the horizon of each of its five layers from top to bottom, giving a clue only for the A and B horizons.
Pairs compare labels with a neighboring pair and settle any difference by the clue.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: 0–4 cm O (litter); 4–18 cm A (dark, crumbly, humus); 18–70 cm B (yellow-brown, clay coats grains); 70–120 cm C (weathered rock fragments); below, bedrock. Common error: calling the dark layer B. Clues are asked for A and B only.
shown: A hypothetical profile: 0–4 cm: fallen leaves and partly rotted plant matter. 4–18 cm: dark, crumbly, rich in humus. 18–70 cm: yellow-brown, sticky, clay coating the grains. 70–120 cm: angular rock fragments with some weathering. Below 120 cm: solid rock.

segments.title: Design a soil
segments.description:
Each student makes up a setting for the thickest, most developed soil they can, choosing parent material, climate, organisms, topography and time, and giving a reason for the two choices they think matter most.
Groups of three compare settings and agree on one.
Two groups report, and the instructor compares them with a thin soil on a steep, cold, young surface.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: warm, wet climate; dense vegetation; gentle slope so the soil stays; a parent material that weathers readily (basalt over quartz sandstone); long time. Tropical red soils can be many meters thick. Steep slopes lose soil to mass wasting.
shown: Design the thickest, most developed soil you can. Choose parent material, climate, organisms, topography and time, and give a reason for the two that matter most.

segments.title: Summary and the lab ahead
segments.description:
Students write one sentence linking a soil horizon to the process that makes it.
The instructor says that next time is the lab, where pairs study weathered hand samples, sediment grains and soil profiles.
Lab reports: Igneous rocks and volcanoes is due at the start of that lab.
segments.teacherNotes: Remind pairs of closed-toe shoes and goggles whenever the acid bottle is out.

segments.title: Report due, safety and pairs
segments.description:
Lab reports: Igneous rocks and volcanoes is due now, at the start of this lab.
The instructor reviews the rules: closed-toe shoes, goggles whenever the acid bottle (dilute HCl) is out, and hand samples stay in their trays and go back where they came from.
Students sit in their lab pairs and collect a hand lens.
segments.teacherNotes: Safety: goggles on before anyone opens the acid bottle; keep it at the instructor’s bench and use only dropper amounts. Report spills immediately and follow the department’s spill procedure. For eye or skin exposure, begin flushing immediately at the eyewash or safety shower and alert the instructor; do not apply baking soda. Nobody tastes samples. Wipe benches dry. Sweep up chalk dust; do not blow it.
shown: Rules: Closed-toe shoes. Goggles whenever the acid bottle is out. Samples stay in their trays and go back where they came from.

segments.title: Method: evidence of weathering in a hand sample
segments.description:
The instructor demonstrates on a spare weathered sample not in the pairs’ trays, thinking aloud at each step. The steps are describing the surface and an existing fresh broken face, testing with a drop of dilute HCl under goggles, and judging whether the rock is physically broken, chemically altered, or both. Explain that fizz identifies carbonate; evidence of natural dissolution must come from features such as pitting.
Pairs take the Weathered samples record sheet.
The instructor shows how to read grain shape on the roundness chart.
segments.teacherNotes: Record what is seen before naming a process. Calcite fizzes in dilute HCl; quartz and feldspar do not. A rusty rind means oxidation. A crumbly, sandy surface (grus) means disintegration. Use the sample’s fresh broken face for color.

segments.title: Predict, then shake: how fast do edges round?
segments.description:
Pairs write a prediction: what will happen to five angular pieces of soft limestone shaken in water, and what will the water look like?
Each pair seals five limestone pieces, each about 2 cm across, and 100 mL of water in a 250 mL plastic jar. Partners take turns shaking it hard for five minutes.
Pairs pour off and record the water’s appearance, the corner shape and the size of the pieces. They link the result to abrasion and to the fine sediment that stays in the water.
segments.teacherNotes: Use pieces confirmed as calcite by the fizz test; some commercial chalk is gypsum. Expected: slight loss of material and softened corners, and cloudy water from suspended fine particles. Cloudiness alone does not establish particle size. The jar models abrasion during transport, not a measured duration of river wear. Safety: use screw-cap plastic jars only, wipe floors. Collect the rinse water and pieces in a labeled sediment waste container for disposal under the department’s procedure.

segments.title: Weathered samples and the fizz test
segments.description:
Pairs work through the numbered samples from the department’s first tray, using the method just shown. They record fizz, surface color or rind, hardness and weathering type for each.
The instructor circulates and asks each pair for the evidence behind its call.
segments.teacherNotes: Suggested set, adjust to trays: fresh and weathered granite, limestone, quartz sandstone, rusty basalt. Expected: limestone fizzes because it contains calcite; pitting would support natural dissolution. Weathered granite with altered feldspar and clay supports hydrolysis; rusty basalt supports oxidation. Quartz grains do not fizz, but calcite cement in sandstone can. Pairs often call color change physical.

segments.title: Break
segments.description: Students leave samples in their trays and step away from the benches.
segments.teacherNotes: Acid bottle capped and moved to the instructor’s bench.

segments.title: Sediment grains: roundness and sorting
segments.description:
Pairs examine three samples from the second tray of sediment samples with a hand lens. For each they record roundness (angular to well rounded) and sorting (poor to well).
Pairs then propose a transport agent for each sample, with one piece of evidence.
For one sample of their choice, they also name an alternative interpretation.
segments.teacherNotes: Suggested set, adjust to trays: river gravel, dune sand, a poorly sorted mixed sample. Expected: well-sorted, frosted sand is consistent with wind transport; rounded gravel is consistent with abrasion during water transport; poorly sorted angular material is consistent with nearby rockfall or debris-flow deposition. These observations do not uniquely establish an agent or distance. Pairs judge by color alone.

segments.title: Soil profile cards
segments.description:
Pairs get four profile cards of hypothetical soils, each with its horizon evidence and a short site description. For each they label the horizons from top to bottom with one clue each.
Pairs then name the controls (climate, parent material, organisms, topography or time) that the site evidence supports for each profile, and may name more than one.
Two pairs share a card, and the class checks it against the clues.
segments.teacherNotes: Card A: site is a gently sloping broadleaf forest on granite. Leaf litter 3 cm; dark crumbly layer to 15 cm; yellow-brown clay-coated layer to 60 cm; broken rock to 100 cm. Answer: O, A, B, C; organisms, granitic parent material and gentle topography are supported; climate and surface age cannot be established from this card. Card B: site is a spruce forest on sandy parent material with high rainfall. Thin litter; dark layer 5 cm; pale gray sand layer 10 cm; reddish clay-rich layer; crumbly rock. Answer: O, A, E, B, C; leaching fits; accept organisms, climate or sandy parent material. Card C: site is dry shrubland with windblown dust and low rainfall. No litter; pale soil 8 cm; white carbonate nodules at 30–50 cm; broken rock. Answer: A, B with carbonate, C; dust supplies carbonate and little water flushes it deeper. Card D: site is a flat upland under tropical forest on granite. 0–0.3 m slightly darker, little humus; 0.3–2 m red, clay-rich; 2–3 m soft rotted rock keeping the granite texture; hard rock below. Answer: A, B, C; warm climate, forest organisms, granitic parent material and flat topography are supported. Heavy rainfall and a long surface age are possible explanations, but neither is established by the card. All four are invented, not real sites.

segments.title: Finish recording and clean up
segments.description:
Pairs finish their tables and check each entry against the evidence they saw.
Samples go back into their trays and to where they came from, and lenses, jars and benches are wiped.
segments.teacherNotes: Count samples against the tray list before pairs leave. Acid bottle returned and capped; collect used dropper tips and acid waste in the department’s designated waste containers for disposal under its procedure.

segments.title: Assignments and what comes next
segments.description:
The Lab reports assignment for this lab is set now. Lab reports counts for 30% of the course grade. This assignment is due at the start of the lab of Sedimentary rocks. Each student writes their own.
Weekly online quizzes is set now and counts for 10% of the course grade. It is due at the first meeting of Sedimentary rocks. Each student does their own work, scored alone, and submits online before that meeting.
The instructor announces Midterm exam 1 (15%), taken at Sedimentary rocks, on what has been taught so far. It is marked in points. The teacher will announce what students may bring or use. Before then, students read Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, ch. 6 (Sediments and Sedimentary Rocks).
The instructor says that later in the course students will study clastic, chemical and biochemical sedimentary rocks and their environments. A practice quiz on this lesson is open after class and counts toward no grade.
segments.teacherNotes: Do not list exam topics. Say nothing about the exam beyond what is given here.

keyIdeas: Weathering breaks rock down where it sits. Physical weathering (frost wedging, unloading, root wedging, abrasion) breaks it into smaller pieces without changing its minerals. Chemical weathering (dissolution, hydrolysis, oxidation) changes the minerals themselves.

Physical weathering speeds chemical weathering because it exposes more surface. Cutting a 1 cm cube into 1 mm cubes raises its surface from 6 cm² to 60 cm². Minerals that crystallize first in Bowen’s reaction series (olivine) weather fastest at the surface, and quartz survives longest.

Erosion is the movement of weathered material by water, wind, ice and gravity. Mass wasting is gravity-driven movement (rockfall, slump, debris flow, creep). Transport can round and sort grains. Grain shape and sorting provide evidence about transport history.

Soil is weathered material mixed with organic matter. It forms layers called horizons: O (organic), A (topsoil), E (leached), B (accumulation of clay and iron), C (partly weathered parent material), above bedrock.

Soil develops under five controls: parent material, climate, organisms, topography and time. Over comparable periods on stable surfaces, granite generally undergoes more chemical weathering in a warm, wet climate than in an arid climate. Carbonate can accumulate in arid soils when a source, such as windblown dust, supplies it.

vocabulary.definition: The breakdown of rock at or near Earth’s surface into smaller pieces or new minerals, without the pieces being moved far.
Physical weathering in which water freezes in a crack, expands and pries the rock apart.
Chemical weathering in which water reacts with a mineral, as when feldspar turns to clay.
Chemical weathering in which iron in a mineral reacts with oxygen to form rusty iron oxides.
The removal and transport of weathered material by water, wind, ice or gravity.
The downslope movement of rock and soil under gravity, such as rockfall, slump, debris flow and creep.
A layer of soil, distinguished from those above and below by color, texture and composition, such as the O, A, E, B and C horizons.
The rock or sediment from which a soil develops.

sides.title: Sample 1: fresh granite
points: Pink and white crystals interlocked, hard, a ringing sound when struck.

sides.title: Sample 2: granite from a hillside outcrop
points: A rusty-brown surface, crumbling loose grains, white powdery patches, a crack along one side.

visual.ask: What has changed in the second sample, and what might have caused it?

slides.title: Physical weathering and surface area
bullets: Frost wedging, unloading, root wedging, salt wedging, abrasion
A 1 cm cube cut into 1 mm cubes: what happens to the total surface area?
slides.notes: Present each process and say what force breaks the rock: frost wedging (ice expanding in cracks), unloading (exfoliation, as in Half Dome in Yosemite, where rock expands as the load above is removed), root wedging, salt wedging (growing salt crystals) and abrasion. For each, say that no new mineral forms. Use the chain to walk through frost wedging. Water expands about 9% when it freezes, and frost wedging needs repeated freeze-thaw cycles around 0 °C. Then stop at the cube question. Students predict by how much the total surface rises and write a number. Common error: ‘about double’. Then work it on the board: one cube has 6 cm². There are 1,000 small cubes of 6 mm² each, so 6,000 mm², which is 60 cm². Stress that more surface lets water and acid attack faster, so physical weathering feeds chemical weathering.

Answer: before 6 × 4 = 24 cm²; eight cubes of 6 cm² each give 48 cm², so the surface doubles. The gain is smaller than the tenfold gain for 1 mm cubes. bullets: Rainwater is weakly acidic: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid)

slides.notes: Walk through the table row by row: dissolution takes limestone (calcite) into solution; hydrolysis turns feldspar into clay; oxidation turns iron in olivine and pyrite into rusty iron oxides. Then pose the last bullet. Both minerals are in Bowen’s reaction series from last time. Students write a prediction before you build the answer. Expected: olivine weathers fastest and quartz survives longest. Link the order to silicate structure and to the conditions where each mineral formed: minerals that crystallize at the highest temperatures are furthest from surface conditions. Quartz persists as sand, and clay forms from feldspar. Warm, wet climates weather faster than cold, dry ones.

study.overview: Rock that formed deep in Earth is unstable at the surface, so it breaks down where it sits. This is weathering. Erosion then moves the broken material by water, wind, ice and gravity. What stays in place, mixed with organic matter, becomes soil. This guide covers four ideas: how physical and chemical weathering differ, how surface area links them, what grain shape and sorting tell you about transport, and how soil layers and soil-forming controls work. Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, covers all of this in its chapter on weathering and soil.

points.heading: Physical and chemical weathering change rock in different ways
points.explanation:
Physical weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces without changing its minerals. Frost wedging is the standard case. Water enters a crack, freezes and expands by about 9%, and widens the crack. Repeated freeze-thaw cycles around 0 °C eventually pry a block loose. Root wedging, abrasion and unloading (as in the curved sheets on Half Dome in Yosemite) are also physical.

Chemical weathering changes the minerals themselves. Rainwater is weakly acidic because CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid). Dissolution removes calcite from limestone and leaves a pitted surface. Hydrolysis turns feldspar into clay, so granite crumbles to loose grus and clay. Oxidation turns iron in olivine or pyrite into rusty iron oxides. A color change like this is not cosmetic, because new minerals have formed.

A quick test is to ask whether the minerals are the same afterward. If they are, the weathering is physical. If new ones appeared, it is chemical. Rock can show both at once, so record what you see before you name a process.

points.heading: Surface area links the two kinds of weathering
points.explanation:
Physical weathering speeds up chemical weathering because it exposes more surface to water and acid. Take a 1 cm cube with 6 cm² of surface. Cut it into 1 mm cubes. Each small cube has 6 mm² of surface, and there are 1,000 of them, so the total is 6,000 mm², which is 60 cm². The surface has grown tenfold and the amount of rock has not changed. The smaller the final pieces, the larger the gain. A common mistake is to guess that the area only doubles.

Minerals also differ in how fast they weather. Those that crystallize first in Bowen’s reaction series, such as olivine, formed at the highest temperatures. They are furthest from surface conditions and weather fastest. Quartz survives longest, so it persists as sand while feldspar becomes clay.

points.heading: Erosion moves material, and grains record the journey
points.explanation:
Weathering breaks rock down in place. Erosion is the movement of the weathered material by water, wind, ice and gravity. If a block falls from a cliff, the cracking was weathering and the fall is erosion.

Water can carry clay up to boulders. Wind lifts sand by saltation and carries silt as dust, as in the 1930s Dust Bowl. Size classes run from clay (under 0.004 mm) through silt (to 0.0625 mm) and sand (to 2 mm) to gravel above that. Mass wasting is gravity-driven movement: rockfall, slump, debris flow and creep. The 1903 Frank Slide at Turtle Mountain, Alberta, is a rockslide in which many people died.

Grain shape and sorting are evidence of transport history. Well-sorted, frosted sand is consistent with wind. Poorly sorted, angular debris is consistent with nearby rockfall or debris flow. Treat these as tendencies, not proof. Floods can deposit poorly sorted water-laid sediment, and gravity deposits are not always angular. Roundness and sorting do not uniquely identify an agent or a distance, so name an alternative interpretation when you can.

points.heading: Soil forms in horizons under five controls
points.explanation:
Soil is weathered material mixed with organic matter. It forms layers called horizons, from the top down:
- O: organic litter.
- A: dark topsoil with humus.
- E: a pale layer from which water has leached clay, iron and aluminum.
- B: the layer where clay and iron oxides accumulate.
- C: partly weathered parent material.
- Bedrock below.

Not every soil has an E horizon. As a practice case, take a hypothetical profile: 0–4 cm of fallen leaves, 4–18 cm of dark, crumbly, humus-rich material, 18–70 cm of yellow-brown material with clay coating the grains, 70–120 cm of angular, partly weathered rock fragments, and solid rock below 120 cm. Read it top to bottom as O, A, B, C and bedrock. The common error is to call the dark layer B. Its color comes from humus, so it is the A horizon.

Five controls decide how a soil develops: parent material, climate, organisms, topography and time. Compare two settings. A gentle slope under dense tropical forest, on rock that weathers readily, with a very long time to develop, can produce red soils many meters thick. A steep, cold, young surface gives a thin soil, because mass wasting strips it away and little time has passed. Soil takes centuries to thousands of years to form, so lost soil is hard to replace. Climate and age are not always readable from a profile. Carbonate can build up in dry soils when a source such as windblown dust supplies it and little water flushes it deeper.

handouts.title: Predict, then shake: how fast do edges round?
handouts.usedIn: Predict, then shake: how fast do edges round?

blocks.text: Work with your partner. Write your prediction before you touch the jar.

blocks.hint: Prediction: what will happen to five angular pieces of soft limestone shaken in water, and what will the water look like?

blocks.text: Procedure

items: Take five limestone pieces, each about 2 cm across, that your instructor has checked. Look at their corners and sizes first.
Put the five pieces and 100 mL of water in a 250 mL plastic screw-cap jar. Seal it tightly.
Partners take turns shaking the jar hard for five minutes in total.
Pour off the water into a clear container and look at it. Do not pour any pieces down the sink.
Look at the pieces again. Compare corner shape and size with what you saw before.
Put the rinse water and the pieces in the labeled sediment waste container. Wipe up any water from the floor.

blocks.hint: Link your results to abrasion, and say what happened to the fine sediment that stays in the water.

handouts.key:
Prediction: Collisions should chip or wear the limestone, soften some corners and release fine particles into the water. The pieces may become slightly smaller. The water should become cloudy. Accept a reasoned prediction even if the observed change is small.

Results, in table order:
Appearance of the water: Typically cloudy, with suspended particles; some material may settle. Record the actual appearance.
Corner shape of the pieces: Typically slightly less sharp or more rounded. Accept little visible change if that is what occurred.
Size of the pieces: Typically a slight decrease, possibly too small to see clearly. No numerical decrease is required because the procedure includes no size measurement.

Link to abrasion and suspended sediment: Repeated collisions between pieces and contact with the jar wear edges and release particles. Some fine particles remain suspended, making the water cloudy; others may settle. Cloudiness alone does not establish their grain-size class. A common slip is to call the cloudy material dissolved limestone. Another is to treat the shaking interval as an equivalent river travel time.

handouts.title: Weathered samples record
handouts.usedIn: Weathered samples and the fizz test

blocks.text: Use the numbered samples from the first tray and the method sheet. Goggles on before the acid bottle is opened. Record what you see, then decide the weathering type: physical, chemical or both. Give the evidence behind each call.

blocks.caption: One row for each numbered sample

handouts.key:
Rows 1–5: Each row must match the numbered department sample examined. Apply the following criteria to every row, in column order.

Sample: Record the tray number accurately.
Fizz: Record the observed reaction, including no visible fizz where appropriate. Calcite-bearing limestone should fizz. Quartz and feldspar do not fizz; sandstone may fizz if it contains calcite cement.
Surface color or rind: Describe the observed color, staining or rind before interpreting it. Possible observations include orange-brown staining, pale altered feldspar, pits or a crumbly surface.
Hardness: Describe the observed resistance to scratching or crumbling. Surface crumbliness alone does not establish a mineral's Mohs hardness.
Weathering type: Physical, chemical or both, supported by the sample's features.
Evidence for your call: Link the classification to observations. Cracks or grain separation support physical breakdown. Altered feldspar with clay supports chemical weathering by hydrolysis. A rusty alteration rind supports oxidation. Dissolution pits support chemical weathering. Use both only when evidence supports both breakdown and chemical alteration.

For any row containing fresh granite, little visible weathering is an acceptable conclusion if supported by its condition. For weathered granite, distinguish loose grains from feldspar alteration. For limestone, distinguish a positive acid test from evidence of natural dissolution. For quartz sandstone, distinguish resistant quartz grains from potentially reactive cement. For rusty basalt, connect an alteration rind to oxidation rather than treating color alone as conclusive.

Common slips: Using fizz as proof of natural dissolution; calling oxidation physical because only color appears to change; assigning a process from the rock name without describing evidence.

handouts.title: Sediment grains record

blocks.text: Examine three samples from the second tray with a hand lens. Record roundness (angular, subangular, subrounded, rounded, well rounded) and sorting (poor, moderate, well). Then propose a transport agent (water, wind or gravity) and one piece of evidence for it.

blocks.hint: For one sample of your choice, name the sample and give an alternative interpretation of how it was transported or deposited.

handouts.key:
Rows 1–3: Match each entry to the actual numbered sediment sample. Apply these criteria in column order.

Sample: Record the tray number.
Roundness: Use angular, subangular, subrounded, rounded or well rounded, based on grain edges and corners. Accept a supported range if grains vary.
Sorting: Use poor, moderate or well, based on the spread of grain sizes. A narrow size range is well sorted; a broad range is poorly sorted.
Transport agent: Propose water, wind or gravity as an interpretation supported by the observations.
One piece of evidence: Connect a visible feature to the proposed agent. Rounded gravel is consistent with abrasion during water transport. Well-sorted sand is consistent with wind transport, especially if frosting is visible. Poorly sorted angular material is consistent with nearby rockfall or debris-flow deposition. These features do not uniquely identify an agent.

Alternative interpretation: Name one examined sample and give another plausible transport or deposition history. For example, well-sorted sand could have been sorted by waves or river flow rather than wind. Poorly sorted sediment could have been deposited rapidly by a flood rather than a debris flow. Rounded gravel could have inherited its shape from an older deposit before being moved again.

Common slips: Confusing roundness with sorting; using color alone to identify transport; treating a plausible agent as proven; assigning an exact travel distance from grain shape.

handouts.key:
Card A
Horizons from top to bottom, with clues: O—3 cm of leaf litter; A—dark, crumbly material extending to 15 cm; B—yellow-brown material with clay coatings extending to 60 cm; C—broken parent rock extending to 100 cm.
Supported controls: Organisms—broadleaf forest and litter; parent material—granite; topography—gentle slope. Climate and time cannot be established from this description. Common slip: Adding an E horizon without a pale, leached layer.

Card B
Horizons from top to bottom, with clues: O—thin litter; A—dark layer 5 cm thick; E—pale gray sand layer 10 cm thick; B—reddish, clay-rich layer; C—crumbly parent material.
Supported controls: Organisms—spruce forest; parent material—sandy material; climate—high rainfall. Downward leaching is consistent with the pale E horizon above the reddish B horizon. Topography and time are not established. Common slip: Calling the pale layer C because it is sandy, while overlooking its position and evidence of leaching.

Card C
Horizons from top to bottom, with clues: A—upper pale soil, 8 cm thick; B—subsurface carbonate accumulation indicated by white nodules at 30–50 cm; C—broken parent rock. No O horizon is described.
Supported controls: Climate—low rainfall limits downward flushing; organisms—shrubland vegetation; parent material inputs—windblown dust supplies material, including carbonate. The underlying rock type, topography and time are not established. Common slips: Labeling carbonate accumulation as E; assuming every A horizon must be dark; adding a litter layer that is not described.

Card D
Horizons from top to bottom, with clues: A—slightly darker surface material at 0–0.3 m, with little humus; B—red, clay-rich material at 0.3–2 m; C—soft, rotted rock at 2–3 m that retains granite texture; R or bedrock—hard rock below 3 m.
Supported controls: Climate—tropical conditions support warmth; organisms—forest vegetation; parent material—granite; topography—flat upland. Heavy rainfall and a long period of soil development are possible explanations, but neither is established by the card. Common slips: Calling the soft, rotted granite bedrock despite its weathering; inferring a specific soil age from thickness; assuming tropical forest necessarily establishes high rainfall.

Each student first writes one sentence predicting what turns a loose bed of sand into solid rock.

The teacher links the rounding and sorting met in the weathering and erosion lesson to transport: rounded, well-sorted grains suggest substantial abrasion and sorting during transport or repeated reworking.

segments.title: Chemical and biochemical rocks
segments.description:
The teacher explains two ways dissolved ions leave water. Chemical rocks form when minerals precipitate as water evaporates, giving rock salt (halite) and rock gypsum in a drying lagoon.
Biochemical rocks form when organisms build shells and skeletons from dissolved calcium carbonate or silica, giving fossiliferous limestone, coquina, chalk and much chert.
The teacher shows that calcite (CaCO₃) fizzes in dilute HCl and chert does not.
Students tell a partner for two minutes how a limestone of shell fragments differs from rock salt, and which test shows calcite.

segments.title: Find and fix the field note
segments.description:
Each student reads a field note that holds two mistakes and writes a corrected version alone for five minutes.
Pairs then compare corrections for two minutes.
Two pairs name the clue that decided each fix.
segments.teacherNotes: Fixes: whole shells make it fossiliferous (biochemical) limestone, not chemical; angular gravel makes it breccia; angularity suggests limited abrasion but does not establish transport distance. Common slip: calling all limestone chemical because calcite precipitates. Accept any wording that names the clue.

segments.title: What structures and fossils record
segments.description:
The teacher shows a photograph of cross-bedded sandstone, and each student writes a guess at the setting before any explanation.
The teacher then covers bedding, cross-bedding, ripple marks, graded bedding, mud cracks and fossils, and what each says about water, wind or climate.
The teacher stresses that one feature narrows the possible settings and several together strengthen an interpretation.
segments.teacherNotes: Cross-beds dip downcurrent; asymmetric ripples show a one-way current, symmetric ones show waves. Fossils help only if the organism lived where it was buried, not if it was swept in. Brachiopods show marine water only; reef-building corals add warm, shallow, clear water.

segments.title: Infer the setting
segments.description:
Each student writes a likely setting and a two-word clue for each of three hypothetical beds, about one minute a bed.
Pairs compare answers for one minute.
The teacher hears one pair on a bed where they disagree, and the class settles it from the evidence.
segments.teacherNotes: Answers: 1 desert dune (large cross-beds, rounded frosted grains, no fossils); 2 marine setting with little sand or mud supply; warm, shallow water would require evidence such as reef-building corals; 3 floodplain or lake margin that dried out. For Bed 3, also accept a tidal flat if the explanation links the cracks to exposure and drying. Bed 2 requires a marine interpretation. Keep the disagreement round to two minutes.

segments.description:

segments.description:
Each pair records grain size, rounding and a rock name for every clastic sample in the tray.
The pair then picks the sample that shows the most abrasion and sorting, and gives one observation that supports the choice.
The teacher circulates and checks the first sample with each pair.

segments.title: Chemical and biochemical station

segments.title: Identify three unknowns

keyIdeas: Sedimentary rocks form when loose sediment is compacted and cemented (lithification), or when minerals come out of water or organisms build shells and skeletons. Rocks are grouped by origin as clastic, chemical or biochemical.

Clastic rocks are named by grain size and composition: conglomerate and breccia (gravel), sandstone (sand), shale and mudstone (silt and clay). Rounded clasts show abrasion during transport or repeated reworking; angular clasts show less abrasion. Rounding alone does not establish transport distance.

Chemical and biochemical rocks are named by composition and origin. Rock salt and rock gypsum form by evaporation; limestone, chalk and some chert are built from the remains of organisms. Dilute HCl fizzes on calcite but not on chert.
Sedimentary structures and fossils record the environment of deposition: cross-bedding, ripple marks, graded bedding, mud cracks and marine fossils each narrow the likely setting.

vocabulary.definition: Made of broken fragments (clasts) of older rock or minerals, such as the grains in sandstone.
The change of loose sediment into solid rock by compaction and cementation.
The binding of grains by minerals such as silica, calcite or iron oxide that precipitate in the spaces between them.
A sedimentary rock built from the shells or skeletons of organisms, such as fossiliferous limestone.
A chemical sedimentary rock, such as rock salt or rock gypsum, formed as water evaporates and minerals precipitate.
Layering in sedimentary rock that records changes in the sediment laid down over time.
Inclined layers within a bed, formed as sand migrates in dunes or ripples, dipping in the direction of flow.
The setting where sediment accumulated, such as a river channel, desert dune or shallow sea.
