study.overview: Sedimentary rocks record how loose material, dissolved ions and living organisms end up as solid rock at Earth’s surface. Rocks are grouped by origin: clastic (compacted and cemented fragments), chemical (minerals precipitated from water) and biochemical (built from shells and skeletons). Each rock is named from grain size, composition and a few simple tests. Structures and fossils in the beds then show the setting where the sediment collected. This guide follows Earle, Physical Geology, in the chapter on sedimentary rocks.

points.heading: Clastic rocks are named by grain size and composition
points.explanation: Clastic means made of broken fragments (clasts) of older rock or mineral. It does not mean made of clay. Loose sediment becomes rock by lithification. It is buried, compacted, and then cemented when minerals such as silica, calcite or iron oxide crystallize in the pore spaces between grains. Grain size gives the main name: gravel over 2 mm gives conglomerate (rounded clasts) or breccia (angular clasts), sand from 0.0625 to 2 mm gives sandstone, and silt and clay under 0.0625 mm give shale (splits into thin sheets) or mudstone (breaks in blocks). Composition refines the name, so a sandstone that is mostly quartz is a quartz arenite. Clast shape needs care. Rounding shows abrasion during transport or repeated reworking. Angular clasts show less abrasion. Rounding alone does not tell you how far the grains traveled. Example: suppose a hand sample has grains too small to see without a lens, no visible layering, and breaks into blocky chunks. It is made of silt and clay but is not fissile, so it is mudstone rather than shale.

points.heading: Chemical and biochemical rocks are named by composition and origin
points.explanation: Not all sedimentary rock is made of fragments. Chemical rocks form when minerals precipitate from water, as in the evaporation of a drying lagoon that leaves rock salt or rock gypsum. Biochemical rocks form when organisms build shells and skeletons from dissolved calcium carbonate or silica, giving fossiliferous limestone, coquina, chalk and much chert. A few quick tests separate them. Calcite (CaCO₃) fizzes in dilute HCl and has a Mohs hardness of 3. Quartz-rich chert does not fizz and has a hardness of 7, so it resists a steel nail (about 5.5). Gypsum is scratched by a fingernail (about 2.5). Always test acid on a fresh surface, with goggles on and one small drop. Dolostone reacts only weakly with cold acid, so powdering a little makes the reaction easier to see. Origin comes from the evidence in the rock, not from a single test. Limestone can also form chemically (travertine, ooids) and chert can precipitate directly. Example: a dense gray rock with a conchoidal fracture that a steel nail cannot scratch and that does not fizz is not limestone. It is consistent with chert, and its origin still needs further evidence.

points.heading: Structures and fossils narrow the depositional environment
points.explanation: Features in the beds record the water, wind or climate present when the sediment was laid down. Cross-bedding shows sand moved by wind or flowing water, and the beds dip downcurrent. Asymmetric ripple marks show a current in one direction, and symmetric ripples show back-and-forth wave motion. Graded bedding, coarse at the base and fine at the top, shows a current that slowed, as in a deep-sea turbidity current or a flood deposit. Mud cracks show mud that dried in air. Fossils help only if the organism lived where it was buried and was not swept in. Fossils also differ in how much they tell you, because reef-building corals point to warm, shallow, clear water while many marine fossils show only that the water was marine. One feature fits several settings, and several features together strengthen the interpretation. Example: suppose a sandstone bed has large cross-beds with a layer above that grades upward from coarse to fine. The cross-beds show moving sand and the grading shows a slowing current. Together they favor a flowing-water setting such as a river channel over a still lake, though you would still look for more evidence before settling on one.

handouts.title: Find and fix the field note
handouts.usedIn: Find and fix the field note

blocks.text: Read the field note below. It is a hypothetical note, written for this exercise. It holds two mistakes in how the rocks were named or interpreted. Work alone. Then write a corrected version of the note.
Field note

Unit A (lower): pale gray rock in a road cut. It fizzes in dilute HCl. Whole brachiopod shells are packed in a fine-grained matrix. I recorded it as a chemical limestone, because calcite precipitates from seawater.
Unit B (above A): gravel-sized clasts, all with sharp corners, in a sandy matrix. I recorded it as a conglomerate. This shows the clasts were carried a long way from their source.

blocks.hint: Write the corrected note. Keep what is right. Change only what the evidence does not support.

handouts.key:
Unit A: Pale gray rock that fizzes in dilute HCl, with whole brachiopod shells packed in a fine-grained matrix. Identify it as fossiliferous limestone of biochemical origin. The shells supply the evidence for that origin; fizz supports the presence of calcite. Brachiopods support a marine source, although transport must be considered when interpreting the burial environment.

Unit B: Gravel-sized, angular clasts in a sandy matrix identify breccia. Angularity suggests limited abrasion; it does not establish transport distance. Replace the claim of long transport with that qualified interpretation.

Look for a corrected note that preserves the observations and changes the classifications and unsupported transport inference. Common slips: classifying all limestone as chemical; overlooking clast shape; treating angularity as proof of a particular transport distance.

handouts.title: Infer the setting

blocks.text: Each bed below is hypothetical. For each, write the most likely depositional setting and a two-word clue from the description that supports it. Spend about one minute on each bed. Then compare with your partner.
Bed 1
Sandstone with cross-beds up to several meters thick. The grains are well rounded and have frosted surfaces. No fossils.

blocks.hint: Setting, and a two-word clue

blocks.text: Bed 2
Fine-grained gray limestone that fizzes in dilute HCl. Whole brachiopod shells occur throughout. There are no sand or mud layers and no corals.

blocks.hint: Setting, and a two-word clue

blocks.text: Bed 3
Thin layers of shale. The top surface of one layer shows a network of polygon-shaped cracks, filled with sand from the layer above. No marine fossils.

blocks.hint: Setting, and a two-word clue

handouts.key:
Bed 1 — Setting: desert sand dune. Two-word clue: “frosted surfaces.” Large cross-beds and well-rounded grains strengthen the interpretation of wind-deposited sand. Common slip: treating cross-bedding alone as proof of a desert environment.

Bed 2 — Setting: marine carbonate environment with little input of sand or mud, assuming the shells represent organisms that lived there. Two-word clue: “brachiopod shells.” Do not require warm or shallow water: the description does not establish either. Common slip: treating all fossiliferous limestone as evidence of a warm, shallow reef.

Bed 3 — Setting: intermittently exposed floodplain or lake margin; a tidal flat is also defensible. Two-word clue: “polygon-shaped cracks.” Sand-filled cracks record drying and exposure of the mud before deposition of the overlying sand. Common slip: treating the absence of marine fossils as proof of freshwater deposition.

handouts.title: Sedimentary rock identification sheet: clastic rocks

blocks.text: Work with your partner and the department's hand samples. Keep every sample in its tray. Do not break samples. Record your observations before you name a rock.
Equipment and safety

items: Hand lens
Grain-size card or millimeter ruler
Steel nail for hardness
Dilute HCl bottle with dropper: goggles on before you touch the bottle, a fresh surface, one small drop per test
Closed-toe shoes at all times

blocks.text: Method

blocks.hint: In your own words, write the steps for describing a sedimentary rock, in the order you will do them.

blocks.text: Clastic grain-size table

rows: Conglomerate if clasts are rounded; breccia if angular
Sandstone (quartz arenite if mostly quartz; arkose if rich in feldspar)
Shale if it splits into thin sheets; mudstone if it breaks in blocks
blocks.caption: Clastic sediment and the rocks it forms

blocks.text: Record: every clastic sample in your tray

blocks.label: Sample that shows the most abrasion and sorting

blocks.hint: One observation that supports your choice

handouts.key:
Method blank — An acceptable sequence is: record the sample identifier; use a hand lens and grain-size card or millimeter ruler to describe grain size; record rounding and sorting; examine mineral composition; assess hardness and, where useful, fizz on an already exposed fresh surface; describe structures and fossils; then assign a rock name and interpret its origin. Keep samples in their trays and do not break them. Wear goggles before touching the dilute HCl bottle and use one small drop per test. Look for observations recorded before identification.

Recording table — Enter the identifier on each department sample in the Sample column. Match each row to its observed properties. Expected entries for the described tray are:
• Conglomerate: gravel clasts larger than 2 mm; rounded; conglomerate. Record the size of the gravel clasts separately from the finer matrix.
• Breccia: gravel clasts larger than 2 mm; angular; breccia.
• Quartz arenite: sand-sized grains, 0.0625–2 mm; rounding as observed; quartz arenite. Mostly quartz is the compositional clue.
• Arkose: sand-sized grains, 0.0625–2 mm; rounding as observed; arkose. Abundant feldspar is the compositional clue; pink color alone is insufficient.
• Shale: silt- and clay-sized sediment, smaller than 0.0625 mm; rounding generally not resolvable with a hand lens; shale. Fissility is the diagnostic texture.
• Mudstone: silt- and clay-sized sediment, smaller than 0.0625 mm; rounding generally not resolvable with a hand lens; mudstone. It lacks fissility and commonly breaks into blocks.

Sample showing the most abrasion and sorting — Give the identifier of the sample with the best combination of rounded grains and a narrow grain-size range. A well-rounded, well-sorted quartz arenite is a suitable choice if those properties are present.

Supporting observation blank — Accept, for example: Most grains have rounded edges and are similar in size. Look for an observation that supports the selected sample. Common slips: equating sorting with rounding; inferring rounding from rock name alone; claiming that quartz abundance proves the greatest transport distance.

handouts.title: Sedimentary rock identification sheet: chemical and biochemical rocks

blocks.text: Work with your partner and the department's hand samples. Keep every sample in its tray. Never taste a sample. Test acid only on a fresh surface, with goggles on, using one drop per sample.
Hardness guide
Record: every sample in your tray
For Origin, write chemical or biochemical.

blocks.hint: Two lines: how can you tell limestone from chert using fizz and hardness?

handouts.key:
Recording table — Use each department sample's identifier and match the remaining cells to observations. Expected entries for the described tray are:
• Rock salt: no fizz; Mohs hardness about 2.5; crystalline, with three cleavage directions at right angles and commonly cubic fragments; rock salt; chemical.
• Rock gypsum: no fizz; Mohs hardness 2, scratched by a fingernail; crystalline, with texture varying from massive to visibly crystalline; rock gypsum; chemical.
• Fossiliferous limestone: fizz with dilute HCl; calcite hardness 3; visible shells or shell fragments in a carbonate matrix; fossiliferous limestone; biochemical.
• Chalk: fizz with dilute HCl; calcite hardness 3, although the porous rock commonly crumbles or marks easily; very fine-grained, commonly white and powdery; chalk; biochemical.
• Chert: no fizz; Mohs hardness about 7; dense, microcrystalline silica, commonly with conchoidal fracture; chert; biochemical or chemical, depending on evidence of origin. Either origin is acceptable when the hand sample supplies no diagnostic evidence.

Two-line answer — Calcite limestone fizzes with dilute HCl and has mineral hardness 3, so a steel nail scratches it.
Chert does not fizz and has hardness about 7, so a steel nail does not scratch it.

Look for a distinction between mineral hardness and the ease with which a porous rock crumbles. Common slips: identifying any white rock as chalk; confusing cubic cleavage with crystal shape; assigning a definite origin to chert from hardness and fizz alone.

handouts.title: Sedimentary rock identification sheet: structures and environments

blocks.text: Examine each department slab or projected photograph with your partner. For each, record the structure, what it shows about water or wind, and a likely setting. Be ready to share one inference with the class.

handouts.key:
For A, B and C, match the row to the slab or photograph displayed under that letter. The expected sets of cells are:
• Asymmetric ripple marks | A predominantly one-way water current moved sediment | River channel or tidal flat; another current-dominated setting is acceptable with a supporting explanation.
• Polygonal mud cracks | Wet mud dried during exposure; the feature does not establish flow direction | Floodplain, lake margin or exposed tidal flat.
• Brachiopod fossils in limestone | Marine organisms supplied skeletal material; fossils alone do not establish current direction | Marine carbonate environment, provided the fossils represent the local community. If reef-building corals are also present and preserved in growth position, warm, shallow, clear marine water is supported.

Look for each interpretation to follow the visible evidence. Common slips: calling asymmetric ripples wave ripples; interpreting mud cracks as evidence of permanently submerged sediment; inferring warm, shallow water from brachiopods alone; ignoring possible fossil transport.

handouts.title: Sedimentary rock identification sheet: three unknowns

blocks.text: Your pair has three unlabeled samples. For each, run the method you wrote earlier on this sheet set. Then name the rock, give its group (clastic, chemical or biochemical), and say where it likely formed. Goggles on for any acid test.

handouts.key:
Enter the name, group and likely setting for the actual sample under each identifier. For the example set, in the order described in the plan:
1 | Conglomerate | Clastic | River channel or gravel beach. Rounded gravel clasts larger than 2 mm are the diagnostic observation; either setting is plausible rather than uniquely established.
2 | Fossiliferous limestone | Biochemical | Marine carbonate environment if the shells are marine and represent the local community. Visible shells and fizz support the identification, but do not alone establish shallow water. Without identifiable marine fossils or other environmental evidence, accept a qualified carbonate setting, including a lake.
3 | Rock gypsum | Chemical | Evaporating saline basin. Fingernail scratching, no fizz and the absence of cubic cleavage support the identification; gypsum has Mohs hardness 2.

Look for names supported by recorded observations and settings expressed at the certainty the sample permits. Common slips: calling rounded gravel breccia; treating all limestone as chemical; identifying gypsum as halite without examining cleavage; treating one hand sample as proof of a unique depositional setting.

ready: Teacher: department hand samples in trays for each pair (clastic, then chemical and biochemical), plus three unlabeled samples per pair for the last check
Teacher: dilute HCl bottle with dropper, and goggles for every student
Teacher: hand lenses, grain-size cards or millimeter rulers, and steel nails for each pair
Teacher: department slabs and projected photographs showing ripple marks, mud cracks and fossils
Teacher: one tray sample for modeling the method, and a limestone sample with an exposed fresh surface for the fizz prediction

l_81884a8d6bb4.title: Metamorphic rocks and the rock cycle
l_81884a8d6bb4.summary: How heat, pressure and fluids change rocks, how foliated and non-foliated rocks form, and how all rock types link in the rock cycle.
readings: Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, ch. 7 (to confirm) (Metamorphic Rocks)

segments.title: Quiz due now and a marble puzzle
segments.description:
Weekly online quizzes: Sedimentary rocks is due now; it was submitted online before this meeting.
The teacher puts two rocks side by side on the screen.
Each student writes one sentence on what could turn the first rock into the second.
Two students read their sentence aloud.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: heat and pressure recrystallize the calcite and destroy the shells. Do not correct vocabulary yet; the next segment supplies it. Both rocks fizz because both are calcite, so the change is texture, not composition.
shown: Side by side: Fossiliferous limestone: mostly calcite; whole shells visible; fizzes in dilute HCl | Marble: mostly calcite; interlocking crystals; no shells; fizzes in dilute HCl
Both rocks are mostly calcite. In one sentence, what could turn the first into the second?

segments.title: Heat, pressure and fluids
segments.description:
The teacher defines metamorphism as change in the solid state, from a protolith to a new rock, and gives the temperature range from about 200 °C up to the start of melting.
The teacher separates heat from the geothermal gradient (about 25 °C per km) and from intrusions, confining pressure from differential stress, and the role of hot fluids carrying ions.
Before contact and regional metamorphism are explained, each student writes whether shale baked beside a granite intrusion would be foliated, and why.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected prediction: not foliated, because heat acts without differential stress, so hornfels forms. Common error: metamorphism means melting. If partial melting starts, melt forms while some minerals remain solid. The melt enters the igneous part of the cycle when it cools and crystallizes. Link to Earle, ch. 7.

segments.title: Match the setting to the agent
segments.description:
Each student writes the type of metamorphism (contact, regional, hydrothermal or burial) for each of four settings.
The teacher hears two answers, each with the main agent of change behind it, and the class settles any disagreement.
segments.teacherNotes:
Answers:
1 Contact (hornfels); agent heat.
2 Regional (schist or gneiss); agents heat and differential stress.
3 Hydrothermal alteration, neither contact nor regional; agent fluids.
4 Burial; agent confining pressure with rising temperature.
Accept a second agent if the student reasons from the setting.
shown: 1. Mudstone in a thin halo against the edge of a granite intrusion
2. Shale in the core of a mountain belt where two continents collided
3. Basalt on a mid-ocean ridge flank, circulated by hot seawater
4. Sandstone buried under about 10 km of sediment in a deep basin

segments.title: Foliation and the grade sequence
segments.description:
The teacher shows how differential stress aligns platy minerals perpendicular to the greatest compressive stress, which gives foliation.
Students predict what shale becomes at slightly higher temperature, and which feature changes, before the sequence goes up.
The teacher then gives slate, phyllite, schist and gneiss with the index minerals, and the non-foliated rocks marble, quartzite and hornfels.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected prediction: slate, with tiny aligned mica and chlorite. Grain size grows with grade. Gneiss bands are light quartz and feldspar alternating with dark biotite and amphibole. Common error: calling visible calcite crystals in marble foliation. Marble has no alignment.
shown: Steps: shale → slate, dull, splits flat → phyllite, silky sheen → schist, visible mica, garnet → gneiss, light and dark bands
Steps: chlorite → biotite → garnet → staurolite → kyanite → sillimanite, rising grade
Table: Parent rock | Non-foliated product / limestone | marble / quartz sandstone | quartzite / mudstone beside an intrusion | hornfels

segments.title: Which has the higher grade?
segments.description:
For each of two pairs of rocks, each student writes which has the higher grade and the clue that decided it (four minutes).
Pairs compare their choices for two minutes.
The teacher hears two or three explanations (two minutes).
segments.teacherNotes:
Pair 1: Rock B. Visible mica and garnet mean coarser grains and higher grade than the silky, fine phyllite.
Pair 2: Rock B, if these are comparable shale-derived rocks from the same Barrovian metamorphic sequence. The kyanite zone represents higher grade than the garnet zone in that sequence. Across unrelated samples, kyanite versus garnet alone does not establish relative grade; pressure, bulk composition, and the full mineral assemblage also matter.
Common slip: choosing by color. Grade is shown by grain size, foliation type and index minerals.
shown: Pair 1. Rock A: phyllite, silky sheen, grains too small to see. Rock B: schist, visible mica flakes and garnet crystals.
Pair 2. Rock A: a schist whose key mineral is biotite with garnet. Rock B: a schist whose key mineral is kyanite.

segments.title: Work backward from the rock
segments.description:
Each student reads two rock descriptions and writes the rock name and a likely parent rock for each (five minutes).
Pairs compare for two minutes.
The teacher hears two pairs, asks the conditions behind each rock, and the class settles any disagreement from the evidence (three minutes).
segments.teacherNotes:
Rock X: gneiss, parent shale or granite; conditions: high grade with differential stress.
Rock Y: quartzite, parent quartz sandstone; heat and pressure recrystallized the grains, and foliation is not needed.
Accept granite or shale for X if reasoned.
Quartzite breaks through grains; sandstone breaks around them.
shown: Rock X: banded; light bands of quartz and feldspar alternate with dark bands of biotite and amphibole; grains visible; no fizz.
Rock Y: light, not foliated; interlocking quartz grains; breaks through the grains, not around them; no fizz; not scratched by a steel nail.

segments.title: Summary and what the next lecture does
segments.description:
The teacher recaps agents, foliated versus non-foliated, and the grade sequence.
Students are told the next lecture places these rocks in plate settings and links all three rock types in the rock cycle.
segments.teacherNotes: Ask for the clue students find hardest to apply, and use it to open the next lecture.

segments.title: Granite in a collision zone
segments.description:
The teacher puts a prompt on the screen.
Each student writes a rock name and says whether it is foliated.
Two students share an answer.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: gneiss, foliated; quartz, feldspar and mica align and segregate into bands. A student who answers granite gneiss is right. Do not explain settings yet.
shown: Granite is buried and squeezed in a collision zone. Name the rock it could become and say whether it is foliated.

segments.title: Where metamorphism happens
segments.description:
The teacher links three settings to plate tectonics from earlier in the course: contact halos around intrusions, regional belts in collision zones, and subduction zones.
Students then tell a partner for two minutes which setting makes a wide belt and which a narrow halo, and why.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: regional is wide because whole crust is heated and squeezed; contact is narrow because heat travels only a short way from the intrusion. Subduction zones give high pressure at low temperature because cold crust sinks fast. Link to Earle, ch. 7.
shown: Table: Setting | Main agents | Typical rocks / Contact, beside an intrusion | heat, fluids | hornfels, marble / Regional, collision zone | heat, differential stress | slate, schist, gneiss / Subduction zone | high pressure, low temperature | blueschist

segments.title: Name the rock
segments.description:
Each student writes the likely rock for each of four protolith and condition pairs.
The teacher hears two answers with the clue used, and the class says whether each rock is foliated.
segments.teacherNotes:
Answers:
1 Shale, low grade with differential stress: slate, foliated.
2 Limestone beside an intrusion: marble, not foliated.
3 Quartz sandstone, heated and buried: quartzite, not foliated.
4 Granite, high grade with differential stress: gneiss, foliated.
shown: 1. Shale, low temperature, differential stress
2. Limestone beside a hot intrusion
3. Quartz sandstone, heated and deeply buried
4. Granite, very high temperature, strong differential stress

segments.title: The rock cycle and its processes
segments.description:
The teacher draws the three rock types on the board and labels every arrow with its process.
Before the shortcuts are drawn, each student lists the routes an igneous rock can take.
The teacher then adds the shortcuts and stresses that no path is compulsory.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected routes: weathering to sediment; metamorphism to a metamorphic rock; remelting to magma. Shortcuts: igneous to metamorphic without sediment; sedimentary rock to sediment through uplift, exposure, weathering and erosion, then to another sedimentary rock through deposition and lithification. Error: the cycle runs in one direction only. Uplift brings buried rock to the surface.
shown: Table: Process | From | To / Weathering, erosion, deposition | any rock | sediment / Lithification | sediment | sedimentary rock / Metamorphism | any rock | metamorphic rock / Melting | any rock | magma / Crystallization | magma | igneous rock

segments.title: Trace a quartz grain
segments.description:
Each student writes the path of a quartz grain from granite to quartzite and names the process at each step (six minutes).
Partners check each other’s lists (one minute).
The teacher hears two pairs (two minutes).
segments.teacherNotes: Expected path: uplift and exposure; weathering; erosion and river transport; deposition; burial and lithification into quartz sandstone; metamorphism into quartzite; uplift and weathering again. Quartz survives weathering, as taught earlier in the course. Accept wind transport if reasoned.
shown: Follow one quartz grain: granite → ? → quartzite. Write each step and name the process.

segments.title: Invent a shortcut journey
segments.description:
Each student picks a starting rock and invents a journey that skips at least one rock type, naming the process on every arrow (six minutes).
Partners check that each arrow has a real process (two minutes).
The teacher hears two or three journeys, and the class tests each one (two minutes).
segments.teacherNotes: Example answers: basalt buried and heated becomes metamorphic rock without any sediment stage; limestone exposed by uplift and erosion undergoes physical weathering; its carbonate fragments are transported, deposited and lithified into clastic limestone; gneiss melts to magma, which cools and crystallizes slowly into granite. Reject any arrow with no process named.

segments.title: Summary and the lab ahead
segments.description:
The teacher recaps the grade sequence, the non-foliated rocks and the cycle’s processes.
Students are told the next meeting is the lab, done in pairs with the department’s hand samples.
The teacher reminds them that Lab reports: Sedimentary rocks is due at the start of the lab, and that goggles are required for the acid bottle.
segments.teacherNotes: Ask students which pair of rocks they find hardest to tell apart, and use it to open the lab.

segments.title: Report due, safety and pairs
segments.description:
Lab reports: Sedimentary rocks is due now, at the start of this lab.
The teacher states the rules: closed-toe shoes, the dilute HCl bottle used only with goggles on, and samples kept in their trays and returned where they came from.
Students form pairs, and each pair takes a tray set and the Metamorphic rock identification sheet: bench method, which holds the lab rules, the tests and how much of each to use, and room for the pair's own steps.
Each pair writes its pair members and tray number on the sheet.
segments.teacherNotes:
A missed lab can be made up in the same week’s open lab hour.
Safety: check shoes at the door. Goggles go on before the acid bottle is touched; one small drop per test. Rinse skin or eyes with water at once and report it. Samples have sharp edges; handle them over the tray. Taste nothing.
The pair's own steps are written later, after the method is modeled.

segments.title: Method: describing a metamorphic rock
segments.description:
The teacher models the method on one tray sample that students will not meet later.
With goggles on, the teacher runs the fizz test on a fresh surface with one drop.
Pairs predict the fizz result on a second sample, then watch the test.
Pairs write the steps in their own words on the sheet.
segments.teacherNotes: Record observations before naming the rock. Foliation first: is there alignment? Then grain size, visible minerals, hardness (steel nail), fizz. Test a fresh surface. Infer a likely parent rock last. Estimate grade only where the texture and mineral assemblage support it; record grade as undetermined for samples whose observations do not establish it. Wipe the acid dropper after each test and cap the bottle.
shown: Steps: foliation, present or not → grain size → visible minerals → hardness → fizz on a fresh surface → parent rock and grade

segments.title: Foliated rocks station
segments.description:
Each pair records foliation type, grain size, visible minerals, rock name and likely parent rock for every foliated sample in the tray.
The pair then orders the samples from lowest to highest grade and writes the clue for each step.
The teacher circulates and checks the first sample with each pair.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected samples: slate (dull, splits flat); phyllite (silky sheen); schist (visible mica, garnet may show); gneiss (light and dark bands). If the tray differs, the method holds. Grade order follows grain size and foliation type.

segments.title: Break
segments.description: Students step away from the benches. Samples stay in their trays and goggles are put aside.
segments.teacherNotes: Use the time to set out the non-foliated trays and the parent-rock trays.

segments.title: Non-foliated rocks station
segments.description:
Each pair records fizz, hardness, texture, rock name and likely parent rock for each non-foliated sample in the tray.
Acid is used on a fresh surface, one drop per sample, goggles on.
Pairs then write two lines on how to tell marble from quartzite.
segments.teacherNotes:
Expected samples and answers: marble, fizzes, scratched by a steel nail, parent limestone; quartzite, no fizz, not scratched by the nail, parent quartz sandstone; hornfels, fine-grained, hard and non-foliated, commonly derived from mudstone or shale; verify the color and acid response of the department’s specimen before using them as identification clues.
Marble: crystals shine in a bright light; quartzite breaks through grains.

segments.title: Parent and product
segments.description:
Pairs match each metamorphic sample to its likely parent rock from the sedimentary and igneous trays, or from photographs if a parent is missing.
For each match, they write what changed in the rock and which agent caused it.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected matches: shale to slate; limestone to marble; quartz sandstone to quartzite; granite to gneiss. Changes: recrystallization, new minerals, alignment. The new rock often retains approximately the parent’s bulk composition, but fluids can change it. Composition supports a possible match; it does not prove the parent rock.

segments.title: Identify three unknowns
segments.description:
Each pair receives three unlabeled samples from the department’s hand samples.
For each, they run the method, name the rock, say whether it is foliated, and give its parent rock.
The teacher checks each pair’s names against the key.
segments.teacherNotes:
Example set and key:
banded, light and dark, visible grains: gneiss, foliated, parent granite or shale.
silvery flakes with garnet crystals: garnet schist, foliated, parent shale.
white granular rock, fizzes, scratched by a nail: marble, not foliated, parent limestone.
Swap in available samples.

segments.title: Trace one sample around the rock cycle
segments.description:
Each pair picks one sample from its tray and writes the path from its parent rock to that sample, then on to a new rock.
The pair names the process on every arrow.
One pair shares its path with the class.
segments.teacherNotes: Example answer for marble: shell fragments accumulate on a sea floor and undergo burial, compaction and cementation to form limestone; heat from an intrusion causes metamorphism to marble; uplift and erosion expose it; physical weathering produces carbonate fragments; transport, deposition and lithification form a new clastic limestone. Check every arrow has a process.

segments.title: Clean-up, assignments and what comes next
segments.description:
Pairs return samples to their trays and trays to where they came from, wipe benches and put goggles away.
The teacher sets Lab reports (30%), each student’s own work, done and scored alone, due at the start of the lab of Geologic time and how rocks are dated.
The teacher sets Weekly online quizzes (10%), each student’s own work, done and scored alone, due at the first meeting of Geologic time and how rocks are dated, submitted online before that meeting.
Students read Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, ch. 8 (Measuring Geological Time) before that lesson.
Later in the course, students will study relative dating principles, unconformities, radiometric dating with half-lives, and the geologic time scale from the Hadean to the present.
A short practice quiz on this lesson can be taken after class; it counts toward no part of the grade.
segments.teacherNotes: Count trays and goggles before students leave. Make sure the acid bottle is capped and stored.

keyIdeas: Metamorphism changes a rock in the solid state, without melting it. Heat, pressure and hot fluids make its minerals recrystallize or react to form new ones. The starting rock is the protolith.

Foliation forms when differential stress aligns platy minerals such as mica and chlorite. Rock grade rises through slate, phyllite, schist and gneiss. Heating without differential stress can produce non-foliated hornfels. Marble and quartzite are generally non-foliated because calcite and quartz do not readily develop a preferred alignment, even under differential stress.

Parent rock and conditions together explain a metamorphic rock. Shale gives slate, limestone gives marble, quartz sandstone gives quartzite, and granite or shale can give gneiss. Index minerals (chlorite, biotite, garnet, staurolite, kyanite, sillimanite) mark rising grade.
Metamorphism occurs in a few plate-tectonic settings. Contact metamorphism makes a narrow halo around an intrusion. Regional metamorphism makes broad belts in collision zones and deep burial.

The rock cycle links igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks through named processes: weathering, erosion, deposition, lithification, metamorphism, melting, crystallization and uplift. It is not a one-way loop, and any rock can take shortcuts.

vocabulary.definition: Change in a rock’s minerals and texture in the solid state, caused by heat, pressure or hot fluids.
The original rock, before metamorphism changed it.
The intensity of metamorphism, shown by grain size, foliation type and index minerals.
Pressure that is stronger in one direction than in others, which aligns platy minerals.
A layered or banded texture caused by aligned minerals in a metamorphic rock.
A high-grade foliated rock with coarse bands of light and dark minerals.
A hard, non-foliated rock formed when quartz sandstone recrystallizes.
The set of processes that change rocks among igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic types.

slides.title: Metamorphic rocks and the rock cycle
bullets: Heat, pressure and fluids change rocks
Reading: Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, ch. 7 (to confirm)
slides.notes: Open by saying what this lecture builds. Students learn how heat, pressure and hot fluids change a rock in the solid state, how foliated and non-foliated rocks form, and how to identify a metamorphic rock from its foliation and its parent rock. The next lecture places these rocks in plate settings and links all three rock types in the rock cycle. The chapter to have read is Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, ch. 7, on metamorphic rocks.

slides.title: Two rocks, mostly calcite
slides.notes:
Weekly online quizzes: Sedimentary rocks is due now. Students submitted it online before this meeting, so nothing is collected in class.

Put the two rocks side by side on the screen. Each student writes one sentence on what could turn the first rock into the second. Then hear two students read their sentences aloud.

Expected: heat and pressure recrystallize the calcite and destroy the shells. Do not correct vocabulary yet; the next part of the lecture supplies it. Point out that both rocks fizz because both are calcite, so the change is in texture, not in composition.

visual.ask: Both rocks are mostly calcite. In one sentence, what could turn the first into the second?

slides.title: Metamorphism: change in the solid state
bullets: A protolith becomes a new rock without melting
Heat: from about 200 °C to the start of melting
Geothermal gradient: about 25 °C per km
Confining pressure versus differential stress
Hot fluids carry ions and speed reactions
slides.notes:
Define metamorphism as change in the solid state, from a protolith to a new rock. Give the temperature range: from about 200 °C up to the start of melting. Separate heat from the geothermal gradient (about 25 °C per km) and from heat given off by intrusions. Separate confining pressure, which squeezes equally from all sides, from differential stress, which is stronger in one direction. Explain the role of hot fluids carrying ions.

Common error: metamorphism means melting. If partial melting starts, melt forms while some minerals remain solid. The melt enters the igneous part of the cycle when it cools and crystallizes.

Before contact and regional metamorphism are explained, each student writes whether shale baked beside a granite intrusion would be foliated, and why. Expected prediction: not foliated, because heat acts without differential stress, so hornfels forms. Take answers after they have written. Link to Earle, ch. 7.

slides.title: Contact, regional, hydrothermal or burial?
bullets: 1. Mudstone in a thin halo against the edge of a granite intrusion
2. Shale in the core of a mountain belt where two continents collided
3. Basalt on a mid-ocean ridge flank, circulated by hot seawater
4. Sandstone buried under about 10 km of sediment in a deep basin
slides.notes:
Each student writes the type of metamorphism for each of the four settings. Then hear two answers, each with the main agent of change behind it, and let the class settle any disagreement.

Answers, for after students have written:
1. Contact (hornfels); the agent is heat.
2. Regional (schist or gneiss); the agents are heat and differential stress.
3. Hydrothermal alteration, neither contact nor regional; the agent is fluids.
4. Burial; the agent is confining pressure with rising temperature.
Accept a second agent if the student reasons from the setting.

slides.title: Rising grade: shale to gneiss
bullets: Foliation: platy minerals aligned by differential stress
slides.notes:
Before this slide goes up, students have predicted what shale becomes at slightly higher temperature and which feature changes. Take their predictions first, then show the sequence.

Expected prediction: slate, with tiny aligned mica and chlorite. Explain that differential stress aligns platy minerals perpendicular to the greatest compressive stress, and that this alignment is foliation. Grain size grows with grade. Gneiss bands are light quartz and feldspar alternating with dark biotite and amphibole.

visual.note: Each step is a rock sample, from shale up to gneiss. Watch the flat layers line up and the grains grow.
parts: Shale: the bottom step
Slate: dull, splits flat
Phyllite: silky sheen
Schist: visible mica, garnet
Gneiss: light and dark bands

slides.title: Index minerals and non-foliated rocks
slides.notes:
Index minerals (chlorite, biotite, garnet, staurolite, kyanite, sillimanite) mark rising grade in a shale-derived sequence. Link them to the rocks on the previous slide: chlorite goes with slate, and garnet can show in schist. Across unrelated samples, one index mineral alone does not settle relative grade, because pressure and bulk composition also matter.

Then turn to the table of non-foliated rocks. Marble and quartzite are generally non-foliated because calcite and quartz do not readily develop a preferred alignment, even under differential stress. Hornfels forms where heat acts without differential stress, as in mudstone or shale baked beside an intrusion.

Watch for students calling the visible calcite crystals in marble foliation. Foliation needs alignment, and marble has none.

slides.title: Index minerals and non-foliated rocks (continued)
slides.notes: Walk the table: limestone gives marble, quartz sandstone gives quartzite, and mudstone baked beside an intrusion gives hornfels. Ask which of the three could also form under differential stress without becoming foliated, and why.

slides.title: Which has the higher grade?
bullets: Pair 1. Rock A: phyllite, silky sheen, grains too small to see. Rock B: schist, visible mica flakes and garnet crystals.
Pair 2. Rock A: a schist whose key mineral is biotite with garnet. Rock B: a schist whose key mineral is kyanite.
slides.notes:
For each pair, each student writes which rock has the higher grade and the clue that decided it (four minutes). Pairs then compare their choices for two minutes, and you hear two or three explanations.

Answers, for after students have written:
Pair 1: Rock B. Visible mica and garnet mean coarser grains and higher grade than the silky, fine-grained phyllite.
Pair 2: Rock B, if these are comparable shale-derived rocks from the same Barrovian sequence. The kyanite zone is higher grade than the garnet zone in that sequence. Across unrelated samples, kyanite versus garnet alone does not establish relative grade; pressure, bulk composition and the full mineral assemblage also matter.

Common slip: choosing by color. Grade shows in grain size, foliation type and index minerals.

slides.title: Name the rock and a likely parent
bullets: Rock X: banded; light bands of quartz and feldspar alternate with dark bands of biotite and amphibole; grains visible; no fizz.
Rock Y: light, not foliated; interlocking quartz grains; breaks through the grains, not around them; no fizz; not scratched by a steel nail.
slides.notes:
Each student reads the two descriptions and writes a rock name and a likely parent rock for each. Pairs compare. Then hear two pairs, ask the conditions behind each rock, and let the class settle any disagreement from the evidence.

Answers, for after students have written:
Rock X: gneiss; parent shale or granite; high grade with differential stress. Accept either parent if the student reasons from the evidence.
Rock Y: quartzite; parent quartz sandstone. Heat and pressure recrystallized the grains, and foliation is not needed. Quartzite breaks through its grains, while sandstone breaks around them.

slides.title: Metamorphic settings and the rock cycle
bullets: Where metamorphism happens in plate settings
How the rock cycle links all three rock types
slides.notes: This meeting builds on the previous lecture of this lesson, where students met the agents of metamorphism, foliation and the grade sequence. Today the rocks are placed in plate-tectonic settings, and then igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks are linked through the rock cycle. The reading remains Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, ch. 7.

slides.title: Granite in a collision zone
bullets: Granite is buried and squeezed in a collision zone. Name the rock it could become and say whether it is foliated.
slides.notes:
Put the prompt on the screen. Each student writes a rock name and says whether it is foliated. Then two students share an answer.

Expected: gneiss, foliated. Quartz, feldspar and mica align and segregate into bands. A student who answers granite gneiss is right. Do not explain settings yet; the next slide does that.

slides.title: Where metamorphism happens
bullets: Which makes a wide belt? Which a narrow halo? Why?
slides.notes:
Link the three settings to plate tectonics from earlier in the course: contact halos around intrusions, regional belts in collision zones, and subduction zones. Then students tell a partner for two minutes which setting makes a wide belt and which a narrow halo, and why.

Expected: regional metamorphism is wide because the whole crust is heated and squeezed. Contact metamorphism is narrow because heat travels only a short way from the intrusion. Subduction zones give high pressure at low temperature because cold crust sinks fast, which is why blueschist forms there. Link to Earle, ch. 7.

slides.title: Name the likely rock for each
bullets: 1. Shale, low temperature, differential stress
2. Limestone beside a hot intrusion
3. Quartz sandstone, heated and deeply buried
4. Granite, very high temperature, strong differential stress
slides.notes:
Each student writes the likely rock for each of the four protolith and condition pairs. Then hear two answers with the clue used, and the class says whether each rock is foliated.

Answers, for after students have written:
1. Slate, foliated (low grade with differential stress).
2. Marble, not foliated.
3. Quartzite, not foliated.
4. Gneiss, foliated (high grade with differential stress).

slides.title: The rock cycle and its processes
bullets: List the routes an igneous rock can take.
slides.notes:
Draw the three rock types on the board and label every arrow with its process, using the table. Before you draw the shortcuts, each student lists the routes an igneous rock can take.

Expected routes: weathering to sediment; metamorphism to a metamorphic rock; remelting to magma. Then add the shortcuts on the board: igneous to metamorphic without any sediment stage; a sedimentary rock returning to sediment through uplift, exposure, weathering and erosion, then becoming another sedimentary rock through deposition and lithification. Stress that no path is compulsory and the cycle does not run in one direction only. Uplift brings buried rock to the surface.

slides.title: Trace a quartz grain
bullets: Follow one quartz grain: granite → ? → quartzite. Write each step and name the process.
slides.notes:
Each student writes the path of a quartz grain from granite to quartzite and names the process at each step (six minutes). Partners check each other’s lists (one minute). Then hear two pairs.

Expected path: uplift and exposure; weathering; erosion and river transport; deposition; burial and lithification into quartz sandstone; metamorphism into quartzite; uplift and weathering again. Quartz survives weathering, as taught earlier in the course. Accept wind transport if the student reasons from it.

slides.title: Invent a shortcut journey
bullets: Pick a starting rock
Invent a journey that skips at least one rock type
Name the process on every arrow
slides.notes:
Each student picks a starting rock and invents a journey. Partners then check that each arrow has a real process. Hear two or three journeys and have the class test each one. Reject any arrow with no process named.

Example answers to compare against:
- Basalt buried and heated becomes metamorphic rock without any sediment stage.
- Limestone exposed by uplift and erosion undergoes physical weathering; its carbonate fragments are transported, deposited and lithified into clastic limestone.
- Gneiss melts to magma, which cools and crystallizes slowly into granite.

slides.title: Summary and the lab ahead
bullets: Grade sequence: slate, phyllite, schist, gneiss
Non-foliated: marble, quartzite, hornfels
Processes link igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
Lab reports: Sedimentary rocks is due at the start of the lab
Next time: lab in pairs; goggles for the acid bottle
slides.notes:
Recap the grade sequence, the non-foliated rocks and the cycle’s processes. Tell students that next time is the lab, done in pairs with the department’s hand samples. Remind them that Lab reports: Sedimentary rocks, which counts toward Lab reports (30%), is due at the start of the lab, and that goggles are required for the acid bottle.

Ask students which pair of rocks they find hardest to tell apart, and use the answer to open the lab.

slides.title: Metamorphic rocks lab: identify and trace
bullets: Done in pairs with the department’s hand samples
Goggles on before the acid bottle is touched
slides.notes: Lab reports: Sedimentary rocks is due now, at the start of this lab. State the rules: closed-toe shoes, the dilute HCl bottle used only with goggles on, and samples kept in their trays and returned where they came from. Pairs then form and take a tray set and the bench method sheet.

slides.title: Method: describing a metamorphic rock
slides.notes:
Model the method on one tray sample that students will not meet later. With goggles on, run the fizz test on a fresh surface with one drop. Pairs predict the fizz result on a second sample, then watch the test. Pairs then write the steps in their own words on the bench method sheet.

Record observations before naming the rock. Foliation first: is there alignment? Then grain size, visible minerals, hardness (steel nail), fizz. Test a fresh surface. Infer a likely parent rock last. Estimate grade only where the texture and mineral assemblage support it; record grade as undetermined for samples whose observations do not establish it. Wipe the acid dropper after each test and cap the bottle.

slides.title: Due and reading
bullets: Lab reports (30%): due at the start of the lab of Geologic time and how rocks are dated
Weekly online quizzes (10%): due at the first meeting of Geologic time and how rocks are dated, submitted online before that meeting
Read before that lesson: Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, ch. 8 (to confirm) (Measuring Geological Time)
slides.notes:
Set both graded pieces before students leave, naming each and when it is due. Each is a student’s own work, done and scored alone. Then give the reading: Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, ch. 8 (Measuring Geological Time). Later in the course, students will study relative dating principles, unconformities, radiometric dating with half-lives, and the geologic time scale from the Hadean to the present. A short practice quiz on this lesson can be taken after class; it counts toward no part of the grade.

Before students leave, count trays and goggles, and make sure the acid bottle is capped and stored.

study.overview: Metamorphism changes a rock in the solid state, without melting it, when heat, pressure and hot fluids make its minerals recrystallize or react to form new ones. Any metamorphic rock is explained by two things together: the parent rock (the protolith) and the conditions that acted on it. The rock cycle then links metamorphic rocks to igneous and sedimentary rocks through named processes. Read this guide with the metamorphic rocks chapter of Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition.

points.heading: Metamorphism: solid-state change driven by heat, pressure and fluids
points.explanation: Metamorphism runs from about 200 °C up to the temperature where melting starts. Heat comes from burial and from nearby intrusions. The geothermal gradient is about 25 °C per km, so a mudstone buried to about 8 km is roughly 200 °C warmer than it was at the surface and is reaching the lower edge of the range. Pressure comes in two kinds. Confining pressure squeezes equally from all sides and does not align minerals. Differential stress is stronger in one direction, and it is what produces alignment. Hot fluids carry dissolved ions in and out of the rock and speed up mineral reactions. The setting tells you which agents dominate. Contact metamorphism makes a narrow halo around an intrusion, because heat travels only a short distance, and it is mostly heat and fluids. Regional metamorphism makes broad belts in collision zones and in deep burial, with heat and differential stress acting over a large volume of crust. Subduction zones give high pressure at low temperature because cold crust sinks quickly, and the typical rock is blueschist. Metamorphism does not mean melting. If partial melting begins, the melt separates from the minerals that stay solid, and it joins the igneous part of the cycle when it cools and crystallizes.

points.heading: Foliation, grade and the non-foliated rocks
points.explanation: Foliation forms when differential stress aligns platy minerals such as mica and chlorite perpendicular to the greatest compressive stress. As grade rises, grain size grows and the rock changes in this order. Slate is dull and splits into flat sheets. Phyllite has a silky sheen but grains too small to see. Schist has visible mica flakes, and garnet may show. Gneiss has light bands of quartz and feldspar alternating with dark bands of biotite and amphibole. Rank two samples by grain size, foliation type and index minerals, never by color. Index minerals mark rising grade; learn their order from your lecture slide and Earle’s chapter. Some rocks are non-foliated. Heating without differential stress, as beside an intrusion, gives a fine-grained, hard rock such as hornfels. Calcite and quartz do not readily develop a preferred alignment, so marble and quartzite are generally non-foliated even under differential stress. Take care with one trap: visible interlocking crystals are a texture, not foliation. Foliation means the minerals are aligned or banded. For example, when a quartz sandstone is heated and buried, its grains recrystallize into an interlocking mosaic with no alignment, and the broken surface cuts through the grains rather than around them.

points.heading: Reading a hand sample: observe first, then infer the parent
points.explanation: Work in a fixed order and record what you see before you name the rock. First check for alignment or banding. Then note grain size and visible minerals. Scratch the sample with a steel nail to test hardness. Last, run the fizz test on a fresh surface with one small drop of dilute HCl and goggles on. Only then infer a likely parent rock and, if the evidence supports it, a grade. Suppose a sample is dark, fine-grained, hard enough that a steel nail does not scratch it, with no alignment and no fizz. That fits hornfels, and a mudstone or shale parent heated by an intrusion is a reasonable inference. Composition supports a possible parent but does not prove it. A new rock often keeps roughly the bulk composition of its parent, but fluids can change that, and different parents can give similar products. If your observations do not establish grade, record it as undetermined rather than guessing. When you write up your own samples, report only what you actually observed and say where more than one identification is possible.

points.heading: The rock cycle: named processes and shortcuts
points.explanation: The cycle links igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks through eight named processes. Weathering, erosion and deposition turn any rock into sediment. Lithification turns sediment into sedimentary rock. Metamorphism turns any rock into metamorphic rock. Melting turns any rock into magma. Crystallization turns magma into igneous rock. Uplift brings buried rock to the surface, where weathering can begin. The cycle is not a one-way loop, and no path is compulsory. When you draw a path, name the process on every arrow and check that each process fits its starting material and its product. For example, only sediment is lithified and only magma crystallizes. Here is a shortcut that skips a rock type. A sandstone or mudstone carried down and heated until it melts to magma is drawn on the cycle as one melting arrow, and the magma cools slowly and crystallizes into an igneous rock. On the diagram this route skips the metamorphic box, although in a real collision zone the rock recrystallizes on its way to melting. A journey back to the surface needs a different set of steps: uplift, then weathering, erosion, deposition and lithification, and these end in a new sedimentary rock.

handouts.title: Metamorphic rock identification sheet: bench method

blocks.text: Keep this sheet at your bench. It holds the lab rules, the tests and how much of each to use, and room for your pair's own version of the method.
Lab rules

items: Wear closed-toe shoes.
Put goggles on before you touch the acid bottle. The bottle holds dilute HCl and is used only with goggles on.
Handle samples over the tray, because they have sharp edges. Samples stay in their trays and go back where they came from.
Taste nothing.
If acid touches skin or eyes, rinse with water at once and tell the teacher.

blocks.text: Tests and amounts

items: Fizz test: use a fresh surface, one small drop of dilute HCl, goggles on. Wipe the dropper after each test and cap the bottle.
Hardness: try to scratch the sample with a steel nail.
Alignment: look for platy minerals lying parallel, or for light and dark bands.
Record what you observe before you name the rock.

blocks.hint: Write the steps of the method in your own words, in the order you would do them.

handouts.key:
Pair members: the names of both students working together.
Tray number: the identifier on the pair’s tray.

Method in the pair’s own words: Accept a clear sequence that records observations before assigning a rock name. A suitable answer is:
1. Keep the sample over its tray. Look for parallel platy minerals, cleavage surfaces, or alternating light and dark mineral bands.
2. Record grain size and visible minerals. Distinguish individual mineral grains from compositional bands.
3. Test whether a steel nail scratches the sample. Record a groove, not merely a metal streak.
4. Put goggles on before touching the acid bottle. Apply one small drop of dilute HCl to a fresh surface and record whether it fizzes. Wipe the dropper after the test and cap the bottle.
5. Use the observations to name the rock and identify a likely parent rock.
6. Estimate metamorphic grade only when texture and mineral assemblage support it. Otherwise record undetermined.
7. Return the sample to its tray and the tray to its original place.

Look for safe handling, the specified test amount, observations before interpretation, and a parent-rock inference supported by composition and texture. Common slips: treating sparkling crystals as foliation; calling a metal streak a scratch; naming the rock before recording evidence; assigning a precise grade from color alone.

handouts.title: Metamorphic rock identification sheet: foliated rocks

blocks.text: Record every foliated sample in your tray. Use one row for each sample and leave unused rows blank. Write what you observe first, then name the rock and its likely parent rock.
Now order your samples from lowest to highest grade. Put the lowest grade in row 1 and the highest grade last. For each row, write the clue that decided its place.

handouts.key:
Rows A–E: Each sample letter refers to the specimen bearing that letter in the pair’s tray. Accept observations and identifications that agree with that specimen. Leave unused rows blank. The following entries give the expected rock descriptions in column order: Foliation | Grain | Minerals | Rock | Parent.

Slate: closely spaced slaty cleavage; splits into flat sheets | very fine; individual metamorphic minerals generally not visible | fine mica and chlorite may be inferred, but need not be identifiable by eye | slate | shale or mudstone.
Phyllite: wavy foliation with a silky sheen | fine; mica generally too small to distinguish individually | fine mica; report only minerals supported by observation | phyllite | shale or mudstone.
Schist: parallel, readily visible platy minerals; schistosity | medium to coarse | visible mica, commonly with quartz; garnet only if present | schist, or garnet schist when garnet is present | commonly shale or mudstone.
Gneiss: alternating light and dark compositional bands | medium to coarse | commonly quartz and feldspar in light bands, with biotite or amphibole in dark bands | gneiss | granite or shale; accept either when supported by mineral composition.
An additional foliated specimen receives its own observation-based entry; it need not represent an additional grade.

Grade-order rows: For the typical shale-derived sequence, enter the actual sample identifiers in this order: slate → phyllite → schist → gneiss. Clues, in the same order: very fine grains and slaty cleavage; silky sheen from fine aligned mica; individually visible mica and possible garnet; compositional banding and a mineral assemblage consistent with high-grade metamorphism. Use only the rows needed. Equivalent specimens may share a position. A granite-derived gneiss is high grade, but its presence does not establish that every specimen shares a parent rock.

Look for texture and minerals supporting each placement. Common slips: using color as the deciding clue; confusing sedimentary bedding with metamorphic foliation; treating grain size alone as a universal measure of grade. Source: Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, section 7.2, [Classification of Metamorphic Rocks](https://opentextbc.ca/physicalgeology2ed/chapter/7-2-classification-of-metamorphic-rocks/).

handouts.title: Metamorphic rock identification sheet: non-foliated rocks

blocks.text: Record every non-foliated sample in your tray. Run the fizz test on a fresh surface with one drop, goggles on. Test hardness with the steel nail. Use one row for each sample and leave unused rows blank.

blocks.hint: Write two lines on how to tell marble from quartzite, using what you observed at the bench.

handouts.key:
Rows A–D: Match each sample letter to the actual specimen in the tray. Leave unused rows blank. Expected entries appear in column order: Fizz | Hardness | Texture | Rock | Parent.

Calcite marble: fizzes with dilute HCl | scratched by a steel nail; calcite has Mohs hardness 3 | interlocking calcite crystals, commonly sugary or crystalline, without preferred alignment | marble | limestone.
Quartzite: no fizz | a steel nail does not scratch the quartz grains; quartz has Mohs hardness 7 | tightly interlocking quartz grains, commonly granular; fractures commonly cut through grains | quartzite | quartz sandstone.
Hornfels: commonly no fizz in a shale-derived specimen; record the observed response | commonly resistant to a steel nail, but mineral composition controls the result | fine-grained, compact, non-foliated; larger crystals may occur | hornfels | commonly shale or mudstone.
A further specimen receives a separate observation-based entry, even if it duplicates a rock type.

Two-line comparison: Calcite marble fizzes with dilute HCl and is scratched by a steel nail; its interlocking calcite crystals may sparkle. Quartzite does not fizz and resists scratching by a steel nail; its interlocking quartz texture commonly makes fractures cut through grains.

Look for both chemical response and hardness, supported by texture. Common slips: identifying either rock from white color alone; mistaking a nail’s metal streak for a scratch; treating sparkling crystals as foliation. Dolomitic marble may react weakly on an intact surface, so accept an identification supported by the specimen’s combined properties.

handouts.title: Parent and product table

blocks.text: Match each metamorphic sample to its likely parent rock from the sedimentary and igneous trays, or from photographs if a parent is missing. For each match, write what changed in the rock and which agent caused the change.

handouts.key:
Each occupied row records the actual metamorphic sample identifier, a plausible parent, the observed or inferred change, and its agent. Row order follows the pair’s specimens. Leave unused rows blank. Expected matches, in column order: Sample | Parent | Change | Agent.

Slate specimen | shale or mudstone | fine minerals recrystallize and grow in a preferred orientation, producing slaty cleavage | heat and differential stress.
Marble specimen | limestone | calcite recrystallizes into interlocking crystals; fossils and sedimentary textures may be lost | heat; confining pressure may also accompany burial.
Quartzite specimen | quartz sandstone | quartz grains and cement recrystallize into an interlocking texture | heat during metamorphism, commonly with burial pressure; differential stress is not required.
Gneiss specimen | granite | minerals recrystallize and develop light and dark compositional bands | heat and differential stress at high grade.

Accept shale as a possible parent for a suitable gneiss. Accept shale → schist or shale → phyllite when those specimens are used, with recrystallization, mineral growth, and alignment attributed to heat and differential stress. Accept shale or mudstone → hornfels, with fine-grained recrystallization attributed mainly to heat near an intrusion.

Look for a specific change and an agent that explains it. Composition supports a possible parent but does not uniquely establish it. Common slips: calling melting the process that forms a metamorphic rock; assuming every non-foliated rock formed without pressure; claiming fluids necessarily changed every specimen’s bulk composition.

handouts.title: Metamorphic rock identification sheet: three unknowns

blocks.text: Your pair has three unlabeled samples. For each one, run the method from your bench sheet: record your observations first, then name the rock, say whether it is foliated, and give its likely parent rock.

handouts.key:
For each row, use the observations of the specimen carrying that unknown identifier. The following is a worked example for the example specimens, in column order: Unknown | Alignment | Grain | Minerals | Fizz | Hardness | Rock | Foliated | Parent.

Unknown 1, if the banded specimen: alternating light and dark mineral bands | medium to coarse, with visible grains | quartz and feldspar in light bands; biotite or amphibole in dark bands when identifiable | normally no fizz | quartz and feldspar resist a steel nail; softer mica may scratch | gneiss | yes | granite or shale.
Unknown 2, if the silvery specimen with garnet: parallel mica flakes; schistosity | visible mica with larger garnet crystals | mica and garnet; quartz if observed | normally no fizz | mica scratches readily; garnet resists a steel nail | garnet schist | yes | shale or mudstone.
Unknown 3, if the white, granular, fizzing specimen: no preferred mineral alignment | visible interlocking grains | calcite | fizzes | scratched by a steel nail | marble | no | limestone.

Look for every cell to distinguish observation from interpretation. A hardness result may differ among minerals in one sample. Mineral names require recognizable evidence; a student may record a visible feature without confidently naming its mineral. Common slips: calling the garnet crystals foliation; identifying marble from color alone; treating granite as the only possible parent of gneiss.

handouts.title: Rock cycle path for one sample
handouts.usedIn: Trace one sample around the rock cycle

blocks.text: Pick one sample from your tray. Write the path from its parent rock to the sample, and then on to a new rock. Name the process on every arrow. Use one row for each arrow and leave unused rows blank.

blocks.caption: Path, one arrow to a row

handouts.key:
Sample blank: the identifier and rock name of the sample selected from the tray.

Accept any geologically plausible path that begins with its likely parent, reaches the chosen metamorphic sample, continues to a new rock, and names a process on every arrow. Leave unused rows blank.

Worked marble example, in table order From | Process | To:
Limestone | contact metamorphism: heat causes solid-state recrystallization of calcite | marble.
Marble | uplift and erosion of overlying material expose the rock | exposed marble.
Exposed marble | physical weathering | carbonate fragments.
Carbonate fragments | transport and deposition | deposited carbonate sediment.
Deposited carbonate sediment | burial, compaction, and cementation | clastic limestone.
Remaining row: blank.

Other valid paths include shale → slate through low-grade metamorphism with differential stress, followed by uplift and exposure, weathering and erosion, deposition, and lithification into a sedimentary rock; or granite → gneiss through high-grade metamorphism with differential stress, followed by partial melting to produce melt and cooling and crystallization to form a new igneous rock.

Look for explicit processes, plausible changes, and a completed route to a new rock. Intermediate sediment or magma is valid, but the path must continue until it forms a rock. Common slips: using time or pressure alone as the label for every arrow; making quartzite directly from loose sand without lithification or metamorphic consolidation; calling melting metamorphism; treating uplift alone as exposure when overlying rock still needs removal.
