Teacher: the dilute HCl bottle with a dropper, and goggles for every student
Teacher: a steel nail for each pair
Teacher: sedimentary and igneous parent-rock trays, or photographs of parent rocks
Teacher: three unlabeled hand samples for each pair, with the answer key
Teacher: the non-foliated trays and parent-rock trays set out during the break

l_89ba5a3d2696.title: Geologic time and how rocks are dated
l_89ba5a3d2696.summary: Relative dating principles, unconformities, radiometric dating with half-lives, and the geologic time scale from the Hadean to the present.
readings: Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, ch. 8 (to confirm) (Measuring Geological Time)
suggestedReadings: Dalrymple, The Age of the Earth (1991)

segments.title: Quiz due now and a stack of layers
segments.description:
Weekly online quizzes: Metamorphic rocks and the rock cycle is due now, and it was submitted online before this meeting.
Show four flat layers. Each student writes which layer is oldest, which is youngest, and one thing that must be true for the answer to hold.
Pairs compare, then two students are heard.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: conglomerate oldest, shale youngest, provided the layers are undisturbed, not overturned and not faulted. Students who only say ‘bottom is oldest’ have the rule but not its conditions. This links to the chapter on measuring geological time, read before this meeting.
shown: Layers: Shale → Sandstone → Limestone → Conglomerate
Prompt: These four layers are flat, with shale on top. Which layer is oldest, which is youngest, and what must be true for you to be sure?

segments.title: Superposition, horizontality, cross-cutting and inclusions
segments.description:
Pose the dike question first. Everyone writes an answer and a reason, then compares with a partner before two are heard.
Present the four principles, drawing one sketch for each on the board, crediting Nicolaus Steno for superposition and original horizontality and describing inclusions by a pebble in a conglomerate.
Students write one line per principle in their own words and do not copy the sketches.
Remind them that folded layers can be overturned, and that graded bedding, ripple marks and mud cracks from earlier in the course show which way was up.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: the dike is younger, because it cuts the layers. A common slip is to date a feature by where it sits rather than by what it cuts. Stress that the dike is younger than the host rock it bakes. The contact metamorphism happened when the dike intruded. One line per principle is enough; the board sketches carry the pictures.
shown: Prompt: A vertical basalt dike cuts across flat layers of sandstone, shale and limestone. Which is older, the dike or the layers? Write your answer and one reason.

Table: Principle | What it says / Original horizontality | Sediment settles in flat layers, so steeply tilted layers were moved later / Superposition | In undisturbed layers the oldest is at the bottom and the youngest is on top / Cross-cutting relationships | A dike, vein or fault is younger than the rocks it cuts / Inclusions | Fragments inside a rock are older than the rock that holds them

segments.title: Unconformities: gaps in the record
segments.description:
Ask students to sketch the events needed to leave tilted layers capped by flat layers. Pairs compare sketches.
The teacher draws the sequence of deposition, tilting, erosion and new deposition, and names it an angular unconformity, using Hutton’s visit to Siccar Point, Scotland, in 1788.
Then show disconformity and nonconformity side by side, and students label each in their notes.
segments.teacherNotes: Key point: an unconformity is a surface, and it stands for missing time, not a layer. Students often call it an event of its own; it is the erosion or non-deposition that left it. Siccar Point: tilted Silurian greywacke under flat Devonian red sandstone.
shown: Side by side: Disconformity: parallel layers above and below an erosion surface; the gap is hard to see | Angular unconformity: tilted older layers cut off by flat younger layers | Nonconformity: sedimentary layers resting on eroded igneous or metamorphic rock

segments.title: Order the events in a cross section
segments.description:
Show the cross section described in the table. Each student writes the seven events from oldest to youngest.
Pairs compare and settle any disagreement by pointing to the relationship that decides it.
The class then names the type of unconformity in the section.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer, oldest to youngest: sandstone, shale, limestone, dike, erosion, siltstone, fault. Principles: superposition for the three layers; the dike cuts them; the siltstone rests on the erosion surface and the dike does not cut it; the fault offsets everything. The surface is a disconformity, since the layers below are not tilted. Common error: placing the fault before the siltstone. It offsets the siltstone, so it is younger.
shown: Table: Feature | What you can see / Sandstone, shale, limestone | Flat layers, with sandstone at the bottom / Basalt dike | Cuts all three layers and ends at a flat erosion surface / Siltstone | Rests on the erosion surface; the dike does not cut it / Fault | Offsets everything, including the siltstone

segments.title: Fossils and correlation
segments.description:
Explain faunal succession through William Smith’s canal surveys in England around 1800, where he found the same fossils in the same order in distant outcrops.
Define an index fossil and show how two outcrops are correlated by one.
Pairs explain to each other why a species that lived for 200 million years would make a poor index fossil, then two are heard.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: it would be found in too wide a range of rocks to separate them. A good index fossil is widespread, abundant, easy to recognise and short-lived. Fossils only match layers; they give older or younger, not a number. That gap leads to the next meeting.
shown: Prompt: Why is a species that lived for 200 million years a poor index fossil? Explain to your partner.

segments.title: Summary and what comes next time
segments.description:
Each student writes one sentence: which principle dates a fault, and what relative dating cannot tell us.
The teacher sums up the principles, unconformities and index fossils.
Next time is half-lives and the geologic time scale: how a ratio of parent to daughter atoms becomes an age in years.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected sentence: cross-cutting dates the fault as younger than what it offsets; relative dating gives no age in years. Collect a few sentences aloud to open the next meeting.

segments.title: From order to numbers
segments.description:
Show the prompt. Each student writes one sentence, then compares with a partner.
Two students are heard, and the teacher links their answers to the need for a clock inside the rock.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: it cannot give how many years ago, or how long a gap lasted. Tie to the metamorphic rocks lesson: heating can reset a mineral’s clock, which is why the dated event matters.
shown: Prompt: Relative dating can show that a dike is younger than a limestone. What can it not tell us?

segments.title: Decay, half-lives and a worked age
segments.description:
Explain isotopes, a parent isotope decaying to a daughter isotope, and half-life as the time for half the parent to decay.
Show the first rows of the decay table. Students fill in only the parent left and the parent : daughter ratio for the rows at three and four half-lives, then check with a partner. The teacher gives the daughter fractions.
Introduce the charcoal calculation as a hypothetical example and work it on the board. Explain that its carbon-14 clock starts when the wood stops exchanging carbon with its surroundings. For the mineral calculations, assume the daughter counted was produced by decay and no parent or daughter atoms entered or escaped after the clock started.
segments.teacherNotes: Answers: 3 half-lives, parent 1/8, daughter 7/8 (given), 1:7; 4 half-lives, 1/16, 15/16 (given), 1:15. Misconception: after two half-lives all the parent is gone. It is a quarter, not none. K-40 only partly decays to Ar-40; the sums here simplify that.
shown: Table: Half-lives passed | Parent left | Daughter made | Parent : daughter / 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 : 0 / 1 | 1/2 | 1/2 | 1 : 1 / 2 | 1/4 | 3/4 | 1 : 3
Worked example: Charcoal from a hearth has 25% of its original carbon-14. 25% = 1/4 = 2 half-lives. Age = 2 × 5,730 years = 11,460 years.

segments.title: Work out the ages
segments.description:
Each student works the three problems alone, showing the number of half-lives for each. The rocks and measurements are hypothetical, and in every problem the daughter atoms counted were produced by decay, with no parent or daughter atoms entering or escaping after the clock started.
In the mica problem, daughter means all atoms produced by potassium-40 decay, including calcium-40 and argon-40; the requested ratio is not potassium-40 to argon-40.
Pairs then compare answers, and any pair that disagrees finds the step that differs.
The teacher goes over the third problem, which runs the calculation backward from a known age.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. 12.5% C-14 left: 3 half-lives, 17,190 years.
2. U-235 : Pb-207 = 1 : 3 (half-life 704 million): 2 half-lives, about 1.41 billion years.
3. Mica 2.5 billion years old, K-40 half-life 1.25 billion: 2 half-lives, 1/4 left, ratio 1 : 3.

segments.title: Which clock for which rock?
segments.description:
Show the isotope table and three cases. Each student chooses an isotope pair or method for each case and writes the reason in one sentence.
Pairs compare choices and settle differences.
Three students are heard, one per case.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. Hearth charcoal, about 9,000 years: carbon-14, since its half-life suits the span; uranium would show almost no decay.
2. Granite, about 3 billion years: U-Pb in zircon; too little carbon-14 remains for routine reliable dating beyond about 50,000 years.
3. Sandstone with fossils: date a volcanic ash bed above or below, not the sand grains, which date their source rocks.
shown: Table: Parent → daughter | Half-life | Useful for / Carbon-14 → nitrogen-14 | 5,730 years | wood, bone and shell younger than about 50,000 years / Uranium-235 → lead-207 | 704 million years | zircon in igneous rocks / Uranium-238 → lead-206 | 4.47 billion years | zircon in igneous rocks / Potassium-40 → argon-40 | 1.25 billion years | micas, feldspars and volcanic ash
Case 1: Charcoal from a hearth thought to be about 9,000 years old.
Case 2: A granite thought to be about 3 billion years old.
Case 3: A fossil-bearing sandstone, with a volcanic ash bed just above it. Do you date the sand grains or the ash?

segments.title: The geologic time scale
segments.description:
Present the four eons and the three eras of the Phanerozoic with their dates.
Point out that the boundaries were first drawn from fossils and later given numbers by radiometric dates.
Students copy the tables and mark which eon lasted longest.
segments.teacherNotes: Dates are rounded and shift slightly between sources; use those in the book. The Phanerozoic is 541 of 4,540 million years, about 12%. Many students think it is most of the story because it is the best known.
shown: Table: Eon | Span | Marker / Hadean | 4.54 to 4.0 billion years ago | Earth forms; oldest minerals, zircons of about 4.4 billion years / Archean | 4.0 to 2.5 billion years ago | oldest well-preserved rocks; first life / Proterozoic | 2.5 billion to 541 million years ago | oxygen builds up; complex cells and first animals / Phanerozoic | 541 million years ago to now | abundant visible fossils
Table: Era of the Phanerozoic | Span / Paleozoic | 541 to 252 million years ago / Mesozoic | 252 to 66 million years ago / Cenozoic | 66 million years ago to now

segments.title: Place the events
segments.description:
Show five events with their ages. Each student names the eon for each.
Pairs compare, then the class checks the answers together.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. Oldest zircons, 4.4 billion years ago: Hadean.
2. Stromatolites, 3.5 billion: Archean.
3. Cambrian explosion, about 540 million: Phanerozoic, at its base.
4. Non-bird dinosaurs die out, 66 million: Phanerozoic.
5. Homo sapiens, about 300,000 years ago: Phanerozoic.
shown: Event 1: The oldest known zircons, about 4.4 billion years ago.
Event 2: Stromatolites in Western Australia, about 3.5 billion years ago.
Event 3: The start of the Cambrian explosion of animals, about 540 million years ago.
Event 4: Non-bird dinosaurs die out, 66 million years ago.
Event 5: The first Homo sapiens, about 300,000 years ago.

segments.title: Summary and the lab ahead
segments.description:
The teacher sums up half-lives, the choice of clock and the time scale.
Weekly online quizzes (10%) is set before students leave. It is each student’s own work, done and scored alone. It is due at the first meeting of Earthquakes and submitted online before that meeting.
Next time is the lab, done in pairs with the department’s hand samples. Students wear closed-toe shoes.
segments.teacherNotes: The lesson’s own practice quiz is left for after class; it is mentioned at the end of the lab. Do not describe the Weekly online quizzes questions.

segments.title: Report due, safety and pairs
segments.description:
Lab reports: Metamorphic rocks and the rock cycle is due now.
Review safety: closed-toe shoes in the lab, and the acid bottle of dilute HCl used only with goggles on. Hand samples stay in their trays and go back where they came from.
Students sit in their lab pairs and collect one tray and one set of tools per bench.
segments.teacherNotes: Acid is not needed in this lab. If a pair wants a fizz test on a limestone clast, they must put on goggles first. Point out the eye-wash station. Coins should be kept off the floor to avoid slips.

segments.title: Method: ordering events from a sample or a section
segments.description:
Show the recording steps. For each feature, pairs write a letter, what they see, the relationship, and the principle that decides it.
Demonstrate on one sample, using a hand lens and a ruler, and find which way was up from graded bedding or ripple marks.
Pairs state their order as ‘A is older than B because...’ before moving on.
segments.teacherNotes: Remind pairs that a sample may be turned any way in the tray; they must find way-up from the rock, not from the tray. Samples go back to the same tray after use.
shown: Steps: Describe each feature → Name the relationship you can see → Write ‘older than’ or ‘younger than’ → Check the order has no contradiction

segments.title: Predict, then test: which is older?
segments.description:
The teacher sets three prepared hand samples on each bench: one with a vein or dike cutting across the rock, one conglomerate or breccia, and one with layers that show way-up.
Pairs write a prediction of the relative ages in each, then check with the lens and record the principle.
The class compares results for the sample that surprised them most.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: the vein is younger than the rock it cuts; clasts in the conglomerate are older than the rock that holds them; the layered sample is oldest at the bottom once way-up is found. If no vein sample is in the department’s trays, use a photo of one. Samples stay in their trays.

segments.title: Order events in cross sections
segments.description:
Pairs work the lab sheet Ordering events in cross sections. It holds two sections: one with a dike cutting tilted layers and truncated at the erosion surface beneath flat layers, and one with sedimentary layers on granite and gneiss, cut by a fault.
For each, they write the events from oldest to youngest and label every unconformity by type.
Pairs check their sequence by reading it aloud to another pair.
segments.teacherNotes: Section 1: sandstone, shale, limestone, tilting, dike, erosion, flat conglomerate, flat sandstone; angular unconformity. Section 2: gneiss, granite cuts it, erosion, sandstone, shale, fault; nonconformity. Common error: dating a layer from the fault rather than from what rests on it.

segments.title: Break
segments.description: Students step away from the benches. Samples stay in their trays.

segments.title: A half-life you can watch
segments.description:
Each pair starts with 64 coins in a cup. Each round they shake, tip out and remove the coins showing heads, which stand for decayed atoms.
They record the coins left after each of six rounds and plot parent left against round.
They then give the parent : daughter ratio after the third round and compare with their results.
segments.teacherNotes: The initial parent count is 64; expected counts after rounds 1 through 6 are 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, but real runs scatter, which is why real dating counts billions of atoms. Ratio after round 3: about 1 : 7. Keep coins on the bench and off the floor.

segments.title: Bracket the age of a shale
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Bracket the age of a shale”.
Show the data for a hypothetical shale resting on an ash bed and cut by a dike. Use a felsic dike in the displayed example, with zircon that crystallized during intrusion, and zircon that crystallized during the ash-producing eruption. Pairs calculate the two ages from the ratios and state the age range of the shale.
They name the eon the range falls in.
Pairs say why the shale itself is not dated directly.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. Ash bed under the shale, U-235 : Pb-207 = 1 : 3: 2 half-lives, 1,408 million years.
2. Dike cutting the shale, 1 : 1: 704 million years.
3. Shale is between 704 million and 1.41 billion years old: Proterozoic.
4. Its grains come from older rocks and date those, not the deposit.

segments.title: A scale model of Earth history
segments.description:
Pairs lay out a paper strip at 1 millimeter for every million years, with the present at one end.
They mark each event in the table at its distance, so 66 million years goes at 66 millimeters.
They then measure the Phanerozoic and write what fraction of the strip it fills.
segments.teacherNotes: Distances in meters: end-Cretaceous 0.066; end-Permian 0.252; Cambrian base 0.541; Great Oxidation 2.4; oldest zircons 4.4; Earth 4.54. The Phanerozoic is 541 mm of 4,540, about 12%. The strip is paper tape, 4.6 m long.

segments.title: Finish recording and clean up
segments.description:
Pairs finish their notes and check that their sequences and calculations agree.
They return every sample to the tray it came from, put coins back in the supply box and roll up the strip.
segments.teacherNotes: Count the trays before pairs leave.

segments.title: Assignments and what comes next
segments.description:
Lab reports (30%) is set now. It is each student’s own work, done and scored alone, due at the start of the lab of Earthquakes.
A short practice quiz on the lesson is there to take after class. It counts toward no grade.
Later in the course: how faults rupture, how P, S and surface waves travel, how magnitude and intensity are measured, and how epicenters are located. Before then, students read the chapter on earthquakes in Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition.

keyIdeas: Relative dating orders events without numbers. Original horizontality, superposition, cross-cutting relationships and inclusions each say which of two features is older, and an unconformity marks a gap in the record.
Fossils extend relative dating across distance. Faunal succession means an index fossil, a species that was widespread and short-lived, lets us match layers in different places.

Radiometric dating gives numeric ages. A parent isotope decays to a daughter isotope at a fixed rate, and a parent-to-radiogenic-daughter ratio of 1:1, 1:3 or 1:7 means one, two or three half-lives have passed, assuming no parent or daughter atoms entered or escaped.

Each isotope pair suits a certain span of time and certain minerals. Igneous rocks and ash beds date their own crystallization, so sedimentary layers are bracketed by dated igneous rocks above and below.

The geologic time scale joins relative and numeric dates into four eons (Hadean, Archean, Proterozoic, Phanerozoic), and the Phanerozoic, home of abundant visible fossils, is only about 12% of Earth’s history.

vocabulary.definition: In undisturbed layered rock, each layer is younger than the one beneath it.
A feature such as a dike, vein or fault is younger than the rock it cuts across.
A surface of erosion or non-deposition that marks a gap in the rock record; the main types are disconformity, angular unconformity and nonconformity.
A fossil of a species that was widespread and lived a short time, used to match and date layers in different places.
The time it takes for half of the parent atoms in a sample to decay to daughter atoms; the basis of radiometric dating.
The radioactive isotope that decays, such as uranium-238 or potassium-40.
The stable isotope made when a parent isotope decays, such as lead-206 or argon-40.
The longest division of the geologic time scale: Hadean, Archean, Proterozoic and Phanerozoic.

study.overview: Geologists date Earth’s rocks in two ways. Relative dating says which of two things is older, using rules about how rocks form and cut each other. Radiometric dating gives an age in years from the steady decay of unstable isotopes inside minerals. The geologic time scale joins the two into one calendar of Earth history, from the Hadean eon to the present. This guide covers the relative dating rules, fossils, half-lives and choosing a clock, and the time scale. For the full treatment, review the chapter on measuring geological time in Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition.

points.heading: Relative dating: four rules and the gaps between layers
points.explanation:
Four principles each tell you which of two features is older. Original horizontality: sediment settles in flat layers, so steeply tilted layers were moved after they formed. Superposition: in undisturbed layers the oldest is at the bottom and the youngest is on top. Cross-cutting relationships: a dike, vein or fault is younger than the rocks it cuts. Inclusions: fragments inside a rock, such as a pebble in a conglomerate, are older than the rock that holds them. Nicolaus Steno is credited with superposition and original horizontality. Superposition holds only if the layers have not been overturned or faulted, so the conditions matter as much as the rule.

An unconformity is a surface that stands for missing time, not a layer. It marks erosion or a pause in deposition. There are three types. A disconformity has parallel layers above and below the surface. An angular unconformity has tilted older layers cut off by flat younger layers. James Hutton recognized one at Siccar Point, Scotland, in 1788, where flat Devonian red sandstone lies on tilted Silurian greywacke. A nonconformity has sedimentary layers resting on eroded igneous or metamorphic rock.

Example: a cross section shows flat layers of sandstone, shale and limestone, with sandstone at the bottom. A basalt dike cuts all three and stops at a flat erosion surface. Siltstone rests on that surface, and the dike does not cut it. A fault offsets everything, including the siltstone. Superposition orders the three layers. The dike cuts them, so it is younger. Erosion then cut off the top of the dike, and the siltstone was laid on that surface. The fault offsets the siltstone, so it is youngest. The order from oldest to youngest is sandstone, shale, limestone, dike, erosion, siltstone, fault. The surface is a disconformity, because the layers beneath it are not tilted. Dating a feature by what it cuts or what rests on it is more reliable than dating it by where it sits.

points.heading: Fossils extend relative dating across distance
points.explanation:
Around 1800, William Smith surveyed canal routes in England and found the same fossils in the same order in outcrops far apart. This is faunal succession: fossil species appear and disappear in a regular sequence. An index fossil is a species that was widespread and short-lived. If two outcrops hold the same index fossil, their layers formed at about the same time, even when the rock types differ or the outcrops are many kilometers apart.

A species that survived for hundreds of millions of years makes a poor index fossil, because it turns up in too wide a range of rocks to separate them. A good one is also abundant and easy to recognize.

The limit is that fossils only match layers. They say older or younger, never how many years ago. Relative dating also cannot say how long a gap in the record lasted. To get numbers, we need a clock inside the rock.

points.heading: Radiometric dating: half-lives, the right clock, and bracketing sediments
points.explanation:
A parent isotope decays to a daughter isotope at a fixed rate. The half-life is the time it takes for half the parent atoms present to decay. After each half-life, half of what remains is lost, so the parent never drops to zero in two steps.

Half-lives passed | Parent left | Daughter made | Parent : daughter
0 | 1 | 0 | 1 : 0
1 | 1/2 | 1/2 | 1 : 1
2 | 1/4 | 3/4 | 1 : 3

A ratio of 1 : 1 means one half-life has passed, and 1 : 3 means two. This assumes that all the daughter atoms counted came from decay and that no parent or daughter atoms entered or escaped after the clock started.

Worked example (hypothetical): charcoal from a hearth has 25% of its original carbon-14. Since 25% = 1/4, two half-lives have passed. The half-life of carbon-14 is 5,730 years, so the age is 2 × 5,730 = 11,460 years. The clock starts when the wood stops exchanging carbon with its surroundings.

Each isotope pair suits a certain span of time and certain materials:
- Carbon-14 → nitrogen-14, half-life 5,730 years: wood, bone and shell younger than about 50,000 years.
- Uranium-235 → lead-207, half-life 704 million years: zircon in igneous rocks.
- Uranium-238 → lead-206, half-life 4.47 billion years: zircon in igneous rocks.
- Potassium-40 → argon-40, half-life 1.25 billion years: micas, feldspars and volcanic ash.

A granite thought to be 3 billion years old needs uranium-lead in zircon. Almost no carbon-14 would remain. Charcoal about 9,000 years old suits carbon-14, whereas uranium would show almost no decay.

Sedimentary rocks are a special case. Sand grains date the older rocks they came from, not the layer. Igneous rocks and ash beds date their own crystallization, so geologists bracket a sedimentary layer between dated igneous units. Suppose an ash bed just above a sandstone gives 300 million years and another ash bed just below it gives 320 million years. These numbers are made up for illustration. The sandstone is younger than 320 million years and older than 300 million years.

points.heading: The geologic time scale and the size of the Phanerozoic
points.explanation:
The time scale joins relative and numeric dates. Its boundaries were first drawn from fossils and later given numbers by radiometric dates. Dates are rounded and shift slightly between sources, so use the values in your textbook.

Eon | Span | Marker
Hadean | 4.54 to 4.0 billion years ago | Earth forms; oldest minerals, zircons of about 4.4 billion years
Archean | 4.0 to 2.5 billion years ago | oldest well-preserved rocks; first life
Proterozoic | 2.5 billion to 541 million years ago | oxygen builds up; complex cells and first animals
Phanerozoic | 541 million years ago to now | abundant visible fossils

The Phanerozoic has three eras: Paleozoic (541 to 252 million years ago), Mesozoic (252 to 66 million years ago) and Cenozoic (66 million years ago to now).

The Phanerozoic is the best known part of Earth’s history because its fossils are abundant, but it is short. It spans 541 million years of 4,540 million, which is about 12%. The Proterozoic is the longest eon at about 2 billion years. On a paper strip at 1 millimeter per million years, the Phanerozoic is only the last 541 millimeters of a strip 4.54 meters long.

To place an event, compare its age with the boundaries. Stromatolites about 3.5 billion years old fall between 4.0 and 2.5 billion years ago, so they belong to the Archean. Non-bird dinosaurs died out 66 million years ago, which is after 541 million years ago, so that event lies in the Phanerozoic, at the boundary between the Mesozoic and Cenozoic.

handouts.title: Work out the ages

blocks.text: Work each problem alone. Show the number of half-lives. The rocks and measurements below are hypothetical. In every problem, assume that the daughter atoms counted were produced by decay and that no parent or daughter atoms entered or escaped after the clock started.
Suppose a piece of charcoal from a hearth has 12.5% of its original carbon-14 left. The half-life of carbon-14 is 5,730 years. How many half-lives have passed, and how old is the charcoal?

blocks.hint: Number of half-lives, working and age

blocks.text: Suppose a zircon crystal has uranium-235 and lead-207 atoms in the ratio U-235 : Pb-207 = 1 : 3. The half-life of uranium-235 is 704 million years. How many half-lives have passed, and how old is the zircon?

blocks.hint: Number of half-lives, working and age

blocks.text: Suppose a mica crystal is 2.5 billion years old. The half-life of potassium-40 is 1.25 billion years. Here "daughter" means all the atoms produced by potassium-40 decay, including calcium-40 and argon-40. How many half-lives have passed, what fraction of the potassium-40 is left, and what is the ratio of potassium-40 to daughter atoms? (This is not the ratio of potassium-40 to argon-40.)

blocks.hint: Number of half-lives, fraction left and ratio, with your working

handouts.key:
Charcoal: 12.5% = 0.125 = 1/8. The parent fraction falls from 1 to 1/2 to 1/4 to 1/8, so 3 half-lives have passed. Age = 3 × 5,730 = 17,190 years. Common slip: treating 12.5% as the fraction that decayed rather than the fraction remaining.

Zircon: U-235 : Pb-207 = 1 : 3 means the parent fraction is 1/(1 + 3) = 1/4. This represents 2 half-lives. Age = 2 × 704 = 1,408 million years, or 1.408 billion years. Common slip: reading three daughter atoms as three half-lives.

Mica: Number of half-lives = 2.5/1.25 = 2. Parent fraction remaining = (1/2)² = 1/4. Daughter fraction = 3/4. Potassium-40 : total daughter atoms = 1 : 3. Look for both calcium-40 and argon-40 included in the daughter total. Common slip: reporting this as the potassium-40 : argon-40 ratio.

blocks.hint: Prediction: which is older, the clasts or the rock that holds them, and why?
What you see with the lens: clast shapes and sizes, and the material around them
Principle that decides it, and your statement: "A is older than B because..."

blocks.hint: Evidence for which way was up (graded bedding or ripple marks), found in the rock and not from the tray
Prediction: which layer is oldest and which is youngest, and why?
Principle that decides it, and your statement: "A is older than B because..."

blocks.text: For the class comparison

blocks.hint: Which sample surprised you most, and what did you predict that the rock did not show?

handouts.key:
Sample with a vein or dike cutting across the rock
Prediction: The host rock is older than the vein or dike because the host existed before the cutting feature formed.
Lens observations: Look for a description of the actual vein or dike boundaries, the host features it crosses, and its visible ends at sample edges or within the rock. A sample edge need not be the feature's original termination.
Principle and statement: Cross-cutting relationships. The host rock is older than the vein or dike because the vein or dike cuts it. Common slip: using position in the tray to decide age.

Conglomerate or breccia sample
Prediction: The clasts are older than the rock containing them because they existed before incorporation into the sediment.
Lens observations: Look for clast shapes, measured sizes with units, and a description of the surrounding matrix or cement. Conglomerate has predominantly rounded gravel-sized clasts; breccia has predominantly angular gravel-sized clasts. Gravel-sized clasts exceed 2 mm.
Principle and statement: Inclusions. The clasts are older than the containing rock because fragments of preexisting rock were incorporated into it. Common slip: treating cement and clasts as having formed together.

Sample with layers that show way-up
Way-up evidence: In a normally graded bed, grains become finer toward the original top. Ripple evidence must distinguish an original bed surface from a cast on the underside of an overlying bed; a ripple pattern alone does not establish way-up.
Prediction: Once original way-up is established, the originally lowest layer is oldest and the originally highest layer is youngest, assuming the sequence remains in depositional order.
Principle and statement: Superposition. The originally lower layer is older than the overlying layer because it was deposited first. Common slip: identifying the layer nearest the bottom of the tray as oldest.

Class comparison
Accept a specific initial prediction, the observed feature that challenged it, and a revised interpretation supported by a relative dating principle. If the observations supported the prediction, accept an explicit statement of that agreement with evidence.

handouts.title: Ordering events in cross sections

blocks.text: For each section, write every event from oldest to youngest. Include events that are not layers. Then label each unconformity by type and name the relationship that decides your order. Check your sequence by reading it aloud to another pair.
Section 1

From the bottom of the section upward: three layers of sandstone, shale and limestone, in that order from the lowest, all tilted at the same steep angle. One dike cuts across all three tilted layers. The tops of the tilted layers and the top of the dike are cut off along one flat, slightly uneven surface. Resting on that surface are two flat layers: conglomerate, then sandstone above it. The dike does not continue into the conglomerate or the sandstone above.

blocks.hint: Events from oldest to youngest
Type of unconformity, and where it lies
The relationship that tells you the dike's place in the order

blocks.text: Section 2

The lowest part of the section is a banded gneiss. A body of granite lies against the gneiss, with narrow granite veins running into the gneiss. Across the tops of both gneiss and granite runs one flat erosion surface. Flat layers rest on it: sandstone, then shale above the sandstone. A steep fault cuts through the shale, the sandstone, the erosion surface, the granite and the gneiss. Every one of them is displaced, with the layers on the left side of the fault lower than the same layers on the right.

blocks.hint: Events from oldest to youngest
Type of unconformity, and where it lies
How you dated the sandstone: what it rests on, and what the fault does to it

handouts.key:
Section 1
Events from oldest to youngest: Deposition of the lower sandstone; deposition of shale; deposition of limestone; tilting; dike intrusion; erosion truncating the tilted layers and dike; deposition of flat conglomerate; deposition of the upper flat sandstone.
Unconformity: Angular unconformity at the erosion surface between the tilted sedimentary layers and the flat conglomerate.
Dike relationship: The dike is younger than the layers it cuts and older than the erosion surface that truncates it and the conglomerate deposited above it. Cutting the sedimentary layers alone does not establish whether intrusion preceded or followed tilting; the listed sequence follows the section's stated description of a dike cutting already tilted layers. Accept an explicit recognition of that evidential limit. Common slip: extending the dike's age past deposition of the conglomerate even though the dike is truncated beneath it.

Section 2
Events from oldest to youngest: Formation of gneiss; granite intrusion, including granite veins into the gneiss; erosion exposing both crystalline rocks; sandstone deposition; shale deposition; fault displacement.
Unconformity: Nonconformity where sedimentary sandstone rests on the eroded granite and gneiss.
Sandstone relationships: The sandstone is younger than the crystalline rocks and their erosion surface because it rests on them. It is older than the shale above it by superposition and older than the fault because the fault cuts and displaces it. Common slip: using displacement to reverse the depositional order of sandstone and shale.

handouts.title: A half-life you can watch

blocks.text: Procedure

items: Put 64 coins in the cup. Each coin is one parent atom. This is round 0.
Shake the cup, then tip the coins out onto the bench. Keep every coin on the bench and off the floor.
Remove all the coins showing heads. These stand for atoms that decayed, so they are now daughter atoms.
Count the coins left (the parent) and write the number in the table. Work out the total number of coins removed so far (the daughter).
Put the remaining coins back in the cup and repeat from step 2. Stop after round 6.

blocks.text: Record your counts

blocks.hint: Plot coins left (vertical axis, 0 to 64) against round (horizontal axis, 0 to 6). Label both axes and join your points.
Your parent : daughter ratio after round 3, from your counts
Compare it with the ratio expected after three half-lives, worked out in lecture by extending the decay table. Explain any difference.

handouts.key:
Record your counts
Round 0: Parent = 64; daughter = 0.
Round 1: Parent = the observed remaining count; daughter = 64 minus that count. Expected values: 32 parent, 32 daughter.
Round 2: Parent = the observed remaining count; daughter = 64 minus that count. Expected values: 16 parent, 48 daughter.
Round 3: Parent = the observed remaining count; daughter = 64 minus that count. Expected values: 8 parent, 56 daughter.
Round 4: Parent = the observed remaining count; daughter = 64 minus that count. Expected values: 4 parent, 60 daughter.
Round 5: Parent = the observed remaining count; daughter = 64 minus that count. Expected values: 2 parent, 62 daughter.
Round 6: Parent = the observed remaining count; daughter = 64 minus that count. Expected values: 1 parent, 63 daughter.
For every row, parent plus daughter must equal 64. Parent counts cannot increase. Once no parent coins remain, later parent counts stay at zero. Common slip: recording only the coins removed in that round instead of the cumulative daughter count.

Plot: Horizontal axis labeled Round, from 0 to 6; vertical axis labeled Parent coins remaining, from 0 to 64. Plot the recorded counts, including (0, 64), and join successive points. The expected sequence is (0, 64), (1, 32), (2, 16), (3, 8), (4, 4), (5, 2), (6, 1). Actual points should follow the pair's observations.

Ratio after round 3: If p coins remain, parent : daughter = p : (64 − p), simplified where possible. For 8 remaining coins, 8 : 56 = 1 : 7. If none remain, the ratio is 0 : 64, or 0 : 1; if none have decayed, it is 64 : 0, or 1 : 0.

Comparison: The theoretical ratio after three half-lives is 1 : 7. Actual ratios may differ because each coin has a probability of 1/2 of being removed in each round; a small sample need not lose exactly half each time. Look for a distinction between the expected decay pattern and the observed counts. Common slip: replacing observed counts with the theoretical values.

handouts.title: Bracket the age of a shale
handouts.usedIn: Bracket the age of a shale

blocks.text: Suppose a shale lies directly on top of an ash bed, and a felsic dike cuts across the shale. The measurements below are hypothetical. Assume that the daughter atoms counted were produced by decay and that no parent or daughter atoms entered or escaped after the clock started.

rows: Crystallized during the eruption that produced the ash
Crystallized during intrusion of the dike
blocks.caption: Data

blocks.text: The half-life of uranium-235 is 704 million years.

blocks.caption: Eons, with boundaries in millions of years ago

blocks.hint: Age of the ash bed: half-lives and age in millions of years
Age of the dike: half-lives and age in millions of years
The age range of the shale
The eon the range falls in
Why the shale itself is not dated directly

handouts.key:
Ash bed: Parent fraction = 1/(1 + 3) = 1/4, representing 2 half-lives. Age = 2 × 704 = 1,408 million years.

Dike: Parent fraction = 1/(1 + 1) = 1/2, representing 1 half-life. Age = 704 million years.

Shale age range: Older than 704 million years and younger than 1,408 million years. Written as an age before the present: 704 million years < shale age < 1,408 million years. Superposition places deposition after the ash-producing eruption; cross-cutting places deposition before dike intrusion. Common slip: reversing the age bounds because larger ages describe earlier events.

Eon: Proterozoic. Both bounds fall between 2,500 and 541 million years ago.

Why not date the shale directly? Its detrital mineral grains generally formed in source rocks before erosion, transport, and deposition. Their radiometric ages generally record events in those source rocks rather than deposition of the shale. The specified zircon ages instead date the eruption beneath the shale and the intrusion cutting it.

readings: Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, the chapter on earthquakes

segments.title: Quiz due now and a puzzle of scale
segments.description:
Weekly online quizzes: Geologic time and how rocks are dated is due now. Weekly online quizzes count for 10% of the course grade. Each student’s own work is submitted online before the lesson it is due at and scored individually.
Students read the puzzle on the screen and each writes one or two sentences that make both statements true, in about three minutes.
They compare answers with a partner for one minute, then two students are heard.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: friction locks the fault while the plates keep moving, so strain builds for decades and is released in seconds. Hypothetical accumulation example: at a steady relative motion of 4 cm per year, 150 years gives 600 cm = 6 m. Accept any one-sentence answer that names stored strain.
shown: Plates move at about 4 cm per year. Yet in the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, the two sides of the San Andreas Fault slipped by several meters within a minute. How can both statements be true?

segments.title: Elastic rebound and the focus
segments.description:
Starting from the students’ answers, explain elastic rebound: rock bends and stores elastic energy until friction on the fault is overcome, then springs back.
Define the focus, where rupture begins, and the epicenter, the point on the surface directly above it.
Use the offset fences and roads that H. F. Reid studied after 1906 as the evidence for the idea.
Students copy the four steps and write the 6 m calculation beside them.
segments.teacherNotes: Common misconception: the epicenter is where the fault slipped. A large rupture runs along tens to hundreds of kilometers of fault, and the epicenter marks only where it began. Rock around a locked fault stores elastic strain as plate motion continues.
shown: Steps: Plates move steadily while the fault stays locked → Rock bends and stores elastic energy → Friction is overcome and the fault slips → Rock springs back and energy radiates as seismic waves
Focus: where the rupture begins. Epicenter: the point on Earth’s surface directly above the focus.

segments.title: Draw the fence across a fault
segments.description:
Each student quickly sketches a straight fence that crosses a fault, seen from above, in four small frames that match the four steps, using a few lines per frame, in about three minutes.
Students then explain their frames to a partner, one minute each way.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: frame 1 straight fence. Frame 2 fence bent near the fault, far ends already displaced. Frame 3 fence breaks as the sides slip. Frame 4 two straight pieces offset by the slip. Common mistake: drawing the offset already in frame 2.
shown: Draw a straight fence that crosses a fault, seen from above, in four frames that match the four steps. Label the frame where energy is stored and the frame where it is released.

segments.title: P, S and surface waves
segments.description:
Draw the push–pull motion of a P wave and the shearing motion of an S wave on the board, and give their typical speeds in the upper crust.
Before the table appears, each student writes a prediction: S waves do not pass through Earth’s outer core, so what does that say about it? Two predictions are heard.
Then present surface waves, Love and Rayleigh, as the slowest and the largest, and show the table.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: the outer core is liquid, because a liquid has no shear strength; this links to Earth’s layers earlier in the course. Surface waves cause most damage because of their large amplitude and long shaking.
shown: Prompt: S waves do not travel through Earth’s outer core. What does that tell you about the outer core? Write your answer.

segments.title: Name the wave
segments.description:
Students decide for each statement on the screen whether it describes a P wave, an S wave or a surface wave.
They work alone for three minutes and compare with a partner for one minute.
Then two students give and defend an answer.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. Particles move back and forth along the direction of travel: P.
2. Cannot pass through the liquid outer core: S.
3. First to arrive at a distant station: P.
4. Slowest, usually the largest shaking and most damage: surface.
5. Moves through Earth’s interior with particles at right angles to travel: S.

3. It is the first to arrive at a distant station.
4. It is the slowest, and usually produces the largest shaking and most damage.
5. It moves through Earth’s interior with particles moving at right angles to its direction of travel.

segments.title: From the S–P interval to a distance
segments.description:
P and S leave the focus together, but P is faster, so the gap between their arrivals grows with distance.
For the classroom calculations and maps, assume a shallow focus and constant wave speeds, so distance to the focus approximates distance to the epicenter. With P at 6.0 km/s and S at 3.5 km/s, the gap grows by about 1 second for every 8.4 km.
Suppose a station records the S wave 10 s after the P wave. That station is about 84 km from the epicenter, drawn as a circle on the board.
Pairs write where the epicenter could be after two circles, then the teacher adds a third circle.
segments.teacherNotes: Derivation: d/3.5 − d/6.0 = interval gives d = 8.4 × interval. Real travel-time curves bend with depth, so the rule is a classroom approximation. Two circles cross at two points; the third picks one. Mistake: reading the circle as a direction.
shown: Rule used in this course: distance (km) ≈ 8.4 × (S–P interval in seconds)
Steps: Read the S–P interval → Multiply by 8.4 km per second → Draw a circle of that radius around the station → Repeat at three stations → The epicenter is where the circles meet
Prompt: A circle is drawn around station 1 and another around station 2. Where could the epicenter be? Write your answer.

segments.title: One station, one number
segments.description:
Each student works alone for three minutes on the question on the screen.
They then compare answers with a partner for one minute.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: 12 × 8.4 ≈ 101 km. One station gives only a circle, with no direction, so the epicenter could be anywhere on it. Common mistake: dividing the interval by 8.4 instead of multiplying.
shown: Suppose a station records the S wave 12 s after the P wave. How far is the epicenter? What can this one station not tell you?

segments.title: Summary and what the next lecture does
segments.description:
Summarize the chain: locked fault, rupture, three kinds of wave, the S–P interval, circles from three stations.
Next time the lecture turns the method around, then compares magnitude with intensity and explains how earthquakes cause damage.

segments.title: Run the method backward
segments.description:
Students are told where an earthquake happened and must predict what two seismographs will record.
Each student works alone for five minutes: find the S–P interval for each station with the rule in about two minutes, then mark the P and S arrivals for both stations on one time axis in about three.
Partners compare and correct for one minute, then two students show their numbers.
segments.teacherNotes: Station X: P at 21 s, S at 36 s, interval 15 s (126 ÷ 8.4 = 15). Station Y: P at 7 s, S at 12 s, interval 5 s (42 ÷ 8.4 = 5). Marks are ticks on one axis, not full traces. Mistakes: giving P and S the same arrival time, or a larger interval at the nearer station.

segments.title: Magnitude: one number per earthquake
segments.description:
Richter’s 1935 scale used the largest wave amplitude on a seismogram, corrected for distance, on a logarithmic scale.
That scale saturates for the largest earthquakes, so seismologists report moment magnitude, based on the rigidity of the rock, the fault area that slipped and the average slip.
Each whole step is 10 times the amplitude and about 32 times the energy.
Examples: 1906 San Francisco about 7.9, 2011 Tohoku 9.1, and 1960 Chile 9.5, the largest recorded.
segments.teacherNotes: Seismic moment = rigidity × fault area × average slip. The energy factor is 10^{1.5} ≈ 32. Mistake: treating the scale as linear, so that a 9 seems slightly bigger than a 7.
shown: Table: Step in magnitude | Ground-motion amplitude | Energy released / 1 unit | 10 times | about 32 times

segments.title: Compare magnitudes
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Compare magnitudes”.
Students work the three comparisons on the sheet alone for three minutes, using the reminder from the table.
They write a number for each in the space for its answer.
They check with a partner for one minute, then two students explain how they used the reminder.
segments.teacherNotes:
1. Amplitude, M5.0 vs M3.0: 10 × 10 = 100 times.
2. Energy, M8.0 vs M7.0: about 32 times.
3. Energy, M9.1 vs M7.1: 32 × 32 ≈ 1,000 times.
Mistake: using 10 for energy.

segments.title: Intensity: the shaking at a place
segments.description:
The Modified Mercalli scale runs from I to XII and rates the effects on people, objects and buildings at one place.
One earthquake has one magnitude but many intensities, drawn as bands on a map.
Pairs write which of two towns has the higher intensity for two minutes, then one pair is heard before the teacher explains why.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: Town B. Soft, saturated fill amplifies and prolongs shaking. Intensity also depends on distance, depth and construction. Mistake: assuming one magnitude means the same intensity everywhere.
shown: Side by side: Magnitude: one value per earthquake; from seismograms and fault slip; logarithmic | Intensity: a different value at every place; from effects on people and buildings; Modified Mercalli, I to XII

Prompt: The same hypothetical magnitude 6.5 earthquake shakes two towns 80 km from the epicenter. Town A stands on bedrock. Town B stands on soft, water-saturated fill. Which has the higher intensity, and why? Write your answer.

segments.title: How earthquakes cause damage
segments.description:
Ground shaking: surface and S waves damage weak buildings, and soft sediment amplifies shaking, as in Mexico City in 1985, about 350 km from the epicenter.
Tsunami: a subduction-zone rupture lifts or drops the sea floor and displaces the water above, as in Sumatra in 2004 and Tohoku in 2011.
Pairs write for two minutes why loose, saturated sand loses strength when dry sand does not, then the teacher explains liquefaction with Niigata in 1964, where apartment blocks tilted nearly intact.
segments.teacherNotes: These events killed many people; keep the focus on mechanism and speak respectfully. Answer to prompt: shaking raises water pressure between grains, so they lose contact. Dry sand has no water to carry the load. Show the steps after pairs answer.
shown: Prompt: Why can loose, water-saturated sand lose its strength during shaking when dry sand does not?

Table: Hazard | Cause | Where worst / Ground shaking | Surface and S waves | Soft sediment, weak buildings / Tsunami | Sudden sea-floor uplift or drop | Low coasts facing a subduction zone / Liquefaction | Rising pore-water pressure | Loose, saturated sand and fill
Steps: Shaking squeezes loose, water-saturated sand → Water pressure between grains rises → Grains lose contact with each other → Ground flows like a liquid and buildings sink or tilt

segments.title: Find and fix the mistakes
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Find and fix the mistakes”.
Students read a short draft summary of the lecture on the sheet, written by an imaginary student.
Each student works alone for six minutes: underline every wrong statement and write a corrected sentence for it.
Partners compare corrections for two minutes, then two students are heard and the class settles each answer.
segments.teacherNotes:
Four statements, each wrong:
1. A magnitude 7 releases twice the energy of a magnitude 6. Fix: about 32 times.
2. The epicenter is the point underground where rock first breaks. Fix: that is the focus; the epicenter is on the surface above it.
3. Each earthquake has one intensity, recorded by a seismograph. Fix: intensity varies by place and comes from effects; magnitude is one value.
4. Liquefaction is worst in dry sand. Fix: it needs loose, water-saturated sand.

segments.title: Summary and the lab ahead
segments.description:
Summarize: magnitude is one logarithmic number, intensity varies by place, and shaking, tsunamis and liquefaction cause the damage.
Next time is the lab: students locate an epicenter in pairs, shake sand trays and read an intensity survey.
Closed-toe shoes are required in the lab.

segments.title: Report due, safety and pairs
segments.description:
Lab reports: Geologic time and how rocks are dated is due now. Lab reports count for 30% of the course grade.
State the rules: closed-toe shoes, hand samples stay in their trays and go back where they came from, and spilled water or sand is wiped up at once.
Pairs form, as in every lab, and each partner keeps their own record of the work.
Outline the day: locate an epicenter, shake sand trays, and read an intensity survey.
segments.teacherNotes: Safety: wet sand makes floors slippery, so keep towels and a dustpan at the sand stations. Compass points are sharp; hand samples stay in their trays.

segments.title: Method: locating an epicenter
segments.description:
Show how to read a seismogram: mark the first P arrival and the first S arrival, then subtract.
Use the demonstration stations D, E and F: convert each interval to a radius and draw circles with a compass at the map scale.
After the circles for D and E are drawn, pairs predict which crossing point station F’s circle will pass through.
Then draw F’s circle, read off the coordinates and enter the values in the recording table.
segments.teacherNotes: Demonstration epicenter (70, 40) km: intervals 9.6, 7.6 and 7.3 s, radii about 81, 64 and 61 km. The other D–E crossing is (70, −40), about 140 km from F. Equipment: compass, ruler, map on a km grid. Mistakes: using arrival times instead of intervals, or the wrong map scale.
shown: Table: Station | Position in km (east, north) | P arrives | S arrives / D | 0, 0 | 13.4 s | 23.0 s / E | 120, 0 | 10.7 s | 18.3 s / F | 60, 100 | 10.1 s | 17.4 s

Steps: Mark the first P arrival → Mark the first S arrival → Subtract to get the S–P interval → Multiply by 8.4 km per second → Set the compass to that radius on the map scale → Draw the circle around the station → The epicenter is where three circles meet
Prompt: The circles for D and E cross at two points. Which one will station F’s circle pass through, and how do you know?

segments.title: Locate the epicenter from three stations
segments.description:
Pairs take the Epicenter location worksheet: arrival times for stations A, B and C, and a map on a kilometer grid with the stations plotted.
One partner reads the arrival times and calls out values while the other converts and draws; they swap roles for each station.
Each partner records the intervals, radii and the epicenter’s coordinates in their own table, and notes how large the uncertainty is.
segments.teacherNotes: Stations A (0, 0), B (100, 0), C (50, 100) km. S–P intervals 6.0, 8.0 and 8.4 s give radii of about 50, 67 and 71 km. Epicenter near (40, 30) km; accept within 5 km. Ask circulating pairs what two stations alone would show.

segments.title: Compare epicenters across the room
segments.description:
Each pair writes its epicenter coordinates on the board.
Each student writes an answer to the prompt for two minutes, then compares with a partner for one minute.
Two or three answers are heard, and the class describes the spread of results on the board.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: pencil line width, compass slip, and picking P or S slightly early or late. One second on the S–P interval changes a radius by about 8 km. Takeaway: an epicenter is a best fit with some uncertainty, and more stations narrow it.
shown: Prompt: Why do the pairs’ epicenters not agree exactly? Suppose station C’s S arrival were picked 1 s too late. How far would its circle move?

segments.title: Break
segments.description:
Students take a break.
Meanwhile the teacher sets out the sand tubs, water, small blocks and sandstone hand sample trays at the benches.

segments.title: Liquefaction in a tray
segments.description:
Pairs predict for two minutes what a small block will do on saturated sand and on dry sand when the tub is shaken.
They tap the side of each tub steadily for 15 to 20 seconds, once on saturated sand and once on dry sand, and record what the block and the water do.
Pairs write an explanation in terms of water pressure between grains, with a labeled sketch.
They then examine a sandstone hand sample in its department tray beside the loose sand, write why cemented rock does not liquefy, and loosen the sand and reset the tubs for the next pair.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: on saturated sand, water rises to the surface and the block tilts or sinks; dry sand only settles slightly. Cement holds grains in contact, so pore pressure cannot free them. Preparation: before class, prepare each matched set with one tub of loose, fully saturated sand with little standing water on top and one tub of loose, dry sand. Use identical blocks and test the tapping method on both conditions. Between pairs, loosen and level the sand in both tubs; restore full saturation with little standing water in the saturated tub, and keep the dry tub dry. Safety: tap gently, never strike; wipe spills at once; keep samples in their trays; keep sand out of the sink and wash hands.

segments.title: Reading an intensity survey
segments.description:
Pairs take the Intensity survey sheet: felt reports from six towns after a hypothetical earthquake, each with its distance and ground type, and a Modified Mercalli key.
Pairs assign a Mercalli level to each town’s report and plot level against distance, marking bedrock and soft-ground towns differently.
They compare the two groups of towns and each partner writes an answer to the prompt in their own record.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: intensity does not fall off with distance alone. Soft-sediment towns plot above bedrock towns at similar distances. Mistake: rating a town by distance alone. Check levels against the key on the sheet.

segments.title: Clean-up, assignments and what comes next
segments.description:
Pairs return tubs, sand and hand samples to where they came from and wipe the benches.
Set the graded assignment Lab reports, which counts toward Lab reports (30%), due at the start of the lab of Folds, faults and mountain building.
Set the graded assignment Weekly online quizzes, which counts toward Weekly online quizzes (10%), due at the first meeting of Folds, faults and mountain building. Each student’s own work is submitted online before that meeting and scored individually.
Midterm exam 2 (15%) is taken at Folds, faults and mountain building, on what has been taught so far, and the teacher announces what to bring.
Read before then Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, the chapter on crustal deformation and mountain building.
The practice quiz on this lesson is taken after class and counts toward no grade.
segments.teacherNotes: Do not list exam topics; the paper alone gives them. Remind students that the practice quiz is separate from the graded online quizzes.

keyIdeas: Earthquakes release strain stored in rock. Plate motion bends a locked fault, friction fails, and the rock springs back (elastic rebound). Waves spread from the focus, and the epicenter is the point on the surface directly above it.

P waves arrive first, S waves second and surface waves last, and surface waves cause the most damage. The S–P interval grows with distance, so one station gives a circle and three stations fix the epicenter.

Magnitude is one logarithmic number for the whole earthquake: each whole step is 10 times the ground-motion amplitude and about 32 times the energy. Intensity is the shaking felt at one place, and it changes with distance, ground and construction.
Earthquakes harm people through ground shaking, which soft sediment amplifies, through tsunamis from sudden sea-floor movement, and through liquefaction of loose, water-saturated sand.

vocabulary.definition: The spring-back of rock that has been bent by stress, when friction on a fault is overcome and the fault slips.
The point inside Earth where an earthquake rupture begins.
The point on Earth’s surface directly above the focus.
The time between the arrival of the first P wave and the first S wave at a station; it grows with distance from the epicenter.
A logarithmic measure of an earthquake’s size, based on the rock’s rigidity, the fault area that slipped and the average slip.
A scale from I to XII that rates intensity at one place by the effects of shaking on people, objects and buildings.
A series of long waves caused by sudden displacement of water, commonly when an earthquake at a subduction zone lifts or drops the sea floor.
The loss of strength of loose, water-saturated sediment when shaking raises the water pressure between grains.

slides.title: A puzzle of scale
bullets: Plates move at about 4 cm per year. Yet in the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, the two sides of the San Andreas Fault slipped by several meters within a minute. How can both statements be true?
slides.notes:
Start by saying that Weekly online quizzes: Geologic time and how rocks are dated is due now. Weekly online quizzes count for 10% of the course grade. It is each student’s own work, submitted online before this meeting and scored individually, so nothing is collected in class.

Then leave the puzzle on the screen. Each student writes one or two sentences that make both statements true, in about three minutes. Partners compare for one minute. Hear two students.

Expected: friction locks the fault while the plates keep moving, so strain builds for decades and is released in seconds. Hypothetical accumulation example: at a steady relative motion of 4 cm per year, 150 years gives 600 cm = 6 m. Accept any one-sentence answer that names stored strain.

slides.title: Elastic rebound
bullets: Focus: where the rupture begins. Epicenter: the point on Earth’s surface directly above the focus.
slides.notes:
Start from the students’ answers. Rock bends and stores elastic energy as plate motion continues, until friction on the fault is overcome. Then it springs back. Define the focus and the epicenter.

Evidence: H. F. Reid studied the offset fences and roads after 1906 and used them to propose the idea.

Students copy the four steps and write the 6 m calculation beside them (4 cm per year × 150 years = 600 cm = 6 m, a hypothetical accumulation).

Common misconception to head off: the epicenter is where the fault slipped. A large rupture runs along tens to hundreds of kilometers of fault, and the epicenter marks only where it began.

steps.title: Rock springs back
steps.detail: and energy radiates as seismic waves

slides.title: Draw the fence across a fault
bullets: Draw a straight fence that crosses a fault, seen from above, in four frames that match the four steps. Label the frame where energy is stored and the frame where it is released.
slides.notes:
Each student sketches quickly, a few lines per frame, in about three minutes. Then they explain their frames to a partner, one minute each way. Walk the room while they draw.

Expected: frame 1 a straight fence. Frame 2 the fence bent near the fault, with the far ends already displaced. Frame 3 the fence breaks as the sides slip. Frame 4 two straight pieces offset by the slip.

Common mistake: drawing the offset already in frame 2.
