study.overview: An earthquake is the sudden release of strain that plate motion has stored in rock around a locked fault. The waves it sends out let us find where it started and how large it was. Those same waves, together with the ground and the buildings they meet, decide how much harm results. This guide follows that chain: rupture, waves, location, size, damage.

points.heading: Elastic rebound, focus and the three kinds of wave
points.explanation:
Plates keep moving while friction locks a fault, so the rock on both sides bends and stores elastic energy. When friction is overcome, the fault slips and the rock springs back. This is elastic rebound. The focus is where the rupture begins. The epicenter is the point on the surface directly above the focus. It marks the start of the rupture, not the whole slip, because a large rupture can run along tens to hundreds of kilometers of fault.

Example (hypothetical): suppose the plates on either side of a locked fault move past each other at 3 cm per year. After 100 years the rock holds 300 cm = 3 m of strain, and it can be released in seconds.

The energy travels as P waves (push–pull, about 6.0 km/s in the upper crust), S waves (shearing at right angles to travel, about 3.5 km/s) and surface waves (Love and Rayleigh, a little slower than S). They arrive in that order, and surface waves usually do the most damage because of their large amplitude and long shaking. S waves cannot cross Earth’s outer core, which shows that it is liquid: a liquid has no shear strength.

points.heading: Locating an epicenter with the S–P interval
points.explanation:
P and S waves leave the focus together, but P is faster, so the gap between their arrivals grows with distance. For a station at distance d, the gap is d/3.5 − d/6.0, which gives the classroom rule distance (km) ≈ 8.4 × S–P interval (s). It assumes a shallow focus and constant wave speeds, so it is an approximation.

Example: a station 168 km away would record P at 168 ÷ 6.0 = 28 s and S at 168 ÷ 3.5 = 48 s after the origin time. The interval is 20 s, and 8.4 × 20 = 168 km. Going the other way, a 4 s interval means about 8.4 × 4 ≈ 34 km. Multiply the interval by 8.4; do not divide.

One station gives only a circle of that radius around it, with no direction. Two circles cross at two points. A third station’s circle passes through one of them and fixes the epicenter. Real picks of P and S arrivals and drawn circles carry small errors, so the result is a best fit with some uncertainty, and more stations narrow it.

points.heading: Magnitude and intensity measure different things
points.explanation:
Magnitude is one number for the whole earthquake, on a logarithmic scale. Richter’s 1935 scale used the largest wave amplitude on a seismogram, corrected for distance. It saturates for the largest earthquakes, so seismologists now report moment magnitude. Moment magnitude is based on the rock’s rigidity, the fault area that slipped and the average slip. Each whole step is 10 times the ground-motion amplitude and about 32 times the energy (10^{1.5} ≈ 32). Examples: 1906 San Francisco about 7.9, 2011 Tohoku 9.1, 1960 Chile 9.5, the largest recorded.

Example: compare a magnitude 7.0 earthquake with a magnitude 4.0. That is three steps. The amplitude ratio is 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000. The energy ratio is 32 × 32 × 32, about 33,000. Treating the scale as linear makes a 7 look only slightly bigger than a 4.

Intensity is the shaking felt at one place, rated on the Modified Mercalli scale from I to XII by effects on people, objects and buildings. One earthquake has one magnitude but many intensities, which can be drawn as bands on a map. Example (hypothetical): in a magnitude 6.0 earthquake, a town on bedrock 40 km away might be rated V, while a town on soft fill the same distance away might be rated VII. Distance, ground and construction all change intensity.

points.heading: How earthquakes cause damage
points.explanation:
Three mechanisms do most of the harm.

Ground shaking, mainly from surface and S waves, damages weak buildings. Soft sediment amplifies and prolongs the shaking. In 1985 Mexico City, about 350 km from the epicenter, was badly hit because it stands on soft sediment.

Tsunamis come from sudden movement of the sea floor. A subduction-zone rupture lifts or drops the sea floor and displaces the water above it, as in Sumatra in 2004 and Tohoku in 2011. Low coasts facing a subduction zone are most at risk.

Liquefaction affects loose, water-saturated sand and fill. Shaking squeezes the sand, the water pressure between the grains rises, the grains lose contact with each other, and the ground flows like a liquid. Dry sand has no pore water to carry the load, and cemented rock holds its grains together, so neither liquefies the same way. At Niigata in 1964, apartment blocks tilted nearly intact as the sand beneath them lost strength. The damage came from the ground failing, not from the buildings breaking.

handouts.title: Run the method backward

blocks.text: Work alone. An earthquake has just happened, and you know where. Predict what two seismographs will record. Take the origin time as 0 s. P waves travel at 6.0 km/s and S waves at 3.5 km/s. Distances are to the epicenter, which you may treat as the distance to the focus.

Step 1: find each S–P interval with the rule (interval = distance ÷ 8.4). Step 2: fill in the P and S arrival times. Step 3: mark both stations' P and S arrivals as ticks on one time axis below, labeling each tick.

blocks.hint: Draw a time axis from 0 s to 40 s. Above it mark Station X's P and S ticks, and below it Station Y's P and S ticks.

handouts.key:
Station X: S–P interval = 126 ÷ 8.4 = 15 s; P arrival = 126 ÷ 6.0 = 21 s; S arrival = 126 ÷ 3.5 = 36 s.
Station Y: S–P interval = 42 ÷ 8.4 = 5 s; P arrival = 42 ÷ 6.0 = 7 s; S arrival = 42 ÷ 3.5 = 12 s.
Time axis: draw a uniformly spaced axis from 0 to 40 s. Above it, label X P at 21 s and X S at 36 s. Below it, label Y P at 7 s and Y S at 12 s.
Look for P arriving before S at both stations and a larger S–P interval at the more distant station. Common slip: plotting the interval as an arrival time.

handouts.title: Compare magnitudes

blocks.text: Work alone. Give a number for each comparison. Reminder from the table: each whole step on the magnitude scale is 10 times the amplitude and about 32 times the energy.

items: Amplitude: how many times larger is the ground motion on a seismogram for a magnitude 5.0 earthquake than for a magnitude 3.0 earthquake?
Energy: about how many times more energy does a magnitude 8.0 earthquake release than a magnitude 7.0 earthquake?
Energy: about how many times more energy does a magnitude 9.1 earthquake release than a magnitude 7.1 earthquake?

blocks.hint: Answer to 1
Answer to 2
Answer to 3

handouts.key:
1. Amplitude ratio = 10^{5.0−3.0} = 100. The magnitude 5.0 amplitude is 100 times as large, with the distance correction understood.
2. Energy ratio ≈ 32^{8.0−7.0} = 32. The magnitude 8.0 earthquake releases about 32 times as much energy.
3. Energy ratio ≈ 32^{9.1−7.1} = 1,024, or about 1,000. Using the unrounded energy relation gives 10^{1.5×2} = 1,000.
Common slips: multiplying the magnitude difference by 10, or using the amplitude factor for energy.

handouts.title: Find and fix the mistakes

blocks.text: Below is a short draft summary of today's lecture, written by an imaginary student. Work alone. Underline every wrong statement, then write a corrected sentence for it in the space after the draft.
Draft summary

items: A magnitude 7 releases twice the energy of a magnitude 6.
The epicenter is the point underground where rock first breaks.
Each earthquake has one intensity, recorded by a seismograph.
Liquefaction is worst in dry sand.

blocks.hint: Corrected sentence for statement 1
Corrected sentence for statement 2
Corrected sentence for statement 3
Corrected sentence for statement 4

handouts.key:
1. A magnitude 7 earthquake releases about 32 times as much energy as a magnitude 6 earthquake.
2. The focus is the point underground where rupture begins. The epicenter is the point on Earth's surface directly above the focus.
3. An earthquake has different intensities at different places. Modified Mercalli intensity describes observed effects on people, objects and structures. Magnitude describes the earthquake's size using seismic measurements.
4. Liquefaction is most likely in loose, water-saturated sediment, especially sand. Shaking raises pore-water pressure and reduces the effective stress holding grains together.
Look for all four statements identified and corrected. Common slips: giving 10 as the energy ratio, reversing focus and epicenter, or describing liquefaction as grains melting.

handouts.title: Epicenter location worksheet
handouts.usedIn: Locate the epicenter from three stations
handouts.copies: One per student; one kilometer-grid map with stations A, B and C plotted per pair

blocks.text: Work in pairs. One partner reads the arrival times from the table and calls out values while the other converts and draws. Swap roles for each station. Each partner fills in their own table. Use the department's compass and ruler, and the scale printed on the map.
Trace readings (seconds after the record began)

columns: Position on map (km east, km north)
blocks.caption: Stations A, B and C

blocks.text: Rule for this exercise
Assume a shallow focus and constant wave speeds, with P at 6.0 km/s and S at 3.5 km/s. Then radius (km) = 8.4 × S–P interval (s).
Steps

items: Subtract each P arrival from its S arrival to get the interval, and enter it in the table.
Convert each interval to a radius in kilometers, and enter it in the table.
Set the compass to the radius at the map scale and draw a circle around each station.
Read the coordinates of the point where the three circles meet.

blocks.hint: Epicenter coordinates (km east, km north)
How large is the uncertainty in your answer, in kilometers, and where do you see it on the map?
If you had only stations A and B, what would the map show?

handouts.key:
Station A: S–P interval = 14.4 − 8.4 = 6.0 s; radius = 8.4 × 6.0 = 50.4 km.
Station B: S–P interval = 19.2 − 11.2 = 8.0 s; radius = 8.4 × 8.0 = 67.2 km.
Station C: S–P interval = 20.2 − 11.8 = 8.4 s; radius = 8.4 × 8.4 = 70.56 km, approximately 70.6 km.
Epicenter coordinates: approximately (40, 30) km east and north. Accept a plotted location within about 5 km of this point. The rounded arrival readings produce circles that nearly intersect in this area.
Uncertainty: accept a numerical estimate in kilometers supported by the plotted overlap, line widths and map scale. A small region a few kilometers across is reasonable for a hand-drawn result. Look for recognition that arrival picking and compass placement also affect the location. A 1 s change in an interval changes its radius by 8.4 km.
With only A and B: the circles intersect at approximately (40.1, 30.5) and (40.1, −30.5) km. Either location fits those two stations; C selects the northern location.
Common slips: multiplying an arrival time rather than the interval by 8.4, treating kilometers as centimeters without applying the map scale, or reporting an exact point with no uncertainty.

handouts.title: Liquefaction in a tray

blocks.text: Work in pairs, each keeping your own record. Wipe spills at once, keep sand out of the sink, and wash your hands afterward. Hand samples stay in their trays.
Procedure

items: Your bench has two tubs: one of loose, fully saturated sand with little standing water on top, and one of loose, dry sand.
Set one small block flat on the surface of the saturated sand. Set an identical block on the dry sand.
Tap the side of each tub steadily and gently for 15 to 20 seconds. Never strike the tub. Do the saturated tub once and the dry tub once.
Watch the block and the water during the tapping and just after it. Record what you see.
Take the sandstone hand sample from its tray and examine it beside the loose sand.
Loosen and level the sand in both tubs for the next pair. Restore the saturated tub to full saturation with little standing water, and keep the dry tub dry.

blocks.hint: Prediction, before you tap: what will a small block do on saturated sand and on dry sand when the tub is shaken?
Explain the difference in terms of water pressure between the grains.
Labeled sketch of the saturated sand before and during shaking. Label the grains, the water and the block.
Why does the cemented sandstone not liquefy?

handouts.key:
Prediction: the block on saturated sand may sink or tilt during tapping, and water may rise to the surface. The block on dry sand may settle slightly as grains pack more closely.
Observations, saturated sand: record the block's actual movement, such as sinking, tilting or remaining level. Record any water rising, pooling or moving around the block.
Observations, dry sand: record the block's actual movement, usually slight settling. There is no pore water to rise or pool. Accept observations that differ from the prediction when clearly recorded.
Explanation: shaking tends to compact loose saturated sand. If water cannot drain quickly, pore-water pressure rises. Effective stress and frictional resistance between grains decrease, so the sand can lose strength and the block can sink or tilt. Dry sand can compact, but it cannot develop excess pore-water pressure.
Sketch: before shaking, show the block supported by contacting grains, with water filling the pore spaces. During shaking, show increased pore-water pressure, reduced grain contact forces, possible upward water movement and a sinking or tilted block. Label grains, water and block.
Sandstone: cement bonds its grains into a coherent rock framework. It does not undergo the grain rearrangement and loss of frictional strength shown by the loose saturated sand in this experiment.
Common slips: claiming that water melts the sand, that dry sand cannot settle, or that all saturated sediment must liquefy.

handouts.title: Intensity survey map
handouts.copies: One per student; one sheet of graph paper per pair

blocks.text: Suppose an earthquake struck a region with six towns. The reports and ground types below are hypothetical. Work in pairs, each keeping your own record. Assign a Modified Mercalli level to each town's report using the key. Then plot Mercalli level against distance from the epicenter on the grid, using one symbol for bedrock towns and another for towns on soft ground, and write each town's name beside its point.
Modified Mercalli key

rows: Felt by a few people at rest, especially on upper floors.
Felt indoors by several people. Hanging objects swing slightly.
Felt indoors by many. Dishes and windows rattle. Parked cars rock.
Felt by nearly everyone. Sleepers wake. Small objects move.
Felt by all. Furniture moves. Some plaster cracks or falls in older houses.
Hard to stand. Negligible damage in well-built structures, considerable damage in poorly built ones. Some chimneys fall.
Considerable damage in ordinary buildings, partial collapse in poorly built ones. Chimneys and walls fall.
Heavy damage. Buildings shift off their foundations. Ground cracks.
Most masonry and frame structures destroyed. Rails bend. Landslides.
Few structures remain standing. Bridges destroyed.
Total damage. Waves seen on the ground surface.

blocks.text: Felt reports and ground type

rows: Everyone felt it. Furniture moved and some plaster cracked in older houses.
Several old brick buildings partly collapsed. Chimneys and walls fell. Cracks opened in the ground.
Many people indoors felt it. Dishes and windows rattled and parked cars rocked.
People found it hard to stand. Poorly built houses were badly damaged and several chimneys fell.
A few people indoors felt it. Hanging lamps swayed slightly.
Nearly everyone felt it. Sleepers woke and small objects moved.
blocks.caption: Ground type at each town.

blocks.hint: Compare the bedrock towns with the soft-ground towns on your graph. If intensity depended on distance alone, what would the graph show? Describe how your graph differs, and explain why.

handouts.key:
Alder Point: VI. Furniture moved and plaster cracked.
Brookfield: VIII. Partial collapse, fallen chimneys and fallen walls are the strongest matching evidence. Ground cracks alone do not establish IX.
Cedar Mills: IV. Dishes and windows rattled, and parked cars rocked.
Delta Landing: VII. People had difficulty standing, poorly built houses suffered considerable damage and chimneys fell.
Eastgate: III. Slight movement of hanging lamps supports III, although the report's reference to only a few people feeling it overlaps with II. Accept II if the student explicitly explains that ambiguity using the key.
Fairview: V. Nearly everyone felt it, sleepers woke and small objects moved.
Graph: points at (10 km, VI) Alder Point, (12, VIII) Brookfield, (30, IV) Cedar Mills, (32, VII) Delta Landing, (55, III) Eastgate and (58, V) Fairview, with bedrock and soft-ground towns marked differently. Accept the justified alternative for Eastgate described above.
Ground-type comparison: Brookfield has stronger reported effects than Alder Point despite being slightly farther away. The same pattern occurs for Delta Landing versus Cedar Mills and Fairview versus Eastgate. In this hypothetical survey, soft sediment is associated with higher intensity than nearby bedrock sites. On the graph the soft-ground towns sit two to three levels above bedrock towns at similar distances, so intensity is not set by distance alone. Look for explanations involving local amplification of shaking, while recognizing that building vulnerability also affects damage reports.
Common slip: assigning intensity from distance alone instead of the reported effects.

l_1fcbc06097c2.title: Folds, faults and mountain building
l_1fcbc06097c2.summary: Midterm exam 2, on sedimentary rocks through earthquakes, is taken in this lesson, followed by rock deformation, geologic maps and orogeny.
readings: Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, the chapter on crustal deformation and mountain building
suggestedReadings: McPhee, Annals of the Former World (1998)

segments.title: Room set-up and exam instructions
segments.description:
Seat students with space between them where the room allows.
Tell them what they may have at their desks for the exam.
Say that Midterm exam 2 (15%) is on what has been taught so far and is marked in points. Announce the teacher’s exam conditions.
Say that Weekly online quizzes: Earthquakes, part of Weekly online quizzes (10%), is due now and is submitted online before this meeting. Then hand out the papers face down and start everyone together.
segments.teacherNotes: Clear the board and screen of earlier work before students enter. Keep spare copies of the paper. Papers stay face down until you say begin.
shown: Midterm exam 2: on what has been taught so far.

segments.title: Midterm exam 2
segments.description:
Students sit Midterm exam 2 under the conditions announced by the teacher.
Announce the time left at the halfway point, ten minutes before the end, and two minutes before the end.
Students who finish early stay seated and check their work until the papers are collected.
segments.teacherNotes: The paper carries its own questions, key and points. Walk the room quietly. Keep nothing on the board or screen that could give an answer.

segments.title: Collect papers and look ahead
segments.description:
Call time and collect every paper.
Say that the next meeting begins rock deformation, with folds and faults.
Remind students that Lab reports: Earthquakes is due at the start of the lab.
segments.teacherNotes: Count papers against the class list before students leave the room. Ask students not to discuss the paper in the corridor until all have finished.

segments.title: Squeeze a stack
segments.description:
Lay a stack of four colored towels flat on the desk, one color per layer. Identify the bottom towel as the oldest layer and each towel above it as successively younger.
Each student sketches what the stack will look like when pushed together from both ends, then compares with a partner.
Push the ends together and show the result.
segments.teacherNotes: Expect rounded upfolds and downfolds side by side. Explain that the towels model folding under compression. Rock deformation also depends on temperature, confining pressure, rock properties and strain rate. The layers start flat because of original horizontality, from earlier in the course.
shown: A flat stack of four colored layers is pushed together from both ends. Sketch the stack afterward.

segments.title: Stress and folds
segments.description:
Name three stresses: compression squeezes, tension pulls apart, shear slides sideways.
Say that hot, deep rock under slow stress bends into folds, while cold, shallow rock breaks along faults.
Define an anticline as an arch and a syncline as a trough, each with two limbs.
Pairs predict which layer lies at the center of the arch and of the trough in the towel stack, before the answer is given.
segments.teacherNotes: Oldest rock at the core of an anticline, youngest at the core of a syncline, if the layers are right way up (superposition, from earlier in the course). Common mistake: reading the name as ‘sinking’ or ‘rising’ instead of the shape.
shown: Side by side: Anticline: arch; limbs dip away from the hinge; oldest rock at the core | Syncline: trough; limbs dip toward the hinge; youngest rock at the core

segments.title: Anticline or syncline?
segments.description:
Put the table of rock ages on the screen, read along a line from the center of a fold outward.
Each student writes anticline or syncline for each section, with no written reason.
Partners compare, and settle any difference by naming the oldest rock in the section.
One answer is heard, with its reason.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. Section P: Jurassic at center, Permian at the outer edges. Syncline, youngest at the core.
2. Section Q: Permian at center, Jurassic at the outer edges. Anticline, oldest at the core.
The reason is one phrase: oldest or youngest at the core. Common slip: forgetting that Permian is older than Jurassic.
shown: Table: Section | Rock at center | Rock in the middle | Rock at outer edges / P | Jurassic | Triassic | Permian / Q | Permian | Triassic | Jurassic

segments.title: Faults and the hanging wall
segments.description:
Define the hanging wall as the block above an inclined fault plane and the footwall as the block below.
Hold two wooden blocks cut at an angle to show a fault. Pairs predict which way the hanging wall moves when the crust is pulled apart.
Show normal, reverse and strike-slip motion with the blocks.
Link strike-slip faults to the San Andreas fence offset from the earthquakes lesson, a right-lateral motion.
segments.teacherNotes: Tension makes room, so the hanging wall slides down. Compression shortens the crust and pushes it up. A thrust fault is a reverse fault with a low dip. A fault is younger than the rocks it cuts (cross-cutting, from earlier in the course).
shown: Table: Fault type | Stress | Motion / Normal | Tension | Hanging wall moves down / Reverse | Compression | Hanging wall moves up / Strike-slip | Shear | Blocks slide past horizontally

segments.title: Name the fault
segments.description:
Four fault descriptions are on the screen.
Each student writes only the fault type for every one.
Partners compare, then one answer is heard.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. Normal fault.
2. Reverse fault.
3. Strike-slip fault.
4. Reverse (thrust) fault; older rock lies over younger.
Common mistake: calling 1 reverse because the block is ‘above’.
shown: 1. The crust is pulled apart. The hanging wall moves down relative to the footwall.
2. The crust is squeezed together. The hanging wall moves up relative to the footwall.
3. Two blocks slide past each other horizontally. A fence built across the fault is offset sideways.
4. Along a gently dipping fault, older rock lies on top of younger rock.

segments.title: Continental collision builds a mountain belt
segments.description:
Pairs predict what happens when a continent riding on a subducting plate reaches the trench, and why.
Explain that continental crust resists subduction because of its buoyancy. During collision, some continental crust can be forced beneath the other continent, while shortening forms folds and thrust faults that stack and thicken the crust.
Use India and Asia: the collision began roughly 50 million years ago, India still moves north at roughly 5 cm per year, and the crust under Tibet is about 70 km thick, twice normal.
End with marine limestone near the summit of Everest, and the eroded Appalachians as an old belt.
segments.teacherNotes: Name the whole episode an orogeny. Regional metamorphism happens in the thick root (earlier in the course). Thick crust floats high, then erosion strips it. Everest is about 8,850 m high. Its summit limestone formed in the sea.
shown: Steps: Ocean closes by subduction → Continents meet → Crust crumples and thrust slices stack → Crust thickens to about 70 km → Belt rises and erodes

segments.title: Find and fix the mistake
segments.description:
Four statements about folds, faults and collision are on the screen, and each contains one or more mistakes.
Each student underlines the mistake in every statement and writes the fix in a few words.
Partners compare in one minute, then two corrections are heard.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and fixes (a few words each is enough):
1. Fix: the oldest rocks are at the core of an anticline.
2. Fix: normal faults form under tension, and the hanging wall moves down.
3. Fix: strike-slip blocks slide horizontally.
4. Fix: continental crust is buoyant, so it crumples and thickens, building mountains.
shown: 1. In an anticline, the youngest rocks are at the center of the fold.
2. A normal fault forms when the crust is compressed, and its hanging wall moves up.
3. A strike-slip fault moves rock up and down along the dip of the fault.
4. When two continents collide, one sinks deep into the mantle like oceanic crust, so no mountains form.

segments.title: Summary and the lab ahead
segments.description:
Review how to tell an anticline from a syncline by the age at the core, and the three fault types by hanging wall motion.
Review why a continental collision makes a thick, high belt.
Say that next time is the lab, where pairs draw cross sections from geologic maps. Lab reports: Earthquakes is due at the start of the lab, and closed-toe shoes are required.

segments.title: Report due, safety and pairs
segments.description:
Lab reports: Earthquakes, part of Lab reports (30%), is due now.
State today’s rules: closed-toe shoes, hand samples stay in their trays and go back where they came from, and goggles on whenever the dilute HCl is used.
Pairs set out a ruler, a protractor, sharp pencils and colored pencils.
Pairs record results together, and each student writes their own report.
segments.teacherNotes: Safety: sharp pencils stay on the bench. Keep paper towels at each bench for spills. Count samples against the tray labels at the start so missing pieces are noticed.

segments.title: Method: reading a geologic map and drawing a section
segments.description:
Explain that a contact is the boundary between two rock units, and that a strike-and-dip symbol gives the bed’s direction and tilt.
Show the steps on the board with a practice map. Lay a paper strip on the section line, mark each contact, then move the strip to the top of the grid.
For these exercises, use section lines perpendicular to the strike of the beds. At each mark, draw the contact at its dip with a protractor, using the same scale across and down.
Pairs find how far west of the surface trace the contact lies at 1 km depth before the teacher draws it.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: 1 ÷ tan 20° ≈ 2.7 km west of the trace, so the contact slopes down toward the west. A dip of 45° puts it as far across as deep. Common mistake: measuring the dip from vertical.
shown: Steps: Choose the line → Mark contacts on a paper strip → Move the strip to the grid → Draw each contact at its dip → Shade and label the units

Practice map: flat ground, section line running west to east. The contact between shale and sandstone crosses the line 2.0 km from the west end. Its strike-and-dip symbol reads strike north–south, dip 20° to the west.

segments.title: Read the symbols
segments.description:
The teacher draws four strike-and-dip symbols on the board.
Each student writes the dip of each bed as one short phrase, such as 30° east.
Partners compare, then the class decides which bed is steepest.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. Long line north–south, tick east, 30: dips 30° east.
2. Long line east–west, tick north, 60: dips 60° north.
3. Long line north–south, tick west, 10: dips 10° west.
4. Long line east–west, tick south, 85: dips 85° south, nearly vertical; steepest.
The strike is the direction of the long line; ask for it aloud only if time allows.

segments.title: Predict, then test: match the map units to samples
segments.description:
Pairs read the sheet Map key: three units, which describes each unit by its grain and its reaction to dilute HCl.
Before any acid is used, each pair writes which sample in their tray they predict will fizz and what makes them say so.
With goggles on, they test each sample with one drop of dilute HCl and watch for bubbles.
Beside each unit they record the sample number from the tray label, the rock name and whether it fizzed.
segments.teacherNotes:
Before class, test the shale and sandstone samples with a drop of acid and set out only ones that do not fizz (some sandstones have calcite cement and some shales are calcareous). The limestone must fizz, so the results match the map key.
Expected record:
Unit 1: shale, no fizz (very fine grains, splits in thin sheets).
Unit 2: sandstone, no fizz (cemented sand-sized grains).
Unit 3: limestone, fizz (fine, compact grains).
Prediction: the limestone, because the key shows only Unit 3 fizzing. Samples go back to their trays.
Safety: goggles on before the bottle is opened. One drop only, wipe spills at once, rinse the sample and dry it.

segments.title: Cross section: tilted layers
segments.description:
Pairs use the sheet Geologic map: tilted sedimentary layers, which holds a map of three units on flat ground with strike-and-dip symbols and the line A–A′ running west to east, plus a section grid.
One partner marks the contacts on the paper strip while the other measures each dip; they switch for the next contact.
Pairs draw the section, shade the units, and write which way the rocks get younger.
They compare with another pair before recording.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: contacts dip 30° east and are drawn without vertical exaggeration. The rocks get younger toward the east. Common errors: contacts drawn vertical, dip drawn the wrong way, or a different scale down than across. Accept small measuring errors.

segments.title: Break
segments.description: Pairs leave the benches. Hand samples stay in their trays.

segments.title: Predict, then draw: a folded region
segments.description:
Pairs use the sheet Geologic map: folded layers, which holds a map where the same three units appear in strips on either side of a central strip, with dips and a section line B–B′.
Before drawing, each student predicts from the map whether the fold is an anticline or a syncline and writes the evidence.
Pairs draw the section, continue the contacts as dashed lines above the ground, and label the fold.
They record the fold name and the age of the rock at its core.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: an anticline. The oldest unit forms the central strip and the dips point away from the center on both sides. The section is a mirror image either side of the axis. Common mistake: dips drawn toward the center.

segments.title: Name the fault from the section
segments.description:
Pairs use the sheet Faults in cross section, which holds two sections of layered rock offset along a dipping fault.
For each section they mark the hanging wall, then name the fault type and the stress that formed it.
They also write whether the fault is older or younger than the layers it cuts.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: section one is a normal fault under tension; section two is a reverse (thrust) fault under compression, with older rock over younger. In both, the fault is younger than the layers it cuts. Common error: identifying the hanging wall by which block appears to move instead of identifying the block above the inclined fault plane.

segments.title: Rocks of a mountain belt
segments.description:
Pairs examine the five samples in their tray: the department's slate, schist, gneiss, marble and fossil-bearing limestone.
In the table on the sheet Rocks of a mountain belt they record the rock name for each sample, and the rock name only.
Pairs then write two sentences on how a continental collision could make the metamorphic rocks in their tray and lift marine limestone to the top of a high range.
Two pairs read their explanations.
segments.teacherNotes:
Table answers, in any order: slate, schist, gneiss, marble, fossil-bearing limestone. The limestone is the one that is not metamorphic.
Expected explanation: collision squeezes and thickens the crust. Heat and pressure at depth cause regional metamorphism. Uplift and erosion expose the rocks, and sea-floor sediments are lifted high, like the limestone on Everest. Samples go back to their trays.

segments.title: Finish recording and clean up
segments.description:
Pairs complete the recording sheets and return every sample to the tray it came from.
They cap the acid bottle, wipe the benches and collect their pencils and protractors.
segments.teacherNotes: Count samples against the tray labels before pairs leave. Safety: rinse the limestone sample used for the fizz test and dry it before it goes back. Put used paper towels in the bin.

segments.title: Assignments and what comes next
segments.description:
Set the assignment Lab reports (30%), due at the start of the lab of Streams and floods. Each student writes their own report, which is scored individually. Set the assignment Weekly online quizzes (10%), due at the first meeting of Streams and floods. Each student completes it individually; it is scored individually and submitted online before the lesson it is due at.
Tell students to read Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, the chapter on streams and floods, before that lesson.
Say that Streams and floods covers drainage basins, stream discharge, erosion and deposition, meanders and floodplains, and flood hazards, tested in a stream table model.
Say that a short practice quiz on this lesson is there to take after class, and that it counts toward no grade.

keyIdeas: Rock under slow, steady compression bends into folds. An anticline is an arch with the oldest rock at its core. A syncline is a trough with the youngest rock at its core.

Faults are classified by the relative motion of the blocks. Normal faults (tension) drop it down, reverse faults (compression) push it up, and strike-slip faults (shear) slide the blocks past each other horizontally.
A geologic map shows the rock units at the surface. Contacts plus strike and dip let you draw a cross section that shows the structure at depth.
When two continents collide, neither subducts easily. The crust crumples, thrust faults stack slices of rock, and the crust thickens and rises as a mountain belt such as the Himalaya.

vocabulary.definition: A fold shaped like an arch. If the beds are right way up, the oldest rock lies in its core.
A fold shaped like a trough. If the beds are right way up, the youngest rock lies in its core.
The block of rock above an inclined fault plane. The block below it is the footwall.
A fault in which the hanging wall moves down relative to the footwall. It forms when the crust is pulled apart by tension.
A fault in which the hanging wall moves up relative to the footwall. It forms under compression. A thrust fault is a reverse fault with a low dip.
A fault in which the blocks slide past each other horizontally. It forms under shear.

The strike is the compass direction of the line where a bed meets a horizontal surface. The dip is the angle at which the bed tilts down from horizontal, measured at right angles to the strike, with its direction.
An episode of mountain building, often caused by plate collision, with folding, faulting, metamorphism and uplift.

slides.title: Squeeze a stack
bullets: A flat stack of four colored layers is pushed together from both ends. Sketch the stack afterward.
slides.notes: Lay a stack of four colored towels flat on the desk, one color per layer. Identify the bottom towel as the oldest layer and each towel above it as successively younger. Each student sketches what the stack will look like when pushed together from both ends, then compares with a partner. Then push the ends together and show the result. Expect rounded upfolds and downfolds side by side. The towels model folding under compression. Rock deformation also depends on temperature, confining pressure, rock properties and strain rate. The layers start flat because of original horizontality, from earlier in the course. Leave this slide up while you move on to the next segment.

slides.title: Anticline and syncline
slides.notes: Before this slide: name three stresses. Compression squeezes, tension pulls apart, shear slides sideways. Say that hot, deep rock under slow stress bends into folds, while cold, shallow rock breaks along faults. Define an anticline as an arch and a syncline as a trough, each with two limbs. Pairs predict which layer lies at the center of the arch and of the trough in the towel stack. Show this slide only after they have predicted. Oldest rock at the core of an anticline, youngest at the core of a syncline, if the layers are right way up (superposition, from earlier in the course). Common mistake: reading the name as ‘sinking’ or ‘rising’ instead of the shape.

Section Q has Permian at the center and Jurassic at the outer edges, so it is an anticline, oldest at the core. The reason is one phrase: oldest or youngest at the core. Explain that continental crust resists subduction because of its buoyancy. During collision, some continental crust can be forced beneath the other continent, while shortening forms folds and thrust faults that stack and thicken the crust. Use India and Asia: the collision began roughly 50 million years ago, India still moves north at roughly 5 cm per year, and the crust under Tibet is about 70 km thick, twice normal. study.overview: Rock responds to stress by bending or breaking. Slow compression of hot, deep rock produces folds. Cold, shallow rock tends to break along faults. Geologists read these structures from the age pattern of rock units and from the motion of blocks. They draw a cross section from a geologic map to show structure at depth. The same compression, on a continental scale, builds mountain belts. This guide covers folds, faults, cross sections and continental collision. Review the chapter on crustal deformation and mountain building in Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, alongside it.

points.heading: Folds: read the age at the core
points.explanation: Compression squeezes layers into folds. Picture a stack of four colored towels laid flat, the bottom towel oldest and each one above it younger. Push the ends together and the stack buckles into rounded upfolds and downfolds side by side. The layers start flat because of original horizontality. An anticline is an arch. Its limbs dip away from the hinge, and the oldest rock is at the core. A syncline is a trough. Its limbs dip toward the hinge, and the youngest rock is at the core. The names describe shape, not ‘rising’ or ‘sinking’. The rule assumes the layers are right way up (superposition). Hypothetical example: a map shows Triassic rock in the central strip, with Permian rock at the outer edges. Permian is older than Triassic, so the youngest rock is at the core and the structure is a syncline. A quick check is to find the oldest unit and ask whether it is in the middle or on the outside.

points.heading: Faults: name them by the motion of the hanging wall
points.explanation: A fault is a fracture along which blocks have moved. On an inclined fault plane, the hanging wall is the block above the plane and the footwall is the block below. Do not pick the hanging wall by which block seems to move. Classify the fault by the relative motion of the blocks. Normal faults form under tension, and the hanging wall moves down. Reverse faults form under compression, and the hanging wall moves up. A thrust fault is a reverse fault with a low dip, so older rock can end up lying on top of younger rock. Strike-slip faults form under shear, and the blocks slide past each other horizontally. A fence built across a strike-slip fault is offset sideways. The San Andreas fault is an example, with right-lateral motion. A fault is younger than the rocks it cuts, because the rocks had to exist before they could be broken (cross-cutting relationships).

points.heading: From geologic map to cross section
points.explanation: A geologic map shows the rock units at the surface. A contact is the boundary between two units. A strike-and-dip symbol gives the bed’s direction (the long line is the strike) and its tilt (the number, with the tick showing the dip direction). The steps are: choose a section line perpendicular to the strike; mark each contact on a paper strip; move the strip to the grid; draw each contact at its dip with a protractor; then shade and label the units. Use the same scale across and down. Measure the dip from horizontal, not from vertical, and draw the contact sloping down in the dip direction. Worked example: the contact between shale and sandstone crosses the line 2.0 km from the west end. The symbol reads strike north–south, dip 20° west. At 1 km depth, the contact lies 1 ÷ tan 20° ≈ 2.7 km west of its surface trace. So the contact slopes down toward the west. A 45° dip would put the contact as far across as it is deep. For a fold, continue the contacts as dashed lines above the ground. They show where eroded layers once arched.

points.heading: Continental collision builds mountain belts
points.explanation: Oceanic plates subduct easily. Continental crust is buoyant and resists it. When an ocean closes and two continents meet, the crust crumples. Folds form and thrust faults stack slices of rock. Some continental crust can be forced beneath the other continent. The overall effect is that the crust shortens, thickens and rises. The whole episode is an orogeny. India and Asia show this. The collision began roughly 50 million years ago, and India still moves north at roughly 5 cm per year. The crust under Tibet is about 70 km thick, twice normal, and the Himalaya stand above it. Heat and pressure in the thick root cause regional metamorphism, which makes rocks such as slate, schist and gneiss. Marine limestone lies near the summit of Everest, about 8,850 m high, because sea-floor sediments were lifted. Erosion eventually strips a belt down. The Appalachians are an old, eroded belt.

Step 2: A is west, at the left; A′ is east, at the right. The ground line is 6 cm long, representing 6 km. The depth axis extends 3 cm below ground, representing 3 km. Both contacts slope downward toward the east at 30° from horizontal. Their depth is the horizontal distance east of their surface trace multiplied by tan 30°, approximately 0.577.

Useful drawing checks: At A′, the Unit 3–Unit 2 contact is approximately 2.60 km below ground: 4.5 × tan 30° ≈ 2.60. The Unit 2–Unit 1 contact is approximately 1.44 km below ground: 2.5 × tan 30° ≈ 1.44. Neither contact reaches the bottom of the grid within the section. Label Unit 1 above the eastern contact, Unit 2 between the contacts, and Unit 3 below the western contact. Use consistent colors and label both ends.

The rocks get younger toward the east. At the surface, Ordovician Unit 3 is followed eastward by Silurian Unit 2 and then Devonian Unit 1. Common slips: reversing the age order, drawing the contacts westward, measuring dip from vertical, or using unequal horizontal and vertical scales.

blocks.text: Step 2: draw the section

On the section grid, draw the ground line 8 km long with B at the left and B′ at the right. Leave 2.2 km of space above the ground line and extend the vertical axis 3 km below it. Mark the contacts and draw each at its dip with a protractor. Continue the contacts as dashed lines above the ground. Shade the units and label the fold.

blocks.hint: Your cross section B–B′ (label the units and the ends of the line).

blocks.text: Step 3: record

blocks.label: Age of the rock at the core of the fold

handouts.key:
Step 1: Anticline. Ordovician Unit 3, the oldest unit, occupies the central strip. Silurian Unit 2 and Devonian Unit 1 occur successively outward on both sides. The western beds dip west and the eastern beds dip east, away from the fold axis. Common slip: identifying the fold from dip alone without checking the ages.

Step 2: Draw B at the west end and B′ at the east end of an 8 cm ground line. Mark contacts at 1.5, 3.0, 5.0 and 6.5 cm from B. Use the same horizontal and vertical scale. The contacts at 1.5 and 3.0 km dip 40° west; those at 5.0 and 6.5 km dip 40° east. Place the fold axis at approximately 4.0 km. Show a symmetric upward fold, with Unit 3 in the core, Unit 2 surrounding it and Unit 1 outside Unit 2. Solid lines show contacts below ground; dashed lines reconstruct their eroded continuation above ground.

For straight-limb extrapolation, the Unit 3–Unit 2 contacts meet 1.0 × tan 40° ≈ 0.84 km above ground at the axis. The Unit 2–Unit 1 contacts meet 2.5 × tan 40° ≈ 2.10 km above ground there. Accept smoothly rounded hinges consistent with the mapped contacts and limb dips; the map does not uniquely determine hinge curvature. Common slips: drawing dips toward the center, placing the youngest unit in the core, or drawing solid contacts through the air.

Step 3:
Fold name: Anticline.
Age of the rock at the core of the fold: Ordovician.

handouts.title: Faults in cross section
handouts.usedIn: Name the fault from the section

blocks.text: Each section is a vertical cross section through layered rock, west on the left and east on the right. Layer A is the youngest, Layer B lies below it and Layer C is the oldest. All three layers were once flat and horizontal.
Section one

The fault plane slopes down toward the east at 60° from horizontal. Layers A, B and C all appear on both sides of the fault. On the east side each layer lies lower than the same layer on the west side.
Section two
The fault plane slopes down toward the west at 25° from horizontal. At the fault, Layer C of the west block lies directly on top of Layer A of the east block.
Your answers
For each section, name the block that is the hanging wall (east or west), the type of fault and the stress that formed it, and say whether the fault is older or younger than the layers it cuts.

columns: Fault older or younger than the layers it cuts

handouts.key:
Section One | East block | Normal fault; tension or extension | Younger than the layers it cuts.

The east block lies above the east-dipping fault plane. Its layers are displaced downward relative to matching layers in the west block.

Section Two | West block | Reverse fault, specifically a thrust fault; compression | Younger than the layers it cuts.

The west block lies above the west-dipping fault plane. Older Layer C has been carried over younger Layer A. The 25° dip supports identifying this reverse fault as a thrust fault.

Common slip: identifying the hanging wall from its elevation or movement instead of its position above the inclined fault plane. Fault age follows cross-cutting relationships.

handouts.title: Rocks of a mountain belt

blocks.text: Examine the five samples in your tray. Record the rock name only. Samples go back to their tray when you finish.

blocks.hint: In two sentences, explain how a continental collision could make the metamorphic rocks in your tray and lift marine limestone to the top of a high range.

handouts.key:
Table: Enter each sample’s actual tray label in the Sample column and its corresponding rock name in the Rock column. The five rock entries, in whichever order the tray presents them, are slate, schist, gneiss, marble and fossil-bearing limestone.

Identification cues: Slate has very fine grains and slaty cleavage; schist has visible aligned platy minerals; gneiss has compositional banding; marble has interlocking carbonate crystals; fossil-bearing limestone contains recognizable fossils. The limestone is sedimentary.

Example two-sentence explanation: Continental collision shortens and thickens the crust, burying rocks where heat and directed stress can produce regional metamorphism, including slate, schist, gneiss and marble from suitable parent rocks. Deformation and uplift can raise marine limestone to high elevations, while erosion exposes rocks that formed deeper in the mountain belt.

Look for crustal shortening and thickening, metamorphism at depth, and uplift of formerly marine rocks. Common slips: saying metamorphism requires melting, treating fossil-bearing limestone as metamorphic, or implying all five samples form successive stages of one metamorphic sequence.

ready: Teacher: four colored towels and two wooden blocks cut at an angle for the demonstrations
Teacher: a practice geologic map for the board, and paper strips for each pair
Teacher: a section grid (graph paper) for each pair, for both cross sections
Teacher: rulers, protractors, sharp pencils and colored pencils for each pair
Teacher: the department's pretested shale, sandstone and limestone samples, and the slate, schist, gneiss, marble and fossil-bearing limestone samples, in labeled trays
Teacher: a bottle of dilute HCl, goggles for every student and paper towels at each bench

l_799e28bdfc8b.title: Streams and floods
l_799e28bdfc8b.summary: Drainage basins, stream discharge, erosion and deposition, meanders and floodplains, and flood hazards, tested in a stream table model.
readings: Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, the chapter on streams and floods
suggestedReadings: Leopold, A View of the River (1994)

segments.title: Quiz due now and a raindrop’s route
segments.description:
Weekly online quizzes: Folds, faults and mountain building is due now; it was submitted online beforehand.
Each student writes the route a raindrop takes from the roof of this building to the sea, naming every stream, river or lake they think it passes through.
Two students read their routes aloud.
segments.teacherNotes: Accept guesses. Routes should run from a gutter to a creek to a larger river. Use the answers to introduce the basin idea. Students were asked to read the Earle chapter on streams and floods, so draw on it.
shown: Prompt: Trace a raindrop from the roof of this building to the sea. Name each stream, river or lake you think it passes through.

segments.title: Drainage basins and divides
segments.description:
Define a drainage basin as all the land that sends its water to one stream. Its edge is a divide, a ridge that splits the flow.
Draw two streams with a ridge between them on the board. Pairs mark the divide and shade each basin before the teacher marks it.
Use the Mississippi as the large case: its basin drains about 40% of the contiguous United States, with the Missouri and Ohio as major tributaries.
Name headwaters, tributary and mouth, and explain that sea level is the lowest level a stream can cut down to (its ultimate base level).
segments.teacherNotes: Common mistake: drawing the divide along a stream instead of along the ridge. Stress that every tributary has its own smaller basin inside the larger one.
shown: Steps: headwaters → tributaries join → main channel → mouth at base level

segments.title: Discharge: width × depth × velocity
segments.description:
Define discharge as the volume of water passing a cross section each second: Q = w × d × v, in m³/s.
Pairs compute the example on the screen before the answer is shown. Then check the units: m × m × m/s gives m³/s, and 1 m³ is 1,000 liters.
Explain how velocity is measured with a float or current meter. A current-meter reading at about 0.6 of the depth below the surface estimates mean velocity in that vertical. Readings across the channel are combined to estimate discharge.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: 8 × 1.5 × 0.6 = 7.2 m³/s, which is 7,200 L/s. Real channels are not rectangles: depth is measured at several points and the strips are summed. Common slip: using the maximum depth.
shown: Q = w × d × v
Example: width 8 m, average depth 1.5 m, velocity 0.6 m/s. Find Q.

segments.title: Calculate discharge, calm and in flood
segments.description:
Pairs split the two problems on the screen: each student calculates one, and the partner checks the units.
They state how many times larger the storm discharge is.
One pair gives its answers.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. 12 × 2.0 × 0.5 = 12 m³/s.
2. 12 × 3.5 × 1.4 = 58.8 m³/s, about 5 times larger.
Say that depth rose 1.75 times and velocity 2.8 times, so velocity mattered more. Numbers are hypothetical.
shown: Suppose a small stream is 12 m wide, 2.0 m deep on average and flowing at 0.5 m/s. Find its discharge.
Suppose the same stream in a storm is still 12 m wide, but 3.5 m deep and flowing at 1.4 m/s. Find its discharge and how many times larger it is than in the first problem.

segments.title: Make up a channel
segments.description:
Each student invents a stream channel, with a width, a depth and a mean velocity, whose discharge is exactly 24 m³/s. The velocity must lie between 0.5 and 3 m/s, and the channel must be wider than it is deep.
Students swap with a partner, who checks the multiplication and judges whether the channel is realistic.
Two made-up channels are heard, and the class checks whether each satisfies the discharge, velocity and width constraints.
segments.teacherNotes: Valid examples: 12 × 2 × 1 = 24; 8 × 1.5 × 2 = 24; 20 × 1.2 × 1 = 24. Watch for mixed units, such as width in cm with depth in m. Ask students to say why a channel is unrealistic, not only that it is.
shown: Prompt: Make up a channel with Q = 24 m³/s. Give its width, depth and velocity. The velocity must be between 0.5 and 3 m/s, and the width must be greater than the depth.

segments.title: What changes downstream
segments.description:
Each student first writes whether gradient, discharge, and channel width and depth rise, fall or stay about the same from headwaters to mouth.
Draw a long profile on the board: steep and narrow with a rocky bed near the headwaters, gentle and wide with a sandy or muddy bed near the mouth.
Explain that discharge usually rises downstream as tributaries and groundwater add water. In dry regions it can fall, as water evaporates and soaks into the ground.
Partners compare predictions with the board profile.
segments.teacherNotes: Common misconception: that a gentler gradient means slower water. Larger channels generally have less boundary friction relative to their flow volume, so mean velocity can increase downstream despite the gentler gradient. Paraphrase Earle’s discussion of the long profile; do not quote.
shown: Prompt: Going downstream from the headwaters to the mouth, does each of these rise, fall or stay about the same: gradient, discharge, channel width and depth?

segments.title: Summary and what comes next
segments.description:
Review the basin and divide, and Q = w × d × v.
Say that next time is about how streams erode and deposit sediment, how meanders and floodplains form, and what makes a flood a hazard.
segments.teacherNotes: Ask for one sentence on what discharge measures before moving on.

segments.title: Fast side, slow side
segments.description:
Each student writes which side of a river bend has the fastest water, where sand will pile up, and which bank will erode.
Two predictions are heard, with no correction yet.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: fastest on the outside of the bend, sand on the inside, erosion of the outside bank. Accept guesses; the prediction frames the meander segment. Common idea: water is fastest on the inside because the path is shorter.
shown: Prompt: A river bends to the right. On which side of the bend does the water move fastest, and where will sand pile up?

segments.title: Erosion, transport and deposition
segments.description:
Describe three ways a stream carries material: dissolved, suspended and bed load.
Explain competence (the largest grain a flow can move) and capacity (the total load it can carry). Both rise with velocity and discharge.
Pairs predict which grain size is picked up by the slowest current: clay, sand or gravel.
Show that fine sand moves at a few tenths of a meter per second. Clay needs faster water to erode because the particles stick together. Gravel needs much faster water because it is heavy.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: sand, which surprises students. Cohesion makes clay hard to lift, but clay stays suspended once moving. Refer to the velocity-and-grain-size diagram in Earle’s chapter; do not redraw numbers from memory.
shown: Table: Load | How it moves | Typical material / Dissolved | carried as ions in the water | calcium and bicarbonate from limestone / Suspended | held up by turbulence | silt and clay / Bed load | rolls, slides and hops along the bed | sand, gravel and cobbles

segments.title: Meanders, point bars and floodplains
segments.description:
Draw a bend in plan view and in cross section. Water is fastest on the outside, which erodes a steep cut bank. It is slowest on the inside, which drops sand and gravel as a gently sloping point bar.
The bend migrates sideways. When the neck narrows and the river cuts across it, the abandoned loop becomes an oxbow lake, as along the lower Mississippi.
Floodplains grow as point bars build outward and as floods lay down silt and clay. Sand dropped beside the channel as the water slows forms natural levees.
Each student sketches the bend with the cut bank, point bar and a flow arrow, and a partner checks the labels.
segments.teacherNotes: Common mistake: swapping cut bank and point bar. Mnemonic: the cut bank is where the river cuts. Bends migrate downstream as well as outward. Link to the first meeting: velocity is highest in the deepest, outer part of the bend.
shown: Steps: erosion at the cut bank → deposition on the point bar → bend migrates sideways → neck narrows → cutoff leaves an oxbow lake

segments.title: Cut bank or point bar?
segments.description:
Each student marks every observation on the screen as a cut bank or a point bar.
Partners compare and give a reason for any answer that differs.
Two answers are heard, each with its reason.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. Steep bank with roots hanging in the air: cut bank.
2. Gentle slope of sand and small gravel, dry at low water: point bar.
3. Where the water is deepest and fastest: cut bank.
4. Side that will lose the field behind it: cut bank.
shown: Table: Observation | Cut bank or point bar? / 1. A steep bank with tree roots hanging in the air | ? / 2. A gentle slope of sand and small gravel, dry at low water | ? / 3. The side of the bend where the water is deepest and fastest | ? / 4. The side that will lose the field behind it over the next decades | ?

segments.title: Floods and recurrence intervals
segments.description:
Define bankfull, flood stage and recurrence interval. A 100-year flood has a 1% chance of happening in any year.
Assuming independent years and a constant 1% annual probability, pairs use a calculator to find the chance of at least one 100-year flood during a 30-year mortgage, as 1 − 0.99³⁰.
Name what raises flood hazard: paved surfaces that speed runoff, levees that confine the flow, and homes on the floodplain. Dams and retention basins reduce peaks.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: 0.99³⁰ ≈ 0.74, so about 26%. Common error: reading 100-year as once every hundred years. Two such floods can come in successive years. Recurrence intervals are estimated from gauge records.
shown: Table: Recurrence interval | Chance in any one year / 10 years | 10% / 50 years | 2% / 100 years | 1%
Prompt: What is the chance of at least one 100-year flood in 30 years?

segments.title: Raise the levee or buy out the lowest homes?
segments.description:
Each student reads the case on the screen and writes a choice and two reasons.
The teacher opens by asking one student who chose the levee, then one who chose the buyout, for their best reason.
Partners argue the opposite side for two minutes. The class then takes three questions in order: who pays and who carries the risk, what a confined river does downstream, and what the bought-out land does in the next flood.
The teacher writes the reasons in two columns on the board and closes by saying that a floodplain is part of the river system, which the river reoccupies in floods.
segments.teacherNotes: Transitions: from the opening choices to the partner argument (“now defend the other side”); from cost to downstream effects; then to the cleared land. Takeaway: raising the levee reduces local inundation while it holds, but excluding floodplain storage can increase downstream flood peaks, and overtopping or failure remains possible. A buyout removes homes from exposure and leaves cleared floodplain available to store floodwater. The town is hypothetical.
shown: Side by side: Raise the levee: keeps the river in its channel; costs money; confines the flow, so flood water stands higher | Buy out the lowest homes: cleared land stays open floodplain that stores floodwater; families must move; no levee to fail
Prompt: Suppose a small town sits on the floodplain of a meandering river. Bought-out land would be cleared and left open to flood. Which option would you choose, and why?

segments.title: Summary and the lab ahead
segments.description:
Review cut bank, point bar, floodplain and recurrence interval.
Say that next time is the lab, where pairs measure discharge on a stream table, watch a channel develop bends, and test what a flood does to it.
Lab reports: Folds, faults and mountain building is due at the start of the lab, and closed-toe shoes are required.
segments.teacherNotes: Remind students that the lab is a small model, so it shows the direction of change, not true scale.

segments.title: Report due, safety and pairs
segments.description:
Lab reports: Folds, faults and mountain building is due now.
State today’s rules: closed-toe shoes, hand samples stay in their trays and go back where they came from, and spills of water are wiped at once.
Pairs record results together, and each student writes their own report.
Pairs set out a ruler, tape, stopwatch, floats and a graduated beaker, and take the sheet Stream table: recording sheet, which holds tables for channel width, depth, float time and outflow.
segments.teacherNotes:
Count hand samples against the tray labels now. Where tables are fewer than pairs, two pairs share one and alternate runs.
Safety: wet floors are a slip hazard, so keep mops ready. Keep pump plugs and power strips off the floor, on a GFCI outlet. Dampen sand before handling to limit dust.
shown: Rules: closed-toe shoes; samples stay in trays; wipe water spills at once

segments.title: Method: running the stream table and measuring discharge
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Stream table: steps and measurements”.
Introduce the equipment: sand bed, adjustable tilt, valve for the water supply, drain to a bucket, floats and a graduated beaker. The sheet has the steps.
Before the demonstration, pairs predict whether raising the slope with the same water makes the stream wider, deeper or faster.
Demonstrate on a spare table with different settings. Suppose width is 4 cm, average depth is 0.8 cm and surface float speed is 6 cm/s. Using surface speed gives an uncorrected estimate of 19.2 cm³/s; compare it with the outflow measurement because surface speed is not mean velocity.
Show the check: catch the outflow for 30 s, and 1 mL equals 1 cm³, so 480 mL gives 16 cm³/s, a little below the surface-speed estimate.
segments.teacherNotes:
Pilot the table beforehand. Wet the sand before cutting a channel. Expect more cutting and faster flow with a steeper slope. Do not use the pairs’ settings in the demonstration.
Safety: keep the area around the pump dry, and send sand to buckets, never down sinks.

segments.title: Predict, then test: discharge in a straight channel
segments.description:
Pairs set a low slope, cut a straight channel and predict whether the outflow caught in the beaker will be larger or smaller than the Q found from width, depth and velocity.
At each of three stations, they measure width and take depths at evenly spaced points across the wetted channel to estimate cross-sectional area. They time a float over 50 cm in three trials, calculate each surface speed and its average, and multiply that average by the average cross-sectional area to estimate Q.
They then catch the outflow for 30 s and compare the two values, and record both.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: the calculated Q runs a little high, because a surface float moves faster than the mean flow. A factor of 0.85 is sometimes used to estimate mean velocity from surface speed, but it is not calibrated for this table. Use timed outflow as the discharge reference and discuss differences caused by surface speed, irregular cross sections and measurement uncertainty. Typical values might be a 5 cm channel, 1 cm deep, floats at 5 cm/s. Check units are cm throughout.

segments.title: Predict, then run: a meandering channel
segments.description:
Pairs lower the slope, smooth the sand and cut a gently curved starter channel with two or three bends. On the grid, each student marks where they predict a cut bank and a point bar will form.
They run the steady flow set for the table for about fifteen minutes, without changing it. They sketch the channel at the start, the middle and the end, and mark any bank collapse and sand deposits.
Pairs compare with the next pair and label cut banks and point bars.
segments.teacherNotes:
Pilot beforehand to fix one slope, sand and flow that every pair uses. Expected: erosion on the outside of bends; sand may collect on the inside, but bars can be small. Before class, prepare photographs that clearly show identifiable point bars, using the pilot run if it produces them or a natural river bend otherwise. If no bar forms, pairs record any observed deposition, state that no point bar formed, and label point bars on the prepared photographs.
Safety: stop the pump before reshaping the bed, and wipe up water at once.

segments.title: Channel, bar and floodplain deposits in hand samples
segments.description:
Pairs examine the department’s conglomerate, sandstone and shale hand samples in their trays. For each, they record grain size and rounding.
They decide which part of a river system could have laid down that material: the channel, a point bar or the floodplain.
Pairs write one sentence explaining how abrasion can round pebbles and why rounding alone does not establish transport distance.
Two pairs report.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: conglomerate with rounded pebbles means a high-energy channel. Sandstone means a point bar or channel sand. Shale means floodplain mud or an oxbow lake. Samples go back to their trays. No acid is needed.

segments.title: Break
segments.description: Pairs leave the benches. Hand samples stay in their trays, and the stream table is left switched off with its channel intact.
segments.teacherNotes: Check that every pump is switched off and the floor is dry before the break.

segments.title: Predict, then test: a flood on the stream table
segments.description:
Each student writes a prediction of what a flow large enough to spill over the banks will do to the channel’s width, its banks at the bends, and where sediment will be dropped.
Pairs measure channel width at three marked stations. They catch the low outflow for 15 s, then raise the flow in steps until water spills onto the level sand beside the channel, catch the outflow again, and run it for about five minutes.
They re-measure the widths, sketch the new channel and deposits, calculate how many times larger the discharge became, and compare with their prediction.
segments.teacherNotes:
Pilot so the starter channel is shallow, with level sand on both sides as a floodplain, and note the valve setting that overtops the banks. Expected: widening, collapsed banks at bends, sand spread on the floodplain and a fan at the mouth. The model shows direction, not real scale.
Safety: stand back from fast flow, keep the pump away from spilled water, and mop immediately.

segments.title: Finish recording and clean up
segments.description:
Pairs complete the recording sheet, then drain the table and shovel the sand into the buckets.
They return every hand sample to the tray it came from, wipe the benches and collect their equipment.
segments.teacherNotes:
Count samples against the tray labels before pairs leave. Sand must not go down any sink. Mop the floor.
Safety: wash hands after handling sand and wet equipment.

segments.title: Assignments and what comes next
segments.description:
Set the assignment Lab reports (30%), due at the start of the lab of Groundwater. Each student writes their own report, scored individually using the rubric on the assignment. Separately, set the assignment Weekly online quizzes (10%), due at the first meeting of Groundwater. Each student completes it individually and submits it online before that meeting; points are given on the quiz itself.
Tell students to read Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, the chapter on groundwater, before the first meeting of Groundwater. Say that later in the course they will study porosity, permeability, the water table, aquifers and wells, groundwater flow, contamination and overpumping.
Say that a short practice quiz on this lesson is there to take after class, and that it counts toward no grade.
segments.teacherNotes: Write the due times on the board. Students should leave knowing the reading.

keyIdeas: A drainage basin is all the land that sends water to one stream, bounded by divides. Discharge is the volume of water passing a cross section each second: Q = w × d × v, in m³/s. It usually grows downstream as tributaries add water.

Moving water erodes, carries and drops sediment according to its velocity and the size of the grains. In a bend the water is fastest on the outside, which erodes a cut bank, and slowest on the inside, which builds a point bar. The bend therefore migrates sideways, and a cutoff can leave an oxbow lake.

A floodplain is built by point bars shifting sideways and by silt and clay laid down when the river overflows. Natural levees form along the channel edge. A flood hazard depends on discharge, recurrence interval, land use and what is built on the floodplain.

In a flood, discharge rises sharply because depth and velocity both increase. The channel widens, banks at bends erode, and sediment is dumped on the floodplain and at the mouth. A stream table shows the direction of these changes in a small model, not real scale.

vocabulary.definition: All the land that sends its surface water to one stream or river, bounded by divides.
The volume of water passing a cross section of a stream each second; Q = width × depth × velocity, in m³/s.
Sand, gravel and cobbles that a stream rolls, slides or hops along its bed.
The steep outer bank of a bend, where the fastest water erodes the channel.
A gently sloping deposit of sand and gravel on the inside of a bend, where the water is slowest.
The flat land beside a channel that is built by the river and flooded when it overflows.
A crescent-shaped lake left when a river cuts across the neck of a meander and abandons the loop.
The average time between floods of a given size; a 100-year flood has a 1% chance of occurring in any year.

Then draw a long profile on the board: steep and narrow with a rocky bed near the headwaters, gentle and wide with a sandy or muddy bed near the mouth. Partners compare their predictions with the profile. Explain that discharge usually rises downstream as tributaries and groundwater add water. In dry regions it can fall, as water evaporates and soaks into the ground. Students often assume that a gentler gradient means slower water. It does not follow: larger channels generally have less boundary friction relative to their flow volume, so mean velocity can increase downstream despite the gentler gradient. Paraphrase Earle’s discussion of the long profile; do not quote.

slides.title: Fast side, slow side
bullets: Prompt: A river bends to the right. On which side of the bend does the water move fastest, and where will sand pile up?
slides.notes: Each student writes an answer, including which bank will erode. Hear two predictions with no correction yet. Expected: fastest on the outside of the bend, sand on the inside, erosion of the outside bank. Accept guesses; the prediction frames the meander segment. Some students will say the water is fastest on the inside because the path is shorter. That idea is not correct, and the next segments show why.

slides.title: How streams carry material
bullets: Competence: the largest grain a flow can move
Capacity: the total load it can carry
slides.notes: Describe the three ways a stream carries material. Explain competence and capacity: both rise with velocity and discharge. Then ask pairs to predict which grain size is picked up by the slowest current: clay, sand or gravel. Answer: sand, which surprises students. Fine sand moves at a few tenths of a meter per second. Clay needs faster water to erode because the particles stick together (cohesion), although clay stays suspended once moving. Gravel needs much faster water because it is heavy. Refer to the velocity-and-grain-size diagram in Earle’s chapter; do not redraw numbers from memory.

rows: carried as ions in the water

slides.title: Meanders, point bars and floodplains
bullets: Floodplain: point bars plus flood silt and clay
Natural levees: sand dropped beside the channel
slides.notes: Draw a bend in plan view and in cross section on the board. Water is fastest on the outside, which erodes a steep cut bank. It is slowest on the inside, which drops sand and gravel as a gently sloping point bar. The bend migrates sideways, and downstream as well as outward. When the neck narrows and the river cuts across it, the abandoned loop becomes an oxbow lake, as along the lower Mississippi. Floodplains grow as point bars build outward and as floods lay down silt and clay. Sand dropped beside the channel as the water slows forms natural levees. Each student sketches the bend with the cut bank, point bar and a flow arrow, and a partner checks the labels. Common mistake: swapping cut bank and point bar. Mnemonic: the cut bank is where the river cuts. Link to the first meeting: velocity is highest in the deepest, outer part of the bend.

Cut bank (steep bank with roots hanging in the air). 2. Point bar (gentle slope of sand and small gravel, dry at low water). 3. Cut bank (where the water is deepest and fastest). 4. Cut bank (the side that will lose the field). Reveal these only after the pairs have compared.

slides.title: Floods and recurrence intervals
bullets: Prompt: What is the chance of at least one 100-year flood in 30 years?
slides.notes: Define bankfull, flood stage and recurrence interval. A 100-year flood has a 1% chance of happening in any year. Assuming independent years and a constant 1% annual probability, pairs use a calculator to find the chance of at least one 100-year flood during a 30-year mortgage, as 1 − 0.99³⁰. Keep the answer off the slide until they finish. Answer: 0.99³⁰ ≈ 0.74, so about 26%. Common error: reading 100-year as once every hundred years. Two such floods can come in successive years. Recurrence intervals are estimated from gauge records. Then name what raises flood hazard: paved surfaces that speed runoff, levees that confine the flow, and homes on the floodplain. Dams and retention basins reduce peaks.

slides.title: Raise the levee or buy out the lowest homes?
bullets: Prompt: Suppose a small town sits on the floodplain of a meandering river. Bought-out land would be cleared and left open to flood. Which option would you choose, and why?
slides.notes: The town is hypothetical. Each student reads the case and writes a choice and two reasons. Open by asking one student who chose the levee, then one who chose the buyout, for their best reason. Then partners argue the opposite side for two minutes (“now defend the other side”). Take three questions in order: who pays and who carries the risk; what a confined river does downstream; and what the bought-out land does in the next flood. Write the reasons in two columns on the board. Close by saying that a floodplain is part of the river system, which the river reoccupies in floods. Takeaway: raising the levee reduces local inundation while it holds, but excluding floodplain storage can increase downstream flood peaks, and overtopping or failure remains possible. A buyout removes homes from exposure and leaves cleared floodplain available to store floodwater.
