study.overview: A stream is a system that collects water from a drainage basin, moves it downstream, and shapes the land as it goes. This guide covers four ideas: how discharge is measured and calculated, how flowing water erodes, carries and drops sediment, how bends build point bars and floodplains, and what makes a flood a hazard. Each idea has a worked example you can redo on your own. For the full treatment, reread the streams and floods chapter of Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition.

points.heading: Drainage basins and stream discharge
points.explanation:
A drainage basin is all the land that sends its water to one stream. Its edge is a divide, a ridge that splits the flow. Every tributary has its own smaller basin inside the larger one, so a divide runs along a ridge and never along a stream. The Mississippi is the large case: its basin drains about 40% of the contiguous United States, with the Missouri and Ohio as major tributaries. Sea level is the lowest level a stream can cut down to (its ultimate base level).

Discharge is the volume of water passing a cross section each second: Q = w × d × v, in m³/s. Use the average depth across the channel, not the maximum, because real channels are not rectangles. Check that all lengths share a unit before multiplying.

Worked example: a channel is 8 m wide, with an average depth of 1.5 m and a velocity of 0.6 m/s. Q = 8 × 1.5 × 0.6 = 7.2 m³/s. Since 1 m³ is 1,000 liters, that is 7,200 L/s.

Discharge usually grows downstream as tributaries and groundwater add water. In dry regions it can fall, because water evaporates and soaks into the ground. Gradient decreases downstream, but mean velocity can still rise, because larger channels lose relatively less energy to friction with their boundaries. Do not assume that a gentler gradient means slower water.

points.heading: How a stream erodes, carries and deposits sediment
points.explanation:
A stream carries material in three ways. Dissolved load travels as ions in the water. Suspended load, mostly silt and clay, is held up by turbulence. Bed load, which is sand, gravel and cobbles, rolls, slides and hops along the bed.

Two terms describe what a flow can do. Competence is the largest grain it can move. Capacity is the total load it can carry. Both rise with velocity and discharge.

The order in which grains start to move surprises many students. Fine sand moves at only a few tenths of a meter per second. Clay needs faster water to lift because its particles stick together (cohesion). Gravel needs much faster water because it is heavy. Once clay is moving, it stays suspended. As the water slows, the largest grains drop out first.

Example using hypothetical numbers: suppose a small stream is 12 m wide, 2.0 m deep and flowing at 0.5 m/s. Then Q = 12 × 2.0 × 0.5 = 12 m³/s. In a storm the width stays at 12 m, but the depth rises to 3.5 m and the velocity to 1.4 m/s. Then Q = 12 × 3.5 × 1.4 = 58.8 m³/s, about 5 times larger. Depth rose 1.75 times and velocity rose 2.8 times, so velocity mattered more. Faster, larger flow has more competence and capacity, so a storm can move coarser grains and far more sediment.

points.heading: Meanders, point bars and floodplains
points.explanation:
In a bend, water is fastest on the outside, where the channel is deepest, and slowest on the inside. The fast outside water erodes a steep cut bank. The slow inside water drops sand and gravel as a gently sloping point bar. A useful memory aid is that the cut bank is where the river cuts. A common wrong idea is that water is fastest on the inside because the path is shorter.

Erosion on one side and deposition on the other make the bend migrate sideways, and also downstream. When the neck of a loop narrows and the river cuts across it, the abandoned loop becomes an oxbow lake, as along the lower Mississippi.

A floodplain is built in two ways. Point bars shifting sideways leave sheets of sand and gravel. When the river overflows, it lays down silt and clay. Sand dropped right beside the channel as the overflow slows forms natural levees along the channel edge.

This also explains what different deposits tell you. Conglomerate with rounded pebbles suggests a high-energy channel. Sandstone suggests a point bar or channel sand. Shale suggests floodplain mud or an oxbow lake. Rounding shows that abrasion occurred, but it does not by itself show how far the pebbles traveled.

points.heading: Floods, hazards and the stream table model
points.explanation:
In a flood, discharge rises sharply because depth and velocity both increase. The channel widens, banks at bends erode, and sediment is dumped on the floodplain and at the mouth of the stream. Flood hazard depends on discharge, recurrence interval, land use and what is built on the floodplain. Paved surfaces speed runoff and raise peaks. Levees confine the flow. Homes on the floodplain increase exposure. Dams and retention basins reduce peaks.

A recurrence interval is estimated from gauge records. A 100-year flood has a 1% chance of happening in any year. It does not mean once every hundred years, and two such floods can come in successive years. Assume independent years and a constant 1% annual chance. The chance of no 100-year flood in 30 years is 0.99³⁰ ≈ 0.74, so the chance of at least one is 1 − 0.99³⁰, about 26%.

A stream table lets you test these ideas in a small model. It shows the direction of change, not real scale. In a hypothetical run, suppose a channel is 4 cm wide with an average depth of 0.8 cm and a surface float speed of 6 cm/s. That gives 4 × 0.8 × 6 = 19.2 cm³/s. Catching 480 mL of outflow in 30 s gives 16 cm³/s, since 1 mL = 1 cm³, so the surface-speed estimate runs a little high, as expected. A float moves at the surface, which is not the mean velocity, so timed outflow is the reference value.

For a hypothetical town on a floodplain, a levee keeps the river in its channel locally, but it confines the flow and removes floodplain storage, which can raise flood peaks downstream. A buyout removes homes from exposure and leaves open floodplain to store floodwater. A floodplain is part of the river system: the river reoccupies it in floods.

handouts.title: Stream table: steps and measurements
handouts.usedIn: Method: running the stream table and measuring discharge

blocks.text: Keep this sheet at your table. It gives the steps and the amounts for every stream table run today. Use centimeters and seconds throughout.
Equipment

items: Stream table with a sand bed, adjustable tilt, water valve and a drain to a bucket
Ruler and tape
Stopwatch
Floats
Graduated beaker
Buckets for sand

blocks.text: Setting up a run

items: Wet the sand before you cut anything, then smooth the surface.
Set the tilt to the slope your instructor gives for the activity.
Cut the starter channel in the sand.
Open the valve to the flow set for the table and let the flow settle before you measure.
Stop the pump before you reshape the bed.

blocks.text: Measuring one cross section

items: Lay the ruler across the wetted channel and read its width in cm.
Take depths in cm at evenly spaced points across the wetted channel.
Mean depth is the average of those depths.
Cross-sectional area (cm²) = width × mean depth.

blocks.text: Measuring surface speed with a float

items: Mark a 50 cm length along the straight channel with tape.
Release the float upstream of the first mark and time it between the marks.
Repeat for three trials.
Surface speed (cm/s) = 50 cm ÷ time in seconds. Average the three speeds.

blocks.text: Measuring outflow

items: Hold the beaker under the outflow and start the stopwatch as the water enters it.
Catch the outflow for the time the activity gives: 30 s for the straight channel, 15 s for the flood run.
Read the volume in mL. 1 mL = 1 cm³.
Outflow (cm³/s) = volume in cm³ ÷ time in seconds.

blocks.text: Discharge from measurements

Q = w × d × v. With width and depth in cm and speed in cm/s, Q is in cm³/s. Check that every length is in cm before you multiply. A float rides on the surface of the stream, so its speed is a surface speed.
Safety and clean-up

items: Wear closed-toe shoes.
Keep the area around the pump dry and keep the pump away from spilled water.
Wipe up spilled water at once. Wet floors are a slip hazard.
Stand back from fast flow.
Dampen sand before handling it. Send sand to the buckets, never down a sink.
Wash your hands after handling sand and wet equipment.

handouts.title: Stream table: recording sheet
handouts.usedIn: Predict, then test: discharge in a straight channel

blocks.text: Record your results together with your partner. Use centimeters and seconds throughout. Each of you writes your own report afterwards.
Prediction
Will the outflow caught in the beaker be larger or smaller than the Q you calculate from width, depth and float speed? Give a reason.

blocks.hint: Write before you cut the channel.

blocks.text: Cross sections
At each station, measure the width of the wetted channel and take four depths at evenly spaced points across it. Mean depth is the average of the four. Area = width × mean depth.

blocks.label: Average cross-sectional area of the three stations (cm²)

blocks.text: Float trials

blocks.hint: Q = average area × average surface speed. Show your working and give the unit.

blocks.text: Outflow
Comparison
Compare the Q from your measurements with the outflow. Which is larger, and by how much? Does this match your prediction?

blocks.hint: One or two sentences.

handouts.key:
Prediction: The measured outflow will usually be smaller than Q calculated using surface float speed. Surface water generally moves faster than the cross section's mean flow. Accept a different prediction if its reasoning identifies a plausible measurement effect.

Cross sections, in table order: For each of Station 1, Station 2 and Station 3, enter the observed wetted width and four measured depths, all in cm. Mean depth = (depth 1 + depth 2 + depth 3 + depth 4) ÷ 4. Area = width × mean depth, in cm². Look for evenly spaced depth measurements that represent the whole wetted cross section. Common slips: using maximum depth, including dry banks in the width, or mixing centimeters and meters.

Average cross-sectional area: (area at Station 1 + area at Station 2 + area at Station 3) ÷ 3, in cm².

Float trials, in table order: Enter the measured time for each trial. Trial 1 speed = 50 ÷ Trial 1 time; Trial 2 speed = 50 ÷ Trial 2 time; Trial 3 speed = 50 ÷ Trial 3 time. Each speed is in cm/s.

Average surface speed: (Trial 1 speed + Trial 2 speed + Trial 3 speed) ÷ 3, in cm/s. Common slip: dividing 50 by the average time instead of averaging the three calculated speeds.

Q: Average cross-sectional area × average surface speed, in cm³/s. Look for substitution of the pair's measured values and the correct unit. This is an uncorrected estimate based on surface speed.

Outflow volume: Enter the measured volume collected during 30 s, in mL.

Outflow: Collected volume ÷ 30, in cm³/s, because 1 mL = 1 cm³. Common slip: reporting collected volume as discharge without dividing by collection time.

Comparison: Identify which calculated discharge is larger. Difference = larger discharge − smaller discharge, in cm³/s. State whether the observed ordering agrees with the prediction. Usually the surface-speed estimate is larger. Accept either ordering when supported by the recorded measurements; irregular cross sections, float timing, changing flow and collection losses can affect the comparison.

handouts.title: Stream table: meander sketches
handouts.usedIn: Predict, then run: a meandering channel

blocks.text: Work with your partner on the table, but draw and label your own sketches. Run the steady flow set for the table for about fifteen minutes, without changing it. Draw each sketch in plan view, with the flow direction marked by an arrow.
Start of the run, with your predictions

blocks.hint: Sketch the starter channel with its two or three bends. Mark where you predict a cut bank (CB) and a point bar (PB) will form. Draw the flow arrow.

blocks.text: Middle of the run

blocks.hint: Sketch the channel now. Mark any bank collapse and any sand deposits.

blocks.text: End of the run

blocks.hint: Sketch the channel. Mark bank collapse and sand deposits. After you compare with the next pair, label the cut banks (CB) and point bars (PB).

blocks.text: Review
Where did the cut banks and point bars form compared with your prediction? If no point bar formed, say so and describe any deposition you saw.

blocks.hint: Two sentences.

handouts.key:
Start of the run, with predictions: Look for a plan-view drawing of the actual starter channel, with two or three bends and an arrow showing downstream flow. Predicted CB labels belong on the outside of bends; predicted PB labels belong on the inside. Common slip: reversing the labels.

Middle of the run: Look for the channel's observed position and shape, with bank collapses and sand deposits marked where they occurred. Outer-bank retreat and inner-bend deposition are expected tendencies, but the drawing should represent the run's actual behavior.

End of the run: Look for the final channel outline, a flow arrow, observed bank collapses and deposits. Label eroding outer banks CB and identifiable inner-bend sand bars PB. A deposit at the channel mouth is not a point bar. If no point bar forms, identify point bars on the prepared photograph: they occupy the inside of a bend opposite the cut bank.

Review: A supported answer compares the predicted locations with the observations. Expected explanation: outer-bank erosion produced cut banks, while deposition on the inside of bends produced point bars where bars developed. If no point bar formed, the answer must state this and describe the location of any observed deposition. Accept departures from the expected pattern when consistent with the sketches.

handouts.title: Channel, bar and floodplain deposits: hand sample sheet
handouts.usedIn: Channel, bar and floodplain deposits in hand samples

blocks.text: Examine the department's conglomerate, sandstone and shale hand samples in their trays. For each, record the grain size and the rounding of the grains. Then decide which part of a river system could have laid down that material: the channel, a point bar or the floodplain. Return every sample to its tray.
Write one sentence explaining how abrasion can round pebbles and why rounding alone does not establish how far they were transported.

blocks.hint: One sentence.

handouts.key:
Conglomerate row: Grain size—gravel clasts larger than 2 mm, commonly within a finer matrix. Rounding—describe the observed rounded or subrounded gravel clasts; matrix grains may differ. River setting—a high-energy channel is a plausible interpretation. Common slip: describing every grain as gravel or treating conglomerate as proof of a river origin.

Sandstone row: Grain size—sand, approximately 0.0625–2 mm. Rounding—record the observed grain shapes where visible; accept 'not resolvable in this hand sample' when individual shapes cannot be distinguished. River setting—a point bar or sandy channel is plausible. Common slip: assigning rounding from the smoothness of the sample's broken surface.

Shale row: Grain size—mud, comprising silt and clay smaller than approximately 0.0625 mm; individual grains are generally too small to resolve by eye. Rounding—not determinable from the hand sample. River setting—a floodplain is plausible; quiet water in an oxbow lake is another possibility. Common slip: calling invisible grains rounded or assuming shale identifies a unique depositional environment.

Abrasion sentence: Collisions and scraping during transport wear down pebble edges, but rounding alone cannot establish transport distance because it also depends on rock resistance, initial shape and earlier transport history.

handouts.title: Stream table: flood record
handouts.usedIn: Predict, then test: a flood on the stream table

blocks.text: Write your own prediction before the run. Then record your results together with your partner. Use centimeters and seconds throughout.
Prediction
A flow large enough to spill over the banks: what will it do to the width of the channel?

blocks.hint: One sentence.

blocks.text: What will it do to the banks at the bends?

blocks.hint: One sentence.

blocks.text: Where will the sediment be dropped?

blocks.hint: One sentence.

blocks.text: Channel width at three marked stations

blocks.caption: Measure before the flood run and again after it.

blocks.text: Outflow

blocks.label: Low flow: volume caught in 15 s (mL)

blocks.hint: How many times larger is the flood discharge than the low discharge? Show your working.

blocks.text: After the run

blocks.hint: Sketch the new channel in plan view. Mark the collapsed banks, the sand spread on the floodplain and any fan at the mouth.

blocks.text: Compare what happened with your prediction.

blocks.hint: One sentence.

handouts.key:
Prediction—channel width: The channel will likely widen as increased flow erodes its banks; the response may vary among stations.

Prediction—banks at bends: Outer banks will likely erode and may collapse as flow undercuts them.

Prediction—sediment deposition: Sediment will likely accumulate on the inundated floodplain where flow slows, with possible deposits inside bends and a fan at the mouth. Some sediment may leave the table.

Channel-width table, in row order: For Station 1, Station 2 and Station 3, enter the measured before and after widths in cm at the same marked location. Look for measurements across the channel using a consistent definition of its edges. Common slip: measuring the entire flooded surface as the new channel width.

Low-flow volume: Enter the volume collected in 15 s, in mL.

Low-flow outflow: Low-flow volume ÷ 15, in cm³/s.

Flood-flow volume: Enter the measured collected volume, in mL.

Flood-flow collection time: 15 s.

Flood-flow outflow: Flood-flow volume ÷ 15, in cm³/s.

Discharge multiplier: Flood-flow discharge ÷ low-flow discharge. With equal collection times, this also equals flood-flow volume ÷ low-flow volume. The ratio has no units. Common slips: reversing the ratio or subtracting the discharges instead of dividing.

After-run sketch: Look for the observed channel outline in plan view, with downstream direction indicated. Mark collapsed banks, sand deposited on the floodplain and any fan at the mouth where present. Identify features that did not form rather than drawing them as observations.

Comparison: State which predictions were supported by the measured widths and observed erosion and deposition. Accept a different response from the expected widening and outer-bank collapse when supported by the recorded observations.

l_6aa58487927c.title: Groundwater
l_6aa58487927c.summary: Porosity, permeability, the water table, aquifers and wells, groundwater flow, and problems such as contamination and overpumping.
readings: Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, the chapter on groundwater

segments.title: Quiz due now and where the rain goes
segments.description:
Weekly online quizzes: Streams and floods is due now, submitted online before this meeting. Weekly online quizzes counts for 10% of the course grade.
Students write two sentences on the question on the slide.
Two or three answers are heard.
segments.teacherNotes: Expect “underground rivers and lakes” and “it just disappears”. Do not correct yet; return to these answers in the summary. Most groundwater sits in the pores of rock and sediment, not in open caverns.
shown: Rain soaks into a field after a storm. Where can that water go next, and how long might it stay underground?

segments.title: Porosity and permeability
segments.description:
Define porosity as pore volume divided by total volume, as a percentage, and permeability as the ease with which fluid passes through connected pores.
Partners first predict which holds more water, clay or gravel, and which lets water through faster. Then go through the table, pointing out that clay is high on one and very low on the other.
Explain that sorting, grain size and cementation control both properties, and that fractures can make a dense rock permeable.
segments.teacherNotes: Point to Earle’s groundwater chapter for the same contrast. Common error: treating the two words as synonyms. Stress that permeability depends on pore size and connection, not only on how many pores exist. The values are typical ranges, not exact.
shown: Porosity (%) = pore volume ÷ total volume × 100

Table: Material | Typical porosity | Permeability / Gravel | 25–40% | very high / Sand | 25–45% | high / Silt | 35–50% | low / Clay | 40–60% | very low / Sandstone | 5–30% | low to moderate / Unfractured granite | under 1% | very low

segments.title: Work out porosity
segments.description:
Each student calculates the porosity of both samples in the table.
Partners compare answers.
The class hears the granite answer, then explains why these porosity values alone cannot establish whether either rock could supply a well.
segments.teacherNotes: Sandstone: 30 ÷ 200 × 100 = 15%. Granite: 2 ÷ 500 × 100 = 0.4%. Watch for dividing by pore volume instead of total volume. Granite yields water only through fractures; link back to the table.

segments.title: The water table and aquifers
segments.description:
Students first sketch a profile of a hill and a valley and mark where they think the water table lies.
The teacher draws the correct profile on the board. It is a subdued copy of the land surface, highest under hills and meeting the surface at streams, springs and wetlands.
Name the unsaturated zone, the saturated zone, recharge and discharge. Show how an aquitard separates a confined aquifer from the one above.
Partners explain to each other why a well must reach below the water table.

segments.title: Report due, safety and pairs
segments.description:

Former pairs form and each collects a tray of the department’s hand samples and a bench kit.
The teacher reviews safety: closed-toe shoes, wipe up water spills at once, and hand samples stay in their trays and go back where they came from.
segments.teacherNotes: Provide dry silt in covered, premeasured containers for the porosity test. Open and transfer it gently without raising dust; keep tested silt damp afterward. Use plastic cylinders where possible, and report any breakage at once. Goggles are needed only if the dilute HCl bottle comes out, which is not part of this lab. Water on the floor is a slipping hazard.

segments.title: Method: measuring porosity and permeability
segments.description:
The teacher demonstrates the porosity test. Fill a 100 mL cylinder with dry material to the 100 mL mark, tap it ten times on a pad, and top it up to 100 mL again. Add water from a second cylinder in portions of about 10 mL, tapping the side of the cylinder gently to free trapped air and waiting a minute after each portion, until a thin film of water just shows at the surface; read the total water added, which estimates the connected pore volume.
Then demonstrate the drainage test. Fill an identical funnel to a 5 cm depth with the material, tapped the same way, with a fine mesh screen at the bottom. Wet it with water and let it drain until it stops dripping, then pour 100 mL of water over it at once from a cup held 5 cm above the surface. Start the timer when the water first touches the surface and collect what drains in 30 seconds.
Show how to record both in the Groundwater lab record sheet, which has tables for the readings, the hand sample ranking and the pumping data.
segments.teacherNotes: Read the meniscus at eye level. Roles: one partner pours and times, the other reads and records. Before class, trial both tests on all three materials: check the screen alone drains 100 mL in a few seconds, and fix the funnel size and fill depth. Drained volume compares materials under one set-up; it is not a measured permeability. Wipe any spills right away.

segments.title: Rank the hand samples
segments.description:
Pairs examine three samples with a hand lens: sandstone, vesicular basalt and granite.
They write a provisional ranking from least to most porous and from least to most permeable. For each placement they record the evidence they see and what the lens cannot show.
The class compares rankings, then says which differences a test would have to settle.
segments.teacherNotes: Rankings are hypotheses. Judge the evidence and stated uncertainty, not a fixed order. Sandstone: visible pores, cement unknown. Basalt: vesicles visible, connection unknown. Granite: tight; fractures may matter. Keep samples in trays and dry.

segments.title: Predict, then test: porosity of gravel, sand and silt
segments.description:
Pairs predict which of the three materials has the highest porosity and write it down.
They measure all three with the cylinder method and record the water added.
The class compares results and discusses what the figures show.
segments.teacherNotes: Expect all three between roughly 30% and 50%, with silt slow to saturate. Add water to silt slowly, as air is trapped. Treat each figure as an estimate of connected pore volume. Compare the measured porosities without requiring them to match. Explain that grain size alone does not determine porosity, while pore size and connectivity strongly affect permeability. Dry the cylinders afterward.

segments.title: Break
segments.description:
Students take a break.
Benches are left set up for the next test.

segments.title: Predict, then test: how fast water drains
segments.description:
Pairs predict which of the three materials drains fastest and which slowest.
They run the drainage test on gravel, sand and silt exactly as demonstrated, with the same depth, funnel, wetting and pour height, recording the volume collected in 30 seconds.
They then compare drained volume with porosity and write one sentence on what the pairing shows.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: gravel drains most, sand next, silt almost nothing. Use the trialed procedure unchanged for every material; do not add filter paper, since it can control the flow. High porosity with low drainage is the point: silt stores water but yields little. Cap tests at 30 seconds.

segments.title: Predict, then draw: drawdown around a pumped well
segments.description:

They calculate the drawdown at each observation well and plot drawdown against distance.
They compare the plot with their sketch, then predict the effect of doubling the pumping rate.
segments.teacherNotes: Data are hypothetical. Static level 8.0 m below ground. Pumped levels: 5 m, 12.5 (drawdown 4.5 m). 20 m, 10.0 (2.0 m). 60 m, 8.8 (0.8 m). Doubling gives deeper and wider drawdown, with cones from nearby wells overlapping.

Samples go back to their trays and the benches are wiped.

keyIdeas: Porosity is the share of a rock or sediment that is empty space. Permeability is how easily fluid moves through it. A clay can have high porosity and still be nearly impermeable, because its pores are tiny and poorly connected.

Below the water table, pores are filled with water. An aquifer is a body of rock or sediment that holds and yields usable water. An aquitard, such as clay or shale, holds water but passes it too slowly to supply a well.

Groundwater flows from where the water table is high to where it is low, slowly, often only centimeters to meters per day. A pumping well draws the water table into a cone of depression, and the drawdown is largest at the well.

Contamination travels with the flow as a plume, so a source upgradient of a well threatens it. Pumping faster than recharge lowers the water table, and near coasts it can draw in salt water. In loose sediment it can also make the land surface sink.

The funnel-shaped dip in the water table around a pumping well.

study.overview: Most groundwater is not found in underground rivers or open caverns. It fills the pores and fractures of rock and sediment below the water table. How much water a material holds and how easily it passes water are separate properties. Both depend on the material’s structure. Water moves slowly, usually from high water table elevation to low. A pumping well bends the water table into a cone of depression, and contamination and overpumping both follow the flow and the balance between withdrawal and recharge. Review these ideas alongside the groundwater chapter in Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition.

points.heading: Porosity is storage; permeability is transmission
points.explanation: Porosity is the share of a material that is empty space: pore volume ÷ total volume × 100. Permeability is how easily fluid moves through the pores, and it depends on pore size and on whether the pores connect. A material can hold a lot of water and still pass it very slowly. Sorting, grain size and cementation control both properties, and fractures can make a dense rock permeable. Example: a sandstone sample with 30 cm³ of pores in 200 cm³ of rock has a porosity of 30 ÷ 200 × 100 = 15%. A granite sample with 2 cm³ of pores in 500 cm³ has 2 ÷ 500 × 100 = 0.4%. A common slip is to divide by the pore volume instead of the total volume. Porosity alone cannot tell you whether a rock can supply a well. Unfractured granite is nearly tight, but if its fractures are connected it can still yield water, and its permeability then comes from the fractures rather than from pore space.

points.heading: The water table, aquifers and aquitards
points.explanation: Above the water table is the unsaturated zone, where pores hold both air and water. Below it is the saturated zone, where pores are full of water. The water table is not flat like a lake surface. It is a subdued copy of the land: highest under hills, and meeting the surface at streams, springs and wetlands. Recharge is water arriving from the surface, and discharge is water leaving at those low points. An aquifer is rock or sediment that holds and yields usable water. An aquitard, such as clay or shale, holds water but passes it too slowly to supply a well. In a typical profile, soil and unsaturated zone lie over the water table, then a saturated sand (an unconfined aquifer), then a clay aquitard, then a second saturated sand (a confined aquifer), then bedrock. A well must reach below the water table, which is why wells go dry in a drought when the table falls beneath their bottoms.

points.heading: Flow, the hydraulic gradient and the cone of depression
points.explanation: Groundwater moves from high water table elevation toward low, at right angles to the contours. It is slow, often only centimeters to meters per day, and its speed depends on both permeability and the hydraulic gradient. The gradient is the drop in water table elevation ÷ the distance, and it has no units. Example: two wells 600 m apart have water table elevations of 105 m and 102 m. The gradient is (105 − 102) ÷ 600 = 0.005, and flow runs from the 105 m well toward the 102 m well. A common error is to use the elevation difference without dividing by distance. Pumping changes the shape of the water table. Drawdown is the drop in water level at a point caused by pumping, and together the drawdowns form a cone of depression around the well. Suppose a hypothetical test begins with the water level 12.0 m below ground everywhere. After days of pumping, the level is 14.5 m below ground at an observation well 10 m away, 13.2 m at 30 m, and 12.4 m at 100 m. Drawdown is the new depth minus the old depth: 2.5 m, 1.2 m and 0.4 m. Because these are depths, a larger number means a lower water level. Drawdown is largest at the well and falls with distance. Pumping faster deepens and widens the cone, and the cones of neighboring wells can overlap.

points.heading: Contamination and depletion
points.explanation: Contaminants include leaking fuel tanks, septic systems, landfill leachate, road salt, and fertilizer, manure and pesticides on farmland. A contaminant moves with the groundwater as a plume, so a source upgradient of a well threatens that well first. Suppose the hypothetical town of Ridgeway has a water table sloping north to south toward a river, with a gas station and an old fuel tank in the middle of town. A well to the south, between the station and the river, lies downgradient and is at greatest risk. A well to the north lies upgradient. A strong pump can still bend the gradient and draw water from several sides. Groundwater does not always clean itself: coarse gravel and fractures filter very little, and the 2000 Walkerton, Ontario, outbreak came from bacteria reaching a shallow municipal well from farm runoff. Depletion means pumping faster than recharge. It lowers the water table, can make wells go dry, and near coasts can draw salt water into the aquifer. In loose, fine-grained sediment, falling groundwater pressure lets layers compact, and the land surface sinks. This subsidence has occurred in California’s San Joaquin Valley. Cleanup is slow and costly, so prevention matters more than repair.

Explanation: Porosity measures how much pore space a rock contains. A productive well also needs connected openings that transmit water readily and a sufficient saturated thickness. Sandstone may have connected pores, but cement can restrict flow. Granite may transmit water through connected fractures despite low matrix porosity.
Common slips: Dividing by pore volume instead of total volume; omitting × 100; assuming that greater porosity always means a greater well yield.

handouts.title: Porosity and drainage tests: bench procedure

blocks.text: Keep this sheet at your bench for both tests. Work in your pair: one partner pours and times, the other reads and records. Use the same procedure for gravel, sand and silt. Record your readings in the Groundwater lab record sheet.
Safety and care

items: Closed-toe shoes stay on for the whole lab.
Wipe up spilled water at once: a wet floor is a slipping hazard.
Open the silt container and transfer the silt gently, so that no dust rises. Keep tested silt damp.
Report any broken glass or plastic at once.
Hand samples stay in their trays and go back where they came from.
Silt and sand slurries go in the labeled waste containers, never down the sink.

blocks.text: Test 1: porosity (connected pore volume)

items: Fill a 100 mL cylinder with dry material to the 100 mL mark.
Tap the cylinder ten times on a pad.
Top up the dry material to the 100 mL mark again.
From a second cylinder, add water in portions of about 10 mL.
After each portion, tap the side of the cylinder gently to free trapped air (do not stir, which changes the packing), then wait one minute.
Stop when a thin film of water just shows at the surface.
Read the total water added, with your eye level with the meniscus. This estimates the connected pore volume.
Porosity (%) = water added (mL) ÷ 100 mL × 100.

blocks.text: Test 2: drainage

items: Use an identical funnel for every material, with a fine mesh screen at the bottom.
Fill the funnel with the material to a depth of 5 cm. Tap it the same way each time.
Wet the material with water and let it drain until it stops dripping.
Hold a cup of 100 mL of water 5 cm above the surface.
Pour all 100 mL at once. Start the timer when the water first touches the surface.
Collect what drains in 30 seconds, then stop. Read the volume collected.
Do not add filter paper. Use the same depth, funnel, wetting and pour height for every material.

blocks.text: The drained volume compares the three materials under one set-up. It is not a measured permeability.

handouts.title: Groundwater lab record sheet: hand samples

blocks.text: Examine the three samples with a hand lens. Rank them from 1 (least) to 3 (most) for porosity and for permeability. Your rankings are provisional. For each ranking, record the evidence you see and what the lens cannot show. Keep the samples in their trays and dry.

columns: Porosity: evidence I see, and what the lens cannot show
Permeability: evidence I see, and what the lens cannot show
blocks.caption: Provisional ranking of hand samples

handouts.key:
Accept provisional ranks supported by observations and uncertainty. One defensible ranking, assuming abundant basalt vesicles and no visible granite fractures, is:
Sandstone: Porosity rank 2; visible spaces between grains suggest pore storage, but the lens cannot establish internal pore volume or the extent of cementation. Permeability rank 3; apparent spaces between grains suggest possible flow paths, but their continuity and internal restrictions require testing.
Vesicular basalt: Porosity rank 3; abundant vesicles suggest substantial void space, but their internal abundance cannot be established with the lens. Permeability rank 2; some openings may connect, but visible vesicles alone do not establish throughgoing flow paths.
Granite: Porosity rank 1; tightly interlocking crystals suggest little matrix pore space, but microscopic cracks are unresolved. Permeability rank 1; few visible openings suggest restricted matrix flow, but connected fractures could change the ranking substantially.
Accept other orders when the actual department samples support them. Look for separate reasoning about storage and transmission, with a limitation stated for every placement. Common slip: Assigning high permeability to basalt solely because it has many vesicles.

handouts.title: Groundwater lab record sheet: porosity of gravel, sand and silt
handouts.usedIn: Predict, then test: porosity of gravel, sand and silt

blocks.text: Predict before you measure. Then measure all three materials with the cylinder method on the bench procedure sheet.

blocks.label: Our prediction: the material with the highest porosity will be

blocks.caption: Porosity test, 100 mL of dry material in each

items: Compare your three figures with your prediction. What do the figures show?

blocks.hint: Treat each figure as an estimate of connected pore volume.

handouts.key:
Prediction blank: Accept gravel, sand or silt as a prediction; look for a reason based on packing, sorting or anticipated pore space.
Gravel row: Record the measured water addition, V_gravel mL. Estimated porosity = V_gravel ÷ 100 × 100 = V_gravel%.
Sand row: Record the measured water addition, V_sand mL. Estimated porosity = V_sand ÷ 100 × 100 = V_sand%.
Silt row: Record the measured water addition, V_silt mL. Estimated porosity = V_silt ÷ 100 × 100 = V_silt%.
Comparison: Identify the highest and lowest measured estimates, state whether the prediction matched, and describe any close results. These figures estimate connected pore volume under the procedure. Grain size alone does not determine porosity; packing and sorting matter. Trapped air, especially in silt, can lower the estimate.
Common slips: Substituting expected values for measurements; reporting water volume without converting it to a percentage; treating the estimates as permeability measurements.

handouts.title: Groundwater lab record sheet: how fast water drains
handouts.usedIn: Predict, then test: how fast water drains

blocks.text: Predict before you test. Then run the drainage test on gravel, sand and silt exactly as demonstrated: same depth, same funnel, same wetting, same pour height. Cap each test at 30 seconds.

blocks.label: Our prediction: the material that drains fastest will be
Our prediction: the material that drains slowest will be

blocks.caption: Drainage test, 5 cm depth, 100 mL poured

items: Compare the drained volume with the porosity of each material. Write one sentence on what the pairing shows.

blocks.hint: One sentence.

handouts.key:
Fastest prediction blank: Gravel is the expected prediction because its larger pore passages usually transmit water readily.
Slowest prediction blank: Silt is the expected prediction because its narrow pore passages restrict flow. Accept other predictions with an explanation.
Gravel row: Copy its measured porosity from the porosity table; record its measured volume collected in 30 s, in mL.
Sand row: Copy its measured porosity from the porosity table; record its measured volume collected in 30 s, in mL.
Silt row: Copy its measured porosity from the porosity table; record its measured volume collected in 30 s, in mL.
Comparison sentence: Accept a statement supported by the recorded results. Expected pattern: Gravel drains more than sand, and silt drains least, even if their porosities are similar, because flow depends strongly on pore passage size and connectivity.
Common slips: Claiming that the material with the highest porosity must drain fastest; calling the collected volume a measured permeability; replacing observations with the expected order.

handouts.title: Groundwater lab record sheet: pumping data
handouts.usedIn: Predict, then draw: drawdown around a pumped well

blocks.text: Suppose a pumping test gave the readings below. They are hypothetical data. The water level before pumping, the static level, was 8.0 m below ground. The pumped levels are also measured in meters below ground, at three observation wells at different distances from the pumped well.

items: Before you calculate, sketch the expected shape of the water table on a cross section through the pumped well, from one side of the well to the other.

blocks.hint: Draw the ground surface, the well and the water table.

items: Calculate the drawdown at each observation well and write it in the table.

blocks.hint: Show your working for each of the three wells.

items: Plot drawdown against distance from the pumped well.

blocks.hint: Put distance on the horizontal axis and drawdown on the vertical axis. Label both axes with units.

items: Compare your plot with your sketch. How are they alike, and how do they differ?

blocks.hint: Two or three sentences.

items: Predict the effect on the drawdown if the pumping rate were doubled.

blocks.hint: A sentence or two.

handouts.key:
Initial sketch: Show a water table dipping toward the pumped well from both sides, with the greatest lowering at the well and progressively less lowering farther away. Label the ground surface, well and water table. Common slip: Drawing an equal drop everywhere.
Drawdown table and working: Drawdown = pumped depth below ground − static depth below ground. At 5 m: 12.5 − 8.0 = 4.5 m. At 20 m: 10.0 − 8.0 = 2.0 m. At 60 m: 8.8 − 8.0 = 0.8 m. Common slip: Reversing the subtraction and reporting negative drawdown.
Plot: Horizontal axis, distance from pumped well (m); vertical axis, drawdown (m). Plot (5, 4.5), (20, 2.0) and (60, 0.8). Drawdown decreases with distance. Do not add an invented value at the pumped well.
Comparison: Both representations show that pumping has its greatest effect near the well. The cross section shows water table elevation on both sides; the graph shows the amount of lowering at measured distances on one side. With drawdown increasing upward on the graph, its curve falls away from the well, while water table elevation rises away from the well in the cross section.
Doubled pumping rate: Expect greater drawdown at each observation well and a larger area affected by substantial lowering. Under an idealized linear aquifer response at the same elapsed pumping time, drawdowns would approximately double to 9.0 m, 4.0 m and 1.6 m, respectively. Accept a qualitative prediction; exact doubling requires assumptions about aquifer conditions.

ready: Teacher: dry gravel, sand and silt, with the silt in covered, premeasured containers
Teacher: a bench kit for each pair, with two 100 mL plastic cylinders, a stirring rod, a tapping pad, a funnel with a fine mesh screen, a cup and a timer
Teacher: a tray of the department's hand samples for each pair (sandstone, vesicular basalt, granite) and a hand lens
Teacher: labeled sediment-waste containers for silt and sand slurries
Students bring a calculator

values.where: Segment 14, Method: measuring porosity and permeability
values.text: Folio could not fix this itself: Stirring changes the packing and bulk volume of the sediment after the 100 mL volume has been fixed. A surface film and one-minute waits also do not establish saturation, especially in silt. The water added therefore does not reliably estimate connected pore volume. Specify a trialed saturation and settling procedure, a final bulk-volume measurement, and an endpoint that checks for remaining air.

values.where: Segment 14, Method: measuring porosity and permeability
values.text: Folio could not fix this itself: The drainage procedure still does not establish comparable starting conditions. Stopping dripping leaves different amounts of retained water and air in different sediments. Pouring from the same height does not control the water head above them. A screen fine enough to retain silt may clog even if it passes clean water quickly. Trial a procedure that controls saturation, packing, funnel geometry and hydraulic head, and checks screen resistance with sediment present. Otherwise the expected ordering cannot reliably be attributed to permeability.

l_b3fe46ca36ef.title: Glaciers and climate
l_b3fe46ca36ef.summary: Glacier formation, movement and landforms, and the links between ice ages and climate; the lesson reviews for the final exam, taken afterwards.
readings: Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, the chapter on glaciers

segments.title: Quiz due now and a share of fresh water
segments.description:
Weekly online quizzes: Groundwater is due now and was submitted online before this meeting.
Each student writes a choice for the slide question and compares it with a neighbor for one minute.
Hear two or three choices, then give the answer: about two thirds of Earth’s fresh water is ice.
Link it to the water followed underground last time: most of the liquid fresh water is groundwater, and the ice holds far more.
segments.teacherNotes: Glaciers and ice sheets hold about 69% of fresh water; groundwater about 30%; lakes and rivers a tiny fraction. Many students pick the middle choice because rivers feel large.
shown: Of all the fresh water on Earth, about what share is held as glacier and ice-sheet ice? A: about 3%. B: about 30%. C: about 70%.

segments.title: From snow to glacial ice
segments.description:
Explain how snow buried by later snowfall compacts into firn and then glacial ice, and how density rises from fresh snow to ice near 0.9 g/cm³.
Draw an alpine glacier on the board with the accumulation zone, the ablation zone and the equilibrium line between them.
Define mass balance as yearly gain minus yearly loss.
Before explaining, pairs predict for one minute where the equilibrium line moves in a warm year, then the answer follows: up-valley.
Name the two main kinds, alpine glaciers and ice sheets; Antarctica holds about 90% of the world’s glacier ice.
segments.teacherNotes: Common mistake: thinking glaciers only form in very cold places. Snow must survive the summer; high mountains in warm latitudes qualify. Fresh snow is about 0.1 g/cm³, firn roughly 0.4 to 0.8, ice about 0.9.
shown: Steps: Snow → Firn → Glacial ice
Side by side: Accumulation zone: snow gain exceeds melt; snow-covered all year | Ablation zone: melt exceeds snow gain; bare ice by late summer

segments.title: Mass balance for one year
segments.description:
Each student works alone to fill in the last column of the table: grew, shrank or steady for glaciers A, B and C.
For glacier B only, each student writes one short answer on what its terminus will tend to do if this balance continues for many years.
Partners compare answers for one minute.
Hear one or two answers and the reasoning.
segments.teacherNotes: Answers: A gains 0.3 m water equivalent and grew; B loses 0.5 m and shrank, so its terminus will tend to retreat; C has zero net balance and is steady. Terminus movement can lag changes in mass balance. Numbers are hypothetical. Slow students: subtract loss from gain first.

segments.title: How ice flows
segments.description:
Explain internal deformation, where ice crystals slip and the mass creeps downhill under its own weight.
Explain basal sliding, where meltwater at the bed lets the glacier slide, and contrast it with cold-based ice frozen to the bed.
Show that the brittle top 50 m or so cracks into crevasses while the ice below flows plastically.
Students sketch the predicted stake line after a year, compare with a partner, then see the answer: the line bows downvalley, center furthest.
segments.teacherNotes: Valley glacier speeds run from centimeters to meters per day; some outlet glaciers move much faster. Common mistake: ice at the edges moves as fast as the center. Friction with the valley walls slows the edges.
shown: Stakes in a straight line across a valley glacier are set out in July. Sketch where the line is one year later.
Side by side: Internal deformation: ice creeps under its own weight; fastest at the surface and center | Basal sliding: meltwater at the bed lowers friction; needs ice at the melting point

segments.title: Find and fix the mistake
segments.description:
Each student writes a corrected version of the note in two or three sentences.
Partners swap, check each other’s fix for the cause of the retreat, and revise for two minutes.
Hear two or three corrections.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected fix: the ice still flows downhill; the terminus retreats because ablation removes ice faster than flow delivers it. Retreat is a balance, not a direction of flow. Ice can climb a bump only because the surface slope, not the bed slope, drives flow.
shown: A student’s note: “This glacier’s terminus has retreated 200 m in ten years, so the ice must have stopped flowing, or be flowing uphill.” Find the mistake and write a corrected sentence.

segments.title: Summary and what comes next time
segments.description:
Each student writes the one sentence that links mass balance to terminus position, then shares it with a partner.
Recap the formation of firn and ice, and the two ways ice moves.
Next time: landforms, ice cores and orbital cycles, plus a mixed review set.
Remind students that the chapter on glaciers in Earle’s Physical Geology supports both meetings.
segments.teacherNotes: Good sentence: sustained gain favors terminus advance and sustained loss favors retreat, but the terminus can respond slowly; ice continues flowing downhill either way.

segments.title: How glaciers shape the land
segments.description:
Students first sketch a river valley cross section and the same valley after a valley glacier has filled it, then compare with a neighbor.
Explain erosion by plucking and abrasion, and show striations, cirques, arêtes, horns, U-shaped valleys, hanging valleys and fjords.
Explain deposition: till is unsorted, terminal moraines mark former ice fronts, while lateral moraines form along glacier sides, erratics are carried boulders, and outwash is sorted by meltwater.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected sketch: V-shaped river valley becomes a wide U with a flat floor and steep walls. Common mistake: calling till sorted. Meltwater sorts outwash during transport and deposition; direct deposition by ice leaves unsorted till. Use photographs of a local glaciated valley if available.
shown: Sketch a river valley cross section, then the same valley after a valley glacier has filled it.
Side by side: Erosion: striations; cirque; arête; horn; U-shaped valley; hanging valley; fjord | Deposition: till; terminal and lateral moraines; erratics; outwash plain; drumlins; eskers

segments.title: Landform or deposit?
segments.description:
Each student matches the four descriptions to terms from the bank, with no reasons needed.
Partners compare and settle any difference by pointing to the process.
Hear the answer for one item.
segments.teacherNotes: 1 cirque. 2 arête. 3 terminal moraine (till). 4 outwash. Mistake to watch for: matching item 3 to outwash because it sits beyond the ice.
shown: Term bank: cirque, arête, terminal moraine, outwash
1. A bowl-shaped hollow at the head of a mountain valley.
2. A knife-edge ridge between two such hollows.
3. An unsorted mix of clay to boulders in a ridge at a glacier’s former front.
4. Well-sorted, rounded gravel spread over a plain beyond the ice.

segments.title: What ice cores record
segments.description:
Students predict how temperature and carbon dioxide would compare along one long core, then explain their prediction to a partner.
Explain that annual snow layers build up and that drilling brings up a core from Greenland or Antarctica.
Explain that snow in colder times has less ¹⁸O, which is temperature evidence, and that trapped bubbles hold ancient air, including CO₂.
Name the Antarctic cores that reach back about 420,000 years (Vostok) and about 800,000 years (EPICA Dome C).
segments.teacherNotes: Reveal: temperature and CO₂ rise and fall together across the glacial cycles. Common mistake: saying the core measures old thermometer readings. The temperature is inferred from isotopes, while CO₂ is measured directly in the air bubbles.
shown: If temperature and CO₂ are both read from one ice core, what pattern over time do you expect? Explain it to a partner.
Steps: Snow layer → Buried and compressed → Air sealed in bubbles → Core drilled and measured

segments.title: Orbital cycles and the ice ages
segments.description:
Present the three Milankovitch cycles: eccentricity, tilt and precession.
Explain that they change where and when sunlight arrives, not the yearly total by much, and that cool northern summers let snow survive.
Show how ice-sheet growth and falling CO₂ amplify the small change.
Partners then explain to each other which cycle is longest and why summer sunshine at high northern latitudes matters.
Note that the last glacial maximum was about 20,000 years ago, with sea level about 120 m lower.
segments.teacherNotes: Common mistake: thinking orbital cycles change total sunlight a lot. They shift its seasonal and latitudinal pattern. The roughly 100,000-year cycle dominates the last 800,000 years of the record.
shown: Table: Cycle | What changes | Length / Eccentricity | shape of the orbit, from near circle to slightly oval | about 100,000 years / Tilt (obliquity) | angle of the axis, 22.1° to 24.5° | about 41,000 years / Precession | wobble of the axis, which season is nearest the Sun | about 23,000 years

segments.title: How fast did CO₂ change?
segments.description:
Each student works out the rate of rise in ppm per year for each of the two periods, alone, from the rises given.
Partners compare rates for one minute.
Each student divides the recent rate by the deglaciation rate to find how many times faster the recent rise is. Hear one answer.
segments.teacherNotes: Deglaciation: about 70 ppm (190 to 260) over 10,000 years, about 0.007 ppm per year. 1850–2023: about 135 ppm (285 to 420) over 173 years, about 0.78 ppm per year. Recent rise is about 111 times faster. Values are rounded.

segments.title: Mixed problems from earlier in the course
segments.description:
Explain that this practice prepares students for the Final exam (30%), which is on what has been taught so far. Each student works the five problems alone for about eight minutes.
Partners compare answers and method for two minutes, then raise any problem on which they disagree.
Go over the problem that most pairs missed.
segments.teacherNotes: 1. 12 × 1.5 × 2.0 = 36 m³/s. 2. q = K × i = 5×10⁻⁵ × 0.02 = 1×10⁻⁶ m/s. 3. 12.5% is three half-lives: 3 × 704 = about 2,100 million years. 4. Sandstone, dike, conglomerate. 5. Normal fault, tension. These are practice only; the exam paper alone gives its topics.

segments.title: Summary and the lab ahead
segments.description:
Recap the link from ice cores to orbital cycles.
Next time is the lab: a flowing-ice model, glacial deposits in hand samples and two valley profiles, done in pairs.
Ask for closed-toe shoes at the lab.

segments.title: Report due, safety and pairs
segments.description:
Lab reports: Groundwater is due now, at the start of this lab.
Students sit in pairs with the department’s hand samples.
Review safety: closed-toe shoes; goggles on whenever the dilute HCl bottle is used; samples stay in their trays and return where they came from.
Preview the three stations and the data to record.
segments.teacherNotes: Safety: syrup spills are slippery; wipe immediately and keep bags off the floor. Nothing in the lab is tasted. Wash hands after handling till and outwash samples.

segments.title: Method: the flowing-ice model
segments.description:
Demonstrate a shallow tray tilted on a block, holding a channel of thick syrup with a dye line laid straight across it.
Mark fixed measurement tracks at the center and near each wall, with a common reference line across the tray. Show how to measure the dye line’s downslope position from that reference at each track, starting at time zero and repeating every five minutes.
Show the recording table and the speed calculation: displacement divided by time, in cm/min.
Stress that the model shows the direction of the pattern, not real ice or real scale.
segments.teacherNotes: Equipment: tray, block, syrup, dye, rulers, timers, paper towels. Adjust tilt beforehand so the line moves about a centimeter a minute; flatten if too fast. Syrup is slippery and sticky: wipe with warm water, never taste, rinse small amounts down the sink.
shown: Steps: Tilt the tray → Lay the dye line → Read center and edges → Repeat every 5 minutes → Calculate speed

segments.title: Predict, then run: where does the model flow fastest?
segments.description:
Each pair writes a prediction for which part of the line moves fastest, and why.
Pairs set up the tray, start the timer and read the three tracks at 0, 5, 10 and 15 minutes, swapping reader and recorder after the 10-minute reading.
They sketch the line’s shape at the final reading, then calculate the three speeds from 0 to 15 minutes and compare with the prediction.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: center fastest, edges slowest, and the line bows downslope like the stake line. If a tray flows too slowly, use the pre-made photographs of the line at later times. Keep units in cm and minutes.

segments.title: Predict, then observe: glacial deposits in hand samples
segments.description:
Identify the trays as till, outwash gravel and sand, and a striated cobble. Before examining them, pairs predict which samples will be sorted and which will be rounded.
They examine till, outwash gravel and sand, and a striated cobble with hand lenses, and record sorting, rounding, striations and the likely setting.
They compare the outwash with the stream deposits seen earlier in the course and return all samples to their trays.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: till is unsorted and may contain clasts with varied rounding; outwash is sorted and commonly rounded; the striated cobble shows parallel scratches. If a limestone erratic is present, the fizz test needs goggles on before the acid bottle is opened. Rinse samples afterward.

segments.title: Break
segments.description: Students leave the trays and the model in place and take a break.

segments.title: Predict, then plot: two valley profiles
segments.description:
Each pair predicts which valley was glaciated by looking at the numbers alone.
They plot both profiles on graph paper with the same scales. For this comparison, define floor width as the horizontal span at or below 5 m above the minimum, using straight lines between plotted points. Calculate each valley’s outer wall slope between 400 m and 600 m from the center as rise divided by horizontal run.
They write one sentence naming the valley that was glaciated and the evidence for it.
segments.teacherNotes: Valley B has the profile more consistent with glacial erosion: a broad, gently sloping floor and steep outer walls. Using the 5 m floor criterion, its floor is 400 m wide, compared with 20 m for Valley A. B’s outer wall slope is 260/200 = 1.3, about 52°. A’s wall slope is 100/200 = 0.5, about 27°, producing a V-shaped profile. Numbers are hypothetical.

segments.title: Finish recording and clean up
segments.description:
Pairs complete all three tables and check the units.
They wipe the tray and rulers, return samples to their trays and clear the benches.
Each student starts their own notes for the report from the shared data.
segments.teacherNotes: Check that every sample is back in its tray and that no syrup is left on the floor. Pairs share data; each student’s report is their own work.

segments.title: Assignments and the final exam
segments.description:
Set Lab reports: Glaciers, part of Lab reports (30%). Pairs collect the data together, and each student writes their own report, scored individually using the rubric on the assignment. This is the last lab, so announce the report’s due date.
Set Weekly online quizzes: Glaciers, part of Weekly online quizzes (10%). Each student completes their own work, scored individually as stated on the assignment. It is submitted online by the deadline the instructor announces.
The Final exam (30%) is a separate written exam taken after the course ends, marked in points, and is on what has been taught so far; the paper alone gives its topics. The instructor announces its date, its room and what students may bring or use.
segments.teacherNotes: Say aloud the date or meeting for each new piece before students leave; the missed-lab policy allows a make-up in the same week’s open lab hour.

keyIdeas: A glacier forms where more snow falls than melts. Buried snow compacts into firn and then glacial ice, and the balance between yearly gain and loss decides whether the glacier grows or shrinks.
Ice flows downhill by internal deformation and by basal sliding. A retreating terminus means melting outpaces delivery of ice, not that the ice has stopped flowing.
Glaciers carve cirques, arêtes, U-shaped valleys and striated bedrock, and they leave till, moraines, erratics and outwash.
Ice cores record past temperature in oxygen isotopes and past air in trapped bubbles. Orbital cycles of about 100,000, 41,000 and 23,000 years pace the ice ages.

vocabulary.definition: Old, compacted granular snow that has survived at least one summer and is partway to becoming glacial ice.
The line on a glacier where yearly snow gain equals yearly melt; above it is the accumulation zone and below it the ablation zone.
Loss of ice and snow from a glacier by melting, sublimation or calving.
Movement of a glacier by sliding over its bed, helped by meltwater.
A bowl-shaped hollow cut into a mountainside at the head of a glaciated valley.
Unsorted sediment deposited directly by ice, ranging from clay to boulders.
A ridge or sheet of till left at the edge or end of a glacier.
Regular changes in Earth’s orbital shape, axial tilt and wobble, lasting about 100,000, 41,000 and 23,000 years, that pace the ice ages.

slides.title: Glaciers and climate
bullets: How glaciers form and flow
Mass balance and terminus position
slides.notes: Welcome students. This meeting covers how snow becomes glacial ice, how ice moves, and what the balance between gain and loss does to a glacier’s terminus. The chapter on glaciers in Earle’s Physical Geology, 2nd edition, supports both meetings.

slides.title: Of all the fresh water on Earth, about what share is held as glacier and ice-sheet ice?
bullets: A: about 3%
B: about 30%
C: about 70%
slides.notes:
Weekly online quizzes: Groundwater is due now and was submitted online before this meeting. Nothing is collected in class.

Each student writes a choice, then compares it with a neighbor for one minute. Hear two or three choices, then give the answer: C. Glaciers and ice sheets hold about 69% of Earth’s fresh water. Groundwater holds about 30%, and lakes and rivers a tiny fraction. Many students pick the middle choice because rivers feel large.

Link to the water followed underground last time: most of the liquid fresh water is groundwater, and the ice holds far more.

slides.title: From snow to glacial ice
slides.notes:
Explain how snow buried by later snowfall compacts into firn and then glacial ice. Density rises from fresh snow at about 0.1 g/cm³, through firn at roughly 0.4 to 0.8 g/cm³, to ice near 0.9 g/cm³.

Common mistake: thinking glaciers form only in very cold places. Snow must survive the summer, so high mountains in warm latitudes qualify.

Name the two main kinds, alpine glaciers and ice sheets. Antarctica holds about 90% of the world’s glacier ice.

visual.note: Each step up is denser. Snow is loose, firn is packed grains, glacial ice is solid with tiny bubbles.
parts: Snow: fresh, loose flakes
Firn: snow packed into rounded grains by the weight above
Glacial ice: dense, with tiny trapped bubbles
Burial: later snowfall piles on top

slides.title: Two zones of an alpine glacier
bullets: Mass balance = yearly gain − yearly loss
slides.notes:
Draw an alpine glacier on the board with the accumulation zone, the ablation zone and the equilibrium line between them. Define mass balance as yearly gain minus yearly loss.

Before explaining, pairs predict for one minute where the equilibrium line moves in a warm year. Then give the answer: up-valley, because melt reaches higher and a larger part of the glacier loses more than it gains.

visual.ask: In a warm year, where does the equilibrium line move?

slides.title: Mass balance for one year
bullets: Work from the sheet “Mass balance for one year”.
slides.notes:
Each student works alone to fill in the last column of the table: grew, shrank or steady for glaciers A, B and C.
For glacier B only, each student writes one short answer on what its terminus will tend to do if this balance continues for many years.
Partners compare answers for one minute.
Hear one or two answers and the reasoning.

slides.title: Where is the stake line a year later?
bullets: Stakes in a straight line across a valley glacier are set out in July. Sketch where the line is one year later.
slides.notes:
Before this slide, explain the two ways ice moves. Internal deformation: ice crystals slip and the mass creeps downhill under its own weight. Basal sliding: meltwater at the bed lets the glacier slide; contrast it with cold-based ice frozen to the bed. Also show that the brittle top 50 m or so cracks into crevasses while the ice below flows plastically.

Students sketch the predicted line alone, then compare with a partner. Do not show the next slide until they have. Valley glacier speeds run from centimeters to meters per day; some outlet glaciers move much faster.

slides.title: How ice moves
slides.notes:
Show after students have sketched and compared. The answer: the line bows downvalley, with the center furthest ahead. Draw it on the board over the straight line.

Common mistake: believing ice at the edges moves as fast as the center. Friction with the valley walls slows the edges. Basal sliding needs ice at the melting point, so it does not happen under cold-based ice.

slides.title: Find and fix the mistake
bullets: A student’s note: “This glacier’s terminus has retreated 200 m in ten years, so the ice must have stopped flowing, or be flowing uphill.”
Find the mistake and write a corrected sentence.
slides.notes:
Each student writes a corrected version of the note in two or three sentences. Partners swap, check each other’s fix for the cause of the retreat, and revise for two minutes. Hear two or three corrections.

Expected fix: the ice still flows downhill. The terminus retreats because ablation removes ice faster than flow delivers it. Retreat is a balance, not a direction of flow. If asked about ice climbing a bump: surface slope, not bed slope, drives flow.

slides.title: How glaciers shape the land
slides.notes:
Explain erosion by plucking and abrasion, then show striations, cirques, arêtes, horns, U-shaped valleys, hanging valleys and fjords.

Explain deposition: till is unsorted, terminal moraines mark former ice fronts, lateral moraines form along glacier sides, erratics are carried boulders, and outwash is sorted by meltwater. Common mistake: calling till sorted. Direct deposition by ice leaves unsorted till; meltwater sorts outwash during transport and deposition.

slides.title: Landform or deposit?
bullets: Term bank: cirque, arête, terminal moraine, outwash
1. A bowl-shaped hollow at the head of a mountain valley.
2. A knife-edge ridge between two such hollows.
3. An unsorted mix of clay to boulders in a ridge at a glacier’s former front.
4. Well-sorted, rounded gravel spread over a plain beyond the ice.
slides.notes:
Each student matches the four descriptions to terms from the bank, with no reasons needed. Partners compare and settle any difference by pointing to the process. Hear the answer for one item.

Answers: 1 cirque, 2 arête, 3 terminal moraine (till), 4 outwash. Watch for students matching item 3 to outwash just because it sits beyond the ice.

slides.title: Temperature and CO₂ in one ice core
bullets: If temperature and CO₂ are both read from one ice core, what pattern over time do you expect? Explain it to a partner.
slides.notes:
Students predict, then explain the prediction to a partner. Do not show the next slide until they have.

Then reveal: temperature and CO₂ rise and fall together across the glacial cycles. Common mistake: saying the core measures old thermometer readings. Temperature is inferred from isotopes, while CO₂ is measured directly in the air bubbles.

slides.title: How an ice core is made
slides.notes:
Explain that annual snow layers build up and that drilling brings up a core from Greenland or Antarctica. Snow in colder times has less ¹⁸O, which is temperature evidence, and trapped bubbles hold ancient air, including CO₂.

Name the Antarctic cores: Vostok reaches back about 420,000 years and EPICA Dome C about 800,000 years.

slides.title: The three orbital cycles
slides.notes:
Present the three Milankovitch cycles. They change where and when sunlight arrives, not the yearly total by much. Cool northern summers let snow survive. Ice-sheet growth and falling CO₂ then amplify the small change.

Note that the last glacial maximum was about 20,000 years ago, with sea level about 120 m lower.

Common mistake: thinking orbital cycles change total sunlight a lot. They shift its seasonal and latitudinal pattern. The roughly 100,000-year cycle dominates the last 800,000 years of the record.

Partners then explain to each other which cycle is longest and why summer sunshine at high northern latitudes matters.

study.overview: Glaciers are ice masses built from snow that survives the summer, and they flow, carve and deposit in patterns you can read in a landscape. The same ice stores a record of past climate: oxygen isotopes give temperature, and trapped bubbles give ancient air. This guide covers how glacial ice forms and how its mass balance is judged, how it moves, which landforms it leaves, and how ice cores and orbital cycles explain the ice ages. It supports Earle, Physical Geology, 2nd edition, the chapter on glaciers. The Final exam (30%) is on what has been taught so far, and the paper alone gives its topics. Your instructor announces its date, its room and what you may bring or use. Lab reports: Glaciers and climate is part of Lab reports (30%); this is the last lab, so the instructor announces its due date. Weekly online quizzes: Glaciers and climate is part of Weekly online quizzes (10%), and your instructor announces its deadline.

points.heading: Snow to ice, and the mass balance that decides growth
points.explanation: A glacier forms where more snow falls than melts, so snow survives the summer. This can happen in cold polar regions or on high mountains in warm latitudes. Later snowfall buries and compacts the older snow into firn, and firn becomes glacial ice. Density rises from about 0.1 g/cm³ for fresh snow, to roughly 0.4 to 0.8 g/cm³ for firn, to about 0.9 g/cm³ for ice. An alpine glacier has an accumulation zone, where snow gain exceeds melt, and an ablation zone, where melt exceeds gain and bare ice shows by late summer. The equilibrium line separates them. Mass balance is yearly gain minus yearly loss. Example (hypothetical numbers): a glacier gains 2.0 m and loses 2.4 m of water equivalent in a year. Its balance is 2.0 − 2.4 = −0.4 m, so it shrank. If years like this continue, the equilibrium line shifts up-valley, as it does in any warm year, and the terminus tends to retreat, though it can respond slowly. Alpine glaciers and ice sheets are the two main kinds. Antarctica holds about 90% of the world’s glacier ice, and glaciers and ice sheets together hold about 69% of Earth’s fresh water.

points.heading: How ice flows, and what a retreating terminus means
points.explanation: Ice moves in two ways. In internal deformation, ice crystals slip and the mass creeps downhill under its own weight. In basal sliding, meltwater at the bed lowers friction and the glacier slides, which requires ice at the melting point. Friction with the valley walls slows the edges, so the center of a valley glacier moves fastest. Example: stakes set in a straight line across a valley glacier in July form a downvalley-bowed curve a year later, with the center stake having traveled furthest and the edge stakes least. Valley glacier speeds run from centimeters to meters per day. Flow and terminus position are separate things. Ice flows downhill all the time, and the terminus sits where delivery of ice balances melting. If melting at the front removes ice faster than flow delivers it, the terminus retreats while the ice still moves forward. A retreat of 200 m in ten years records that imbalance. It does not record a change in flow direction.

points.heading: Landforms and deposits: reading a glaciated landscape
points.explanation: Moving ice erodes by plucking, which pulls blocks of bedrock from the bed, and by abrasion, where rock fragments in the ice scratch the bedrock into striations. Erosional landforms include cirques (bowl-shaped hollows at valley heads), arêtes (knife-edge ridges between cirques), horns, hanging valleys and fjords. A river cuts a V-shaped valley. After a valley glacier fills it, the valley becomes a wide U with a flat floor and steep walls. Deposits divide by process. Ice that drops its load directly leaves till, an unsorted mix from clay to boulders, and moraines are ridges of this material. Meltwater leaving the ice sorts and rounds sediment into outwash, spread over a plain beyond the front. An erratic is a boulder carried by ice and left far from its source. Example (hypothetical): a granite boulder sits on limestone bedrock with no granite outcrop for many kilometers. Ice carried it there, so it is an erratic. Sorting is the clue for telling ice deposits from water deposits.

points.heading: Ice cores, orbital cycles and the speed of today’s CO₂ rise
points.explanation: Annual snow layers build up and are buried, and drilling in Greenland or Antarctica brings up a core. Snow from colder times contains less ¹⁸O, so oxygen isotopes give an inferred temperature. This is not an old thermometer reading. Bubbles trapped in the ice hold ancient air, and CO₂ is measured directly from them. Antarctic cores reach back about 420,000 years (Vostok) and about 800,000 years (EPICA Dome C). Across the glacial cycles, temperature and CO₂ rise and fall together. The pacing comes from three orbital (Milankovitch) cycles. Eccentricity, the orbit’s shape, runs about 100,000 years. Tilt (obliquity), the axis angle between 22.1° and 24.5°, runs about 41,000 years. Precession, the axis wobble that sets which season is nearest the Sun, runs about 23,000 years. They shift where and when sunlight arrives, with little change in the yearly total. Cool summers at high northern latitudes let snow survive, and ice-sheet growth and falling CO₂ amplify the small change. About 20,000 years ago, at the last glacial maximum, sea level was about 120 m lower. Worked comparison from rounded values. At the last deglaciation, CO₂ rose from 190 to 260 ppm over 10,000 years: 70 ÷ 10,000 = 0.0070 ppm per year. From 1850 to 2023 it rose from 285 to 420 ppm over 173 years: 135 ÷ 173 = 0.78 ppm per year. Dividing, 0.78 ÷ 0.0070 is about 111, so the recent rise is roughly 111 times faster.

handouts.title: Mass balance for one year

blocks.text: The numbers below are hypothetical. Each is the yearly total for one glacier, in meters of water equivalent. Mass balance is the yearly gain minus the yearly loss. Work alone, then compare with your partner.
For glacier B only: if this balance continues for many years, what will its terminus tend to do?

blocks.hint: One short answer.

handouts.key:
A: 1.8 − 1.5 = +0.3 m water equivalent; grew.
B: 1.0 − 1.5 = −0.5 m water equivalent; shrank.
C: 1.2 − 1.2 = 0 m water equivalent; steady.
Glacier B’s terminus will tend to retreat if the negative mass balance persists. Its response may lag behind the mass loss. Look for a link between sustained ice loss and retreat. Common slip: saying that retreat means the ice flows uphill.

handouts.title: How fast did CO₂ change?

blocks.text: Atmospheric CO₂ concentration is given for two periods. The values are rounded. Work out the average rate of rise in ppm per year for each period. Give each rate to two significant figures. Work alone first, then compare with your partner.
Divide the recent rate by the deglaciation rate. How many times faster is the recent rise?

blocks.hint: Show the division and your answer.

handouts.key:
Last deglaciation: (260 − 190) ÷ 10,000 = 0.0070 ppm per year, to two significant figures.
1850 to 2023: (420 − 285) ÷ 173 = 0.78 ppm per year, to two significant figures.
Rate comparison: (135 ÷ 173) ÷ (70 ÷ 10,000) = 111.48, or about 111 times faster. Using the rounded rates gives 0.78 ÷ 0.0070 = 111.43; accept about 110 times faster to two significant figures.
Common slips: dividing the final concentration by elapsed time instead of dividing the increase, or reversing the ratio.
