blocks.text: This practice prepares you for the Final exam (30%), which is on what has been taught so far. Work all five problems alone. Show your working and give units where they apply.

items: A stream channel is 12 m wide and 1.5 m deep on average. The water moves at an average of 2.0 m/s. Find the discharge in m³/s.
Groundwater moves through sand with a hydraulic conductivity K of 5×10⁻⁵ m/s. The hydraulic gradient is 0.02. Use Darcy's law, q = K × i, to find the flow rate q in m/s.
A rock sample holds 12.5% of its original U-235. The half-life of U-235 is 704 million years. How old is the sample?

In a cross section, flat sandstone beds are cut by a vertical basalt dike. The top of the dike is eroded flat. A conglomerate lies across the sandstone and the truncated top of the dike, and it contains basalt pebbles. List the three units from oldest to youngest.
In a road cut, the rock above an inclined fault surface has moved down relative to the rock below it. Name the type of fault and the kind of stress that produced it.

blocks.hint: Problem 1
Problem 2
Problem 3
Problem 4
Problem 5

handouts.key:
Stream discharge: Q = width × mean depth × mean velocity = 12 × 1.5 × 2.0 = 36 m³/s. Common slip: reporting cross-sectional area, 18 m², as discharge.
Groundwater: q = K × i = (5 × 10⁻⁵) × 0.02 = 1 × 10⁻⁶ m/s. This is specific discharge, the volumetric flow per unit cross-sectional area. Common slip: treating it as pore-water velocity without accounting for porosity.
Radiometric age: 12.5% = 0.125 = (½)³. Three half-lives have elapsed: 3 × 704 = 2,112 million years, or 2.112 billion years. Accept about 2.1 billion years. Common slip: interpreting the percentage remaining as the percentage decayed.
Relative ages, oldest to youngest: sandstone, basalt dike, conglomerate. The dike cuts the sandstone; the conglomerate overlies the eroded dike and contains basalt pebbles. Common slip: placing the dike after the conglomerate despite its truncated top.
Fault: normal fault; tensional stress, or extension. The hanging wall moved down relative to the footwall. Common slip: identifying the hanging wall by compass direction rather than its position above the inclined fault surface.

handouts.title: Flowing-ice model: record sheet
handouts.usedIn: Predict, then run: where does the model flow fastest?

blocks.text: The model is a tilted tray of thick syrup with a dye line laid straight across the channel. It shows the direction of a pattern, not real ice or real scale. Measure the downslope position of the dye line from the common reference line, in cm, at each fixed track. Read at 0, 5, 10 and 15 minutes. Swap reader and recorder after the 10-minute reading.
Prediction (write before you start the timer)

blocks.hint: Which part of the line will move fastest, and why?

blocks.caption: Position of the dye line from the reference line (cm)

blocks.text: Shape of the line at the final reading

blocks.hint: Sketch the tray walls, the direction of flow and the dye line.

blocks.caption: Speed from 0 to 15 minutes. Speed = displacement ÷ time, in cm/min.

blocks.hint: Compare your speeds with your prediction. Was your prediction right? Explain in one or two sentences.

handouts.key:
Prediction: the center should move fastest because resistance from the channel walls slows flow near the sides. Look for a prediction supported by this mechanism.
Position table: record the measured position in centimeters for the center, near-left-wall and near-right-wall tracks at each stated time. Initial positions need not be zero; each reading uses the common reference line. Actual values depend on the model’s flow.
Final sketch: show both tray walls, a downslope flow arrow and the dye line bowed downslope, with its center farther downstream than its ends under the expected flow pattern. The sketch should represent the observed line.
Center displacement = center position at 15 minutes − center position at 0 minutes; center speed = that displacement ÷ 15, in cm/min.
Near-left-wall displacement = left-track position at 15 minutes − left-track position at 0 minutes; left-track speed = that displacement ÷ 15, in cm/min.
Near-right-wall displacement = right-track position at 15 minutes − right-track position at 0 minutes; right-track speed = that displacement ÷ 15, in cm/min.
Prediction comparison: use the calculated speeds to state whether the center moved fastest. A supported answer may report a different observed pattern and explain a plausible influence, such as uneven tray tilt or inconsistent measurement tracks. Common slips: using final position instead of displacement, dividing by the interval between readings instead of the full elapsed time, or reporting real-glacier speeds from the syrup model.

handouts.title: Glacial deposits: record sheet
handouts.usedIn: Predict, then observe: glacial deposits in hand samples

blocks.text: Use a hand lens. Samples stay in their trays and go back where they came from. If a limestone erratic is present, put goggles on before the acid bottle is opened.
Prediction (write before you examine the samples)

blocks.hint: Which samples will be sorted, and which will be rounded?
Compare the outwash with the stream deposits you saw earlier in the course. What is similar, and what process explains it?

handouts.key:
Prediction: till should be unsorted, with clasts of varied rounding. Outwash gravel and sand should be sorted and commonly rounded, especially the gravel. A striated cobble may be rounded, angular or faceted; its scratches are more diagnostic than its rounding. Sorting cannot be established from one cobble alone.
Till row: sorting—poorly sorted or unsorted, with mixed grain sizes; rounding—variable, based on the sample; striations—record whether scratches are visible on individual clasts; likely setting—direct deposition by glacier ice.
Outwash gravel and sand row: sorting—sorted relative to till, with grain-size separation produced by flowing water; rounding—commonly rounded gravel, with sand-grain rounding recorded only where visible; striations—usually absent or not evident, but record any observed; likely setting—meltwater streams downstream from glacier ice.
Striated cobble row: sorting—not determinable from a single clast; rounding—record its observed shape and any facets; striations—parallel scratches or grooves where visible; likely setting—abrasion during transport at a glacier bed. The cobble alone does not establish its final depositional setting.
Stream comparison: outwash resembles stream deposits in its sorting and commonly rounded gravel. Flowing water transports and separates grains by size and transport conditions; collisions and abrasion can round clasts. Look for an explicit link to meltwater transport. Common slips: calling till sorted, assuming all glacial clasts are angular, or assigning a deposit’s sorting to a single cobble.

handouts.title: Two valley profiles
handouts.usedIn: Predict, then plot: two valley profiles

blocks.text: The numbers below are hypothetical. Each valley is symmetrical about its center line. Elevation is measured above the lowest point of the valley floor.
Prediction (from the numbers alone, before plotting)

blocks.hint: Which valley was glaciated, and what in the numbers makes you think so?

blocks.text: Plot

Plot both profiles on graph paper with the same scales: distance from center from −600 m to +600 m, elevation from 0 to 400 m. Mirror each profile to plot the left side. Join the points with straight lines. Label each valley.
Measure

Floor width is the horizontal span at or below 5 m above the minimum, using straight lines between plotted points. Outer wall slope is rise divided by horizontal run between 400 m and 600 m from the center.

blocks.hint: Write one sentence naming the valley that was glaciated and the evidence for it.

handouts.key:
Prediction: Valley B is more consistent with glacial erosion. Elevation rises only 5 m across the central 200 m on either side, then rises sharply toward the outer walls.
Plot: use matching scales for both profiles. Valley A coordinates are (−600, 300), (−400, 200), (−300, 150), (−200, 100), (−100, 50), (−10, 5), (0, 0), (10, 5), (100, 50), (200, 100), (300, 150), (400, 200), (600, 300). Valley B coordinates are (−600, 400), (−400, 140), (−300, 60), (−200, 5), (−100, 1), (−10, 0), (0, 0), (10, 0), (100, 1), (200, 5), (300, 60), (400, 140), (600, 400). Coordinates are in meters. Join successive points with straight lines and label both valleys. Valley A is V-shaped; Valley B has a broad floor and steep outer walls.
Valley A measurements: floor extends from −10 m to +10 m, so width = 20 m. Outer wall slope = (300 − 200) ÷ (600 − 400) = 100 ÷ 200 = 0.50.
Valley B measurements: floor extends from −200 m to +200 m, so width = 400 m. Outer wall slope = (400 − 140) ÷ (600 − 400) = 260 ÷ 200 = 1.30. Rise/run slopes are dimensionless.
Evidence sentence: Valley B is more consistent with glacial erosion because its 400 m floor is much broader and its outer wall slope of 1.30 is steeper than Valley A’s 20 m floor and slope of 0.50.
Common slips: reporting half the floor width, using different plotting scales, or calculating wall slope from the valley center instead of the specified outer interval.

t_de355519f240.prompt: Why does oceanic lithosphere subduct at a trench while continental lithosphere resists? Use densities and age in your answer.
followUps: Oceanic crust is about 3.0 g/cm³ and the mantle beneath it is about 3.3 g/cm³. How can a plate with a lighter crust than the mantle still sink?
What happens to the density of oceanic lithosphere as it cools and moves away from a ridge, and why does its age matter?
Continental crust is about 2.7 g/cm³. What happens when a continent reaches a trench, and what landform results?

t_e646631f2a8d.prompt: Earth’s mean density is 5.51 g/cm³, but the crust and upper mantle are only about 2.7 to 3.3 g/cm³. Is density alone enough to show that Earth has a dense iron-rich core, or do we need other evidence?
followUps: Pressure squeezes rock into a denser state at depth. Could compression alone raise a rock like peridotite to a mean of 5.51 g/cm³? How would you argue for or against that?
Which other piece of evidence (S waves, meteorites or the magnetic field) would you add first, and what does it tell us that density cannot?
If a classmate says the density result is only a hint and the seismic evidence is the real proof, how would you respond?

t_be7e856c106b.prompt: A seismic station receives P waves from a distant earthquake, but direct S waves do not reach it after traveling through the core. Which conclusion does this evidence support?
t_be7e856c106b.explanation: P waves can travel through liquids, but S waves cannot, so the missing direct S waves support a liquid outer core. The entire mantle is liquid confuses slow flow with melting; the inner core is liquid conflicts with seismic evidence for a solid inner core; the continental crust is liquid does not explain S waves being blocked at the core.

t_d9e3d5a9a9d3.prompt: A block containing oceanic crust and rigid uppermost mantle can form part of the lithosphere.
t_d9e3d5a9a9d3.explanation: The lithosphere includes the crust and the rigid uppermost mantle. A tectonic plate can contain oceanic crust, continental crust, or both.

t_3dc8d1c944e1.prompt: A newly mapped boundary has a deep ocean trench, a chain of volcanic islands, and earthquakes that extend hundreds of kilometers below the surface. Which boundary best fits these observations?
t_3dc8d1c944e1.explanation: Oceanic-oceanic convergence can produce a trench, an island arc, and deep earthquakes as one plate subducts. Oceanic-continental convergence produces a volcanic arc on a continent; continental-continental convergence produces a collision mountain belt; divergence at an ocean ridge produces shallow earthquakes and volcanism rather than a deep trench.

t_5033f2d3c9fc.prompt: A student claims that the Red Sea rift is a transform boundary because earthquakes occur there. The plates on either side are moving apart. Identify the mistake and explain which boundary type fits the stated motion and what landform it produces.
t_5033f2d3c9fc.answer: The boundary is divergent, not transform. Plates move apart at a divergent boundary, producing a rift; earthquakes can occur at both divergent and transform boundaries.
t_5033f2d3c9fc.explanation: Earthquakes alone do not distinguish the two boundary types. The stated motion is separation, which identifies a divergent boundary; at a transform boundary, plates slide past one another.

t_2bc27a839eeb.prompt: A piece of seafloor lies 900 km from a mid-ocean ridge and has moved away from it at a constant rate of 3 cm per year. Using 1 cm per year = 10 km per million years, estimate its age in millions of years.
t_2bc27a839eeb.explanation: A rate of 3 cm per year is 30 km per million years. Divide 900 km by 30 km per million years to obtain 30 million years.

t_3781db46653e.title: Lab reports: Earth's layers and plate tectonics
t_3781db46653e.prompt: Use your lab observations and the evidence discussed in class to prepare your own report. Show your calculations, use units, and explain how your evidence supports your conclusions. Lab reports count for 30% of the course grade. This report is due at the start of the lab of Minerals. It is scored using the rubric below.
steps: Present your pair’s mass, water-level and density measurements for granite, basalt and peridotite or dunite. Show the volume and density calculations for each sample. Compare the measured density ranking with your prediction, and explain any repeated measurements or limits in reading volume.

Use your results and Earth’s mean density of 5.51 g/cm³ to explain what must be true about the density of some material inside Earth. Explain why the sample measurements alone cannot establish the core’s composition.

Consider the Cascade Range, where the Juan de Fuca plate moves beneath North America. Explain how plate motion produces the associated trench, volcanic arc and earthquakes. Use the effects of cooling and density to explain why oceanic lithosphere can sink.

Compare the Cascade Range with the North Anatolian Fault near Istanbul. Explain how plate motion differs and why the expected earthquakes and volcanic activity differ. Use the map evidence and boundary characteristics discussed in class.
t_3781db46653e.answerKey:
1. A strong report records the pair’s actual measurements and calculates volume as water level after minus water level before, then density as mass divided by volume. It compares the measured ranking with the prediction and reports any repeated measurements and volume-reading limits. Typical densities are approximately 2.6–2.7 g/cm³ for granite, 2.8–3.0 g/cm³ for basalt and 3.2–3.4 g/cm³ for peridotite; actual observations should not be replaced with these values. Common mistakes include subtracting in the wrong order, omitting units and treating an unexpected ranking as proof without checking measurement uncertainty.
2. A strong answer recognizes that, if the measured samples are less dense than Earth’s mean, substantial material inside Earth must be denser than those samples. The samples alone do not identify the core’s composition; seismic and meteorite evidence also support an iron-rich core. Common mistakes include assuming every interior layer has the mean density or inferring core composition from density measurements alone.
3. A strong answer identifies oceanic–continental convergence: the Juan de Fuca plate descends beneath North America, producing a trench, earthquakes along the descending slab and a volcanic arc. Cooling and thermal contraction can make old oceanic lithosphere denser overall than the warmer asthenosphere, allowing it to sink. Common mistakes include treating the boundary as divergent or attributing sinking solely to the density of oceanic crust without considering the whole lithosphere.
4. A strong answer contrasts subduction at the Cascades with sideways motion along the transform boundary between the Anatolian and Eurasian plates. Both settings produce earthquakes; the Cascades have a subduction-related volcanic arc, while the transform fault does not itself produce volcanoes. A common mistake is to infer that every earthquake-bearing boundary produces volcanoes.

t_e3a9a8073795.title: Weekly online quizzes: Earth's layers and plate tectonics
t_e3a9a8073795.prompt: Complete your own work and submit it online before the first meeting of Minerals. Weekly online quizzes are worth 10% of the course grade. Choose one answer for each question. Each correct answer earns 1 point, for a total of 4 points.
steps: Which mechanical layer consists of the crust and rigid uppermost mantle? A. Asthenosphere B. Lithosphere C. Outer core D. Lower mantle

At a mid-ocean ridge, matching magnetic stripes occur on opposite sides of the ridge. What does this pattern support? A. New seafloor forms at the ridge and moves outward. B. Continents are made entirely of oceanic crust. C. The outer core is solid. D. Transform faults create new lithosphere.
On a drawing with a scale of 1 cm to 1,000 km, how thick would a 50 km layer be? A. 0.005 cm B. 0.5 cm C. 0.05 cm D. 5 cm

A chain of volcanoes lies within a plate, away from a plate boundary. The volcanoes become progressively older toward the west. Assuming a stationary hot spot formed the chain, which direction has the plate moved? A. East B. North C. South D. West
t_e3a9a8073795.answerKey:
1. B. The lithosphere includes the crust and rigid uppermost mantle.
2. A. Symmetrical magnetic stripes record seafloor spreading as new lithosphere forms and moves away from the ridge.
3. C. 50 km ÷ 1,000 km per cm = 0.05 cm.
4. D. The older volcanoes have moved west from the hot spot, indicating westward plate motion.

t_9883907eccc6.prompt: Design the thickest, most developed soil you can. Choose parent material, climate, organisms, topography and time, and give a reason for the two that matter most.
followUps: If you could fix only one of the five controls, which would you fix first, and what happens to your soil if that control is wrong?
Would basalt or quartz sandstone make a thicker soil in your setting, and what does that tell you about which minerals weather most easily?
Compare your soil with one on a steep, cold, young surface. Which horizons would be thin or missing there, and why?

t_7196014173f5.prompt: You find a pile of well-sorted, frosted sand and a bed of rounded gravel. How far can grain shape and sorting alone tell you which agent carried the grains and how far they traveled?
followUps: What second kind of evidence, such as the setting of the deposit, would make you more confident in your interpretation?
Could a flood or a landslide produce a deposit that breaks the usual pattern for its agent? What would you expect it to look like?
If hand-lens grains look rounded, does that prove a long journey? What else could round them or leave them angular?

t_f5a1e12054c3.prompt: Salt crystals grow in pores in a sandstone block and force grains apart. How should this change be classified?
t_f5a1e12054c3.explanation: Growing salt crystals exert force that breaks the rock apart without changing its minerals. Chemical weathering by dissolution would involve minerals dissolving; chemical weathering by oxidation would involve a reaction with oxygen; physical weathering by unloading follows the removal of overlying rock.

t_71c7ebae770c.prompt: A soil profile has a dark, humus-rich layer above a pale, leached layer and a reddish, clay-rich layer. Which horizon is the reddish, clay-rich layer?
t_71c7ebae770c.explanation: The B horizon is a zone where clay and iron compounds can accumulate. The A horizon is commonly dark and humus-rich; the E horizon is the pale, leached layer; the C horizon consists of partly weathered parent material.

t_e8ad873f9563.prompt: When feldspar in an exposed rock changes into a clay mineral, the change is physical weathering because the rock remains in place.
t_e8ad873f9563.explanation: The formation of clay from feldspar is chemical weathering because the original mineral changes. Both physical and chemical weathering can happen where rock remains in place.

t_1cbbc38aed8d.prompt: Two stable granite surfaces have been exposed for comparable lengths of time. One is warm and wet; the other is arid. Which outcome is generally expected?

choices.text: More chemical weathering on the arid surface
More chemical weathering on the warm, wet surface
Equal chemical weathering because both are granite
No chemical weathering because both are stable

t_1cbbc38aed8d.explanation: Warm, wet conditions generally promote chemical weathering. More chemical weathering on the arid surface reverses the expected climate effect; equal chemical weathering because both are granite ignores climate; no chemical weathering because both are stable confuses surface stability with resistance to weathering.

t_415d6d09a909.prompt: A student writes: “A reddish rind on an iron-bearing rock formed when the rock broke into smaller pieces. Rain then carried the pieces downhill, which is chemical weathering.” Identify and correct the mistakes. Explain how physical weathering could still help produce the rind.
t_415d6d09a909.answer: The reddish rind can form through oxidation, a type of chemical weathering that changes iron-bearing minerals. Rain carrying pieces downhill is erosion. Physical weathering can expose more surface area, allowing chemical weathering to act on more of the rock.
t_415d6d09a909.explanation: Breaking rock into smaller pieces is physical weathering, while oxidation produces new iron compounds. Movement downhill is erosion. The extra surface exposed by breakage gives water and other reactants more access to the rock.

t_7abc631749a9.title: Lab reports: Weathering, erosion and soils
t_7abc631749a9.prompt: Use your pair’s lab observations to prepare your own report. Show how your evidence supports your conclusions. Lab reports count for 30% of the course grade. This report is due at the start of the lab of Sedimentary rocks. It is scored using the rubric below.
steps: Present your observations for two numbered weathered hand samples from your lab tray. For each, describe the surface and any existing fresh broken face, report the fizz and hardness observations, and judge whether the evidence supports physical weathering, chemical weathering or both. Explain how the observations support your judgment and identify any uncertainty.

Use your results from the limestone jar activity and your observations of one sediment sample to explain how abrasion can change grains during transport. Describe the evidence for a possible transport agent for the sediment sample, then give an alternative interpretation. Explain why the observations do not establish one agent with certainty.

Choose one soil profile card and describe its horizons from top to bottom, using a visible clue for each. Explain how two soil-forming controls supported by the site description could influence the profile. Identify one control that cannot be established from the card, or explain why the description does not establish how long the surface has been developing.
t_7abc631749a9.answerKey:
1. A strong answer identifies two samples and reports their actual surface, fresh-face, fizz and hardness observations before interpreting them. It connects breakage or disintegration to physical weathering and altered minerals or a rusty rind to chemical weathering where supported. Fizz supports the presence of carbonate; it does not alone establish natural dissolution. Look for uncertainty when evidence is insufficient. Common mistakes include treating fizz as proof of natural dissolution or assuming every color difference establishes a process.
2. A strong answer uses the pair’s actual before-and-after jar observations to explain abrasion and suspended fine sediment, then uses roundness and sorting observations from a named sediment sample to support a plausible agent and an alternative. The evidence does not uniquely identify an agent or distance; cloudy water alone does not establish particle size. Common mistakes include claiming the jar reproduces a measured period of river transport or assigning an agent with certainty from color alone.
3. A strong answer labels the selected card’s horizons with clues: A: O, A, B, C; B: O, A, E, B, C; C: A, carbonate-accumulating B, C; D: A, B, C, above bedrock. It explains two controls supported by the chosen site and distinguishes evidence from possibilities. For example, card C supports low rainfall and a dust source for carbonate; card D supports granitic parent material and flat topography but does not establish surface age. Common mistakes include requiring an E horizon in every profile, treating carbonate nodules as an E horizon, or asserting an unsupported age.

t_a02ee7aea3a6.title: Weekly online quizzes: Weathering, erosion and soils
t_a02ee7aea3a6.prompt: Complete your own work and submit it online before the first meeting of Sedimentary rocks. Weekly online quizzes are worth 10% of the course grade. Choose one answer for each question. Each correct answer earns 1 point, for a total of 4 points.
steps: A 3 cm cube of rock is cut into 27 cubes, each 1 cm on a side. What is the total surface area of the smaller cubes? A. 54 cm² B. 81 cm² C. 162 cm² D. 270 cm²

Two samples of the same type of gravel travel different distances in a river under comparable conditions. Which sample would generally be more rounded? A. The sample transported farther, because collisions wear down corners. B. The sample transported farther, because its minerals crystallize again. C. The sample transported a shorter distance, because water adds corners. D. The sample transported a shorter distance, because abrasion stops during transport.
A pale layer lies beneath a dark topsoil and above a clay-rich layer. Clay and iron have been carried out of the pale layer. Which horizon is it? A. O B. E C. C D. Bedrock
Loose rock and soil move downslope under gravity as a coherent mass along a curved surface. What type of mass wasting is this? A. Rockfall B. Creep C. Debris flow D. Slump
t_a02ee7aea3a6.answerKey:
1. C. Each small cube has 6 cm² of surface area; 27 × 6 = 162 cm².
2. A. Under comparable conditions, collisions during longer transport generally wear down more corners.
3. B. The E horizon is a leached layer from which material has been carried downward.
4. D. A slump moves as a coherent mass along a curved surface.

t_c4e12a32a977.prompt: A fossil-bearing sandstone has a volcanic ash bed just above it. Do you date the sand grains or the ash?
followUps: What event does a zircon in the ash record, and what event do the zircons in the sand grains record?
If the ash gives an age of 704 million years, is the sandstone older or younger than that, and how do you know?
What second dated layer would you look for to put an upper and a lower limit on the sandstone’s age?

t_03defa385460.prompt: Suppose a mica crystal formed in a granite 2.5 billion years ago. Much later, the rock was buried and heated so strongly that some of the argon-40 inside the mica escaped. Does a potassium-argon age measured on that mica give the age of the granite, the age of the heating, or neither?
followUps: Would the measured age come out older or younger than the true crystallization age, and why?
Which assumption about parent and daughter atoms has failed in this crystal?
How could dating a second mineral from the same rock help you decide which event the mica records?

t_52ad75ceecfe.prompt: A fault cuts a sandstone layer and a limestone layer. An undisturbed shale layer lies across the eroded surface of both layers and is not cut by the fault. Which event happened most recently?
t_52ad75ceecfe.explanation: The fault cuts the sandstone and limestone, so both layers predate fault movement. Erosion then exposed their surface, and the shale was deposited across it. Deposition of the sandstone and deposition of the limestone both occurred before the fault. Movement along the fault occurred before erosion and shale deposition.

t_1db879684aab.prompt: A fragment enclosed in a conglomerate is older than the conglomerate that contains it.
t_1db879684aab.explanation: The fragment had to exist before it was incorporated into the conglomerate. This is the principle of inclusions.

t_3d8e52602958.prompt: A hypothetical zircon contains uranium-235 and radiogenic lead-207 in a parent-to-daughter ratio of 1 : 7. Assume all the lead-207 counted came from decay and no parent or daughter atoms entered or escaped after crystallization. Using a half-life of 704 million years, calculate the zircon’s age in millions of years.
t_3d8e52602958.explanation: A parent-to-daughter ratio of 1 : 7 means one-eighth of the original parent remains. Three half-lives have passed, so the age is 3 × 704 = 2,112 million years.

t_3742b100aec6.prompt: A hypothetical fossil-bearing mudstone lies above a volcanic ash bed dated at 980 million years and is cut by a felsic dike dated at 750 million years. Zircon in each igneous rock crystallized when that rock formed. Give the mudstone’s age range and explain how both relationships constrain it.
t_3742b100aec6.answer: The mudstone is between 980 million and 750 million years old. It is younger than the ash bed beneath it and older than the dike that cuts it.
t_3742b100aec6.explanation: Superposition places the mudstone after the ash deposit. Cross-cutting relationships place it before the dike intrusion. The two numeric ages therefore bracket the mudstone’s deposition.

t_321b86f8ee94.prompt: A hypothetical volcanic rock crystallized 1.8 billion years ago. In which eon did it form?
t_321b86f8ee94.explanation: The Proterozoic spans about 2.5 billion to 541 million years ago, which includes 1.8 billion years ago. Hadean and Archean are earlier eons; Phanerozoic began later, about 541 million years ago.

t_513c4d93097e.title: Lab reports: Geologic time and how rocks are dated
t_513c4d93097e.prompt: Use your pair’s lab observations to prepare your own report. Show how your evidence supports your conclusions. Lab reports count for 30% of the course grade. Complete this report independently; it is scored individually using the rubric below. It is due at the start of the lab of Earthquakes.
steps: Choose two samples your pair examined in the lab. For each, describe the visible features and state the relative order of the features or events. Explain which relationship and dating principle support your order. If you used evidence of way-up, describe that evidence and explain why the position of the sample in its tray cannot establish way-up.

Use your pair’s coin results to report the parent and cumulative daughter counts for rounds 0 through 6. Plot parent count against round and calculate your observed parent : daughter ratio after round 4. Compare your result with the expected ratio of 1 : 15 after four half-lives, and explain why the results can differ.

Use your pair’s Earth-history strip to compare the span from Earth’s formation to the start of the Phanerozoic with the span of the Phanerozoic itself. Give both spans in millions of years and as measured distances on the strip. Explain what the comparison shows about the proportion of Earth’s history represented by the Phanerozoic.
t_513c4d93097e.answerKey:
1. Answers depend on the samples. A strong report describes two observed features, orders each pair correctly, and connects each order to the relevant principle: cross-cutting, inclusions or superposition with evidence of way-up. A sample’s orientation in its tray does not establish its original orientation. Common mistakes include treating the tray’s bottom as the original bottom or reversing the age of a vein and its host rock.
2. Counts depend on the pair’s trial. At each round, parent plus cumulative daughter should total 64. The plot should have round on the horizontal axis and parent count on the vertical axis. The observed round 4 ratio is the recorded parent count to the cumulative daughter count; the expected ratio is 1 : 15. Random variation affects the outcome of a small coin sample. Common mistakes include using only the coins removed in round 4 as the daughter count or claiming every trial must match the expected ratio exactly.
3. The span from Earth’s formation to the start of the Phanerozoic is 4,540 − 541 = 3,999 million years, represented by 3,999 mm. The Phanerozoic spans 541 million years, represented by 541 mm. It occupies 541 ÷ 4,540, or about 12% of the modeled history. Common mistakes include measuring both spans from the present without subtracting, or treating the Phanerozoic as most of Earth’s history.

t_2bbdf568b6e6.title: Weekly online quizzes: Geologic time and how rocks are dated
t_2bbdf568b6e6.prompt: Complete your own work and submit it online before the first meeting of Earthquakes. Weekly online quizzes are worth 10% of the course grade. Choose one answer for each question. Each correct answer earns 1 point, for a total of 4 points.
steps: Which observation provides evidence that a sequence of sedimentary layers has been overturned? A. The layers contain minerals. B. Graded bedding indicates that the original way-up is toward the bottom of the sequence. C. A dike cuts across the layers. D. The layers contain clasts.

A widespread fossil species existed for a relatively short interval of geologic time. Why is it useful for correlating sedimentary layers? A. It gives the layers an exact age in years. B. It shows that every layer containing it formed in the same environment. C. It reveals the original thickness of an eroded layer. D. Its limited time range helps match layers of similar relative age across distant outcrops.

Suppose a mineral contains a parent isotope and its radiogenic daughter in a ratio of 1 : 15. All daughter atoms counted formed by decay, and no parent or daughter atoms entered or escaped after crystallization. If the parent isotope has a half-life of 200 million years, how long ago did the mineral crystallize? A. 800 million years ago B. 400 million years ago C. 200 million years ago D. 3,000 million years ago

Suppose a volcanic ash bed is interlayered with fossil-bearing sedimentary rocks. What does a radiometric age obtained from zircon that crystallized during the ash-producing eruption most directly date? A. The formation of the fossils’ ancestors B. The formation of every sand grain in the sequence C. The eruption that produced the ash D. The deposition of all sedimentary rocks in the region
t_2bbdf568b6e6.answerKey:
1. B. Graded bedding can preserve evidence of the original way-up; evidence pointing toward the present bottom indicates overturning.
2. D. A widespread species with a short time range helps correlate layers of similar relative age across distance.
3. A. A 1 : 15 ratio means 1/16 of the parent remains, so four half-lives have passed. Four × 200 million years = 800 million years.
4. C. The zircon crystallized during the eruption, so its age dates the ash-producing event.

t_4ae4bb06b752.prompt: What happens when a continent riding on a subducting plate reaches the trench, and why?
followUps: Oceanic crust sinks into the mantle at a trench. What property of continental crust changes the outcome?
If some continental crust is forced beneath the other continent while the plates keep converging, what happens to the crust above it? What folds and faults would you expect there?
How would the crust under the collision zone compare in thickness with normal crust, and what would that do to the height of the surface?

t_548f012085d8.prompt: Marine limestone lies near the summit of Everest, about 8,850 m above sea level, and India is still moving north at roughly 5 cm per year. Will the Himalaya keep rising, or is erosion already winning? Argue from what happens in a collision, not from the height alone.
followUps: At 5 cm per year, how far does India move in one million years, and where does that shortening go in the crust?
The crust under Tibet is about 70 km thick, twice normal. What does thick crust do to the height of the surface, and what should happen to that height once the plates stop converging?
The Appalachians are an old, eroded mountain belt. What does their present state suggest about the long-term fate of the Himalaya?

t_eeacd8d9ca51.prompt: A fold in upright sedimentary layers has Ordovician rock at its center, Silurian rock on both sides, and Devonian rock at its outer edges. Ordovician is the oldest and Devonian is the youngest. What is the fold?

choices.text: A syncline, with the oldest rock at its core
An anticline, with the oldest rock at its core
An anticline, with the youngest rock at its core
A syncline, with the youngest rock at its core

t_eeacd8d9ca51.explanation: The oldest rock is at the center, so the fold is an anticline. “A syncline, with the oldest rock at its core” reverses the age pattern of a syncline. “An anticline, with the youngest rock at its core” reverses the age pattern of an anticline. “A syncline, with the youngest rock at its core” describes a syncline, but the center rock here is the oldest.

t_3efd3d7a8905.prompt: Along an inclined fault, the hanging wall has moved down relative to the footwall. Which fault and stress best fit this motion?
t_3efd3d7a8905.explanation: A normal fault typically forms under tension, with the hanging wall moving down. “Reverse fault and compression” would have the hanging wall moving up. “Normal fault and compression” matches the motion but assigns the wrong stress. “Reverse fault and tension” assigns both the wrong fault type and the wrong stress.

t_c1e320fa4181.prompt: On flat ground, a contact crosses a west–east section line. Its strike is north–south and its dip is 35° east. The section uses the same horizontal and vertical scale. How should the contact be drawn below its surface trace?

choices.text: Down toward the east at 35° from horizontal
Down toward the west at 35° from horizontal
Down toward the east at 35° from vertical
Down toward the west at 35° from vertical

t_c1e320fa4181.explanation: The section line is perpendicular to strike, so the contact is drawn in the dip direction at the stated angle from horizontal. “Down toward the west at 35° from horizontal” reverses the dip direction. “Down toward the east at 35° from vertical” measures the angle from the wrong reference. “Down toward the west at 35° from vertical” reverses the direction and uses the wrong reference.

t_57422f874b9b.prompt: A geologic map of upright layers shows the oldest unit in a central strip. Strike-and-dip symbols on both sides show beds dipping away from that strip. A student labels the structure a syncline and draws both limbs dipping toward the center. Identify the fold and explain how the map shows that the label and drawing need to be corrected.
t_57422f874b9b.answer: The fold is an anticline. The oldest unit is at its core, and the beds dip away from the center. The cross section should show limbs dipping away from the fold hinge.
t_57422f874b9b.explanation: Both the age pattern and the dip directions indicate an anticline. A syncline in upright layers has its youngest unit at the core and limbs that dip toward the hinge.

t_def4b1b120f6.prompt: A collision between two continents can produce a high mountain belt as folds and thrust faults shorten and thicken the crust.
t_def4b1b120f6.explanation: Continental crust resists deep subduction because it is buoyant. During collision, shortening folds the crust and thrust faults stack rock slices, thickening the crust and helping raise a mountain belt.

t_60f92f156ae4.title: Midterm exam 2
t_60f92f156ae4.prompt: Time allowed: 42 minutes. This exam covers what has been taught so far and is marked in points. The teacher will announce what you may use. Show your working for calculations and give a reason wherever a question asks for one.
steps: A sedimentary rock contains rounded pebbles larger than 2 mm cemented together. What is the rock called? (1 point)
A layer of shale contains mud cracks. What do these cracks suggest about conditions when the sediment was deposited? Give a reason. (2 points)

A rock contains rounded sand-sized grains cemented together. Which name best fits it? (1 point)
A. Shale
B. Sandstone
C. Conglomerate
D. Slate

Shale is buried during continental collision. It changes in the solid state into a rock with visible, aligned mica flakes. Name a likely metamorphic rock and explain how its foliation formed. (2 points)
A limestone lies beside an igneous intrusion. Heat from the intrusion changes the limestone into marble without melting it. Name the type of metamorphism and the protolith. (2 points)
A granite is exposed at the surface. Describe one possible path by which material from it could become sandstone. Name the processes in order. (3 points)
In an undisturbed sequence, sandstone lies beneath shale, and a basalt dike cuts both layers. List the three rock units from oldest to youngest and explain the evidence for your order. (3 points)

A shale layer lies above an igneous bed dated at 260 million years and below an ash bed dated at 240 million years. Give the range of possible ages for the shale and explain your reasoning. (2 points)

A mineral has a parent-to-radiogenic-daughter isotope ratio of 1:3. Assume no parent or daughter atoms entered or escaped. The parent isotope has a half-life of 400 million years. How old is the mineral? Show your reasoning. (2 points)

Which feature makes a fossil especially useful for matching rock layers across widely separated places? (1 point)
A. It lived in one small region for a long time.
B. It occurs only in igneous rocks.
C. It was widespread and existed for a relatively short time.
D. It belonged to a species that is still living.
Explain how strain can build up on a locked fault and how elastic rebound relates to an earthquake. (2 points)
An earthquake begins 12 km below Earth’s surface. Name the point where rupture begins and the point on the surface directly above it. (2 points)

At one seismic station, P waves arrive at 14:06:10 and S waves arrive at 14:06:46. At another station, P waves arrive at 14:06:18 and S waves arrive at 14:07:10. Calculate each S–P interval and identify which station is farther from the earthquake. Explain your choice. (3 points)

Two towns experience the same earthquake. One reports stronger shaking and more damage than the other. Explain why the earthquake has one magnitude but can have different intensities at the two towns. (2 points)

During strong shaking, water-saturated loose sand temporarily loses strength and a building tilts. What is this process called? (1 point)
A. Elastic rebound
B. Deposition
C. Metamorphism
D. Liquefaction
t_60f92f156ae4.answerKey:
1. Conglomerate. Award 1 point for the name. (1 point)
2. The sediment was exposed to air and dried; shrinking mud formed the cracks. Award 1 point for exposure and drying and 1 point for linking drying or shrinkage to the cracks. (2 points)
3. B. Sandstone. Award 1 point. (1 point)
4. Schist is a likely rock. Differential stress causes platy minerals such as mica to align approximately perpendicular to the greatest stress. Award 1 point for schist and 1 point for the explanation of alignment. (2 points)
5. Contact metamorphism; limestone. Award 1 point for each. (2 points)
6. Weathering breaks down the granite; erosion and transport move the sediment; deposition followed by lithification forms sandstone. Award 1 point for weathering, 1 point for erosion and transport, and 1 point for deposition followed by lithification in the correct order. (3 points)
7. Sandstone, shale, basalt dike. Superposition places the sandstone before the shale; the dike is younger than both because it cuts them. Award 1 point for the correct order, 1 point for superposition, and 1 point for cross-cutting. (3 points)
8. The shale is younger than 260 million years and older than 240 million years. It was deposited after the lower igneous bed and before the overlying ash. Award 1 point for the range and 1 point for the reasoning. (2 points)
9. A 1:3 ratio means one quarter of the parent remains, so two half-lives have passed. Age = 2 × 400 million years = 800 million years. Award 1 point for two half-lives and 1 point for 800 million years. (2 points)
10. C. It was widespread and existed for a relatively short time. Award 1 point. (1 point)
11. Continued motion deforms rock while the fault is locked, storing strain. When the fault ruptures, the rock rebounds as strain is released. Award 1 point for strain accumulation and 1 point for rupture and rebound. (2 points)
12. The focus is where rupture begins; the epicenter is directly above it at the surface. Award 1 point for each. (2 points)
13. The intervals are 36 seconds and 52 seconds, respectively. The second station is farther away because its S–P interval is longer. Award 1 point for each interval and 1 point for the station and explanation. (3 points)
14. Magnitude describes the earthquake’s overall energy release. Intensity describes effects at a particular place, which can vary with factors such as ground conditions, distance and buildings. Award 1 point for magnitude and 1 point for intensity and a source of variation. (2 points)
15. D. Liquefaction. Award 1 point. (1 point)
Total: 29 points

t_0e21041e159e.title: Lab reports: Folds, faults and mountain building
t_0e21041e159e.prompt: Use your pair’s lab observations to prepare your own report. Show how your evidence supports your conclusions. Lab reports count for 30% of the course grade. Complete this report independently; it is scored individually using the rubric below. It is due at the start of the lab of Streams and floods.
steps: Report your pair’s sample identifications and acid-test observations for the three map units. Explain how the grain descriptions and test results supported each identification. If an observation differed from your prediction, state the difference and suggest a possible reason.

Include your cross section A–A′. Report the contact positions and dips, and explain how you transferred the map evidence to the section. Use the unit ages to explain which way the rocks get younger along the surface.

Include your cross section B–B′. Identify the fold and explain how both the ages at the surface and the dip directions support your interpretation. Explain what the dashed contacts above the ground show.

For each section on the fault worksheet, identify the hanging wall, fault type and associated stress. Explain how the position of the blocks supports your identification and why the fault is younger than the layers it cuts.

Use your mountain-belt sample observations to explain how continental collision can produce metamorphic rocks and raise marine limestone to high elevations. Name the samples that support your explanation and connect them to processes during mountain building.
t_0e21041e159e.answerKey:
1. A strong report records the pair’s actual sample numbers and observations: Unit 1 is shale, very fine grained and splitting into thin sheets, with no fizz; Unit 2 is gritty sandstone with cemented sand-sized grains and no fizz; Unit 3 is fine, compact limestone and fizzes. Look for evidence linking observations to names and an explanation of any difference from the prediction. Usual mistakes include treating fizz alone as evidence of grain size or changing recorded observations to fit the expected results.
2. The Unit 3–Unit 2 contact is 1.5 km from A and the Unit 2–Unit 1 contact is 3.5 km from A; both dip 30° east. A strong section uses equal horizontal and vertical scales, marks the contacts on the ground line, extends them downward to the east, and labels the units and endpoints. Rocks get younger eastward along the surface: Ordovician Unit 3, Silurian Unit 2, then Devonian Unit 1. Usual mistakes are drawing the dip westward or using unequal scales.
3. The section is an anticline: Ordovician Unit 3 is oldest and occupies the center, and beds dip away from the center on both sides. Dashed contacts show an inferred continuation above the present ground surface, not exposed rock. Look for labeled endpoints, units and fold, with equal scales. A usual mistake is drawing the limbs dipping toward the center.
4. Section one has the east block as hanging wall and is a normal fault associated with tension; its layers lie lower than their counterparts on the west. Section two has the west block as hanging wall and is a reverse thrust fault associated with compression; older Layer C of the west block lies over younger Layer A of the east block. Each fault is younger than the layers it cuts. A usual mistake is choosing the hanging wall from apparent movement instead of its position above the inclined fault plane.
5. A strong explanation uses the pair’s observations of slate, schist, gneiss, marble and fossil-bearing limestone. Collision shortens and thickens crust; heat and pressure at depth can cause regional metamorphism, while uplift and erosion expose rocks and can raise marine limestone to high elevations. The marine limestone near Everest’s summit is an example. Usual mistakes include calling the fossil-bearing limestone metamorphic or claiming that metamorphism requires melting.

t_5bfbd3f36a27.title: Weekly online quizzes: Folds, faults and mountain building
t_5bfbd3f36a27.prompt: Complete your own work and submit it online before the first meeting of Streams and floods. Weekly online quizzes are worth 10% of the course grade. Choose one answer for each question. Each correct answer earns 1 point, for a total of 4 points.
steps: In an upright sequence of folded sedimentary layers, the youngest rocks lie at the center and the limbs dip toward the center. What is the structure? A. Syncline B. Anticline C. Normal fault D. Thrust fault

A fault cuts a sandstone layer and the shale layer above it. How old is the fault compared with the two layers? A. Older than both layers B. Younger than both layers C. Older than the sandstone but younger than the shale D. The same age as the sandstone

On flat ground, a contact crosses a section line drawn perpendicular to its strike, and it dips 45°. With the same horizontal and vertical scale, how far from its surface trace, measured horizontally, does the contact lie at 1 km depth? A. 0.5 km B. 0.7 km C. 1 km D. 2 km

Marine limestone lies near the summit of Everest. What best explains how it got there? A. Sea level was once about 8,850 m higher than today. B. It formed from volcanic ash erupted at the summit. C. Glaciers carried it up the mountain. D. Continental collision lifted sea-floor sediments as the crust shortened and thickened.
t_5bfbd3f36a27.answerKey:
1. A. A syncline has the youngest upright layers at its core, with limbs dipping toward the hinge.
2. B. A fault is younger than the rocks it cuts (cross-cutting relationships).
3. C. Horizontal distance = depth ÷ tan 45° = 1 km ÷ 1 = 1 km.
4. D. Collision folds, faults and thickens the crust, lifting sea-floor sediments high above sea level.

t_b60c4686fa60.prompt: Suppose a small town sits on the floodplain of a meandering river. Bought-out land would be cleared and left open to flood. Which option would you choose, raising the levee or buying out the lowest homes, and why?
followUps: Who pays for each option, and who carries the risk if it fails?
If a levee confines the river to its channel, what happens to the flood water farther downstream?
What will the cleared land do the next time the river overtops its banks?

t_ed2c9bc9fd88.prompt: Suppose a town on a river had a 100-year flood last spring. A resident says, “We have had our flood, so we are safe for the next 99 years.” Do you agree or disagree?
followUps: If each year has a 1% chance of a flood this size, does last year’s flood change the chance for next year?
Recurrence intervals are estimated from gauge records. How much should we trust an estimate from a short record?
If the land upstream has since been paved, would you still trust the old recurrence interval? Why or why not?

t_6c0fad0dc155.prompt: A hypothetical stream is 10 m wide, has an average depth of 1.2 m, and has a mean velocity of 0.8 m/s. Using Q = width × average depth × mean velocity, calculate its discharge in m³/s.
t_6c0fad0dc155.explanation: Multiply 10 m × 1.2 m × 0.8 m/s. The discharge is 9.6 m³/s.

t_dcfb175f6c90.prompt: In a meandering stream, where would you expect a cut bank and a point bar to form?

choices.text: Cut bank on the outside of a bend; point bar on the inside
Cut bank on the inside of a bend; point bar on the outside
Cut bank and point bar both on the outside of a bend
Cut bank and point bar both on the inside of a bend

t_dcfb175f6c90.explanation: Faster flow erodes the outside bank, while sediment accumulates on the inside. “Cut bank on the inside of a bend; point bar on the outside” reverses erosion and deposition. “Cut bank and point bar both on the outside of a bend” places the deposit on the eroding bank. “Cut bank and point bar both on the inside of a bend” places the eroding bank on the depositional side.

t_a27d78d96b00.prompt: A floodplain beside a meandering river forms only when silt and clay settle from floodwater; migrating point bars do not contribute to it.
t_a27d78d96b00.explanation: Floodplains grow both as point bars migrate sideways and as silt and clay settle from water that overflows the channel.

t_35a32401774c.prompt: In a stream table, water rises over the banks of a curved channel. Which change is most likely during the flood?

choices.text: The inner banks erode and sediment collects on the outer banks.
The outer banks erode and sediment spreads onto the floodplain.
Both banks gain sediment and the channel becomes narrower.
The outer banks remain fixed and all sediment leaves the table.

t_35a32401774c.explanation: Floodwater can erode banks, especially at bends, and deposit sediment beyond the channel. “The inner banks erode and sediment collects on the outer banks” reverses the usual pattern at a bend. “Both banks gain sediment and the channel becomes narrower” overlooks flood erosion. “The outer banks remain fixed and all sediment leaves the table” overlooks bank erosion and floodplain deposition.

t_39f262a532b6.prompt: In a hypothetical stream-table flood, a pair measures discharge from timed outflow before and during overbank flow. A student concludes that the flood could not change the channel because the channel was already curved. Explain the mistake and predict two changes the pair might observe.
t_39f262a532b6.answer: A curved channel can still erode and change during a flood. The pair might observe widening from erosion of the outer banks and sediment deposited on the floodplain.
t_39f262a532b6.explanation: High flow can erode the banks of an existing bend, causing the channel to widen or shift. Water spilling onto the floodplain can slow and deposit sediment there. These are predictions to compare with the pair’s observations.

t_015a4808660d.title: Lab reports: Streams and floods
t_015a4808660d.prompt: Use your pair’s stream table measurements and hand sample observations to prepare your own report. Show how your evidence supports your conclusions. Lab reports count for 30% of the course grade. Complete this report independently; it is scored individually using the rubric below. It is due at the start of the lab of Groundwater.
steps: Report the width, four depths, mean depth and cross-sectional area at each straight-channel station. Show how you calculated the average area, each float speed, the average surface speed and discharge from the measurements. Calculate discharge from the timed outflow, compare the two estimates and explain a likely source of any difference.

Use your meander sketches to describe how the channel changed during the steady-flow run. Compare the observed bank erosion and deposits with your predictions. Identify any cut banks and point bars you observed; if no point bar formed, state that and describe any deposition you saw.

Report the low-flow and flood-flow discharges, show how you calculated how many times larger the flood discharge was, and compare channel widths at the three stations before and after the flood. Use your sketch and observations to explain how the banks and sediment deposits changed, and compare the results with your predictions. Identify one limit of using the stream table to represent a real river.

Report the grain size and rounding you observed in each hand sample. Explain which river setting could have deposited each material and how the observations support your choices. Explain how abrasion rounds pebbles and why rounding alone does not establish transport distance.
t_015a4808660d.answerKey:
1. Look for the pair’s actual widths and four depths at each station. Mean depth is the sum of the four depths divided by four; station area is width × mean depth. Average area is the sum of the three areas divided by three. Each float speed is 50 cm divided by its measured time; average the three speeds, then multiply by average area for the surface-speed discharge estimate in cm³/s. Timed outflow is the volume in mL divided by 30 s, with 1 mL = 1 cm³. A strong comparison gives the difference and explains that surface speed can exceed mean velocity; irregular cross sections and measurement uncertainty can also affect agreement. Common mistakes include using maximum depth, averaging times instead of the three speeds, and mixing units.
2. Look for a comparison grounded in the student’s start, middle and end sketches, including observed erosion and deposition. Cut banks are associated with outer-bend erosion and point bars with inner-bend deposition. If no point bar formed, a strong report says so and describes the deposits actually observed. Common mistakes include reversing the two features or claiming a bar formed without observation.
3. Low-flow discharge is the measured low-flow volume divided by 15 s. Flood discharge is its measured volume divided by the recorded collection time; the ratio is flood discharge divided by low-flow discharge. Look for all three before-and-after width comparisons, observed bank and deposit changes, and a comparison with the prediction. Results may differ from expectations and should be reported as observed. The table shows the direction of possible changes but does not reproduce real river scale. Common mistakes include comparing volumes without accounting for collection time and treating predicted erosion or deposition as an observed result.
4. Look for the actual grain size and rounding observed in each sample. Conglomerate with rounded pebbles can indicate a high-energy channel; sandstone can represent channel or point-bar sand; shale can represent floodplain or oxbow-lake mud. Students should connect their choices to their sample observations and recognize that a rock type can have more than one possible setting. Abrasion removes material from pebble edges through impacts and friction; rounding alone cannot establish transport distance because other factors, including rock durability and transport conditions, also matter. Common mistakes include assigning a unique setting from rock name alone or inferring distance from rounding alone.

t_14d1e621cbe8.title: Weekly online quizzes: Streams and floods
t_14d1e621cbe8.prompt: Complete your own work and submit it online before the first meeting of Groundwater. Weekly online quizzes are worth 10% of the course grade. Choose one answer for each question. Each correct answer earns 1 point, for a total of 4 points.
steps: A ridge separates land draining into two neighboring streams. What is the ridge called? A. A drainage divide B. A point bar C. A floodplain D. A stream mouth
Which material is transported as dissolved load in a stream? A. Gravel rolling along the bed B. Silt held up by turbulence C. Sand hopping along the bed D. Calcium and bicarbonate ions in the water

Assume that a flood has a 1% chance of occurring in each year, with independent years and a constant annual probability. Which expression gives the chance of at least one such flood in 20 years? A. 0.01²⁰ B. 1 − 0.99²⁰ C. 0.99²⁰ D. 1 − 0.01²⁰

A town buys homes on frequently flooded land, clears the buildings and leaves the land open. What is one likely benefit during a future flood? A. The river can no longer overtop its banks. B. Flood discharge stops increasing. C. Fewer homes are exposed, and the land can store floodwater. D. The river can no longer carry sediment.
t_14d1e621cbe8.answerKey:
1. A. A drainage divide separates neighboring drainage basins.
2. D. Calcium and bicarbonate travel as dissolved ions.
3. B. The probability of no such flood in 20 years is 0.99²⁰, so the probability of at least one is 1 − 0.99²⁰.
4. C. Removing homes reduces exposure, and the open floodplain can store floodwater.

t_4414e40e4477.prompt: Glacier ice, window glass, and a crystal of quartz from a granite: which of these are minerals and which are not? Choose one item where you and your partner differ, and give your reason.
followUps: Ice melts at 0 °C. Should that decide whether it counts as a mineral, or should we judge it under the conditions where it occurs?
What does window glass lack that a quartz crystal has, and does it fail more than one criterion?
Which of the five criteria did you use most often, and which did you find hardest to apply?

t_a50a963af288.prompt: Obsidian and quartz are both made mostly of SiO₂. If the chemistry is so similar, why should geologists call quartz a mineral but not obsidian? Argue for or against the line the definition draws.
followUps: What is different about how the atoms are arranged in the two materials?
How would that difference show up when you break a sample or look at it closely in the lab?
Is a definition that excludes obsidian useful to a geologist, or would you rather widen it? What would you lose?

t_9c4076f427a8.prompt: A naturally formed crystal of sulfur is inorganic, solid and has an ordered atomic structure and a definite composition. Which conclusion follows?

choices.text: It is not a mineral because it contains only one element.
It is not a mineral because it contains no silicon.
It is a mineral because every natural solid qualifies.
It is a mineral because it meets all five criteria.

t_9c4076f427a8.explanation: The sulfur crystal meets all five criteria. “It is not a mineral because it contains only one element” mistakes an element for a disqualifying feature; “It is not a mineral because it contains no silicon” treats silicon as required; “It is a mineral because every natural solid qualifies” overlooks the other criteria.

t_1a1d4b6c56ac.prompt: A naturally formed substance is a mineral if it has a definite chemical composition, even when its atoms have no repeating, ordered arrangement.
t_1a1d4b6c56ac.explanation: A mineral must have both a definite chemical composition and a crystalline structure. Meeting the composition criterion does not replace the requirement for an ordered atomic arrangement.

t_a877fe18147d.prompt: Two translucent minerals look alike. Sample A has hardness 3 and three cleavage directions that do not meet at right angles. Sample B has hardness 2.5 and three cleavage directions that meet at right angles. An unknown is scratched by a copper coin and has three cleavage directions at right angles. Which identification is best supported?

choices.text: Sample B, because its cleavage angles match.
Sample A, because its hardness is close.
Sample A, because it has three cleavages.
Sample B, because its color is translucent.

t_a877fe18147d.explanation: Both samples are soft enough to be scratched by the coin, but the right-angle cleavages distinguish sample B. “Sample A, because its hardness is close” relies on a test that does not distinguish the samples; “Sample A, because it has three cleavages” overlooks their angles; “Sample B, because its color is translucent” relies on a feature both share.

t_e97b6b83cd40.prompt: A student says, “A dark mineral with two cleavage directions meeting at about 90° must have a double-chain silicate structure.” Identify the mistake and explain the better interpretation.
t_e97b6b83cd40.answer: The cleavage angles point to a single-chain structure, such as pyroxene. Double-chain amphibole has cleavage angles of about 56° and 124°.
t_e97b6b83cd40.explanation: Pyroxene has two cleavages near 90°, while amphibole has two at about 56° and 124°. The student has reversed the structures associated with these cleavage angles.

t_8c04f02ababd.prompt: In a sheet silicate, each tetrahedron shares three of its four oxygen atoms with neighboring tetrahedra. Which description best explains why mica splits readily in one direction?

choices.text: Bonds between sheets are stronger than bonds within sheets.
Each tetrahedron is separate from every neighboring tetrahedron.
Bonds within sheets are stronger than bonds between sheets.
Each oxygen is shared equally in all directions.

t_8c04f02ababd.explanation: Mica splits parallel to its sheets because bonds between them are weaker. “Bonds between sheets are stronger than bonds within sheets” reverses the relationship; “Each tetrahedron is separate from every neighboring tetrahedron” describes isolated units rather than sheets; “Each oxygen is shared equally in all directions” describes a framework rather than a sheet.

t_f76b0160c40b.title: Lab reports: Minerals
t_f76b0160c40b.prompt: Use your lab observations and the evidence discussed in class to prepare your own report. Explain how your evidence supports your conclusions. Lab reports count for 30% of the course grade. This report is due at the start of the lab of Igneous rocks and volcanoes. It is scored using the rubric below. Complete your own work; it will be scored alone.
steps: Choose two unknown samples from your lab observations. For each, report its original name and the properties you observed or tested. Explain how at least two properties support each identification. Note any property you did not test and any correction you recorded after comparing with the key.

Choose one of your unknowns and explain how you would distinguish it from another mineral in the Mineral properties reference table that shares at least one of its properties. Identify a useful observation or test, predict the result for each mineral, and explain why the result would help distinguish them.

Explain how the five criteria for a mineral apply to a naturally formed specimen of halite. Then describe one observation or test from the lab that helps identify halite and explain why that test alone cannot establish all five criteria.
t_f76b0160c40b.answerKey:
1. Look for two actual unknowns, their original names, observed or tested properties, at least two relevant properties supporting each identification, untested properties and any recorded corrections. Results depend on the samples. Common mistakes include treating color alone as proof, presenting an untested property as an observation, or changing an original identification without noting a recorded correction.
2. Look for a mineral in the reference table that shares a property with the chosen unknown, a test or observation that distinguishes them, and accurate predictions for both. For example, galena and halite both have three cleavage directions at 90°, but galena has metallic luster and halite has vitreous luster. Common mistakes include choosing a property that overlaps for both minerals or claiming a test result that the reference table does not support.
3. Naturally formed halite is naturally occurring, inorganic, solid, crystalline and has a definite chemical composition, NaCl. A useful observation is its three cleavage directions at 90°. Cleavage supports identification but does not by itself establish natural occurrence, inorganic character, solid state, crystal structure and composition. Common mistakes include treating cleavage as proof of every criterion or omitting one criterion.

t_b8529b3e3bfc.title: Weekly online quizzes: Minerals
t_b8529b3e3bfc.prompt: Complete your own work and submit it online before the first meeting of Igneous rocks and volcanoes. Weekly online quizzes are worth 10% of the course grade. Choose one answer for each question. Each correct answer earns 1 point, for a total of 4 points.
steps: An oxygen atom has 8 protons and 8 electrons. It gains 2 electrons. What ion does it form? A. O²⁺, with 8 protons and 6 electrons B. O²⁻, with 8 protons and 10 electrons C. O²⁻, with 10 protons and 8 electrons D. O²⁺, with 10 protons and 8 electrons

In a single chain of silicate tetrahedra, each tetrahedron shares two oxygen atoms with neighboring tetrahedra. Counting each shared oxygen as half for each tetrahedron, what is the silicon-to-oxygen ratio? A. 1:2 B. 1:2.5 C. 1:3 D. 1:4
An unknown mineral scratches gypsum but is scratched by calcite. What is its hardness range on the Mohs scale? A. Between 2 and 3 B. Between 3 and 4 C. Between 4 and 5 D. Between 1 and 2

A student rubs a mineral on an unglazed porcelain streak plate. Which observation is the mineral’s streak? A. The color of light reflected from a fresh face B. The shape of a cleavage fragment C. The depth of a scratch on glass D. The color of the mineral’s powder
t_b8529b3e3bfc.answerKey:
1. B. Gaining two electrons leaves 8 protons and 10 electrons, giving a charge of 2−.
2. C. Two unshared oxygens plus two shared halves give three oxygens per silicon, a ratio of 1:3.
3. A. Gypsum has hardness 2 and calcite has hardness 3, so the unknown lies between them.
4. D. Streak is the color of the mineral’s powder.

t_ba881dd5fe85.prompt: In your own words, how does a limestone made of shell fragments differ from rock salt, and which test shows calcite?
followUps: Rock salt and limestone both come from dissolved ions leaving water. What is different about how the ions leave?
A rock fizzes in dilute HCl. Does that prove it is biochemical, or only that it contains calcite? What would you look for in the rock to decide?
Chert does not fizz. What second test, using a steel nail, would separate it from limestone, and what result would you expect for each?

t_2a9dbc9f07d7.prompt: A well-rounded, well-sorted quartz arenite sits beside a breccia with sharp-cornered clasts. A classmate says the sand grains must have traveled much farther than the breccia clasts. Do you agree?
followUps: Rounded, well-sorted grains show substantial abrasion and sorting. Is distance the only way to get that?
Could a beach or a desert dune produce rounded sand grains without a long journey from the source? What evidence in the rock would support that?
What would you need to see in the field, such as structures, fossils or other layers, before you committed to a transport distance?

t_eeeb5b1ab1a8.prompt: Which hazards can people escape? Look at the three records: Nevado del Ruiz in 1985, Mount St. Helens in 1980 and Mount Pinatubo in 1991. For each one, what response does the record support, and what question does it leave open? These deaths are real, so argue from decisions and evidence. Then agree with your partner on what these records can and cannot settle.
followUps: Which of the three records gives the strongest support for its response, and what in the record makes it strong?
At Mount St. Helens, closed zones reduced exposure, yet the blast passed their edge. What does that tell you about how a zone should be drawn?
Suppose the same response were proposed for a different volcano. What would you need to know about travel time, warning, rain or wind before you accepted it?

t_735b3e8bd3f6.prompt: Mauna Loa erupts runny basaltic lava, and Mount St. Helens erupts sticky magma that holds its gas. A neighbor says, “Living beside a shield volcano is basically safe.” Do you agree? Take a side and defend it with the magma’s silica, viscosity and gas, and with the hazard that results.
followUps: If lava flows are slow enough to walk away from, what exactly is still at risk, and who bears that risk?
Does a hazard that is rare but possible, such as an explosive Hawaiian eruption, change your answer? How much should rarity count?
What measurement or observation about a volcano would make you change your mind about how safe it is?

t_3749daefc37b.prompt: A rock has visible crystals several millimeters across and contains quartz and K-feldspar. Which name and silica class best fit it?
t_3749daefc37b.explanation: Visible crystals indicate a phaneritic texture, and quartz and K-feldspar indicate felsic composition, so the rock is granite. Rhyolite; felsic has the right composition but is typically aphanitic. Gabbro; mafic has the right texture but the wrong composition. Basalt; mafic has both the wrong texture and the wrong composition.

t_dae4cd80cb00.prompt: A volcanic rock with large crystals surrounded by a fine-grained groundmass can record an initial period of slow cooling followed by faster cooling.
t_dae4cd80cb00.explanation: The large crystals could grow during slow cooling at depth. The fine groundmass could form when the remaining melt cools faster after eruption.

t_865a35f13f37.prompt: A magma cools and crystallizes calcium-rich plagioclase and pyroxene. Which interpretation best fits Bowen’s reaction series?

choices.text: These minerals form relatively late at low temperatures.
These minerals must crystallize after quartz forms.
These minerals form relatively early at high temperatures.
These minerals cannot occur together in one rock.

t_865a35f13f37.explanation: Calcium-rich plagioclase and pyroxene crystallize relatively early in Bowen’s reaction series. These minerals form relatively late at low temperatures reverses their position in the series. These minerals must crystallize after quartz forms reverses the usual sequence. These minerals cannot occur together in one rock overlooks their overlapping crystallization ranges.

t_0104f71b0bd3.prompt: Which description best matches a typical shield volcano?

choices.text: Steep slopes built mainly by low-viscosity mafic lava
Broad slopes built mainly by low-viscosity mafic lava
Broad slopes built mainly by high-viscosity felsic lava
Steep slopes built mainly by high-viscosity felsic lava

t_0104f71b0bd3.explanation: Fluid mafic lava can spread widely and build a broad shield. Steep slopes built mainly by low-viscosity mafic lava pairs fluid lava with the wrong typical profile. Broad slopes built mainly by high-viscosity felsic lava pairs a shield profile with the wrong typical magma. Steep slopes built mainly by high-viscosity felsic lava better fits a stratovolcano.

t_99189b18b099.prompt: A hypothetical volcano above a subduction zone erupts intermediate magma. After an explosive eruption, heavy rain begins falling on loose ash on its slopes. A student says that only the area immediately beside the vent needs attention because lava is the sole hazard. Identify two problems with that claim and explain a response the evidence supports.
t_99189b18b099.answer: An explosive eruption can produce ash fall and fast pyroclastic flows, so lava is not the sole hazard. Rain can also mobilize loose ash into lahars that travel down valleys beyond the vent. The evidence supports warning and moving people away from threatened slopes and valleys.
t_99189b18b099.explanation: Intermediate magma at a stratovolcano can erupt explosively. Loose volcanic material mixed with heavy rain can form lahars that follow valleys, so hazard planning must consider areas beyond the vent. The evidence does not specify exact travel times or safe routes.

t_9357e6da42a9.title: Lab reports: Igneous rocks and volcanoes
t_9357e6da42a9.prompt: Use your lab observations and the evidence discussed in class to prepare your own report. Explain how your evidence supports your conclusions. Lab reports count for 30% of the course grade. This report is due at the start of the lab of Weathering, erosion and soils. It is scored using the rubric below. Complete your own work; it will be scored alone.
steps: Use your texture station record to compare two reference rocks with different textures. Report the texture and observed grain size, vesicles or glass for each. Explain what those observations suggest about how each rock cooled or formed.

Use your composition and reaction series record to compare granite and gabbro. Report the minerals you observed and your estimates of dark mineral percentages. Place the observed minerals on Bowen’s reaction series and explain how the observations support the rocks’ different compositions.

Choose one rock from your lab observations and propose a tectonic setting where it could form. Explain a melting mechanism that could produce its magma and how the rock’s texture supports a cooling history. Identify one limitation of the evidence available from the hand sample.
t_9357e6da42a9.answerKey:
1. Look for two actual reference samples with different textures, supported by recorded observations. For example, visible crystals in gabbro support slow cooling at depth; glass in obsidian supports very rapid cooling. Accept other supported pairs. Common mistakes include treating dark color as proof of large crystals or interpreting vesicles as crystals.
2. Look for the student’s observed minerals and dark-mineral estimates, with granite minerals such as quartz and K-feldspar placed late and gabbro minerals such as pyroxene and calcium-rich plagioclase placed earlier. Estimates may differ among samples. The explanation should connect the observations to felsic and mafic composition. Common mistakes include assuming every mineral forms in every magma or placing quartz at the high-temperature end.
3. Accept a plausible setting, melting mechanism and cooling history supported by the chosen sample. For example, gabbro can form beneath a mid-ocean ridge where decompression melting produces magma that cools slowly at depth. A limitation is that a hand sample alone may not establish its unique tectonic setting; fine-grained rocks may also require microscopy or chemical analysis for firm classification. Common mistakes include inferring a unique setting from texture alone or equating melting with heating in every setting.

t_58c12830eea3.title: Weekly online quizzes: Igneous rocks and volcanoes
t_58c12830eea3.prompt: Complete your own work and submit it online before the first meeting of Weathering, erosion and soils. Weekly online quizzes are worth 10% of the course grade. Choose one answer for each question. Each correct answer earns 1 point, for a total of 4 points.
steps: At a mid-ocean ridge, hot mantle rises as plates move apart. Which change can cause some of the mantle rock to melt? A. A decrease in pressure B. A decrease in silica content C. An increase in pressure D. The crystallization of quartz
A magma contains 64% SiO₂. Which silica class does it belong to? A. Ultramafic B. Mafic C. Felsic D. Intermediate
A volcanic rock is dark and fine-grained, with approximately 50% SiO₂. Which intrusive rock has a similar composition? A. Granite B. Gabbro C. Diorite D. Rhyolite

A hypothetical eruption produces a fast-moving, hot mixture of gas, ash and rock fragments that travels down a volcano’s flank. What is this hazard called? A. Ash fall B. A lava flow C. A lahar D. A pyroclastic flow
t_58c12830eea3.answerKey:
1. A. As hot mantle rises, pressure decreases, allowing partial melting by decompression.
2. C. Felsic magma contains more than 63% SiO₂.
3. B. Gabbro is the coarse-grained intrusive counterpart of mafic basalt.
4. D. A pyroclastic flow is a fast-moving, hot mixture of gas, ash and rock fragments.

t_b7b474ab1fef.prompt: A clastic rock contains sand-sized grains composed mostly of feldspar and quartz. Which name best fits it?
