t_b7b474ab1fef.explanation: Arkose is a feldspar-rich sandstone. Quartz arenite is composed mostly of quartz; conglomerate contains rounded gravel-sized clasts; mudstone is made mainly of silt and clay.

t_d22bbc6cd388.prompt: A rock contains visible shell fragments cemented together and fizzes in dilute HCl. Which classification best fits the evidence?
t_d22bbc6cd388.explanation: Shell fragments indicate a biochemical origin, and the fizz supports identification as calcite-rich limestone. Chemical rock salt forms from dissolved minerals; clastic sandstone consists of sand-sized fragments; biochemical chert is silica-rich and does not fizz.

t_06e74fd49f62.prompt: Angular gravel-sized fragments in a rock indicate limited abrasion, but they do not establish how far the fragments traveled.
t_06e74fd49f62.explanation: Angular fragments have undergone limited abrasion. Rounding and angularity alone cannot establish transport distance because transport conditions and repeated reworking also affect abrasion.

t_13d827bd566c.prompt: A bed of fine sedimentary rock contains mud cracks and asymmetric ripple marks. Which interpretation best accounts for both features?

choices.text: A deep-sea floor with persistent underwater currents
A tidal flat with currents and periods of exposure
A desert dune with wind-blown sand and no surface water
A lake floor with waves and continuous submergence

t_13d827bd566c.explanation: Asymmetric ripples indicate a current, and mud cracks indicate exposure and drying; both can occur on a tidal flat. A deep-sea floor remains submerged; a desert dune does not account well for the muddy bed and its cracks; a continuously submerged lake floor cannot explain drying cracks.

t_32e0075efc6d.prompt: A field note says: “This limestone contains brachiopod fossils, so it must have formed in a warm, shallow sea.” Identify the overstatement and give an interpretation supported by the fossils.
t_32e0075efc6d.answer: Brachiopod fossils support a marine interpretation, but they do not by themselves establish warm, shallow water. The interpretation is stronger if the brachiopods lived where they were buried rather than being transported there.
t_32e0075efc6d.explanation: Brachiopods indicate marine water, but their presence alone does not establish temperature or water depth. Transported fossils may also record a different place from the one where they originally lived.

t_b56e2eef16a2.title: Midterm exam 1
t_b56e2eef16a2.prompt: Time allowed: 43 minutes. This exam covers what has been taught so far. The teacher will announce what you may use. Answer every question. Show your calculations and give reasons where requested. The point value for each question is shown.
steps: A rock contains an igneous dike that cuts across several sedimentary layers. Which is older, the dike or the layers? Explain how you can tell. (2 points)
A material occurs naturally as solid crystals of an inorganic substance with a definite chemical composition. Does it meet the definition of a mineral? Explain using the criteria. (2 points)

A mineral scratches glass but does not split along flat planes. Which properties have been observed? Choose one answer. (1 point)
A. Streak and color
B. Hardness and lack of cleavage
C. Luster and streak
D. Cleavage and color
Explain why color alone is unreliable for identifying a mineral. Name one other property that could help distinguish minerals. (2 points)

A magma rises beneath a spreading ridge. The surrounding pressure falls, but no water is added and no external heat is supplied. Name the melting mechanism and explain why melting can occur. (2 points)

An igneous rock has visible crystals and a mafic composition. Choose the best name and explain what its texture indicates about cooling. (2 points)
A. Rhyolite
B. Basalt
C. Gabbro
D. Granite

A magma crystallizes as it cools. According to Bowen’s reaction series, which generally crystallizes at a higher temperature: olivine or quartz? What does this imply about how commonly they occur together in one igneous rock? (2 points)
A volcano erupts a gas-rich, viscous magma. Explain why this magma can produce an explosive eruption, and name one hazard such an eruption can generate. (2 points)
Water freezes in a crack and forces it wider. Is this physical or chemical weathering? Explain your choice. (2 points)

A cube of rock has sides 2 cm long. Its surface area is 6 × side². It is cut into eight cubes, each with sides 1 cm long. Calculate the total surface area before and after cutting, and explain how the change can affect chemical weathering. (3 points)
A soil profile has a dark surface layer rich in organic matter above a lighter leached layer. Name the surface mineral-soil horizon and the leached horizon. (2 points)

Two comparable granite surfaces have been exposed for similar periods. One is in a warm, wet climate; the other is in a dry climate. Which would generally undergo more chemical weathering? Give a reason. (2 points)

A mass of loose rock moves downhill primarily under gravity. What general process is this? Choose one answer. (1 point)
A. Mass wasting
B. Hydrolysis
C. Cementation
D. Crystallization
A sand deposit contains grains of many sizes mixed together. Describe its sorting. Can grain shape alone establish how far its grains traveled? Explain briefly. (2 points)
t_b56e2eef16a2.answerKey:
1. The sedimentary layers are older (1 point). The dike cuts across them and therefore formed after them (1 point). Naming the principle of cross-cutting relationships is not required; it is taught later, with geologic time. (2 points)
2. Yes (1 point). It is naturally occurring, inorganic, solid, crystalline, and has a definite chemical composition (1 point). (2 points)
3. B. Hardness and lack of cleavage (1 point). (1 point)
4. The same mineral can occur in several colors (1 point). One useful property is hardness, cleavage, luster, or streak (1 point). (2 points)
5. Decompression melting (1 point). The pressure decrease allows some mantle rock to melt as it rises (1 point). (2 points)
6. C. Gabbro (1 point). Its visible crystals indicate relatively slow cooling at depth (1 point). (2 points)
7. Olivine crystallizes at a higher temperature (1 point). Olivine and quartz rarely occur together in one igneous rock (1 point). (2 points)
8. High viscosity impedes gas escape, allowing pressure to build (1 point). A possible hazard is ash fall, a pyroclastic flow, a lahar, or volcanic gas (1 point). (2 points)
9. Physical weathering (1 point). The rock is broken apart without changing its minerals (1 point). (2 points)
10. Before cutting: 6 × 2² = 24 cm² (1 point). After cutting: 8 × 6 × 1² = 48 cm² (1 point). The increased exposed surface gives water and other reactants more area on which to act, potentially speeding chemical weathering (1 point). (3 points)
11. The dark surface mineral-soil layer is the A horizon (1 point). The leached layer is the E horizon (1 point). (2 points)
12. The granite in the warm, wet climate (1 point). Water supports chemical reactions, and warmer conditions generally increase reaction rates (1 point). (2 points)
13. A. Mass wasting (1 point). (1 point)
14. The deposit is poorly sorted (1 point). Grain shape alone cannot establish transport distance because rounding can result from abrasion or repeated reworking (1 point). (2 points)
Total: 27 points

t_c1ee4bc7a1e7.title: Lab reports: Sedimentary rocks
t_c1ee4bc7a1e7.prompt: Use your pair’s lab observations to prepare your own report. Show how your evidence supports your conclusions. Lab reports count for 30% of the course grade. This report is due at the start of the lab of Metamorphic rocks and the rock cycle. It is scored using the rubric below.
steps: Present your observations for two numbered sedimentary hand samples from your lab tray that have different origins. For each, describe the relevant texture, composition, fizz and hardness observations; name the rock and its origin. Explain how the observations support your identification and identify any uncertainty.

Choose one slab or photograph from the structures and environments station. Describe the visible structure or fossils and explain what they suggest about the depositional environment. Give one other setting consistent with the evidence, or explain what additional evidence would help narrow your interpretation.
t_c1ee4bc7a1e7.answerKey:
1. Look for observations from two numbered samples with different origins, appropriate rock names and origins, and links between diagnostic evidence and each identification. A strong report distinguishes observed properties from inferred origin and acknowledges uncertainty where evidence is insufficient. Usual mistakes include naming a rock without supporting observations or assigning chert a biochemical origin solely because it does not fizz.
2. Look for an accurate description of a structure or fossils, a setting supported by that evidence, and either another plausible setting or additional evidence that would narrow the interpretation. For example, mud cracks indicate exposure and drying but can occur in several settings. Usual mistakes include treating a single structure as proof of one setting or assuming marine fossils alone establish warm, shallow water.

t_a256efbb759c.title: Weekly online quizzes: Sedimentary rocks
t_a256efbb759c.prompt: Complete your own work and submit it online before the first meeting of Metamorphic rocks and the rock cycle. Weekly online quizzes are worth 10% of the course grade. Choose one answer for each question. Each correct answer earns 1 point, for a total of 4 points.
steps: Which process binds loose sediment into solid rock by depositing minerals in the spaces between grains? A. Erosion B. Cementation C. Evaporation D. Abrasion
A fine-grained rock splits into thin sheets. Which name best fits this property? A. Conglomerate B. Breccia C. Rock gypsum D. Shale

A basin of salty water dries repeatedly, leaving beds of halite. How is the resulting rock classified? A. Chemical sedimentary rock B. Biochemical sedimentary rock C. Clastic sedimentary rock D. Igneous rock

A sandstone contains symmetric ripple marks. What movement most directly explains their shape? A. Sediment falling from a glacier B. Mud drying in air C. Back-and-forth wave motion D. Flow in one constant direction
t_a256efbb759c.answerKey:
1. B. Cementation deposits minerals in pore spaces and binds grains together.
2. D. Shale splits into thin sheets; this property is fissility.
3. A. Halite precipitated as the water evaporated, forming a chemical sedimentary rock.
4. C. Symmetric ripples form through back-and-forth wave motion.

t_6d60482cd659.prompt: A contact halo beside a granite intrusion, a regional belt in a continental collision zone, and a subduction zone all make metamorphic rock. Which setting makes a wide belt and which makes a narrow halo, and why?
followUps: How far can heat from an intrusion travel into the surrounding rock before it stops changing it?
Why would the same shale become slate or schist in a collision zone but hornfels beside an intrusion?
In a subduction zone, why do rocks reach high pressure without reaching high temperature?

t_3d2d56bf1726.prompt: Many diagrams draw the rock cycle as a circle: igneous to sediment to sedimentary to metamorphic to magma and back. Follow a quartz grain from granite to quartzite. Is ‘cycle’ the right word for its journey, or is the circle misleading?
followUps: Which arrow lets a rock skip a whole rock type, and what process is named on it?
Can a sedimentary rock become another sedimentary rock without passing through magma or metamorphism? What would have to happen?
Does any rock have to take every step before it can be uplifted and weathered again? What evidence from a hand sample would tell you which path it took?

t_b63c1733fa2c.prompt: A non-foliated rock has interlocking calcite crystals and fizzes in dilute HCl. Which identification and likely parent rock fit the evidence?
t_b63c1733fa2c.explanation: Calcite crystals and fizzing identify marble, which commonly forms from limestone. Quartzite from quartz sandstone is quartz-rich and does not fizz; hornfels from mudstone is typically fine-grained rather than a rock of interlocking calcite crystals; gneiss from granite is foliated and commonly banded.

t_fe988e397ac2.prompt: A fine-grained rock splits into flat sheets and contains tiny aligned mica and chlorite grains. Which identification and likely parent rock best fit?
t_fe988e397ac2.explanation: Slate commonly forms from shale at low metamorphic grade; aligned fine grains give it flat splitting surfaces. Marble from limestone is generally non-foliated; quartzite from quartz sandstone is generally non-foliated; hornfels from mudstone is typically non-foliated.

t_d432fbbd7f6e.prompt: A buried sandstone must melt before it can become quartzite.
t_d432fbbd7f6e.explanation: Quartz sandstone can recrystallize in the solid state to become quartzite. Melting produces magma rather than metamorphic rock.

t_57ab38b00953.prompt: Which sequence could turn buried schist into sedimentary rock?

choices.text: Uplift, weathering, erosion, deposition and lithification
Uplift, melting, crystallization, deposition and lithification
Burial, metamorphism, melting, deposition and lithification
Weathering, crystallization, erosion, burial and metamorphism

t_57ab38b00953.explanation: Uplift can expose the schist; weathering and erosion produce and transport sediment, which can be deposited and lithified. Uplift, melting, crystallization, deposition and lithification omits weathering and erosion after crystallization; burial, metamorphism, melting, deposition and lithification does not explain how sediment forms from the melt; weathering, crystallization, erosion, burial and metamorphism uses crystallization and metamorphism in place of the processes needed to form sedimentary rock.

t_81922357fab2.prompt: A student proposes this path: basalt → melting → gneiss → lithification → granite. Identify both incorrect arrows and replace them with processes and intermediate materials that make a possible path from basalt to gneiss and then to granite.
t_81922357fab2.answer: Basalt → metamorphism → gneiss → melting → magma → crystallization → granite.
t_81922357fab2.explanation: Metamorphism can change basalt into gneiss in the solid state under suitable conditions. Gneiss can then melt to form magma, which cools and crystallizes into granite. Melting does not directly produce gneiss, and lithification turns sediment into sedimentary rock rather than gneiss into granite.

t_cf271a2d49e0.title: Lab reports: Metamorphic rocks and the rock cycle
t_cf271a2d49e0.prompt: Use your pair’s lab observations to prepare your own report. Show how your evidence supports your conclusions. Lab reports count for 30% of the course grade. This report is due at the start of the lab of Geologic time and how rocks are dated. It is scored using the rubric below.
steps: Present your observations for two metamorphic hand samples from your lab tray, one foliated and one non-foliated. For each, describe the relevant alignment, grain size, visible minerals, fizz and hardness observations. Name the rock and a likely parent rock. Explain how the evidence supports your identification and identify any uncertainty.

Choose one of your samples and describe a possible path from its parent rock to the sample and then to a new rock. Name the process on every arrow. Explain how the conditions of metamorphism changed the parent rock, and identify one observation that supports your interpretation.
t_cf271a2d49e0.answerKey:
1. A strong answer reports the pair’s actual observations for one foliated and one non-foliated sample, then uses alignment, grain size, minerals, fizz and hardness as relevant to justify each identification and likely parent. It recognizes uncertainty where observations permit more than one parent or identification. For example, a banded rock with light and dark minerals may be gneiss with granite or shale as a possible parent; composition alone does not prove which parent. Common mistakes include treating visible crystals as foliation, claiming a parent is certain from composition alone, or inventing observations.
2. A strong answer gives a geologically possible path, names every process, and links heat, pressure or fluids to changes supported by an observation. For example, granite can undergo regional metamorphism under heat and differential stress to form gneiss; the gneiss can melt to magma, which crystallizes to form an igneous rock. Light and dark banding supports the gneiss identification. Other paths and samples are acceptable when supported by the student’s observations. Common mistakes include treating metamorphism as melting, leaving arrows unlabeled, and claiming that every rock must pass through all three rock types.

t_94e78124e802.title: Weekly online quizzes: Metamorphic rocks and the rock cycle
t_94e78124e802.prompt: Complete your own work and submit it online before the first meeting of Geologic time and how rocks are dated. Weekly online quizzes are worth 10% of the course grade. Choose one answer for each question. Each correct answer earns 1 point, for a total of 4 points.
steps: A rock beside a granite intrusion is heated strongly but experiences little differential stress. Which type of metamorphism is most likely? A. Contact B. Regional C. Burial D. Hydrothermal
In a collision zone, platy minerals grow in a preferred orientation as a rock is compressed. What feature can this produce? A. Vesicles B. Foliation C. Fossil shells D. Ripple marks
Hot seawater circulates through basalt near a mid-ocean ridge. Which agent most directly carries ions through the rock? A. Wind B. Glacial ice C. Hot fluids D. Surface runoff

A geologist compares shale-derived rocks from the same Barrovian metamorphic sequence. Which index mineral indicates the highest grade among these choices? A. Chlorite B. Biotite C. Garnet D. Sillimanite
t_94e78124e802.answerKey:
1. A. Heat from an intrusion produces contact metamorphism in the surrounding rock.
2. B. Differential stress can produce foliation by aligning platy minerals.
3. C. Hot fluids carry ions through the basalt and promote mineral reactions.
4. D. Sillimanite occurs at the highest grade of the listed minerals in this sequence.

t_9314e29d210d.prompt: The same hypothetical magnitude 6.5 earthquake shakes two towns 80 km from the epicenter. Town A stands on bedrock. Town B stands on soft, water-saturated fill. Which has the higher intensity, and why?
followUps: Suppose Town A’s buildings are old and poorly built, and Town B’s are well built. Does your answer hold? What would you want to know before deciding?
Both towns felt the same earthquake. Which number describes it for both towns, and which number differs from town to town?
Which of the three damage mechanisms from today would you worry about most in Town B, and what in the ground makes you say so?

t_b50401f57218.prompt: Suppose a magnitude 7.0 earthquake strikes a thinly populated region of bedrock, and a magnitude 6.0 earthquake strikes a city built on soft, water-saturated fill. Which is the bigger earthquake, and which is likely to be the bigger disaster? Should a news report lead with magnitude?
followUps: The magnitude 7.0 earthquake releases about 32 times the energy of the magnitude 6.0. Does that settle which one causes more damage? Why or why not?
What would you add to a magnitude in a public report so that a person in either place knew what to expect where they live?
Where would you argue that magnitude is the more useful number, and where would you argue intensity is?

t_da23a9a59591.prompt: Three stations record a hypothetical shallow earthquake. The S–P intervals are 5 s at station R, 10 s at station S, and 15 s at station T. Using distance (km) ≈ 8.4 × S–P interval (s), which set of circle radii would you draw to locate the epicenter?

choices.text: R: 84 km; S: 42 km; T: 126 km
R: 42 km; S: 84 km; T: 126 km

t_da23a9a59591.explanation: Multiply each interval by 8.4 to get 42, 84, and 126 km. “R: 84 km; S: 42 km; T: 126 km” swaps the first two radii. “R: 13.4 km; S: 18.4 km; T: 23.4 km” adds 8.4 instead of multiplying. “R: 1.7 km; S: 0.8 km; T: 0.6 km” divides 8.4 by each interval.

t_a51b87456eef.prompt: On a map, circles drawn from two seismic stations intersect at two points. A third station’s circle passes near one intersection but not the other. Explain how you would locate the epicenter and why your result has some uncertainty.
t_a51b87456eef.answer: Locate the epicenter near the intersection that also lies close to the third circle. Treat it as a best-fit location because arrival-time picks, pencil lines, and compass placement have uncertainty.
t_a51b87456eef.explanation: Two station circles leave two possible locations. The third circle selects the intersection consistent with all three distances. Small measurement and drawing errors can keep the circles from meeting at exactly one point.

t_c0c51626f86f.prompt: Two earthquakes have magnitudes 6.0 and 8.0. Using the lesson’s magnitude comparison, about how much more energy did the larger earthquake release?
t_c0c51626f86f.explanation: A two-unit increase gives about 32 × 32, or roughly 1,000 times the energy. “About 2 times as much” treats magnitude as linear. “About 10 times as much” uses the amplitude factor for one unit. “About 100 times as much” uses the amplitude factor for two units.

t_35bb6b426f86.prompt: A single earthquake must have the same Modified Mercalli intensity in every town that feels it.
t_35bb6b426f86.explanation: Intensity describes effects at a particular place. It can vary among towns with distance, ground conditions, and construction, even though the earthquake has one magnitude.

t_f35239b09271.prompt: During a hypothetical earthquake, a building tilts as the loose, water-saturated sand beneath it loses strength. Which process best explains the damage?

choices.text: Falling pore-water pressure reduces contact between grains.
Rising pore-water pressure cements the grains together.
Falling pore-water pressure cements the grains together.
Rising pore-water pressure reduces contact between grains.

t_f35239b09271.explanation: Shaking can raise pressure in water between sand grains, reducing their contact and allowing the ground to lose strength. “Falling pore-water pressure reduces contact between grains” reverses the pressure change. “Rising pore-water pressure cements the grains together” mistakes a loss of strength for cementation. “Falling pore-water pressure cements the grains together” reverses the pressure change and mistakes it for cementation.

t_0ecb4022f9ea.title: Lab reports: Earthquakes
t_0ecb4022f9ea.prompt: Use your pair’s lab observations to prepare your own report. Show how your evidence supports your conclusions. Lab reports count for 30% of the course grade. Complete this report independently; it is scored individually using the rubric below. It is due at the start of the lab of Folds, faults and mountain building.
steps: Use your pair’s epicenter map to report the S–P interval and calculated radius for each station, along with your estimated epicenter coordinates. Describe the uncertainty in your location and identify evidence of it on the map. Suppose a station’s S arrival were picked 2 seconds too late. Explain how that error would change its circle.

Compare your observations of the saturated and dry sand tubs. Describe what happened to each block and to the water. Use a labeled sketch to explain how shaking changes pressure and contact between grains in saturated sand. Explain why the sandstone hand sample behaved differently from the loose sand.

Use the intensity survey to compare one town on bedrock with one on soft sediment. Report each town’s distance, assigned Modified Mercalli level and observed effects. Explain how the ground type may help account for the difference, and distinguish these local intensity ratings from the earthquake’s magnitude.

Suppose a magnitude 6.4 earthquake and a magnitude 7.4 earthquake occur in different regions. Compare their approximate ground-motion amplitudes and energy releases using the lesson’s whole-step rule. Explain why those magnitude values alone cannot establish which region experienced more damage. Include ground shaking and a possible tsunami in your explanation.
t_0ecb4022f9ea.answerKey:
1. A strong report gives intervals of 6.0, 8.0 and 8.4 s and radii of 50.4, 67.2 and 70.56 km for A, B and C, respectively; the epicenter is near (40, 30) km. The student describes uncertainty using the spread or failure of the drawn circles to meet at exactly one point. An S arrival picked 2 s late increases the interval by 2 s and the radius by 16.8 km. Common mistakes include using an arrival time as the interval or treating the circle as a direction.
2. A strong report states the pair’s actual observations, even if the blocks did not behave as predicted. It explains that shaking can raise pore-water pressure and reduce grain contact in saturated sand, allowing it to lose strength; dry sand has no pore water to carry the load in this way. The sketch labels grains, water and block. Cement binds grains in the sandstone. Common mistakes include claiming that water itself liquefies or replacing observations with expected results.
3. A strong report accurately cites two town reports and their levels and uses the ground types as evidence while recognizing that distance also differs. For example, Cedar Mills is 30 km away on bedrock and rates IV; Delta Landing is 32 km away on saturated river sediment and rates VII. Their effects match the survey key, and soft sediment can amplify shaking. Intensity describes local effects; magnitude is one value for the earthquake. A common mistake is attributing intensity solely to distance or treating intensity as magnitude.
4. A one-unit magnitude difference corresponds to approximately 10 times the ground-motion amplitude and 32 times the energy under the lesson’s rule. A strong explanation connects damage to local shaking, ground conditions and construction, and notes that a tsunami requires sudden sea-floor movement and can damage exposed coasts. Magnitude alone does not establish local effects or whether a tsunami occurred. A common mistake is using the amplitude factor for energy or assuming the larger event necessarily caused more damage.

t_3bd5ebab4c20.title: Weekly online quizzes: Earthquakes
t_3bd5ebab4c20.prompt: Complete your own work and submit it online before the first meeting of Folds, faults and mountain building. Weekly online quizzes are worth 10% of the course grade. Choose one answer for each question. Each correct answer earns 1 point, for a total of 4 points.
steps: A fault remains locked while the plates on either side continue to move. What happens to the surrounding rock before the fault slips? A. It bends and stores elastic strain. B. It stops moving permanently. C. It changes into liquid. D. It releases all its stored energy.

A seismic station records a P wave 10 seconds after an earthquake begins. At the same station, the S wave arrives 17 seconds after the earthquake begins. Using distance (km) ≈ 8.4 × S–P interval (s), approximately how far is the station from the epicenter? A. 84 km. B. 143 km. C. 59 km. D. 227 km.

Why do S waves fail to pass through Earth’s liquid outer core? A. Liquids transmit only surface waves. B. Liquids cannot support the shearing motion of S waves. C. S waves travel faster than P waves. D. S waves travel only along Earth’s surface.

What can generate a tsunami during an earthquake? A. A change in the earthquake’s magnitude after the rupture. B. Shaking that moves furniture inside coastal buildings. C. Sand grains becoming cemented together. D. Sudden uplift or subsidence of the sea floor that displaces water.
t_3bd5ebab4c20.answerKey:
1. A. Continued plate motion bends rock around the locked fault and stores elastic strain.
2. C. The S–P interval is 17 − 10 = 7 s; 8.4 × 7 = 58.8 km, or approximately 59 km.
3. B. Liquids cannot support the shear motion carried by S waves.
4. D. Sudden vertical movement of the sea floor displaces the water above it.

t_4361f77a2320.prompt: If temperature and CO₂ are both read from one ice core, what pattern over time do you expect? Explain it to a partner.
followUps: Temperature is inferred from the oxygen isotopes in the snow layers, while CO₂ is measured in the trapped air bubbles. Are these the same kind of evidence, and does that change how far you trust each record?
If the two curves rise and fall together, does that show which one changed first? What else would you need to know?
The Antarctic cores reach back about 420,000 years (Vostok) and about 800,000 years (EPICA Dome C). What could the longer record show that a short one could not?

t_390d48bcdad0.prompt: A student’s note reads: “This glacier’s terminus has retreated 200 m in ten years, so the ice must have stopped flowing, or be flowing uphill.” Do you agree with the conclusion? Defend your answer using accumulation, ablation and flow.
followUps: If the ice at the front is still moving downhill, what has to be true about how fast melting removes ice compared with how fast flow delivers it?
Two glaciers both have a retreating terminus. Could one be flowing fast and the other barely at all? What would you measure to tell them apart?
Ice can pass over a bump in its bed even though it flows downhill. What drives the flow if it is not the slope of the bed?

t_13e7f04b543f.prompt: Snow remains through the summer on a high mountain. Over many years, snowfall adds more mass than melting removes. What is most likely to happen as the snow is buried?

choices.text: It melts into water and then forms firn.
It compacts into till and then glacial ice.
It freezes into bedrock and then forms ice.
It compacts into firn and then glacial ice.

t_13e7f04b543f.explanation: Buried snow compacts into firn and then glacial ice. “It melts into water and then forms firn” reverses the process; firn forms by compaction of snow. “It compacts into till and then glacial ice” confuses snow with sediment deposited by ice. “It freezes into bedrock and then forms ice” confuses glacial ice with the rock beneath it.

t_e887d55c8f63.prompt: A glacier whose terminus has retreated for several years must have ice flowing uphill.
t_e887d55c8f63.explanation: Ice can continue to flow downhill while the terminus retreats. Retreat occurs when ice is lost at the terminus faster than flow delivers it.

t_a2047838ee1a.prompt: A geologist finds an unsorted mixture of clay, sand and boulders in a ridge marking a former glacier front. Which interpretation best fits the evidence?

choices.text: Till deposited in a terminal moraine
Outwash deposited on a meltwater plain
Gravel sorted along a meltwater stream

t_a2047838ee1a.explanation: Unsorted sediment deposited at a former ice front is till in a terminal moraine. “Outwash deposited on a meltwater plain” and “Gravel sorted along a meltwater stream” describe sediment sorted by meltwater, unlike the mixture here. “Bedrock exposed by glacial abrasion” is eroded rock, not a deposit of mixed sediment.

t_7b941d8fad84.prompt: A researcher measures oxygen isotopes in an ice layer and carbon dioxide in bubbles from the same depth. What do these measurements provide?

choices.text: A direct temperature reading and a sample of ancient air
An inferred temperature and a record of ocean salinity
An inferred temperature and a sample of ancient air
A direct temperature reading and a record of ocean salinity

t_7b941d8fad84.explanation: Oxygen isotopes in ice provide evidence used to infer past temperature; bubbles preserve ancient air whose CO₂ can be measured. The choices with “a direct temperature reading” mistake an inference for a thermometer measurement. The choices with “a record of ocean salinity” misidentify what the trapped air records.

t_73003d230e4c.prompt: A student argues: “An orbital cycle caused an ice age because it greatly reduced the total sunlight Earth receives each year. Cooler summers at high northern latitudes would not matter.” Correct the argument. Explain how summer sunlight can affect ice-sheet growth and name one process that can amplify the initial change.
t_73003d230e4c.answer: Orbital cycles mainly change the seasonal and geographic distribution of sunlight, rather than greatly changing the annual total. Cooler summers at high northern latitudes allow more snow to survive and accumulate into ice. Growing ice sheets or falling atmospheric CO₂ can amplify the initial cooling.
t_73003d230e4c.explanation: Snow that survives summer can accumulate over years. Orbital changes can favor this survival by altering summer sunlight at high northern latitudes. Ice-sheet growth and falling CO₂ can then amplify the cooling.

t_80d3bc8a6da7.title: Final exam
t_80d3bc8a6da7.prompt: Time allowed: 117 minutes. The teacher will announce what you may bring or use. Answer every question. Show your working for calculations, give units where they apply, and explain your reasoning where asked. This exam is on what has been taught so far.
steps: Describe one difference between Earth’s crust and mantle in composition or physical state. Explain why the lithosphere and asthenosphere are distinguished by physical behavior rather than by composition alone. (4 points)
At a mid-ocean ridge, two plates move apart. Explain how new oceanic crust forms there. Predict how the age of oceanic crust changes as you move away from the ridge, and give a reason. (4 points)
An oceanic plate converges with a continental plate. Describe the likely motion of the oceanic plate and explain how this setting can produce a volcanic mountain chain. (4 points)

A mineral scratches glass. Its crystals break along flat, repeated surfaces. Name the property tested by scratching and the property shown by the flat break surfaces. Explain how each property helps identify the mineral. (4 points)

Two clear mineral samples have the same color. Sample X has a white streak and breaks into irregular surfaces. Sample Y has a white streak and breaks along flat planes. Which observation best distinguishes them? Explain why color alone is a weak basis for identification. (3 points)

A dark igneous rock contains crystals too small to distinguish without magnification. Another rock of similar composition has crystals several millimeters across. Compare their cooling histories and explain how crystal size supports your interpretation. (4 points)
Compare a basaltic magma with a silica-rich rhyolitic magma. Which is generally more viscous? Explain how viscosity can affect the escape of gas and the explosiveness of an eruption. (4 points)

A rock outcrop develops cracks as water freezes and expands in them. Nearby, rainwater reacts with feldspar and produces clay minerals. Identify the type of weathering in each case and explain the difference between the processes. (4 points)

After a hillside is cleared of vegetation, a storm carries loose soil into a stream. Distinguish weathering from erosion in this situation. Give one way vegetation can reduce the loss of soil. (3 points)

A sedimentary rock contains rounded sand-sized grains cemented together. Name the rock and describe two steps that can turn loose sand into this rock. What does the rounded shape suggest about the grains’ transport? (4 points)

A geologist finds a sequence with coarse gravel at the bottom, sand above it, and mud at the top. Assuming the layers were deposited in their present order, explain what the change in grain size suggests about the energy of the depositing water. Give a reason. (3 points)

A shale is buried and metamorphosed until it becomes slate. Describe how metamorphism changes the original rock without melting it. Explain why slate may split along planes that differ from the original sedimentary bedding. (4 points)
Describe a path by which an exposed granite could become sandstone and then a metamorphic rock. Name the processes required at each change. (4 points)

A rock contains 25% of its original radioactive parent isotope. The isotope’s half-life is 500 million years. Assuming no parent or daughter isotope entered or left the sample, calculate the rock’s age. Show your working. (3 points)

In an undisturbed sequence, a shale layer lies beneath a limestone layer. A fault cuts both layers. A horizontal sand layer lies across the eroded tops of the shale, limestone and fault. Put the shale, limestone, faulting, erosion and sand deposition in order from oldest to youngest. State the principles that support your order. (5 points)
An earthquake releases energy along a fault. Explain the difference between the focus and the epicenter. Describe one difference between P waves and S waves. (3 points)

At two seismograph stations, the difference between the arrival times of P and S waves is 20 seconds at station A and 50 seconds at station B. Which station is farther from the earthquake? Explain your reasoning. Why are distances from several stations useful for locating an epicenter? (4 points)
In a folded sequence, the oldest beds occur at the center of an arch. Name the fold. Explain how compression can produce this structure and why the age of the beds helps identify it. (3 points)

In a rock exposure, the block above an inclined fault has moved upward relative to the block below. Name the upper block, identify the fault, and name the kind of stress commonly associated with it. (3 points)
Two continents converge after the ocean between them closes. Explain why the collision can build a high mountain belt. Include the roles of faulting and crustal thickness. (4 points)

On a geologic map, a contact separates two rock units. Strike and dip symbols appear within each unit. What does the contact show? What do strike and dip describe? Explain how these observations help a geologist draw a cross section. (4 points)

A stream is 8 m wide and has an average depth of 1.2 m. Its average water velocity is 1.5 m/s. Calculate discharge using Q = width × average depth × average velocity. Show your working and units. (3 points)
Describe where erosion and deposition tend to occur on opposite sides of a stream bend. Explain how these processes can change the position of the bend over time. (4 points)

Explain how a drainage divide relates to a drainage basin. During a flood, both the average depth and velocity of water in a channel increase. Explain what happens to discharge, assuming channel width stays the same. (4 points)

A dry sediment sample has a total volume of 200 mL and a pore volume of 60 mL. Calculate its porosity as a percentage. Explain why porosity alone does not establish whether the sediment will transmit water easily. (4 points)

Groundwater flows through a material with hydraulic conductivity K = 2×10⁻⁴ m/s and hydraulic gradient i = 0.03. Use Darcy’s law, q = K × i, to calculate the flux q. State the direction of groundwater flow in relation to hydraulic head (the water table elevation). (4 points)

A well pumps from an aquifer. Describe the shape of the resulting change in the water table. Explain how heavier pumping can affect a nearby well and how pumping faster than recharge can affect the aquifer over time. (4 points)

A glacier gains 1.6 m of water equivalent and loses 1.9 m of water equivalent in one year. Calculate its mass balance and state whether it gained or lost mass. If that balance persists, what will its terminus tend to do? Explain why the terminus response may not be immediate. (4 points)

A line of stakes is placed straight across a valley glacier. A year later, the line bows downvalley, with its center farther downvalley than its ends. Explain what this pattern shows about differences in ice speed and give a reason for those differences. Name the two main mechanisms by which glacier ice moves. (4 points)

A valley has a broad, relatively flat floor and steep sides. Its bedrock has parallel scratches. Describe two processes by which a glacier can erode rock. Explain how the valley shape and scratches support an interpretation of past glaciation. (4 points)

A field team compares two deposits. Deposit P contains clay, sand and angular to rounded boulders mixed together. Deposit Q contains layers of relatively well-sorted sand and rounded gravel. Identify the more likely directly deposited glacial sediment and the more likely meltwater deposit. Explain the evidence for each choice. (4 points)

An ice-core record contains alternating periods with different inferred temperatures and different concentrations of atmospheric CO₂. Describe the broad relationship between temperature and CO₂ across glacial cycles in the records discussed. Name the three orbital cycles and give the approximate length of each. Explain how ice sheets and CO₂ can amplify a climate change initiated by a shift in the seasonal distribution of sunlight. (6 points)

During the last deglaciation, atmospheric CO₂ rose by about 70 ppm over 10,000 years. During a different interval, it rose by 90 ppm over 150 years. Calculate the average rise in ppm per year for each interval. Divide the second rate by the first to compare them. Show your working. (4 points)
t_80d3bc8a6da7.answerKey:
1. The crust is compositionally distinct from the mantle; for example, mantle rock is generally richer in iron and magnesium than continental crust (1 point). The lithosphere is the rigid outer layer, including crust and uppermost mantle (1 point). The asthenosphere is weaker mantle beneath it that can deform and flow slowly (1 point). Both include mantle material, so their boundary is based on mechanical behavior (1 point). (4 points)
2. Mantle rises beneath the separating plates and partially melts as pressure decreases (1 point). Magma cools to form new oceanic crust (1 point). Crust becomes older with distance from the ridge (1 point) because it moves away as new crust forms at the ridge (1 point). (4 points)
3. The denser oceanic plate subducts beneath the continental plate (1 point). Water released from the descending slab helps cause partial melting in the mantle above it (1 point). Magma rises (1 point) and erupts or solidifies beneath the continent, building a volcanic mountain chain (1 point). (4 points)
4. The scratch test assesses hardness (1 point), which can be compared with materials of known hardness (1 point). The flat break surfaces show cleavage (1 point), whose directions and quality can be compared with known mineral properties (1 point). (4 points)
5. The break pattern distinguishes them: X fractures irregularly and Y has cleavage (1 point). Color alone is weak because different minerals can share a color, or one mineral can occur in several colors (2 points). (3 points)
6. The fine-grained rock cooled relatively quickly, commonly at or near the surface (1 point). The coarse-grained rock cooled more slowly underground (1 point). Rapid cooling leaves less time for crystals to grow (1 point), while slow cooling allows larger crystals to develop (1 point). (4 points)
7. Rhyolitic magma is generally more viscous (1 point). Its high viscosity makes gas escape more difficult (1 point), allowing pressure to build (1 point) and increasing the potential for an explosive eruption (1 point). (4 points)
8. Freezing and expansion cause physical weathering (1 point): the rock breaks without requiring a change in mineral composition (1 point). The reaction of feldspar with water is chemical weathering (1 point): minerals are altered or new minerals form (1 point). (4 points)
9. Weathering produces or alters material in place (1 point); erosion removes and transports the loose material (1 point). Vegetation can reduce soil loss by holding soil with roots or reducing the impact and flow of water (1 point). (3 points)
10. The rock is sandstone (1 point). Burial and compaction press the grains together (1 point), and cementation binds them with minerals deposited between grains (1 point). Rounding suggests that grains were worn during transport (1 point). (4 points)
11. The sequence suggests a general decrease in water energy or velocity over time (1 point). Gravel requires stronger flow to transport than sand (1 point), while mud can settle in relatively quiet water (1 point). (3 points)
12. Heat and pressure alter the rock while it remains solid (1 point). Minerals can recrystallize or new minerals can form (1 point). Directed pressure can align platy minerals (1 point), producing foliation that need not be parallel to bedding (1 point). (4 points)
13. Weathering breaks down the granite (1 point). Erosion and transport move the sediment, which is deposited (1 point). Compaction and cementation turn sand into sandstone (1 point). Heat and pressure can then metamorphose the sandstone while it remains solid (1 point). (4 points)
14. 25% remains after two half-lives: 100% → 50% → 25% (2 points). Age = 2 × 500 million years = 1,000 million years (1 point). (3 points)
15. Oldest to youngest: shale, limestone, faulting, erosion, sand deposition (3 points: 1 for shale before limestone, 1 for faulting after both, 1 for erosion before sand deposition). Superposition places shale below limestone and sand above the eroded surface (1 point). Cross-cutting places the fault after the rocks it cuts; its truncation places erosion after faulting (1 point). (5 points)
16. The focus is the location within Earth where rupture begins (1 point). The epicenter is the point on Earth’s surface directly above it (1 point). P waves travel faster than S waves, or P waves pass through liquids while S waves do not (1 point). (3 points)
17. Station B is farther away (1 point). P waves travel faster than S waves (1 point), so the gap between their arrivals grows with travel distance (1 point). Distances from several stations can be combined to find where their distance circles intersect and locate the epicenter (1 point). (4 points)
18. It is an anticline (1 point). Compression shortens the rock sequence and can bend layers into a fold (1 point). An anticline has older rocks at its core, which helps distinguish it from a syncline (1 point). (3 points)
19. The upper block is the hanging wall (1 point). The fault is a reverse fault (1 point). It is commonly associated with compression (1 point). (3 points)
20. Continental crust resists easy subduction because it is relatively buoyant (1 point). Compression folds and shortens the crust (1 point). Thrust faults stack slices of rock (1 point), thickening the crust and contributing to uplift (1 point). (4 points)
21. The contact shows where the units meet at the surface (1 point). Strike gives the direction of a horizontal line on a rock layer (1 point), and dip gives the direction and angle at which the layer slopes downward (1 point). Together with the mapped contacts, they help project the units beneath the surface in a cross section (1 point). (4 points)
22. Q = 8 m × 1.2 m × 1.5 m/s (1 point) = 14.4 m³/s (2 points, including the unit). (3 points)
23. Faster water on the outside erodes a cut bank (1 point). Slower water on the inside deposits sediment as a point bar (1 point). Erosion removes material from the outer bank (1 point), while deposition builds the inner bank, so the bend migrates sideways (1 point). (4 points)
24. A drainage basin is the land that drains to a stream (1 point), and a divide marks its boundary with a neighboring basin (1 point). Discharge increases (1 point) because discharge is width × depth × velocity and both depth and velocity increase (1 point). (4 points)
25. Porosity = pore volume ÷ total volume × 100 (1 point) = 60 ÷ 200 × 100 = 30% (1 point). Water must move through connected pores (1 point), and small or poorly connected pathways can give low permeability even when pore space is abundant (1 point). (4 points)
26. q = 2×10⁻⁴ m/s × 0.03 (1 point) = 6×10⁻⁶ m/s (2 points, including the unit). Groundwater flows from higher hydraulic head toward lower hydraulic head (1 point). (4 points)
27. Pumping produces a cone of depression, with the greatest drawdown at the pumping well (1 point). Heavier pumping can deepen or expand the drawdown (1 point), lowering water levels in a nearby well (1 point). Pumping faster than recharge can deplete the aquifer over time (1 point). (4 points)
28. Mass balance = gain − loss = 1.6 − 1.9 = −0.3 m water equivalent (1 point). The glacier lost mass (1 point). Sustained negative balance favors terminus retreat (1 point), although the terminus can respond slowly to a change in mass balance (1 point). (4 points)
29. The center moved faster than the edges (1 point). Friction with the valley walls slows ice near the edges (1 point). The two mechanisms are internal deformation (1 point) and basal sliding (1 point). (4 points)
30. Plucking removes pieces of bedrock (1 point), and abrasion scrapes or grinds bedrock with debris carried by ice (1 point). A broad U-shaped valley is consistent with glacial erosion (1 point), and parallel scratches are consistent with abrasion by debris in moving ice (1 point). (4 points)
31. P is more likely till, deposited directly by ice (1 point); its wide mixture of grain sizes is poorly sorted (1 point). Q is more likely outwash deposited by meltwater (1 point); moving water sorts grains, and transport commonly rounds them (1 point). (4 points)
32. Temperature and CO₂ generally rise and fall together across glacial cycles (1 point). Eccentricity varies on a cycle of about 100,000 years (1 point), tilt or obliquity about 41,000 years (1 point), and precession about 23,000 years (1 point). Growing ice sheets reflect more sunlight, reinforcing cooling (1 point). Falling atmospheric CO₂ reduces greenhouse warming and can reinforce cooling (1 point). (6 points)
33. Deglaciation rate = 70 ÷ 10,000 = 0.007 ppm per year (1 point). Second rate = 90 ÷ 150 = 0.60 ppm per year (1 point). Ratio = 0.60 ÷ 0.007 ≈ 86 (1 point). The second average rise was about 86 times as fast (1 point). (4 points)
Total: 127 points

t_bc07c8231a98.title: Lab reports: Glaciers and climate
t_bc07c8231a98.prompt: Use your pair’s flowing-ice model measurements, glacial deposit observations and valley profile plots to prepare your own report. Show how your evidence supports your conclusions. Lab reports count for 30% of the course grade. Complete this report independently; it is scored individually using the rubric below. This is the last lab of the course, so it is due on the date the instructor announces.
steps: Report your prediction and the dye-line positions at each track and time. For each track, show the displacement from 0 to 15 minutes and calculate speed as displacement ÷ 15 minutes. Describe the final shape of the line, compare the speeds with your prediction, and explain how friction with the tray walls helps account for the pattern. Identify one limit of the model as a representation of glacier flow.

Report your prediction and observations of sorting, rounding and striations for the till, outwash gravel and sand, and striated cobble. Use the observations to explain the likely setting of each sample. Compare the outwash with the stream deposits you saw earlier in the course and explain the process that could produce their similarities.

Present your plots of both valley profiles on the same scales. Report the floor width and outer wall slope for each valley, showing how you found them. State which profile is more consistent with glacial erosion and explain how the floor and walls support your interpretation. Identify one reason a valley profile alone is not conclusive evidence of glaciation.

Explain how the ice-flow model, deposit observations and valley profiles together help reconstruct a glaciated landscape. Distinguish evidence of ice movement, erosion and deposition, and identify one additional observation from the lab that would strengthen your interpretation of a valley.
t_bc07c8231a98.answerKey:
1. Look for the pair’s actual positions, each displacement calculated as the 15-minute position minus the initial position, and each speed as displacement ÷ 15 minutes in cm/min. A line that bows downslope with its center moving fastest is consistent with drag near the walls. Results may differ; students should use their measurements rather than substitute the expected pattern. A valid limit is that syrup is not glacier ice or that the tray is not at glacier scale. Common mistakes include treating position as displacement and omitting units.
2. Look for the student’s actual observations and prediction. Till is typically unsorted and can contain clasts of varied rounding; outwash is commonly sorted and rounded by meltwater; parallel scratches on the cobble are evidence of abrasion. Outwash and stream deposits can both be sorted and rounded by flowing water. Do not require every clast to be rounded or every sample to show striations. A common mistake is calling till sorted by meltwater.
3. Both profiles should be mirrored and plotted on the same scales. Using the 5 m criterion, A has a 20 m floor and B a 400 m floor. Outer wall slopes are A: (300 − 200) ÷ (600 − 400) = 0.5, and B: (400 − 140) ÷ (600 − 400) = 1.3. B is more consistent with glacial erosion because it has a broad floor and steeper outer walls. Valley shape alone does not establish the full history; additional evidence such as striated bedrock or glacial deposits would strengthen the interpretation. Common mistakes include using only one side for floor width and treating slope as an elevation difference without dividing by horizontal distance.
4. A strong synthesis uses the model as an analogy for differential flow, the profiles as evidence consistent with erosion, and the samples as evidence of deposition or abrasion. It connects an additional observation, such as striations on bedrock or till, to the valley interpretation while recognizing that the model itself is not evidence that either hypothetical valley was glaciated. Common mistakes include treating outwash as direct deposition by ice or presenting a model result as a field observation.

t_118b73bbd99b.title: Weekly online quizzes: Glaciers and climate
t_118b73bbd99b.prompt: Complete your own work and submit it online before the deadline announced by the instructor. Weekly online quizzes are worth 10% of the course grade. Choose one answer for each question. Each correct answer earns 1 point, for a total of 4 points.
steps: A glacier bed is frozen to the rock beneath it. Which movement mechanism can still allow the glacier to flow? A. Sorting by meltwater B. Internal deformation of the ice C. Basal sliding over a wet bed D. Deposition of outwash
A ridge of glacial debris runs alongside a valley glacier. What is this ridge called? A. An esker B. A cirque C. A terminal moraine D. A lateral moraine

Why can crevasses form near the surface of a glacier? A. The upper ice can fracture as it moves. B. All glacier ice is liquid beneath the surface. C. The ice at the surface cannot move downhill. D. Meltwater sorts the ice into layers.

Which description best distinguishes an ice sheet from an alpine glacier? A. An ice sheet forms only where no snow melts. B. An ice sheet moves only by basal sliding. C. An ice sheet covers a broad land area, while an alpine glacier occupies mountainous terrain. D. An ice sheet consists of firn, while an alpine glacier consists of ice.
t_118b73bbd99b.answerKey:
1. B. Ice can move by internal deformation even when frozen to its bed.
2. D. A lateral moraine forms along the side of a glacier.
3. A. Near-surface ice can fracture, producing crevasses.
4. C. Ice sheets cover broad land areas; alpine glaciers occupy mountainous terrain.

t_f24f8a1e942d.prompt: The hypothetical town of Ridgeway must site one new well. Its water table slopes from north to south toward a river. A gas station with an old fuel tank lies near the middle of town, and a cornfield lies east of it. Site 1 is north of the gas station, 400 m upgradient. Site 2 is east of the gas station, beside the cornfield. Site 3 is south of the gas station, between it and the river. Which site would you choose, and why?
followUps: A strong pump bends the gradient and draws water from every side. Does that change how safe Site 1 is, 400 m upgradient of the tank?
Site 2 sits beside the cornfield. What would you need to know about the flow direction to decide whether the field is upgradient or downgradient of the well?
Which site do you rank last, and what assumption about the fuel plume does that ranking rest on?

t_b1a6ba4f6ff4.prompt: A town needs a new well. One option is a thick silt layer with a porosity of 35–50%. The other is unfractured granite with a porosity under 1%. Which would you drill into, and what would you want to know before you commit?
followUps: If silt holds a lot of water but drains very little in a 30-second test, what does that say about its pores?
Under what condition would the granite become the better choice, and could you see that condition in a hand sample?
What would you measure in the field to settle your disagreement?

t_ea59f9ebd928.prompt: A layer of clay and a layer of gravel both contain water-filled pores. Why is gravel generally more useful as an aquifer?

choices.text: Its total pore volume must be greater.
Its grains prevent water from draining away.
Its pores contain water only below a well.
Its connected pores let water flow more easily.

t_ea59f9ebd928.explanation: Gravel generally has larger, connected openings that allow water to flow readily. “Its total pore volume must be greater” confuses permeability with porosity; clay can have greater porosity. “Its grains prevent water from draining away” describes poor water transmission. “Its pores contain water only below a well” misstates where saturated pores occur.

t_4f383f4fbbf8.prompt: A hypothetical observation well has a water level 6.5 m below ground before pumping and 8.2 m below ground after pumping. What is the drawdown in meters?
t_4f383f4fbbf8.explanation: Both readings are depths below ground, so subtract the original depth from the depth during pumping: 8.2 − 6.5 = 1.7 m.

t_b4c4dd06ce1d.prompt: After sustained pumping in an unconfined aquifer, the water table can dip toward the pumping well, with the greatest drawdown at the well.
t_b4c4dd06ce1d.explanation: Pumping lowers the water table around the well, forming a cone of depression. The drop is greatest at the pumping well and generally decreases with distance.

t_4bf895cfc4a0.prompt: A hypothetical fuel tank leaks into an unconfined aquifer. The water table slopes eastward. Which existing well is most directly threatened by the plume, assuming pumping does not change the flow direction?

choices.text: A well west of the tank.
A well north of the tank.
A well east of the tank.
A well south of the tank.

t_4bf895cfc4a0.explanation: Groundwater and the contaminant plume move downgradient, toward the east. “A well west of the tank” is upgradient. “A well north of the tank” and “A well south of the tank” lie across the stated flow direction rather than directly downgradient.

t_6fea1a89da2d.prompt: A hypothetical coastal community pumps groundwater faster than recharge. A resident argues that adding a deeper well will prevent both water-level decline and saltwater intrusion. Identify the mistake and explain two possible effects of continued overpumping.
t_6fea1a89da2d.answer: A deeper well does not stop the aquifer from being depleted if pumping remains faster than recharge. Continued pumping can lower groundwater levels and draw salt water into the coastal aquifer.
t_6fea1a89da2d.explanation: The balance between withdrawal and recharge controls whether groundwater storage declines. A deeper well may reach water as levels fall, but it does not remove the pumping excess. Lower groundwater levels can also allow salt water to move into a coastal aquifer.

t_92fb6dd08a3d.title: Lab reports: Groundwater
t_92fb6dd08a3d.prompt: Use your pair’s groundwater lab measurements and hand sample observations to prepare your own report. Show how your evidence supports your conclusions. Lab reports count for 30% of the course grade. Complete this report independently; it is scored individually using the rubric below. It is due at the start of the lab of Glaciers and climate.
steps: Report your prediction and the water added and estimated porosity for gravel, sand and silt. Show the calculation for each material. Compare the results with your prediction and explain one limitation of treating water added as a measure of total pore volume.

Report your predictions and the volume collected in 30 seconds for each material. Compare the drainage and porosity results, and explain what they show about the relationship between porosity and permeability. State why the drainage volumes are comparisons under this setup rather than measurements of permeability.

Present your provisional porosity and permeability rankings for sandstone, vesicular basalt and granite. Explain the visible evidence for each ranking and identify what a hand lens cannot establish about the connections between pores or fractures.

Use the hypothetical pumping test in the groundwater lab record sheet to report the drawdown calculations and a labeled plot of drawdown against distance. Compare the plot with your water table sketch and predict how doubling the pumping rate could change the drawdown.
t_92fb6dd08a3d.answerKey:
1. Look for the pair’s prediction and actual water-added readings for all three materials. Each estimated porosity is water added ÷ 100 mL × 100%. Compare the figures with the prediction. Trapped air or incomplete saturation can cause the added water to underestimate pore space; the test estimates connected pore volume. Do not require identical results across pairs. A common mistake is to treat the estimate as an exact measurement of all pore space.
2. Look for both predictions, all three collected volumes and comparisons with the corresponding porosities. A strong explanation recognizes that material can have substantial pore space but drain slowly, because pore size and connections affect flow. The collected volume compares drainage under the specified setup; it is not a measured permeability. Common mistakes are to equate high porosity with fast drainage or to report the collected volume as permeability.
3. Look for both rankings and sample-specific visible evidence. Sandstone may show pores, vesicular basalt shows vesicles, and granite may appear tight or show fractures. A hand lens cannot establish the extent or connectivity of pores and fractures throughout a sample. Rankings are hypotheses; assess their evidence and uncertainty rather than imposing a fixed order. A common mistake is to assume visible vesicles are connected.
4. Drawdown is pumped depth minus the static depth: 12.5 − 8.0 = 4.5 m at 5 m, 10.0 − 8.0 = 2.0 m at 20 m, and 8.8 − 8.0 = 0.8 m at 60 m. The plot has distance in meters on the horizontal axis and drawdown in meters on the vertical axis. Both plot and sketch show less drawdown farther from the well, but the plot shows positive drawdown on one side while the cross section shows water-level elevation on both sides. A higher pumping rate could produce deeper, wider drawdown. Common mistakes are reversing the subtraction or treating the drawdown plot as the water table itself.

t_2b40ff1ccddc.title: Weekly online quizzes: Groundwater
t_2b40ff1ccddc.prompt: Complete your own work and submit it online before the first meeting of Glaciers and climate. Weekly online quizzes are worth 10% of the course grade. Choose one answer for each question. Each correct answer earns 1 point, for a total of 4 points.
steps:
A sandstone sample has a pore volume of 24 cm³ and a total volume of 160 cm³. What is its porosity? Porosity (%) = pore volume ÷ total volume × 100.
A. 6.7%
B. 15%
C. 24%
D. 67%

In an unconfined aquifer, what does the water table mark?
A. The boundary between an aquitard and bedrock
B. The bottom of every well
C. The upper surface of the saturated zone
D. The depth below which rock has no pores

Two observation wells are 400 m apart. The water table elevation is 112 m at well P and 110 m at well Q. What is the hydraulic gradient between them? Hydraulic gradient = drop in water table elevation ÷ distance.
A. 0.005
B. 0.02
C. 2
D. 200

A well taps a confined aquifer. Under what condition will water flow from the well at the ground surface without pumping?
A. When the aquifer has high porosity
B. When the aquifer is made of sand
C. When the water table intersects a nearby stream
D. When pressure raises the water level above ground level
t_2b40ff1ccddc.answerKey:
1. B. 24 ÷ 160 × 100 = 15%.
2. C. The water table is the upper surface of the saturated zone in an unconfined aquifer.
3. A. (112 − 110) ÷ 400 = 0.005. The gradient has no units.
4. D. Confined-aquifer pressure must raise the water level above the ground surface for the well to flow without pumping.

r_720fa4850cee.title: Lab reports: Earth's layers and plate tectonics

descriptors.x_42855ef44a0f: Reports observations and calculated results accurately, with appropriate units and no consequential errors.
descriptors.x_d15abf4e8114: Reports observations and results accurately overall, with a minor error that does not change the conclusions.
descriptors.x_e63e1c08f16b: Reports some correct observations or results, but errors or omissions affect the conclusions.

f_a1fc41638929.question: If the mantle is solid rock, how can it flow and let plates move?
f_a1fc41638929.answer: The mantle is solid. Under high temperature and pressure, solid rock can creep very slowly, over millions of years, without melting. The asthenosphere, just below the rigid lithosphere, is the weakest part, so the plates above it can slide. Only the outer core is liquid. Volcanic magma forms in local pockets where rock melts. It is not a mantle-wide ocean of liquid rock.

f_1ceb8a96ed81.question: Is a plate the same thing as a continent?
f_1ceb8a96ed81.answer: No. A plate is a piece of lithosphere: crust plus the rigid uppermost mantle, about 100 km thick. Many plates carry both continental and oceanic crust. For example, the North American plate includes the continent and the seafloor out to the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. That is why a plate boundary can run through an ocean basin and not along a coastline.

f_b279d35dcf85.question: Volcanoes mark plate boundaries, so why is Hawaii in the middle of the Pacific plate?
f_b279d35dcf85.answer: Most volcanoes and earthquakes do follow boundaries, but a hot spot is an exception. It is a plume of hot mantle rising beneath the interior of a plate. The hot spot stays fairly fixed while the plate moves over it, so volcanoes form one after another and then are carried away. The island chain therefore records the direction and speed of plate motion. Yellowstone is another hot spot, beneath the North American plate.

f_53d0e44b0092.question: Weathering and erosion both wear rock away. What is the difference?
f_53d0e44b0092.answer: Weathering breaks rock down or chemically changes it where it sits. Erosion is the movement of the broken or altered material by water, wind, ice or gravity. A limestone ledge can be pitted by rain and stay exactly where it is, which is weathering with no erosion. Sand carried off by a river is erosion. Ask whether the material moved or only changed.

f_0489749410e0.question: Cutting a rock into smaller pieces leaves the same amount of rock. Why does that speed up chemical weathering?
f_0489749410e0.answer: Chemical weathering happens at surfaces, where water, dissolved CO₂ and oxygen touch minerals. Smaller pieces expose more surface for the same volume. A 1 cm cube has 6 cm² of surface. Cut into 1 mm cubes, the same rock has 60 cm². That is ten times as much surface for reactions, so physical weathering prepares rock for chemical weathering.

f_43104c4841a9.question: Does every soil have all of the horizons O, A, E, B and C?
f_43104c4841a9.answer: No. The sequence O, A, E, B, C above bedrock is a full profile, and many soils show only part of it. The E horizon, for example, is missing in many soils. A young or thin soil may have little more than an A horizon over weathered parent material. Read the layers you can see and match each to its clues, such as dark humus, pale leached material or accumulated clay and iron oxides. Do not force a missing layer into the profile.

f_3070fbe86324.question: If half of the parent is gone after one half-life, why isn’t it all gone after two?
f_3070fbe86324.answer: A half-life is the time for half of whatever parent is left to decay. It is not a fixed number of atoms. Suppose a sample starts with 80 parent atoms. After one half-life, 40 remain. After a second, half of those 40 decay, so 20 remain. The parent shrinks by half each time and never reaches zero in a whole number of half-lives. After two half-lives, one quarter of the parent is left, and the parent to daughter ratio is 1 : 3.

f_12ee3ce0eb2a.question: Why can’t we just date a sandstone or shale directly?
f_12ee3ce0eb2a.answer: The grains in a sedimentary rock come from older rocks that were weathered and eroded. A radiometric date on the grains tells you when those source rocks formed, not when the sediment was deposited. Igneous rocks and volcanic ash beds are different, because their minerals crystallize at a known moment. Geologists therefore date igneous layers above and below a sedimentary layer. The sedimentary layer must lie between those two ages.

f_e80701d6b7b4.question: Is an unconformity a layer or an event?
f_e80701d6b7b4.answer: It is neither. An unconformity is a surface that represents missing time. The time is missing because erosion removed rock or because no sediment was deposited. The erosion or non-deposition is what produced the surface. When you order events, you can place the erosion in the sequence. The surface itself marks the gap in the record, and it is classed by what lies above and below it: angular unconformity, disconformity or nonconformity.

f_2b50cd1e5cc7.question: How do I tell an anticline from a syncline when the ground is flat and the fold has been eroded away?
f_2b50cd1e5cc7.answer: Read the ages, then check the dips. Assuming the layers are right way up, an anticline has the oldest rock at its core, and the beds dip away from the hinge on both sides. A syncline has the youngest rock at its core, and the beds dip toward the hinge. Judge the shape of the structure, not the name. ‘Anticline’ does not mean ‘rising’ and ‘syncline’ does not mean ‘sinking.’ If you forget which is older, check the order of the geologic time scale first.

f_96f12b98b5c1.question: How do I decide which block is the hanging wall, and does that tell me the fault type?
f_96f12b98b5c1.answer: The hanging wall is the block above an inclined fault plane. The footwall is the block below it. Pick the block by where it sits relative to the plane, not by which block looks as if it moved. Then ask how the hanging wall moved relative to the footwall. If it slid down, the crust was pulled apart and the fault is normal. If it moved up, the crust was squeezed and the fault is reverse. A thrust is a reverse fault with a low dip. If the blocks slid past each other horizontally, it is a strike-slip fault. In every case the fault is younger than the rocks it cuts.

f_05b9fd835b42.question: Continental crust is too buoyant to subduct easily, so why does a continental collision still build a huge mountain belt?
f_05b9fd835b42.answer: The crust has nowhere easy to go, so it shortens and thickens. Folds form and thrust faults stack slices of rock on top of one another. Some crust may also be forced beneath the other continent. Thick crust floats high, like a deep iceberg, so the surface rises. India and Asia show this. The collision began roughly 50 million years ago, India still moves north at roughly 5 cm per year, and the crust under Tibet is about 70 km thick, twice normal. Heat and pressure in the thick root cause regional metamorphism. Over time, erosion strips the belt down, as in the old, eroded Appalachians.

f_9d76fdb80c3c.question: My width is in centimeters but my depth is in meters. How do I get discharge?
f_9d76fdb80c3c.answer: Convert every length to the same unit before you multiply. Q = w × d × v only works if width, depth and velocity use the same length unit. For field streams use meters and m/s, which gives m³/s (1 m³ is 1,000 liters). On the stream table use centimeters and seconds, which gives cm³/s (1 mL is 1 cm³).

f_7f1cc0d5feac.question: Does a 100-year flood happen once every hundred years?
f_7f1cc0d5feac.answer: No. It means a 1% chance of a flood that size in any single year. The years are independent, so two such floods can come in successive years, or none for two centuries. Recurrence intervals are estimated from gauge records, so they carry uncertainty, especially for rare floods.

f_fed97bb1b275.question: The slope of a river gets gentler downstream. Doesn’t that mean the water moves slower?
f_fed97bb1b275.answer: Not necessarily. Larger downstream channels lose less energy to friction against the bed and banks relative to the volume of water they carry, and tributaries add discharge. Mean velocity can stay the same or even increase downstream despite the gentler gradient. Earle’s discussion of the long profile treats this.

f_74d4d2bd7982.question: If the stream table is only a small model, why trust what it shows?
f_74d4d2bd7982.answer: Trust the direction of change, not the numbers. Steeper slopes cut more, bends migrate, and floods widen channels and spread sand, in the model and in real rivers. Speeds, depths and grain behavior do not scale up directly, so do not compare your values with a real river’s discharge.

f_c5bb0c286aa4.question: Ice melts at 0 °C. How can glacier ice be a mineral?
f_c5bb0c286aa4.answer: A mineral must be solid under the conditions where it occurs. In a glacier the temperature is below freezing, so the ice is a solid. It also forms naturally, it is not an organic compound, it has a definite formula (H₂O), and its molecules sit in a repeating hexagonal pattern. It meets all five criteria. Ice in a freezer fails only the first one, because people made it.

f_7d531bae8e7d.question: Does “inorganic” mean that no living thing could have been involved in making the mineral?
f_7d531bae8e7d.answer: No. In the mineral definition, “inorganic” means the substance is not an organic compound, that is, not the carbon-based material that makes up coal or wood. Many organisms build shells and skeletons from calcite (CaCO₃). That calcite still has a crystal structure and a definite formula, so it is a mineral.

f_5bb25f74bd19.question: A mineral in my lab tray looks gray, but my partner’s sample of the same mineral looks red. Can I still use color to name it?
f_5bb25f74bd19.answer: Color alone is a poor guide, because one mineral can show many colors. Hematite, for example, can look gray, black or red, yet its powder is always red-brown. Streak, the color of the powder, is more reliable. Use color as a first clue, then check hardness, cleavage, luster and streak before you decide. Remember that very hard minerals such as quartz do not leave a true streak on a porcelain plate.

f_6f9318f36663.question: Obsidian looks like a hard, shiny stone. Why is it called a rock but not a mineral?
f_6f9318f36663.answer: A mineral has atoms arranged in an ordered crystal structure. Obsidian formed when lava chilled so fast that atoms had no time to organize into crystals, so it is volcanic glass. Glass has no crystal structure, which is why it breaks along smooth, curved (conchoidal) surfaces. It is still a rock, because a rock is a natural solid material made of minerals or of other solid matter such as glass.

f_86e29672233c.question: Do mafic magmas ever erupt explosively, or is that only a problem with felsic magma?
f_86e29672233c.answer: Mafic magma is runny, so its gas usually escapes quietly. But silica is not the only control. A mafic magma that carries a lot of dissolved gas, or that meets groundwater or seawater, can still erupt violently. Slow lava flows are also not harmless, because they can bury and destroy roads and buildings. Silica content shapes the typical hazard, but each volcano has to be judged on its own evidence.

f_52dfdd1a0c88.question: Does Bowen’s reaction series mean every magma passes through every mineral, ending in quartz?
f_52dfdd1a0c88.answer: No. The series gives the order in which minerals crystallize as a magma cools, but a magma only reaches the minerals its composition allows. Many mafic magmas never reach quartz, which is one reason olivine and quartz rarely share a rock. Early crystals also do not always disappear. They may react with the melt only partly, or settle out, so several minerals from different parts of the series can coexist in one rock. Read the series as a sequence of crystallization, not as a list of rock types.

f_474c7c588006.question: If a rock fizzes in dilute HCl, does that tell me how it formed?
f_474c7c588006.answer: No. Fizz shows that calcite (CaCO₃) is present, so limestone and chalk fizz and chert does not. It says nothing about origin. Limestone can be biochemical, built from shells and skeletons, or chemical, as in travertine and ooids. To decide, look at the rock itself for whole shells, fragments, or a precipitated texture. Test a fresh surface with goggles on and one small drop.

f_c7f4521a9e6c.question: Do rounded grains mean the sediment traveled a long way?
f_c7f4521a9e6c.answer: Not by themselves. Rounding shows that grains were abraded, either during transport or by being reworked again and again, for example on a beach. Rounded grains tell you abrasion was substantial. They do not give you a distance. Treat rounding as one clue and look for others, such as sorting, composition and sedimentary structures.

f_5cb34e61a77a.question: Can one sedimentary structure tell me the exact environment?
f_5cb34e61a77a.answer: Usually it narrows the choices without settling them. Cross-bedding, for example, fits a river channel, a desert dune or a beach. Add the other evidence you can see, such as grain shape, sorting, other structures and whether fossils are present, and the interpretation gets stronger. A fossil helps only if the organism lived where it was buried and was not swept in.
