f_5d097566bd93.answer: The Lab reports piece for this lab is due at the start of the lab of Metamorphic rocks and the rock cycle. It is your own work, scored alone. If you miss a lab, you can make it up in the same week’s open lab hour.

f_9cfe35cb56dd.question: If I can see big crystals in a rock, does that make it foliated?
f_9cfe35cb56dd.answer: No. Foliation means alignment: platy minerals such as mica lying parallel, or light and dark bands. Crystal size does not matter. A rock can be coarse and sparkling, with crystals pointing in every direction, and have no foliation at all. Look for a preferred orientation first, then describe the grain size separately.

f_638de42ffb81.question: How sure can I be about a metamorphic rock’s parent rock?
f_638de42ffb81.answer: Treat it as a likely parent, not a certainty. The rock’s texture and minerals give you evidence, and a new rock often keeps roughly the bulk composition of its protolith. But different parent rocks can produce similar-looking products, and fluids can change the composition. Write what you observed, say which parent it best supports, and note any other parent that would fit.

f_3aff5909eb9f.question: Does the rock cycle always go igneous, then sedimentary, then metamorphic, then back to igneous?
f_3aff5909eb9f.answer: No. The cycle has no fixed order, and any rock can take a shortcut. A sedimentary rock can be uplifted, weathered and eroded, and its debris can be deposited and lithified into a new sedimentary rock without ever being metamorphosed or melted. An igneous rock can be metamorphosed without passing through a sediment stage. When you trace a path, name the process on every arrow, for example metamorphism, melting, crystallization, uplift, weathering, erosion, deposition or lithification.

f_72e76a19a722.question: Is the epicenter where the fault slipped?
f_72e76a19a722.answer: Not necessarily. The focus is the point underground where the rupture begins. The epicenter is the point on the surface directly above the focus. A large earthquake ruptures tens to hundreds of kilometers of fault, so the slip can extend far from the epicenter, which marks only where it started.

f_a230f5213c8b.question: The news says Richter scale, but the textbook says moment magnitude. Which is right?
f_a230f5213c8b.answer: Richter’s 1935 scale used the largest wave amplitude on a seismogram, corrected for distance. It saturates for the largest earthquakes. Seismologists now report moment magnitude, which is based on the rigidity of the rock, the fault area that slipped and the average slip. Both are logarithmic. Each whole step is 10 times the ground-motion amplitude and about 32 times the energy. Media often still say Richter out of habit.

f_c8ae77fe4b9f.question: P waves arrive first, so why do surface waves cause the most damage?
f_c8ae77fe4b9f.answer: Arrival order depends on speed, not strength. P waves are the fastest, so they reach a station first. Surface waves (Love and Rayleigh) are the slowest, but they have large amplitude and shake the ground for a long time. That combination is what damages buildings.

f_502554b26479.question: What does “meters of water equivalent” mean in the mass balance problem?
f_502554b26479.answer: It is the depth of liquid water you would get if the snow or ice melted. Snow, firn and ice have different densities, so measuring them in water equivalent lets you compare gain and loss in one unit. For example, fresh snow is about 0.1 g/cm³, so a meter of fresh snow melts to only about a tenth of a meter of water. Glacial ice is about 0.9 g/cm³.

f_15bb9e3a5e52.question: Why was sea level about 120 m lower at the last glacial maximum, around 20,000 years ago?
f_15bb9e3a5e52.answer: A great deal of water was stored as ice on land, mainly in large ice sheets, instead of in the oceans. Less water in the oceans means a lower sea surface. Melting land ice returns that water to the oceans. Floating sea ice is different: it already displaces its own weight of water, so its melting barely changes sea level.

f_35df533e5d1d.question: Are porosity and permeability the same thing?
f_35df533e5d1d.answer: No. Porosity is the share of a material that is empty space. Permeability is how easily fluid moves through it, which depends on pore size and on whether the pores connect. Pumice is a good example. It is full of gas bubbles, so its porosity is high, but the bubbles are mostly isolated, so water passes through it poorly.

f_9d1dd265a1cf.question: Is groundwater an underground river or lake?
f_9d1dd265a1cf.answer: Usually not. Most groundwater fills the tiny pores and fractures in rock and sediment below the water table, much like water in a wet sponge. Open underground channels do exist in some limestone regions, but they are the exception.

f_9e0852130830.question: How fast does groundwater move?
f_9e0852130830.answer: Much more slowly than a stream. It often moves only centimeters to a few meters per day. Its speed depends on how permeable the material is and on the hydraulic gradient, the drop in water table elevation divided by the distance. This slow movement is also why a contaminant plume can take years to reach a well and why cleanup is slow.
